docs.title: Java Design Patterns Handbook
docs.text:
From your first new keyword to defending architecture choices in a design review. GoF, concurrency, architecture and microservice patterns in Java 21 and Spring Boot 3, with 3 real-world examples per pattern, runnable code, exact output and interview prep.

The code always matches the docs

docs.title: Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
An anti-pattern is a common response to a recurring problem that looks reasonable but usually makes things worse. Recognizing them is half the value of learning patterns, and senior interviews often ask "what would you flag in this code review?".

Each entry: symptoms → why it hurts → what to do instead.

docs.title: God Object / God Class
docs.text:
• Symptoms: OrderManager with 4,000 lines and 120 methods; every feature touches it; merge conflicts daily.
  • Why it hurts: violates Single Responsibility; impossible to test in isolation; one change breaks unrelated features.
  • Instead: split by responsibility and bounded context; extract Strategies, States, a Facade per use case; keep domain logic in domain objects.

docs.title: Golden Hammer (pattern overuse)
docs.text:
• Symptoms: a Factory for a class with one implementation; an Abstract Factory with one family; Visitor for two types that never change.
  • Why it hurts: indirection without benefit; newcomers can't find the code that runs.
  • Instead: apply YAGNI. Introduce a pattern when the second variation arrives. Patterns are responses to forces, not goals.

docs.title: Copy-Paste Programming
docs.text:
• Symptoms: the same if ladder for payment methods in checkout, refunds and reconciliation; a bug fixed in one copy but not the others.
  • Why it hurts: drift and inconsistent behavior (the classic "fixed it in 51 of 54 places").
  • Instead: one definition: Factory Method, Template Method, Specification.

docs.title: Primitive Obsession
docs.text:
• Symptoms: double amount, String currency, String email, int status passed everywhere; validation repeated (or forgotten).
  • Why it hurts: floating-point money errors, invalid values deep in the system, unclear APIs (transfer(String, String, double)).
  • Instead: small immutable value objects (Money, Email, OrderId) with validation in the constructor. See Immutable Object.

docs.title: Boolean Flag Explosion
docs.text:
• Symptoms: isPaid, isShipped, isCancelled, isRefunded on one entity; impossible combinations ("cancelled and delivered").
  • Why it hurts: 2ⁿ states, most invalid; rules scattered.
  • Instead: a single status with an explicit State machine.

docs.title: Service Locator and Global State
docs.text:
• Symptoms: AppContext.getInstance().getOrderService() inside business methods; singletons holding mutable maps.
  • Why it hurts: hidden dependencies, untestable code, order-dependent tests, concurrency bugs.
  • Instead: constructor injection; DI-managed singletons; immutable shared state. See Singleton.

docs.title: Anemic Domain Model (debated)
docs.text:
• Symptoms: entities with only getters and setters; all rules in *Service classes that manipulate them.
  • Why it hurts: invariants can be broken from anywhere (order.setStatus(DELIVERED) on a cancelled order).
  • Instead: put behavior and invariants on the domain objects (order.cancel() enforces its rules). Keep services for orchestration.

docs.title: Magic Numbers and Strings
docs.text:
• Symptoms: if (code == 51), "356", 0.18 scattered across code.
  • Why it hurts: meaning is lost; values change in one place and not another.
  • Instead: named constants, enums, configuration, and Adapters that translate vendor codes once.

docs.title: Swallowed Exceptions / Exceptions as Control Flow
docs.text:
• Symptoms: catch (Exception e) {}; using exceptions to exit loops; returning null on errors.
  • Why it hurts: silent failures; impossible debugging; NPEs far from the cause.
  • Instead: let exceptions propagate or translate them into domain errors; return result types (Optional, sealed results); use Null Object only where "nothing" is genuinely correct.

docs.title: Lava Flow
docs.text:
• Symptoms: dead code and abandoned abstractions nobody dares to delete ("might still be used").
  • Why it hurts: cognitive load; false leads during incidents.
  • Instead: delete with tests and usage metrics as a safety net; feature flags with expiry dates.

docs.title: 2. Concurrency anti-patterns
docs.text: Anti-pattern Symptoms Instead Unbounded queues new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(), Executors.newFixedThreadPool; OOM under load Bounded queues with an explicit full policy (Producer-Consumer, Thread Pool) DCL without volatile Rare NPEs or half-initialized objects under load volatile, holder idiom, computeIfAbsent (DCL) I/O while holding a lock Periodic latency spikes; threads waiting on locks Prepare outside the lock, swap inside (Read-Write Lock) Shared mutable state Races, "impossible" values Immutable objects, confinement, concurrent collections Busy waiting while (!ready) {} burning CPU BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, CompletableFuture, wait/notify if around wait() Lost or spurious wakeups, hangs Always while (!condition) wait(); Blocking in the common pool Parallel streams and async tasks freeze together Dedicated executor or virtual threads for I/O (Future / Promise) Removing implicit limits Virtual threads overwhelm the database Explicit semaphores and pools (Virtual Threads) ThreadLocal leaks User A's tenant ID shows up in user B's request try/finally remove(), ScopedValue, context propagation

docs.title: 3. Distributed-system and microservice anti-patterns
docs.text: Anti-pattern Symptoms Why it hurts Instead Distributed monolith Services must deploy together; one change touches 6 repos All the costs of microservices, none of the benefits Boundaries by business capability; async events; consumer-driven contracts Shared database Several services read and write the same tables Hidden coupling; schema changes break other teams Database per service; integrate through APIs and events Chatty services One page makes 40 synchronous calls Latency and failure probability multiply Coarse-grained APIs, BFF/Facade, caching, batching Synchronous call chains A → B → C → D, all blocking Availability = product of all availabilities; cascading failures Async messaging, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads Dual writes Save to DB, then publish to Kafka (or call another service) One succeeds, the other fails: inconsistency Transactional outbox / CDC Retry storms Retries at every layer, no backoff A slowdown becomes an outage (5 × 3 × 3 = 45 calls) One retry layer, exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets, circuit breakers Missing idempotency Duplicate charges after timeouts At-least-once delivery is the norm Idempotency keys, de-duplication, conditional updates Silent defaults Unknown status codes treated as success; default: in critical switches Revenue leaks and data corruption found months later Fail loudly; exhaustive switch; alerts on unknown values Client-trusted state Prices or permissions in cookies or tokens without signatures Tampering Server-side state; signed tokens (HMAC); re-validate on the server

docs.title: 4. A code-review checklist
docs.text:
Use this when reviewing pull requests, and in "review this code" interview rounds:

  • Does each class have one reason to change?
  • Are there switch/if chains on types or statuses repeated in several places?
  • Are money, IDs and emails value objects, or raw primitives?
  • Are shared objects immutable, or is mutable state shared between threads?
  • Are all queues, pools and caches bounded, with a defined overload behavior?
  • Are external calls protected by timeouts, and are retries idempotent?
  • Do unknown inputs (codes, types, states) fail loudly?
  • Is anything written to two systems without an outbox or compensation?
  • Is there a pattern here with only one implementation and no realistic second (pattern overuse)?

docs.title: Pattern Comparisons
docs.text: Interviewers love "X vs. Y" questions because they test understanding, not memorization. Many patterns have the same class diagram and differ only in intent. For each pair below: a table, the key difference in one line, and a sentence you can say out loud.

docs.title: Strategy vs. State
docs.text:
Strategy State Intent Choose an algorithm Behavior depends on current state Who switches The client (or config) The state objects themselves, on events Do variants know each other? No Yes: states know their successors Example Delivery fee: standard / express / member Order: placed → packed → out for delivery

Say: "Same structure: a context delegating to an interface. In Strategy the caller picks the behavior; in State the object changes its own behavior as it moves through a lifecycle."

checkout.setFeeStrategy(EXPRESS);   // Strategy: chosen from outside
order.dispatch();                   // State: PACKED decides the next state is OUT_FOR_DELIVERY

docs.title: Decorator vs. Proxy vs. Adapter vs. Facade
docs.text:
Decorator Proxy Adapter Facade Interface Same Same Different (converted) New, simpler Wraps One object One object One object A subsystem Purpose Add behavior Control access Make it fit Simplify Stacking Common (Fraud(Retry(Logging(x)))) Rare No No Who creates it Usually the client Usually a framework or factory Integration code Application code Example Retry + logging around payments @Transactional, lazy loading Legacy bank SDK CheckoutFacade.placeOrder()

Say: "Adapter changes the interface, Decorator keeps it and adds behavior, Proxy keeps it and controls access, Facade gives a new, simpler interface to many classes."

docs.title: Factory Method vs. Abstract Factory vs. Builder vs. Prototype
docs.text:
Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder Prototype Creates One product A family of products One complex product Copies Decides Which class Which family How it's assembled What to copy Typical API create(type) cloud.storage(), cloud.queue() Order.builder()...build() template.copy() Signal switch on type Products that must match Many optional parameters Expensive setup, small changes

Say: "Factory Method answers which class, Abstract Factory which family, Builder how to assemble a complex object step by step, and Prototype start from a copy."

docs.title: Template Method vs. Strategy
docs.text:
Template Method Strategy Varies Steps of a fixed algorithm The whole algorithm Mechanism Inheritance (subclass overrides steps) Composition (inject an object or lambda) Bound at Compile time Runtime Example DataImporter.run() with parse()/validate() DeliveryFeeStrategy

Say: "Template Method fixes the skeleton and lets subclasses fill steps; Strategy swaps the entire algorithm by composition. In modern Java I often get a template's benefits with callbacks, like JdbcTemplate."

docs.title: Observer vs. Mediator vs. Pub/Sub
docs.text:
Observer Mediator Pub/Sub (broker) Shape Subject → many observers Peers ↔ one coordinator Publishers → topic → subscribers Knowledge Observers subscribe to the subject Peers know only the mediator Both know only the topic Logic location In each observer Centralized in the mediator In each subscriber Scope In-process In-process / orchestrator Across processes (Kafka, SNS)

Say: "Observer broadcasts changes; Mediator coordinates peers with central rules; pub/sub is Observer across processes with a broker in between."

docs.title: Composite vs. Decorator
docs.text:
Composite Decorator Children Many One wrapped object Purpose Part–whole trees Add behavior Combines results? Yes (sum, any, all) Wraps a single result Example Bundle of products and bundles Retry around a payment processor

Say: "Both use recursive composition. A composite holds many children to represent a whole; a decorator wraps exactly one object to extend it."

docs.title: Bridge vs. Adapter vs. Strategy
docs.text:
Bridge Adapter Strategy When designed Up front After the fact Up front Hierarchies Two, both evolving One target, one adaptee One context, many algorithms Purpose Avoid M × N classes Make incompatible interfaces work Swap behavior Example Reports × renderers (CSV, HTML) Legacy SDK → PaymentGateway Routing by fee vs. success rate

Say: "Bridge separates two dimensions that both grow; Adapter retrofits an existing interface; Strategy swaps one algorithm."

docs.title: Command vs. Strategy
docs.text:
Command Strategy Represents A request (what to do, with its data) An algorithm (how to do it) Lifecycle Queued, logged, undone, replayed Called immediately Example Transfer(id, from, to, amount) in a batch queue MatchingStrategy.nearest()

Say: "A command is a request turned into data so it can be queued, undone or replayed; a strategy is an interchangeable way of computing something."

docs.title: Chain of Responsibility vs. Decorator
docs.text:
Chain of Responsibility Decorator Forwarding A handler may stop the chain Usually always forwards Purpose Decide who handles Add behavior Example Loan escalation, validation, servlet filters Logging and retry layers

Say: "Structurally similar; the difference is that chain handlers can short-circuit and the goal is finding a handler."

docs.title: Singleton vs. Static Utility Class vs. Spring Singleton Bean
docs.text:
Singleton (GoF) Static utility class Spring singleton bean Instances 1 per class loader 0 1 per ApplicationContext Implements interfaces / polymorphism ✅ ❌ ✅ Testability (mocking) Hard Hard ✅ Easy State Allowed Shouldn't have any Allowed (thread-safe!) Use for True per-process invariants Pure functions (Math) Almost every service

Say: "In Spring apps I rely on singleton-scoped beans with constructor injection; I reserve the GoF Singleton for rare per-process invariants and use enums or the holder idiom when I do."

docs.title: Flyweight vs. Object Pool vs. Singleton
docs.text: Flyweight Object Pool Singleton Instances Few shared, one per distinct state Several, borrowed exclusively Exactly one Mutable? No Yes, while borrowed Maybe Goal Save memory Reuse expensive objects, limit count One global instance Example Map icons, Integer.valueOf cache DB connections Config

docs.title: Interpreter vs. Specification
docs.text:
Interpreter Specification Input Text in a small language (parsed) Rule objects built in code Users Business users write rules Developers compose rules Shared structure AST of AND/OR/comparisons AND/OR/NOT tree of predicates

Say: "A specification is like an interpreter without the parser: same rule tree, built in code instead of parsed from text."

docs.title: Visitor vs. Sealed Types + Pattern Matching (Java 21)
docs.text:
Classic Visitor Sealed + switch Boilerplate accept() in every element + visitor interface None Exhaustiveness Compiler forces every visit overload Compiler checks the switch over sealed types Works across modules / libraries ✅ Only if you own the sealed hierarchy Double dispatch over two hierarchies ✅ Awkward

Say: "For closed hierarchies I own, sealed types with pattern matching give me Visitor's safety with far less code; classic visitors remain useful across library boundaries."

docs.title: Concurrency comparisons
docs.text:
Question Short answer Thread pool vs. virtual threads Pools for CPU-bound work and hard caps (bulkheads); virtual threads for I/O-bound concurrency, with explicit resource limits CompletableFuture vs. virtual threads Futures for composition, timeouts and async APIs; virtual threads for simple blocking fan-out with readable code Read-write lock vs. immutable snapshot RW lock when updating in place under a lock; immutable snapshot + AtomicReference for wait-free reads of read-mostly data synchronized vs. ReentrantLock synchronized is simpler; ReentrantLock adds tryLock, timeouts, fairness, multiple conditions, and avoids pinning on JDK 21–23 DCL vs. holder idiom vs. computeIfAbsent Instance field: DCL with volatile; static: holder; per key: computeIfAbsent BlockingQueue.put vs. offer put blocks when full; offer returns false (or times out), which is better at system edges

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Short, practical definitions of terms used across the handbook, with links to where they matter.

Abstraction (Bridge) The high-level side of a Bridge: what a thing does (a report's contents), delegating how to an implementor (CSV, HTML). Aggregate (DDD) A cluster of domain objects treated as one unit for changes, with one root entity (an Order and its lines). Invariants are enforced inside the aggregate. Anti-Corruption Layer A set of Adapters and translators that keeps an external or legacy system's model out of your domain model. Back-pressure A way for a slow consumer to tell a fast producer to slow down: a full bounded queue, HTTP 429/503, or request(n) in reactive streams. See Producer-Consumer. Bounded Context (DDD) A boundary inside which a model and its terms have one consistent meaning ("customer" in billing vs. in support). Bulkhead Isolating resources (thread pools, connection pools, semaphores) per tenant or dependency so one can't exhaust everything. See Thread Pool. Carrier Thread A platform thread that runs virtual threads; virtual threads mount on it while running and unmount when they block. Circuit Breaker A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while (open), tests it occasionally (half-open), and resumes when healthy (closed). Cohesion How closely the responsibilities inside a class or module belong together. High cohesion is good. Composition over Inheritance Prefer building behavior by combining objects (has-a) instead of extending classes (is-a). The basis of Strategy, Decorator, Bridge and more. Contract Test A test that checks an integration against the agreed request/response format (Pact, WireMock recordings), so vendor or service changes break the build, not production. Coupling How much one module depends on the internals of another. Low coupling is good. CQRS Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate models for writes (commands) and reads (queries). Double Dispatch Choosing a method based on two runtime types, the mechanism behind Visitor (element.accept(v) → v.visit(this)). Effectively Immutable An object that's technically mutable but never modified after safe publication. Eventual Consistency Replicas or services may disagree briefly but converge if no new updates happen. Extrinsic / Intrinsic State In Flyweight: intrinsic state is shared and immutable (an icon); extrinsic state is per use and passed in (position). Fail-Fast Iterator An iterator that throws ConcurrentModificationException when the collection is modified during iteration. See Iterator. Happens-Before The Java Memory Model rule that guarantees one action's effects are visible to another (unlock → lock, volatile write → read, thread start, join). Hook Method An optional step with a default implementation in a Template Method. Idempotency Doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. Essential for retries, queues and webhooks. See Command. Immutability State that can't change after construction. See Immutable Object. Inversion of Control (IoC) A framework calls your code rather than your code calling the framework ("don't call us, we'll call you"). Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) Subtypes must be usable wherever their base type is expected, without surprising callers. Little's Law Average items in a system = arrival rate × average time in the system. Used to size pools and queues. MVCC Multi-Version Concurrency Control: databases keep row versions so readers see snapshots and don't block writers. Open/Closed Principle (OCP) Software should be open for extension but closed for modification: add new behavior with new code. Outbox (Transactional) Write a business change and the event describing it in the same database transaction; a relay publishes the event later. Prevents dual-write inconsistencies. Pinning A virtual thread that can't unmount from its carrier while blocking (inside synchronized before JDK 24, or native frames). Poison Pill A special item placed on a queue to tell a consumer to stop. Race Condition A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads (check-then-act, read-modify-write without synchronization). Saga A sequence of local transactions across services with compensating actions to undo completed steps when a later step fails. Sealed Types Java 17+ classes or interfaces that restrict which classes may extend them, enabling exhaustive switch with pattern matching. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) A class should have one reason to change. SOLID Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion. See OOP & SOLID. Structured Concurrency Treating a group of related concurrent tasks as one unit with a clear lifetime: fork, join, cancel siblings on failure (StructuredTaskScope). Thread Confinement Keeping data accessible to only one thread, so no synchronization is needed. Ubiquitous Language (DDD) The shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts, used in code, conversations and documents. Value Object An immutable object defined by its values, not identity (Money, Email, DateRange). Virtual Thread A lightweight, JVM-scheduled thread (Java 21). See Virtual Threads. YAGNI "You Aren't Gonna Need It": don't build flexibility until it's needed.

docs.title: Pattern Selection Guide
docs.text:
Knowing 30 patterns is easy; picking the right one under interview pressure or in a design review is the real skill. This guide works backwards: start from the symptom in your code or the requirement in the problem, and find the pattern.

Two rules before you pick any pattern

  1. Name the force first. "Payment methods keep being added" (a variation point) or "two threads update this" (shared state). A pattern is a response to a force, not a decoration.
  2. Start simple. If an if statement is clear and won't grow, keep it. Introduce the pattern when the second or third variation shows up (YAGNI).

docs.title: 1. From code smell to pattern
docs.text: You see this in the code... Consider Why if/else or switch on a type to decide which class to new Factory Method Centralize creation; new types without editing callers Constructors with 6+ parameters, many nulls Builder Readable, validated, immutable construction Objects that must always be used together (AWS storage + AWS queue) Abstract Factory Guarantees consistent families new ExpensiveThing() copied with small changes Prototype Copy a configured template A connection/session created per request Object Pool Reuse expensive, limited resources if/else choosing an algorithm (fees, routing, sorting) Strategy Swap algorithms at runtime switch (status) repeated in many methods State Behavior lives with each state; illegal transitions closed Several classes copy the same workflow with small differences Template Method One final skeleton, variable steps A method that calls 5 services in a fixed order, copied in many clients Facade One task-level entry point A vendor SDK's types and error codes all over your code Adapter Translate at the boundary LoggingRetryingCachingService subclasses Decorator Stack behaviors at runtime Security checks / lazy loading mixed into business code Proxy Control access transparently instanceof checks to treat a single item and a group differently Composite Uniform part-whole trees Class names that are two nouns glued together (SalesCsvReport) Bridge M + N classes instead of M × N Millions of objects repeating the same heavy data Flyweight Share immutable intrinsic state One service calls email, inventory, analytics after saving Observer Publish an event; listeners react Widgets/peers calling each other in a tangle Mediator Centralize coordination A request must be queued, retried, undone or logged Command Request as an object Validation/approval handled by a growing if ladder Chain of Responsibility Ordered, independent handlers Undo, drafts, checkpoints Memento Snapshots without breaking encapsulation Many operations added to a stable class hierarchy Visitor / sealed + switch New operations without touching types if (x != null) everywhere for an optional collaborator Null Object Neutral behavior, no checks Business rules duplicated in Java and SQL Specification Named, composable rules Business users want to write rules or formulas Interpreter Small DSL with an AST Paginated or merged data consumed in loops Iterator Lazy, uniform traversal Exactly one instance must exist per process Singleton (or DI singleton scope) One instance, global access

docs.title: 2. From concurrency symptom to pattern
docs.text: Symptom Consider Bursty work arriving faster than it can be processed Producer-Consumer with a bounded queue new Thread() per task, or CPU oversubscribed Thread Pool (CPU-bound) Thousands of tasks mostly waiting on I/O Virtual Threads + explicit resource limits Calling several services one after another Future / Promise (parallel + timeouts) Read-mostly shared data with multi-field updates Read-Write Lock or immutable snapshots Data shared between threads that "never changes" but has setters Immutable Object Expensive lazy initialization under concurrency Double-Checked Locking / holder / computeIfAbsent

docs.title: "I need to create objects"
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q{What is hard about creating it?} -->|Must be exactly one| S[Singleton / DI singleton]
    Q -->|Many optional parameters or must be immutable| B[Builder]
    Q -->|Which class depends on input or config| F[Factory Method]
    Q -->|Several related objects must match| AF[Abstract Factory]
    Q -->|Setup is expensive; a copy would do| P[Prototype]
    Q -->|Creation is expensive and count is limited| OP[Object Pool]

docs.title: "Behavior varies"
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q{What varies?} -->|The whole algorithm, chosen by the caller| ST[Strategy]
    Q -->|Behavior depends on the object's current state| S[State]
    Q -->|A few steps of a fixed process| TM[Template Method]
    Q -->|Who handles a request| COR[Chain of Responsibility]
    Q -->|Operations over a stable set of types| V[Visitor / sealed + switch]
    Q -->|Rules combined with and/or/not| SP[Specification]

docs.title: "I'm wrapping something"
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q{Why wrap it?} -->|Its interface doesn't fit mine| A[Adapter]
    Q -->|Add behavior, possibly stacked| D[Decorator]
    Q -->|Control access: lazy, security, remote, cache| P[Proxy]
    Q -->|Hide many classes behind one simple API| F[Facade]

docs.title: "Objects need to talk"
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q{Communication shape?} -->|One change, many interested parties| O[Observer]
    Q -->|Many peers coordinating with rules| M[Mediator]
    Q -->|Request must be stored, queued, undone| C[Command]
    Q -->|Request passed along until handled| COR[Chain of Responsibility]

docs.title: 4. Patterns behind classic interview problems
docs.text:
These are common choices, not the only correct ones; explain the force behind each.

Problem (LLD round) Patterns that usually fit Parking lot Strategy (pricing, spot allocation), Factory (vehicle/spot types), Singleton/DI (the lot), Observer (display boards), State (spot status) Elevator system State (moving up/down, idle, doors), Strategy (scheduling: nearest car, SCAN), Command (floor requests), Mediator/Observer (controller and panels) Vending machine State (idle, has money, dispensing, sold out), Strategy (payment), Chain of Responsibility (change-making by denomination) Food / grocery delivery State (order lifecycle), Strategy (delivery fee, rider matching), Observer (tracking, notifications), Facade (checkout), Builder (order), Saga (distributed order flow) Splitwise / expense sharing Strategy (split equally, exact, percentage), Immutable Money, Observer (balance updates), Factory (expense types) Rate limiter Strategy (token bucket, sliding window), Proxy/Decorator (wrap the API), Singleton per key or computeIfAbsent LRU cache Hash map + doubly linked list; Decorator/Proxy (caching layer); Strategy (eviction policy) Logger Singleton/DI, Chain of Responsibility (levels/appenders), Strategy (formatters), Producer-Consumer (async appender), Decorator Notification system Bridge (type × channel), Strategy (channel selection), Observer (events), Template Method (send pipeline), Decorator (retry/rate-limit) Payment system Strategy/Factory (methods), Adapter (gateways), State (payment lifecycle), Command (queued instructions), Proxy (security), Template Method (flow) Movie / ticket booking State (seat status), Strategy (pricing), Observer (seat map updates), Builder (booking), locking/optimistic concurrency for seats Chess / board games Strategy (move rules per piece), Command (moves with undo), Memento (save game), State (game phase), Factory (pieces) Document editor Command (undo/redo), Memento (versions), Composite (document tree), Visitor (export), Flyweight (styles)

How to present a pattern in an interview

  1. State the force: "Payment methods will grow, and each has different rules."
  2. Name the pattern: "So I'll use Strategy behind a PaymentMethod interface."
  3. Show the extension point: "Adding wallets is one new class; checkout doesn't change."
  4. Mention the trade-off: "A factory chooses the strategy; for two fixed methods I'd keep a simple switch."

docs.title: 5. When NOT to use a pattern
docs.text:
• One implementation and no realistic second: skip Strategy, Factory and Abstract Factory.
  • Simple, stable conditionals: a 3-case switch expression on a sealed type is often clearer than State or Visitor.
  • DI already gives it to you: Spring singletons, profiles (Abstract Factory), AOP (Proxy/Decorator).
  • The language gives it to you: lambdas (Strategy, Command), records (immutable values), sealed + pattern matching (Visitor), streams (Iterator).
  • Performance-critical inner loops: measure before adding layers of indirection.

docs.text:
Progress: 71 of 71 items (100%)

Every planned item is done: all Creational (6), Structural (7), Behavioral (13), Concurrency (7), Microservices (18) and Architecture (5) patterns, the guides, the full Interview section (company guides, 12 LLD problems, system design patterns, top 100 questions, cheat sheet) and the FreshCart capstone. Every example runs: ./run-demos.sh --check verifies all outputs, and CI runs over 200 unit and ArchUnit tests.

docs.title: Architecture Patterns
docs.text:
Design patterns organize classes; architecture patterns organize whole applications: where business rules live, which way dependencies point, how parts communicate, and how the codebase can grow without turning into a big ball of mud. These five styles cover most architecture discussions in interviews and in real Java projects.

Pattern Core idea Best for Interview frequency Status Layered Presentation → business → persistence, dependencies point down CRUD apps, simple domains ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) Core owns ports; adapters plug in on both sides Many integrations, testability, swapping vendors ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Clean Architecture Concentric circles; dependencies point inward; presenters Complex, long-lived domains ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Event-Driven Components react to events through a broker Integration, real-time processing, decoupling ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Modular Monolith One deployable, enforced business modules New products, growing teams, pre-microservices ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅

Architecture rules are tested, not just drawn

The architecture module includes ArchUnit tests that fail the build if the examples break their own rules: layers calling upward, the hexagon's core importing an adapter, inner Clean Architecture circles depending on outer ones, or the billing module depending on ordering. Run them with mvn -f code/pom.xml test -pl architecture.

docs.title: How they relate
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    L[Layered] -->|invert the DB dependency| H[Hexagonal]
    H -->|name the circles,<br/>add presenters| C[Clean]
    L -->|package by feature,<br/>enforce boundaries| M[Modular Monolith]
    M -->|extract modules| MS[Microservices]
    E[Event-Driven] -.->|integration style for| M
    E -.-> MS
  • Layered, Hexagonal and Clean answer "how is one application organized inside?"
  • Modular Monolith answers "how do we split a large application by business capability?" (and each module can use any of the three above inside).
  • Event-Driven answers "how do parts communicate?", between modules or between services.

docs.title: Choosing quickly
docs.text:
If you have... Start with A CRUD admin app, a small team Layered (package by feature) Several external systems or vendors you may swap Hexagonal Rich business rules that must outlive frameworks Clean (or Hexagonal with a rich domain) A new product, unclear boundaries, 1–3 teams Modular monolith Many teams needing independent deployment and scaling Microservices, split along proven module boundaries Many consumers reacting to the same business facts Event-driven integration

Anti-Corruption Layer Start: Layered Architecture

docs.title: Clean Architecture
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Architecture Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Arrange code in concentric circles: entities (enterprise rules) → use cases (application rules) → interface adapters (controllers, presenters, gateways) → frameworks and drivers (web, DB, UI). Source-code dependencies may only point inward. Business rules don't know about the web, the database or the framework, so those can change, and the rules can be tested in isolation.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the coupon rules of a grocery app are written inside a Spring controller, read data via JPA entities, and return a JSON map. Adding a mobile app with a different response shape means duplicating the rules; upgrading Spring breaks business logic; nobody can say where "the rules" actually are.

Definition (Robert C. Martin, Clean Architecture):

The Dependency Rule: source code dependencies must point only inward, toward higher-level policies. Nothing in an inner circle can know anything at all about something in an outer circle.

Circle Contains Example Entities Enterprise-wide business rules Coupon.evaluate(), Account.withdraw() Use cases Application-specific rules; input/output boundaries; request/response models; gateway interfaces ApplyCoupon.Interactor Interface adapters Controllers, presenters, gateway implementations; convert data between use cases and the outside CouponController, WebPresenter Frameworks & drivers Web framework, DB, UI, devices Spring MVC, PostgreSQL, Android

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A country's constitution, laws and offices

The constitution (entities) changes rarely and doesn't mention any specific government office. Laws (use cases) build on the constitution. Government offices and forms (adapters) implement the laws for citizens, and the buildings and computers (frameworks) can be replaced without changing a single law.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph F["Frameworks & drivers"]
      subgraph A["Interface adapters"]
        subgraph U["Use cases"]
          E["Entities"]
        end
      end
    end
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Controller (adapter)
    participant I as Interactor (use case)
    participant G as Gateway (interface in use-case circle)
    participant En as Entity
    participant P as Presenter (adapter)
    C->>I: Request model
    I->>G: load data
    I->>En: apply rules
    I->>P: Response model (via output boundary)
    P->>P: build view model

Flow of control vs. dependencies: control flows outward (interactor → presenter), but the interactor only knows the output boundary interface defined in its own circle; the presenter implements it. That's dependency inversion.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@PostMapping("/cart/{id}/coupon")
Map<String, Object> apply(@PathVariable String id, @RequestParam String code) {
    CartEntity cart = cartJpaRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    CouponEntity c = couponJpaRepo.findByCode(code.toUpperCase());
    if (c.getExpires().isBefore(LocalDate.now())) return Map.of("error", "expired");   // rule + clock
    long discount = Math.min(c.getMax(), cart.getSubtotal() * c.getPercent() / 100);   // rule
    return Map.of("total", "₹" + (cart.getSubtotal() - discount) / 100);              // formatting
}

docs.title: Example 1: Apply a Coupon, Two Presenters (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The Coupon entity knows the rules (expiry, minimum basket, percentage, cap). The ApplyCoupon interactor loads data through gateway interfaces and reports a response model through an output boundary. A web presenter turns it into a detailed JSON view model; a mobile presenter into a one-line toast. The calendar is a gateway too, so the use case is deterministic in tests.

Full Code:

Coupon.java (entity)ApplyCoupon.java (use case)CouponAdapters.java (interface adapters)CleanCouponDemo.java (main) 
package com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.entities;

import java.time.LocalDate;

/**
 * Entity (innermost circle): enterprise-wide business rules that would exist even without this app.
 * No dependencies on anything outside this circle.
 */
public record Coupon(String code, int percentOff, long minSubtotalPaise, long maxDiscountPaise, LocalDate expires) {

    public sealed interface Outcome permits Discount, NotApplicable {
    }

    public record Discount(long paise) implements Outcome {
    }

    public record NotApplicable(String reason) implements Outcome {
    }

    public Outcome evaluate(long subtotalPaise, LocalDate today) {
        if (today.isAfter(expires)) {
            return new NotApplicable("coupon expired on " + expires);
        }
        if (subtotalPaise < minSubtotalPaise) {
            return new NotApplicable("add ₹" + (minSubtotalPaise - subtotalPaise) / 100 + " more to use " + code);
        }
        return new Discount(Math.min(maxDiscountPaise, subtotalPaise * percentOff / 100));
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.usecase;

import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.entities.Coupon;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * Use-case circle: the boundaries (input/output ports), request/response models, the gateways the
 * use case needs, and the interactor. It depends only on entities.
 */
public final class ApplyCoupon {

    private ApplyCoupon() {
    }

    public record Request(String cartId, String couponCode) { // (1)!
    }

    public record Response(boolean applied, long subtotalPaise, long discountPaise, String message) {
    }

    public interface InputBoundary {
        void apply(Request request, OutputBoundary presenter);
    }

    public interface OutputBoundary { // (2)!
        void present(Response response);
    }

    public interface CartGateway {
        Optional<Long> subtotalOf(String cartId);
    }

    public interface CouponGateway {
        Optional<Coupon> find(String code);
    }

    public interface Calendar {
        LocalDate today();
    }

    public static final class Interactor implements InputBoundary {
        private final CartGateway carts;
        private final CouponGateway coupons;
        private final Calendar calendar;

        public Interactor(CartGateway carts, CouponGateway coupons, Calendar calendar) {
            this.carts = carts;
            this.coupons = coupons;
            this.calendar = calendar;
        }

        @Override
        public void apply(Request request, OutputBoundary presenter) {
            long subtotal = carts.subtotalOf(request.cartId()).orElse(0L);
            Optional<Coupon> coupon = coupons.find(request.couponCode().trim().toUpperCase());
            if (coupon.isEmpty()) {
                presenter.present(new Response(false, subtotal, 0, "unknown coupon " + request.couponCode()));
                return;
            }
            switch (coupon.get().evaluate(subtotal, calendar.today())) { // (3)!
                case Coupon.Discount d -> presenter.present(new Response(true, subtotal, d.paise(), "coupon applied"));
                case Coupon.NotApplicable n -> presenter.present(new Response(false, subtotal, 0, n.reason()));
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. Request model: plain data crossing the boundary; no HTTP types.
  2. Output boundary: implemented by presenters in the outer circle (dependency inversion).
  3. The entity's sealed Outcome lets the compiler check that every case is handled.
package com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.adapters;

import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.entities.Coupon;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.usecase.ApplyCoupon;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * Interface-adapters circle: controllers turn web/app input into request models, presenters turn
 * response models into view models, gateways implement the use case's data interfaces.
 */
public final class CouponAdapters {

    private CouponAdapters() {
    }

    /** Controller: knows the HTTP shape of the input, nothing about rules. */
    public static final class CouponController {
        private final ApplyCoupon.InputBoundary useCase;

        public CouponController(ApplyCoupon.InputBoundary useCase) {
            this.useCase = useCase;
        }

        public void post(Map<String, String> form, ApplyCoupon.OutputBoundary presenter) {
            useCase.apply(new ApplyCoupon.Request(form.get("cart"), form.getOrDefault("code", "")), presenter);
        }
    }

    /** Web presenter: a detailed view model with rupee strings for the desktop basket page. */
    public static final class WebPresenter implements ApplyCoupon.OutputBoundary {
        public String viewModel;

        @Override
        public void present(ApplyCoupon.Response r) { // (1)!
            viewModel = String.format("{\"ok\":%s,\"subtotal\":\"₹%,.2f\",\"discount\":\"-₹%,.2f\",\"total\":\"₹%,.2f\",\"note\":\"%s\"}",
                    r.applied(), r.subtotalPaise() / 100.0, r.discountPaise() / 100.0,
                    (r.subtotalPaise() - r.discountPaise()) / 100.0, r.message());
        }
    }

    /** Mobile presenter: one short line for a toast message. */
    public static final class MobileToastPresenter implements ApplyCoupon.OutputBoundary {
        public String viewModel;

        @Override
        public void present(ApplyCoupon.Response r) {
            viewModel = r.applied() ? "🎉 You saved ₹" + r.discountPaise() / 100 : "⚠ " + r.message();
        }
    }

    /** Gateways: in-memory here; JPA, Redis or a remote API in production. */
    public static ApplyCoupon.CartGateway carts(Map<String, Long> subtotals) {
        return id -> Optional.ofNullable(subtotals.get(id));
    }

    public static ApplyCoupon.CouponGateway coupons(Map<String, Coupon> byCode) {
        return code -> Optional.ofNullable(byCode.get(code));
    }

    public static ApplyCoupon.Calendar fixedCalendar(LocalDate date) {
        return () -> date;
    }
}
  1. The presenter owns formatting: currency, wording, JSON shape. The use case never formats.
package com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon;

import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.adapters.CouponAdapters;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.adapters.CouponAdapters.CouponController;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.adapters.CouponAdapters.MobileToastPresenter;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.adapters.CouponAdapters.WebPresenter;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.entities.Coupon;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.usecase.ApplyCoupon;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;

public class CleanCouponDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // "Main" component: the only place that knows every concrete class.
        var useCase = new ApplyCoupon.Interactor(
                CouponAdapters.carts(Map.of("CART-1", 144_700L, "CART-2", 39_900L)),
                CouponAdapters.coupons(Map.of(
                        "MANGO20", new Coupon("MANGO20", 20, 50_000, 20_000, LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 31)),
                        "DIWALI10", new Coupon("DIWALI10", 10, 0, 50_000, LocalDate.of(2025, 11, 5)))),
                CouponAdapters.fixedCalendar(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 14)));
        var controller = new CouponController(useCase);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: one use case, two presenters ===");
        WebPresenter web = new WebPresenter();
        controller.post(Map.of("cart", "CART-1", "code", "mango20"), web);
        System.out.println("web    CART-1 MANGO20  -> " + web.viewModel);

        MobileToastPresenter mobile = new MobileToastPresenter();
        controller.post(Map.of("cart", "CART-1", "code", "MANGO20"), mobile);
        System.out.println("mobile CART-1 MANGO20  -> " + mobile.viewModel);
        controller.post(Map.of("cart", "CART-2", "code", "MANGO20"), mobile);
        System.out.println("mobile CART-2 MANGO20  -> " + mobile.viewModel);
        controller.post(Map.of("cart", "CART-1", "code", "DIWALI10"), mobile);
        System.out.println("mobile CART-1 DIWALI10 -> " + mobile.viewModel);
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: one use case, two presenters ===
web    CART-1 MANGO20  -> {"ok":true,"subtotal":"₹1,447.00","discount":"-₹200.00","total":"₹1,247.00","note":"coupon applied"}
mobile CART-1 MANGO20  -> 🎉 You saved ₹200
mobile CART-2 MANGO20  -> ⚠ add ₹101 more to use MANGO20
mobile CART-1 DIWALI10 -> ⚠ coupon expired on 2025-11-05

Why Clean here:

  • Rules live in one place (entity), application flow in another (interactor), formatting in presenters.
  • A new channel = a new presenter; no rule changes.
  • Fully testable without Spring or a database (ArchUnit enforces the dependency rule in the tests).

docs.title: Example 2: Transfer Funds, One Response for Two Audiences (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The Account entity enforces balance and daily-limit rules. The interactor orchestrates the transfer and produces one response model. The API presenter shows customer-friendly messages with HTTP codes; the audit presenter writes a detailed compliance line. Both receive the same facts.

Full Code:

TransferFunds.javaTransferDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Banking transfer in Clean Architecture terms. The entity enforces account rules; the interactor
 * orchestrates; TWO presenters render the same response model for different audiences.
 */
public final class TransferFunds {

    private TransferFunds() {
    }

    /** Entity: rules that hold for every application the bank builds. */
    public static final class Account {
        private final String id;
        private long balance;
        private long withdrawnToday;
        private final long dailyLimit;

        public Account(String id, long balance, long dailyLimit) {
            this.id = id;
            this.balance = balance;
            this.dailyLimit = dailyLimit;
        }

        void withdraw(long paise) {
            if (paise > balance) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
            }
            if (withdrawnToday + paise > dailyLimit) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("daily transfer limit exceeded");
            }
            balance -= paise;
            withdrawnToday += paise;
        }

        void deposit(long paise) {
            balance += paise;
        }

        public long balance() {
            return balance;
        }

        public String id() {
            return id;
        }
    }

    public record Request(String from, String to, long paise, String channel) {
    }

    public record Response(boolean ok, String from, String to, long paise, String reason, long fromBalanceAfter) {
    }

    public interface Presenter {
        void present(Response response);
    }

    public interface AccountGateway {
        Account load(String id);

        void save(Account account);
    }

    /** Interactor: application-specific orchestration. Knows nothing about HTTP or logs. */
    public static final class Interactor {
        private final AccountGateway accounts;

        public Interactor(AccountGateway accounts) {
            this.accounts = accounts;
        }

        public void transfer(Request r, Presenter presenter) {
            Account from = accounts.load(r.from());
            Account to = accounts.load(r.to());
            try {
                from.withdraw(r.paise()); // (1)!
                to.deposit(r.paise());
                accounts.save(from);
                accounts.save(to);
                presenter.present(new Response(true, r.from(), r.to(), r.paise(), "", from.balance()));
            } catch (IllegalStateException rule) {
                presenter.present(new Response(false, r.from(), r.to(), r.paise(), rule.getMessage(), from.balance()));
            }
        }
    }

    /** Presenter 1: the mobile API, with HTTP status and customer-friendly text. */
    public static final class ApiPresenter implements Presenter {
        public String output;

        @Override
        public void present(Response r) {
            output = r.ok() ? "200 {\"message\":\"Sent ₹" + r.paise() / 100 + "\"}"
                    : "422 {\"message\":\"Transfer failed: " + r.reason() + "\"}";
        }
    }

    /** Presenter 2: the compliance audit log, with everything an auditor needs. */
    public static final class AuditPresenter implements Presenter {
        public String output;

        @Override
        public void present(Response r) {
            output = String.format("AUDIT result=%s from=%s to=%s amount=%d reason=%s balance_after=%d",
                    r.ok() ? "OK" : "REJECTED", r.from(), r.to(), r.paise(), r.reason().isEmpty() ? "-" : r.reason(),
                    r.fromBalanceAfter());
        }
    }

    /** Gateway implementation (interface-adapters circle). */
    public static final class InMemoryAccounts implements AccountGateway {
        private final Map<String, Account> accounts = new HashMap<>();

        public InMemoryAccounts with(Account a) {
            accounts.put(a.id(), a);
            return this;
        }

        @Override
        public Account load(String id) {
            return accounts.get(id);
        }

        @Override
        public void save(Account account) {
            accounts.put(account.id(), account);
        }
    }
}
  1. Rules are enforced by the entity; the interactor only coordinates and reports.
package com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer;

import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.Account;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.ApiPresenter;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.AuditPresenter;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.InMemoryAccounts;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.Interactor;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.Presenter;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.Request;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.transfer.TransferFunds.Response;

public class TransferDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var accounts = new InMemoryAccounts()
                .with(new Account("A-1", 10_000_000, 5_000_000))
                .with(new Account("B-2", 0, 5_000_000));
        var interactor = new Interactor(accounts);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: one interactor, a response model rendered twice ===");
        for (long paise : new long[] {2_000_000, 4_000_000, 20_000_000}) {
            ApiPresenter api = new ApiPresenter();
            AuditPresenter audit = new AuditPresenter();
            interactor.transfer(new Request("A-1", "B-2", paise, "app"), both(api, audit));
            System.out.println(api.output);
            System.out.println("  " + audit.output);
        }
    }

    private static Presenter both(Presenter a, Presenter b) {
        return (Response r) -> {
            a.present(r);
            b.present(r);
        };
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: one interactor, a response model rendered twice ===
200 {"message":"Sent ₹20000"}
  AUDIT result=OK from=A-1 to=B-2 amount=2000000 reason=- balance_after=8000000
422 {"message":"Transfer failed: daily transfer limit exceeded"}
  AUDIT result=REJECTED from=A-1 to=B-2 amount=4000000 reason=daily transfer limit exceeded balance_after=8000000
422 {"message":"Transfer failed: insufficient funds"}
  AUDIT result=REJECTED from=A-1 to=B-2 amount=20000000 reason=insufficient funds balance_after=8000000

Why Clean here:

  • Customer messaging and compliance logging evolve independently, without touching rules.
  • Entities are reusable across apps (branch system, mobile app, batch).

docs.title: Example 3: Prescription Refills with a Sealed Result (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A modern-Java variation: instead of an output-boundary callback, the use case returns a sealed Result (Approved, NeedsDoctor, Rejected). The outermost web layer maps each case to an HTTP status with an exhaustive switch. Controlled substances always go to the doctor; expired prescriptions too; other patients' prescriptions are invisible.

Full Code:

RefillPrescription.javaRefillDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.clean.refill;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * A modern-Java variation: instead of an output boundary, the use case returns a sealed Result.
 * The web layer (outermost circle) maps each case to HTTP. Same dependency rule: inner code never
 * mentions HTTP.
 */
public final class RefillPrescription {

    private RefillPrescription() {
    }

    public record Prescription(String id, String patient, String drug, int refillsLeft, LocalDate validUntil,
                               boolean controlledSubstance) {
    }

    public sealed interface Result permits Approved, NeedsDoctor, Rejected {
    }

    public record Approved(String drug, int refillsLeft) implements Result {
    }

    public record NeedsDoctor(String reason) implements Result {
    }

    public record Rejected(String reason) implements Result {
    }

    public interface Prescriptions {
        Prescription find(String id);
    }

    /** Use case: pure rules + gateway calls; trivially unit-testable. */
    public static Result refill(Prescriptions repo, String prescriptionId, String patient, LocalDate today) {
        Prescription p = repo.find(prescriptionId);
        if (p == null || !p.patient().equals(patient)) {
            return new Rejected("no such prescription for this patient"); // (1)!
        }
        if (today.isAfter(p.validUntil())) {
            return new NeedsDoctor("prescription expired on " + p.validUntil());
        }
        if (p.controlledSubstance()) {
            return new NeedsDoctor("controlled substance: doctor must approve each refill");
        }
        if (p.refillsLeft() == 0) {
            return new NeedsDoctor("no refills left");
        }
        return new Approved(p.drug(), p.refillsLeft() - 1);
    }

    /** Outermost circle: the web controller maps results to HTTP. */
    public static String httpResponse(Result result) {
        return switch (result) { // (2)!
            case Approved a -> "200 refill approved: " + a.drug() + " (" + a.refillsLeft() + " left)";
            case NeedsDoctor n -> "202 sent to your doctor: " + n.reason();
            case Rejected r -> "404 " + r.reason();
        };
    }

    public static Prescriptions inMemory(Map<String, Prescription> data) {
        return data::get;
    }
}
  1. The same answer for "doesn't exist" and "belongs to someone else", so the API doesn't leak which prescriptions exist.
  2. An exhaustive switch over a sealed type: add a new result and the compiler shows every place to update.
package com.handbook.architecture.clean.refill;

import com.handbook.architecture.clean.refill.RefillPrescription.Prescription;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;

public class RefillDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var repo = RefillPrescription.inMemory(Map.of(
                "RX-1", new Prescription("RX-1", "PAT-5", "Metformin 500 mg", 3, LocalDate.of(2027, 3, 1), false),
                "RX-2", new Prescription("RX-2", "PAT-5", "Alprazolam 0.25 mg", 2, LocalDate.of(2027, 3, 1), true),
                "RX-3", new Prescription("RX-3", "PAT-5", "Atorvastatin 10 mg", 1, LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 30), false)));
        LocalDate today = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 14);

        System.out.println("=== Healthcare: refill use case returning a sealed Result ===");
        for (String[] req : new String[][] {{"RX-1", "PAT-5"}, {"RX-2", "PAT-5"}, {"RX-3", "PAT-5"}, {"RX-1", "PAT-9"}}) {
            var result = RefillPrescription.refill(repo, req[0], req[1], today);
            System.out.printf("%s by %s -> %s%n", req[0], req[1], RefillPrescription.httpResponse(result));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Healthcare: refill use case returning a sealed Result ===
RX-1 by PAT-5 -> 200 refill approved: Metformin 500 mg (2 left)
RX-2 by PAT-5 -> 202 sent to your doctor: controlled substance: doctor must approve each refill
RX-3 by PAT-5 -> 202 sent to your doctor: prescription expired on 2026-09-30
RX-1 by PAT-9 -> 404 no such prescription for this patient

Why this variation:

  • Simpler than presenters when there's one consumer; still no HTTP in the use case.
  • Sealed results make error handling explicit and type-checked (no exceptions for expected outcomes).
Tests (ArchUnit enforces the dependency rule) 
package com.handbook.architecture;

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.domain.JavaClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ClassFileImporter;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses;
import static com.tngtech.archunit.library.Architectures.layeredArchitecture;

/** The architecture of the examples, enforced by ArchUnit on every build. */
class ArchitectureRulesTest {

    private final JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter()
            .withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
            .importPackages("com.handbook.architecture");

    @Test
    void groceryLayersOnlyCallDownwards() {
        layeredArchitecture().consideringOnlyDependenciesInLayers()
                .layer("Web").definedBy("..layered.grocery.web..")
                .layer("Service").definedBy("..layered.grocery.service..")
                .layer("Repository").definedBy("..layered.grocery.repository..")
                .whereLayer("Web").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
                .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Web")
                .whereLayer("Repository").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void hexagonCoreNeverDependsOnAdapters() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.domain..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.port..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void cleanArchitectureDependencyRulePointsInwards() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.entities..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..", "..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void billingModuleDoesNotDependOnOrdering() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.billing..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.ordering..")
                .check(classes);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Output boundary vs. return values: presenters (Example 1–2) suit multiple outputs or streaming; returning a sealed Result (Example 3) is simpler and idiomatic in Java 21.
  • Records for request/response models; sealed interfaces for outcomes; pattern matching in adapters.
  • Screaming architecture: top-level packages named after use cases and domain (coupons/, transfers/), not frameworks (controllers/).
  • Spring at the edge: controllers and @Configuration live in the outer circle; use cases are plain classes registered as beans in configuration.
  • Cross-cutting concerns (transactions, security, logging) as decorators around use cases (see the coding challenge).

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Clean Architecture Android (Google's app architecture guide) Domain layer with use cases, data layer with repositories Spring Boot projects Plain use-case classes + adapters; ArchUnit onionArchitecture() jMolecules Expresses architecture concepts (layers, ring) in code and verifies them iOS (VIPER, Clean Swift) Interactor/Presenter separation inspired by Clean Architecture

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Business rules independent of frameworks, UI, DB Boilerplate: boundaries, request/response models, presenters Very testable; fast tests Indirection can confuse newcomers Long-lived systems survive framework changes Overkill for CRUD Clear place for every kind of code Risk of "ceremony over substance"

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Entities that are just JPA rows

If entities have only getters/setters and all rules are in interactors, you have an anemic model with extra layers. Put invariants in entities.

Use cases returning view models or HTTP codes

Then they depend on the outer circle. Return response models (or sealed results); let presenters/controllers decide formats and status codes.

Mapping everything three times by default

Request → entity → response → view model for a trivial read is ceremony. Be pragmatic about reads; apply full rigour to complex writes.

Frameworks imported 'just for annotations'

@Transactional in a use case looks harmless but couples it to Spring. Prefer decorators/AOP configured in the outer circle if strict independence matters to you.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Policy vs. detail. Martin's core idea: high-level policy (rules) shouldn't depend on low-level detail (I/O). Every inward dependency arrow you protect buys the freedom to postpone or replace a detail.

Where to be pragmatic. Many teams allow JPA annotations on entities, or skip presenters and return DTOs, to reduce mapping. That's fine if it's a deliberate, documented decision enforced by tests, not an accident.

Use cases as the unit of design. Name them after what users do (ApplyCoupon, TransferFunds); each one is a transaction boundary, a test suite and a security boundary. This also maps neatly onto API endpoints and messages.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design / architecture round)
docs.text:
"I'd organize the service around use cases. Entities hold invariants (account limits, coupon rules). Each use case is a plain class with request and response models and gateway interfaces for data it needs. Controllers translate HTTP into requests; presenters or the controller translate responses into views and status codes. Spring, JPA and Kafka live only in the outer circle. ArchUnit enforces that dependencies point inward. Cross-cutting concerns like transactions and authorization are applied as decorators around use cases in configuration."

War story: the framework upgrade that rewrote the business

A logistics firm's routing rules lived in Struts actions and EJB session beans. When the platform reached end of life, migrating to Spring meant rewriting 600 classes, including the rules, because rules and framework code were interleaved. The migration took two years, and several rules changed by accident. What they did next time: entities and use cases as plain Java with 2,000 fast tests; frameworks only in adapters. The next migration (Spring Boot 2 → 3, javax → jakarta) touched only adapters and took three weeks. Lesson: frameworks come and go; protect the rules from them.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Clean Hexagonal Onion Layered Center Entities, then use cases Application core Domain model — Outer things Adapters, frameworks Adapters on ports Infrastructure, UI, tests Lower layers Signature idea Presenters, request/response models Symmetric ports Concentric domain layers Horizontal layers

See Hexagonal, Layered and the in-process Strategy/Decorator patterns used in the challenge.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Entities → Use cases → Interface adapters → Frameworks; dependencies point inward.
  • Request/response models at the boundary; presenters format.
  • Gateways are interfaces in the use-case circle, implemented outside.
  • Java 21: records + sealed results + pattern matching.
  • Cross-cutting concerns as decorators at the edge.

docs.text:
