docs.title: Example 3: Closed vs. Open Layers for Reports (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A statement report is a pure read. With strictly closed layers, the presentation calls a service method that just forwards to the query: the architecture sinkhole anti-pattern. Marking the read-only query layer as open lets presentation read it directly, while writes (transfers) still must go through the service layer and its rules.

Full Code:

StatementLayers.javaOpenLayerDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Closed vs. open layers for a read-only report. In strict (closed) layering every call passes
 * through the service layer, even when it adds nothing: the "architecture sinkhole".
 * Marking a query layer as OPEN lets the presentation layer read it directly.
 */
public final class StatementLayers {

    public record Txn(String date, String description, long paise) {
    }

    /** Data layer: a read-optimized query (in a real app, a SQL view or a reporting replica). */
    public static final class StatementQueries {
        private final Map<String, List<Txn>> data = Map.of("ACC-1", List.of(
                new Txn("2026-10-01", "Salary", 5_000_000),
                new Txn("2026-10-03", "Rent", -1_250_000),
                new Txn("2026-10-07", "Groceries", -89_900)));

        public List<Txn> forAccount(String account) {
            return data.getOrDefault(account, List.of());
        }
    }

    /** Service layer method that only forwards: no rules, no transaction, no transformation. */
    public static final class StatementService {
        private final StatementQueries queries;
        int passThroughCalls;

        public StatementService(StatementQueries queries) {
            this.queries = queries;
        }

        public List<Txn> statement(String account) {
            passThroughCalls++; // (1)!
            return queries.forAccount(account);
        }
    }

    public static String render(Supplier<List<Txn>> source) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Txn t : source.get()) {
            sb.append(String.format("  %s %-10s %,12.2f%n", t.date(), t.description(), t.paise() / 100.0));
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    private StatementLayers() {
    }
}
  1. A layer that only forwards adds code, tests and indirection with no value. If most requests look like this, the layering is too strict.
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting.StatementLayers.StatementQueries;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting.StatementLayers.StatementService;

public class OpenLayerDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StatementQueries queries = new StatementQueries();
        StatementService service = new StatementService(queries);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: statement report through closed vs. open layers ===");
        System.out.println("Closed layering (presentation -> service -> queries):");
        System.out.print(StatementLayers.render(() -> service.statement("ACC-1")));
        System.out.println("service methods that only forwarded: " + service.passThroughCalls);

        System.out.println("Open query layer (presentation -> queries, read-only):");
        System.out.print(StatementLayers.render(() -> queries.forAccount("ACC-1")));
        System.out.println("Same output, one less layer to maintain for a pure read.");
        System.out.println("Writes (transfers, payments) still go through the service layer and its rules.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: statement report through closed vs. open layers ===
Closed layering (presentation -> service -> queries):
  2026-10-01 Salary        50,000.00
  2026-10-03 Rent         -12,500.00
  2026-10-07 Groceries       -899.00
service methods that only forwarded: 1
Open query layer (presentation -> queries, read-only):
  2026-10-01 Salary        50,000.00
  2026-10-03 Rent         -12,500.00
  2026-10-07 Groceries       -899.00
Same output, one less layer to maintain for a pure read.
Writes (transfers, payments) still go through the service layer and its rules.

Why it matters:

  • Mark Richards' rule of thumb: if more than about 20% of requests are simple pass-throughs, consider opening some layers.
  • Open layers must be explicit and documented, or every shortcut becomes a precedent.
Unit and ArchUnit Tests ArchitectureRulesTest.javaArchitectureExamplesTest.java 
package com.handbook.architecture;

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.domain.JavaClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ClassFileImporter;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses;
import static com.tngtech.archunit.library.Architectures.layeredArchitecture;

/** The architecture of the examples, enforced by ArchUnit on every build. */
class ArchitectureRulesTest {

    private final JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter()
            .withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
            .importPackages("com.handbook.architecture");

    @Test
    void groceryLayersOnlyCallDownwards() {
        layeredArchitecture().consideringOnlyDependenciesInLayers()
                .layer("Web").definedBy("..layered.grocery.web..")
                .layer("Service").definedBy("..layered.grocery.service..")
                .layer("Repository").definedBy("..layered.grocery.repository..")
                .whereLayer("Web").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
                .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Web")
                .whereLayer("Repository").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void hexagonCoreNeverDependsOnAdapters() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.domain..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.port..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void cleanArchitectureDependencyRulePointsInwards() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.entities..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..", "..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void billingModuleDoesNotDependOnOrdering() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.billing..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.ordering..")
                .check(classes);
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture;

import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.entities.Coupon;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.refill.RefillPrescription;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.refill.RefillPrescription.Prescription;
import com.handbook.architecture.eventdriven.dlq.RetryingConsumer;
import com.handbook.architecture.eventdriven.iot.MeterWindowing;
import com.handbook.architecture.eventdriven.iot.MeterWindowing.Reading;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out.InMemoryOrderRepository;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.CheckoutService;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.Order;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in.PlaceOrderUseCase.PlaceOrderCommand;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.rules.LayerRules;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.rules.LayerRules.Dependency;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.cycles.ModuleGraph;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ArchitectureExamplesTest {

    @Test
    void hexagonCoreRunsWithTestAdaptersOnly() {
        List<String> sms = new ArrayList<>();
        var core = new CheckoutService((c, p, r) -> p < 1000, new InMemoryOrderRepository(), (phone, m) -> sms.add(m));
        assertThat(core.placeOrder(new PlaceOrderCommand("C", "P", 500)).status()).isEqualTo(Order.Status.PAID);
        assertThat(core.placeOrder(new PlaceOrderCommand("C", "P", 5000)).status()).isEqualTo(Order.Status.PAYMENT_DECLINED);
        assertThat(sms).hasSize(2);
    }

    @Test
    void couponEntityCapsDiscount() {
        var coupon = new Coupon("X", 50, 0, 10_000, LocalDate.of(2030, 1, 1));
        assertThat(coupon.evaluate(100_000, LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1))).isEqualTo(new Coupon.Discount(10_000));
    }

    @Test
    void controlledSubstancesAlwaysNeedADoctor() {
        var repo = RefillPrescription.inMemory(Map.of("R", new Prescription("R", "P", "D", 5, LocalDate.of(2030, 1, 1), true)));
        assertThat(RefillPrescription.refill(repo, "R", "P", LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1)))
                .isInstanceOf(RefillPrescription.NeedsDoctor.class);
    }

    @Test
    void lateEventsLandInTheirEventTimeWindow() {
        var w = new MeterWindowing(300, 10);
        w.accept(new Reading("M", 10, 2));
        w.accept(new Reading("M", 320, 4));
        w.accept(new Reading("M", 250, 4)); // late
        assertThat(w.advanceWatermark(300)).singleElement().extracting(MeterWindowing.WindowResult::avgKw).isEqualTo(3.0);
    }

    @Test
    void poisonMessageGoesToDlqAndOthersContinue() {
        List<String> handled = new ArrayList<>();
        var consumer = new RetryingConsumer<String>(e -> {
            if (e.equals("bad")) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("x");
            }
            handled.add(e);
        }, 2);
        consumer.consume(List.of("a", "bad", "b"));
        assertThat(handled).containsExactly("a", "b");
        assertThat(consumer.deadLetters()).hasSize(1);
    }

    @Test
    void upwardDependencyIsAViolation() {
        var rules = new LayerRules().layer("w").layer("s");
        assertThat(rules.violations(List.of(new Dependency("s.A", "w.B")))).hasSize(1);
        assertThat(rules.violations(List.of(new Dependency("w.B", "s.A")))).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void cycleIsDetected() {
        assertThat(new ModuleGraph().dependsOn("a", "b").dependsOn("b", "a").findCycle()).isPresent();
        assertThat(new ModuleGraph().dependsOn("a", "b").buildOrder()).containsExactly("b", "a");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Package by layer (controller/, service/, repository/) vs. package by feature (orders/, customers/ with layers inside each). Package by feature scales better and leads naturally to a modular monolith.
  • Enforce layers with ArchUnit (layeredArchitecture(), see the tests above) or Java modules (JPMS).
  • DTO mapping between layers with records and MapStruct; keep JPA entities out of API responses.
  • Evolve towards Hexagonal or Clean when the domain logic grows and you want it independent of persistence.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Layering Spring MVC / Spring Boot @Controller → @Service → @Repository stereotypes Jakarta EE JAX-RS resources → EJB/CDI services → JPA OSI / TCP-IP network stacks Each layer uses only the one below Classic enterprise apps (n-tier) Web tier, application tier, data tier on separate servers

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Simple, universally understood Tends to become database-centric (design starts from tables) Clear separation of technical concerns Changes often cut through all layers (a new field touches every one) Easy to test layers in isolation Sinkhole layers that only forward Good default for CRUD-heavy apps Business logic leaks into controllers or repositories

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Fat controllers

Rules in controllers can't be reused by other channels (Example 2) and are hard to test. Controllers translate; services decide.

Anemic domain with transaction scripts everywhere

Services full of if statements over data-only entities. Fine for simple CRUD; for rich domains, move rules into domain objects (see Clean Architecture).

Leaking persistence types upward

Returning JPA entities from controllers couples your API to your schema and triggers lazy-loading surprises. Map to DTOs.

Upward dependencies

A repository importing a web DTO creates cycles and breaks layering. Catch it automatically (see the coding challenge and ArchUnit).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Layers are technical, not business, boundaries. They tell you how code is organized, not what it does. In large systems, slice by business capability first (modules or services), then layer inside each slice.

Where layered architecture breaks down. When the core logic is complex, the dependency of business on persistence (service → repository implementation) makes the domain hard to test and evolve. Dependency inversion (the service owns a repository interface) is the first step toward Hexagonal/Clean.

Governance. Write the rules down (closed/open layers, allowed dependencies) and enforce them with ArchUnit in CI. Unenforced rules decay within months.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design / architecture round)
docs.text:
"For a CRUD-heavy internal app, I'd use classic layering: REST controllers translate HTTP, services hold use cases and transaction boundaries, repositories handle persistence. I'd package by feature with layers inside, map entities to DTOs at the edge, and enforce layer rules with ArchUnit. Read-only reporting can use an open query layer to avoid pass-through services. If the domain logic grows complex, I'd invert the persistence dependency and move toward hexagonal."

War story: the controller that knew too much

An insurance portal's quote controller contained 1,100 lines of pricing logic. When the company launched a broker API, a developer copied the logic into a second controller. Six months later the two channels quoted different prices for the same customer, because a tax change had only been applied to one copy. A regulator asked why. Fix: pricing moved to a QuoteService used by both controllers; ArchUnit rule "controllers may not contain classes ending in Calculator"; a test comparing both channels' quotes. Lesson: business rules live in the business layer, once.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Layered Hexagonal Clean Modular Monolith Organizes by Technical layer Core vs. adapters Concentric policy levels Business module Domain depends on DB? Usually yes No (ports) No (gateways) Depends on inner style Best for CRUD, simple domains Many integrations, testability Complex domains, long-lived apps Large codebases, many teams

See Hexagonal, Clean, Modular Monolith and the in-process Facade.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Presentation → Business → Persistence; dependencies point down.
  • Controllers translate; services decide (and own transactions); repositories store.
  • Closed vs. open layers; avoid sinkholes.
  • Package by feature; DTOs at the edge; ArchUnit to enforce.
  • Next step for complex domains: invert dependencies (Hexagonal/Clean).

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a CancelOrder use case to Example 1 and decide what each layer does.
  • Add a phone-bot front end to Example 2 that books "tomorrow at 9".
  • Add an ArchUnit rule: classes in ..service.. must not use java.sql directly.

docs.title: Modular Monolith
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Architecture Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

One deployable application, split internally into modules along business capabilities. Each module has a small public API, hides its internals, owns its data, and talks to other modules through APIs or in-process events. You get most of the design benefits of microservices (clear boundaries, team ownership) without the operational cost of distributed systems, and modules can be extracted into services later if needed.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a classic monolith turned into a "big ball of mud": any class calls any other, the billing code reads the catalog's tables, and a change anywhere can break anything. The usual reaction, "let's do microservices", trades that for network failures, distributed transactions and 30 deployment pipelines, often before anyone knows where the right boundaries are.

Definition (Simon Brown; Spring Modulith documentation):

A modular monolith is a monolith that is built with well-defined, loosely coupled modules that align with business domains, enforced so that the modules don't depend on each other's internals.

Rule How it's enforced Modules follow business capabilities Package structure by domain (catalog, ordering, billing) Modules expose a small public API Package-private internals, Java modules (JPMS), Spring Modulith No access to other modules' internals or tables ArchUnit / Spring Modulith verification; schema per module Communication via API calls or events In-process events, ideally transactional Acyclic module dependencies Verified in CI (see the coding challenge)

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A department store vs. a mall

A department store (modular monolith) has separate departments, each with its own staff, stock room and manager, under one roof with one entrance and one checkout system. A mall (microservices) has independent shops with their own doors, tills and opening hours. The department store is cheaper to run; a department can later move out and become its own shop if it grows enough.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph App["One deployable (one JVM)"]
      subgraph Catalog
        CA[CatalogApi] --- CI[internals]
      end
      subgraph Ordering
        OA[OrderingApi] --- OI[internals]
      end
      subgraph Billing
        BI[BillingModule]
      end
      OI -->|API call| CA
      OI -->|OrderPlaced event| BUS((in-process events))
      BUS --> BI
    end
    DB[(One database<br/>schema per module)]
    App --> DB

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// billing code in a big-ball-of-mud monolith
var product = productRepository.findById(sku);          // reaches into catalog internals
var order = em.createQuery("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN Customer c ...");  // joins across domains
orderService.markInvoiced(order);                        // billing mutates ordering's state

docs.title: Example 1: Catalog, Ordering and Billing with Enforced Boundaries (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Each module is a Java package with one public API and package-private internals: code in other packages literally cannot reference CatalogService or ProductTable, because the compiler forbids it. Ordering calls CatalogApi.priceOf() and publishes OrderPlaced; billing reacts to the event and never depends on ordering.

Full Code:

CatalogApi.javaCatalog internals (package-private)Ordering moduleBillingModule.javaShared eventsModularShopDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.catalog;

import java.util.Optional;

/** The catalog module's ONLY public surface. Everything else in this package is package-private. */
public interface CatalogApi {

    Optional<Long> priceOf(String sku);

    static CatalogApi create() { // (1)!
        return new CatalogService(new ProductTable());
    }
}
  1. A factory on the API: the only way for other modules to get a catalog, without seeing its implementation.
package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.catalog;

import java.util.Optional;

/** Package-private: other modules cannot even name this class. */
class CatalogService implements CatalogApi {

    private final ProductTable table;

    CatalogService(ProductTable table) {
        this.table = table;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<Long> priceOf(String sku) {
        return table.find(sku).filter(ProductTable.Row::active).map(ProductTable.Row::pricePaise);
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.catalog;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Package-private: the catalog's own tables (its own schema in the shared database). */
class ProductTable {

    record Row(String sku, long pricePaise, boolean active) {
    }

    private final Map<String, Row> rows = Map.of(
            "MANGO-1KG", new Row("MANGO-1KG", 39_900, true),
            "RICE-5KG", new Row("RICE-5KG", 64_900, true),
            "OLD-SKU", new Row("OLD-SKU", 1_000, false));

    Optional<Row> find(String sku) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(rows.get(sku));
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.ordering;

import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.catalog.CatalogApi;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared.ModuleEvents;

import java.util.Map;

/** The ordering module's public API. It depends on the catalog's API, never on its internals. */
public interface OrderingApi {

    String placeOrder(String customerId, Map<String, Integer> items);

    static OrderingApi create(CatalogApi catalog, ModuleEvents events) {
        return new OrderingService(catalog, events);
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.ordering;

import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.catalog.CatalogApi;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared.ModuleEvents;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared.OrderPlaced;

import java.util.Map;

class OrderingService implements OrderingApi {

    private final CatalogApi catalog;
    private final ModuleEvents events;
    private int nextId = 1;

    OrderingService(CatalogApi catalog, ModuleEvents events) {
        this.catalog = catalog;
        this.events = events;
    }

    @Override
    public String placeOrder(String customerId, Map<String, Integer> items) {
        long total = 0;
        for (var item : items.entrySet()) {
            long price = catalog.priceOf(item.getKey()) // (1)!
                    .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("not for sale: " + item.getKey()));
            total += price * item.getValue();
        }
        String id = "ORD-" + nextId++;
        events.publish(new OrderPlaced(id, customerId, total)); // (2)!
        return id;
    }
}
  1. Ordering depends on catalog's API, never its tables.
  2. Downstream reactions happen via an event, so ordering doesn't know billing exists.
package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.billing;

import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared.ModuleEvents;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared.OrderPlaced;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Billing reacts to OrderPlaced. It doesn't depend on the ordering module at all. */
public final class BillingModule {

    private final List<String> invoices = new ArrayList<>();

    public BillingModule(ModuleEvents events) {
        events.on(OrderPlaced.class, this::invoice); // (1)!
    }

    private void invoice(OrderPlaced e) {
        long gst = e.totalPaise() * 5 / 100;
        invoices.add(String.format("INV-%s %s ₹%.2f + GST ₹%.2f", e.orderId(), e.customerId(),
                e.totalPaise() / 100.0, gst / 100.0));
    }

    public List<String> invoices() {
        return List.copyOf(invoices);
    }
}
  1. Billing subscribes to the published event type; ArchUnit verifies billing never imports ordering.
package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/** In-process event bus shared by modules (Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher in a real app). */
public final class ModuleEvents {

    private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<Object>>> listeners = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <E> void on(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> listener) {
        listeners.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e -> listener.accept((E) e));
    }

    public void publish(Object event) {
        listeners.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of()).forEach(l -> l.accept(event));
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared;

/** A published event: part of the ordering module's public contract. */
public record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String customerId, long totalPaise) {
}

package com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop;

import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.billing.BillingModule;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.catalog.CatalogApi;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.ordering.OrderingApi;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.shop.shared.ModuleEvents;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class ModularShopDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ModuleEvents events = new ModuleEvents();
        CatalogApi catalog = CatalogApi.create();
        OrderingApi ordering = OrderingApi.create(catalog, events);
        BillingModule billing = new BillingModule(events);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: one deployable, three modules with enforced boundaries ===");
        Map<String, Integer> basket = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        basket.put("MANGO-1KG", 2);
        basket.put("RICE-5KG", 1);
        System.out.println("ordering.placeOrder -> " + ordering.placeOrder("CUST-42", basket));
        try {
            ordering.placeOrder("CUST-42", Map.of("OLD-SKU", 1));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("ordering.placeOrder -> rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("billing invoices    -> " + billing.invoices());
        System.out.println("(new CatalogService() from the ordering package would not compile: it is package-private)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: one deployable, three modules with enforced boundaries ===
ordering.placeOrder -> ORD-1
ordering.placeOrder -> rejected: not for sale: OLD-SKU
billing invoices    -> [INV-ORD-1 CUST-42 ₹1447.00 + GST ₹72.35]
(new CatalogService() from the ordering package would not compile: it is package-private)

Why a modular monolith here:

  • Boundaries are enforced by the compiler, not by good intentions.
  • One deployment, one database transaction where needed, simple debugging.
  • Each module could become a service later, because its interactions are already explicit.

docs.title: Example 2: Extraction-Ready Events (HR & Payroll)
docs.text:
Scenario: HR publishes EmployeeHired through an EventPublisher port. In the monolith, the publisher delivers in-process to payroll. When payroll is extracted into its own service (different scaling, compliance and release needs), the same HR module class is wired with an outbox publisher instead. Only wiring changes.

Full Code:

PayrollModules.javaExtractionReadyDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.modular.payroll;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * HR and Payroll modules communicate only through an EventPublisher port. Today it's in-process;
 * when payroll is extracted into its own service, only the publisher implementation changes.
 */
public final class PayrollModules {

    private PayrollModules() {
    }

    public record EmployeeHired(String employeeId, String name, long monthlySalaryPaise) {
    }

    public interface EventPublisher {
        void publish(EmployeeHired event);
    }

    /** Wiring today: a direct in-process call to the subscriber. */
    public static EventPublisher inProcess(Consumer<EmployeeHired> subscriber) {
        return subscriber::accept;
    }

    /** Wiring after extraction: events go to an outbox table and Kafka (here: a list). */
    public static EventPublisher outbox(List<String> outboxTable) {
        return e -> outboxTable.add("topic=hr.employee-hired key=" + e.employeeId() + " payload=" + e);
    }

    /** HR module: hires people and announces it. Unchanged across both wirings. */
    public static final class HrModule {
        private final EventPublisher publisher;

        public HrModule(EventPublisher publisher) {
            this.publisher = publisher;
        }

        public void hire(String id, String name, long monthlySalaryPaise) {
            // ...HR's own records, contracts, onboarding tasks...
            publisher.publish(new EmployeeHired(id, name, monthlySalaryPaise)); // (1)!
        }
    }

    /** Payroll module: keeps its own copy of what it needs. */
    public static final class PayrollModule {
        private final List<String> payees = new ArrayList<>();

        public void on(EmployeeHired e) {
            payees.add(e.employeeId() + " " + String.format("₹%,d/month", e.monthlySalaryPaise() / 100));
        }

        public List<String> payees() {
            return List.copyOf(payees);
        }
    }
}
  1. HR publishes a fact; it doesn't know whether the subscriber is in the same JVM or behind Kafka.
package com.handbook.architecture.modular.payroll;

import com.handbook.architecture.modular.payroll.PayrollModules.HrModule;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.payroll.PayrollModules.PayrollModule;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ExtractionReadyDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== HR & Payroll: modules today, services tomorrow ===");

        PayrollModule payroll = new PayrollModule();
        HrModule hr = new HrModule(PayrollModules.inProcess(payroll::on));
        hr.hire("EMP-101", "Meera Nair", 9_500_000);
        hr.hire("EMP-102", "Arjun Das", 7_200_000);
        System.out.println("Modular monolith, in-process events -> payroll has " + payroll.payees());

        List<String> outbox = new ArrayList<>();
        HrModule extractedHr = new HrModule(PayrollModules.outbox(outbox)); // same HrModule class
        extractedHr.hire("EMP-103", "Sara Khan", 8_100_000);
        System.out.println("After extracting payroll, HR writes to the outbox:");
        outbox.forEach(row -> System.out.println("  " + row));
    }
}

Output:

=== HR & Payroll: modules today, services tomorrow ===
Modular monolith, in-process events -> payroll has [EMP-101 ₹95,000/month, EMP-102 ₹72,000/month]
After extracting payroll, HR writes to the outbox:
  topic=hr.employee-hired key=EMP-103 payload=EmployeeHired[employeeId=EMP-103, name=Sara Khan, monthlySalaryPaise=8100000]

Why design for extraction:

  • You don't have to decide now which modules become services.
  • Event-based integration between modules already looks like integration between services.

docs.title: Example 3: Verifying Module Boundaries in CI (Education platform)
docs.text:
Scenario: An LMS has modules courses, enrollment, certificates and payments, each declaring the modules it may depend on. A verifier (like Spring Modulith's ApplicationModules.verify()) checks dependencies found in the code against the declarations and flags undeclared dependencies and access to internal packages. The build fails until they're fixed.

Full Code:

ModuleVerifier.javaModuleVerifyDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.modular.verify;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * Like Spring Modulith's ApplicationModules.verify(): compares the dependencies a module DECLARES
 * with the ones found in the code (from bytecode analysis), and flags access to another module's
 * internal packages.
 */
public final class ModuleVerifier {

    /** A type reference found in the code: from module + type, to module + package. */
    public record Reference(String fromModule, String fromType, String toModule, String toPackage) {
    }

    private final Map<String, Set<String>> declared;

    public ModuleVerifier(Map<String, Set<String>> declaredDependencies) {
        this.declared = declaredDependencies;
    }

    public List<String> verify(List<Reference> references) {
        List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Reference r : references) {
            if (r.fromModule().equals(r.toModule())) {
                continue;
            }
            if (!declared.getOrDefault(r.fromModule(), Set.of()).contains(r.toModule())) {
                problems.add(r.fromType() + ": undeclared dependency " + r.fromModule() + " -> " + r.toModule());
            } else if (r.toPackage().contains(".internal")) {
                problems.add(r.fromType() + ": uses internal package " + r.toPackage());
            }
        }
        return problems;
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.modular.verify;

import com.handbook.architecture.modular.verify.ModuleVerifier.Reference;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

public class ModuleVerifyDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var verifier = new ModuleVerifier(Map.of(
                "enrollment", Set.of("courses"),
                "certificates", Set.of("enrollment"),
                "payments", Set.of()));

        List<Reference> found = List.of(
                new Reference("enrollment", "EnrollmentService", "courses", "lms.courses"),
                new Reference("certificates", "CertificateIssuer", "enrollment", "lms.enrollment"),
                new Reference("certificates", "CertificatePdf", "courses", "lms.courses"),
                new Reference("enrollment", "SeatChecker", "courses", "lms.courses.internal.jpa"),
                new Reference("payments", "RefundPolicy", "enrollment", "lms.enrollment"));

        System.out.println("=== Education platform: verifying module boundaries in CI ===");
        List<String> problems = verifier.verify(found);
        problems.forEach(p -> System.out.println("FAIL " + p));
        System.out.println(problems.isEmpty() ? "All module boundaries respected" : problems.size() + " violations: build fails");
    }
}

Output:

=== Education platform: verifying module boundaries in CI ===
FAIL CertificatePdf: undeclared dependency certificates -> courses
FAIL SeatChecker: uses internal package lms.courses.internal.jpa
FAIL RefundPolicy: undeclared dependency payments -> enrollment
3 violations: build fails

Why verification matters:

  • Without automated checks, module boundaries erode within months.
  • Declared dependencies double as documentation of the architecture.
Tests (ArchUnit: billing must not depend on ordering) 
package com.handbook.architecture;

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.domain.JavaClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ClassFileImporter;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses;
import static com.tngtech.archunit.library.Architectures.layeredArchitecture;

/** The architecture of the examples, enforced by ArchUnit on every build. */
class ArchitectureRulesTest {

    private final JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter()
            .withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
            .importPackages("com.handbook.architecture");

    @Test
    void groceryLayersOnlyCallDownwards() {
        layeredArchitecture().consideringOnlyDependenciesInLayers()
                .layer("Web").definedBy("..layered.grocery.web..")
                .layer("Service").definedBy("..layered.grocery.service..")
                .layer("Repository").definedBy("..layered.grocery.repository..")
                .whereLayer("Web").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
                .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Web")
                .whereLayer("Repository").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void hexagonCoreNeverDependsOnAdapters() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.domain..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.port..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void cleanArchitectureDependencyRulePointsInwards() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.entities..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..", "..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void billingModuleDoesNotDependOnOrdering() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.billing..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.ordering..")
                .check(classes);
    }
}

docs.text:
// Spring Modulith (reference): each top-level package under the main package is a module
@SpringBootApplication
class ShopApplication { }

@Transactional
public String placeOrder(...) { ...; events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(id, customer, total)); }

Option Notes Package-private + ArchUnit Works everywhere; simplest Spring Modulith Module detection, verification, event publication registry, module integration tests, documentation Java Platform Module System module-info.java with exports; strongest encapsulation, more friction with frameworks Multi-module Maven/Gradle Separate build modules per business module; compile-time boundaries Schema per module Each module owns its tables; no cross-module joins

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Modular monolith Spring Modulith ApplicationModules, @ApplicationModuleListener, @ApplicationModuleTest Shopify's Rails monolith Componentized into domain components with enforced boundaries (Packwerk) JPMS module-info.java exports/requires ArchUnit / jMolecules Rules for slices and cycles (slices().should().beFreeOfCycles())

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Simple operations: one deploy, one runtime, local calls Shared fate: one memory leak or bad deploy affects all modules Clear boundaries, team ownership Scaling is per application, not per module Local transactions where needed One technology stack for all modules Easy refactoring of boundaries before they harden Requires discipline and tooling to keep boundaries Extraction to services is straightforward Build and test times grow with size

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Modules by technical layer

controllers, services, repositories modules aren't business modules. Modules should be capabilities (catalog, ordering), with layers inside.

Shared tables

If billing queries ordering's tables, the modules are coupled through the database, and extraction later becomes a data migration project. One owner per table.

A giant 'common' module

Everything "shared" ends up in common, which everything depends on. Keep shared kernels tiny (IDs, money types, event contracts).

Synchronous chains between modules

A → B → C → D calls inside one request recreate a distributed monolith in-process. Prefer events for reactions.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
"Monolith first." Martin Fowler and others observe that many successful microservice systems started as monoliths whose boundaries were discovered over time. A modular monolith is how you do that deliberately: cheap to change boundaries while you learn the domain.

When to extract a module. Different scaling profile, different release cadence, different team, different compliance needs, or a different technology need. If none apply, keep it in.

Transactional events. Publishing events within the business transaction and handling them after commit, with a persisted publication log (Spring Modulith's event publication registry), gives outbox-like reliability inside the monolith, and makes the later switch to Kafka trivial.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design / architecture round)
docs.text:
"For a new product with one or two teams, I'd start with a modular monolith in Spring Boot: modules per business capability (catalog, ordering, billing, customers), each with a small public API and package-private internals, owning its own schema. Modules integrate through APIs for queries and events for reactions, using Spring Modulith's transactional event publication. CI verifies module boundaries and forbids cycles. When a module needs independent scaling or a separate team, we extract it: its API becomes REST, its events go to Kafka via the outbox."

War story: microservices on day one

A startup split its MVP into 14 microservices before launch, with 4 engineers. Most features changed 3–5 services at once; local development needed 20 containers; a third of the engineering time went into infrastructure. Boundaries turned out to be wrong: "pricing" and "promotions" were constantly called together. What they did: merged into a modular monolith with 6 modules, enforced boundaries with ArchUnit, and later extracted only search (different scaling) and payments (compliance). Lesson: you can't design good service boundaries before you understand the domain. Modules let you learn cheaply.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Modular monolith Big ball of mud Microservices Deployables 1 1 Many Boundaries Enforced modules None Network Transactions Local where needed Anywhere Sagas Operational cost Low Low High Changing boundaries Cheap (refactor) n/a Expensive (migrate data, APIs)

See Decomposition, Strangler Fig, Database per Service and Layered.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One deployable, many business modules with enforced boundaries.
  • Public API + hidden internals + own data per module.
  • APIs for queries, events for reactions; no cycles.
  • Verify in CI (Spring Modulith, ArchUnit).
  • Extract to services only when there's a reason.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a shipping module that reacts to OrderPlaced and exposes a ShippingApi.eta(orderId).
  • Add an ArchUnit rule that the modules under modular.shop are free of cycles (hint: slices().matching(...).should().beFreeOfCycles()).
  • Make ModuleEvents record publications and re-deliver unhandled ones on restart (like Spring Modulith's registry).

docs.title: Behavioral Patterns
docs.text:
Behavioral patterns are about how objects collaborate and share responsibility: who decides, who reacts, and how requests and changes flow through a system.

Pattern Problem it solves Interview frequency Status Chain of Responsibility Pass a request along handlers until one deals with it ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Command Turn a request into an object (queue, undo, log, retry) ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Interpreter Evaluate sentences in a small language (rules, filters) ⭐⭐ ✅ Iterator Traverse a collection without exposing its structure ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Mediator Centralize complex communication between objects ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Memento Capture and restore an object's state (undo, drafts) ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Observer Notify many objects when one changes ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ State Change behavior when internal state changes ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Strategy Swap algorithms at runtime ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Template Method Fixed algorithm skeleton, customizable steps ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Visitor Add operations to a class hierarchy without changing it ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Null Object Replace null checks with a do-nothing object ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Specification Combine business rules with and/or/not ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ 
flowchart TD
    Q{What varies or needs decoupling?} -->|The algorithm| S[Strategy]
    Q -->|Behavior depends on current state| ST[State]
    Q -->|Steps of a fixed process| T[Template Method]
    Q -->|Who handles a request| C[Chain of Responsibility]
    Q -->|Reacting to changes| O[Observer]
    Q -->|A request must be queued, undone or logged| CMD[Command]
    Q -->|Many objects talk to each other| M[Mediator]
    Q -->|Operations over a stable hierarchy| V[Visitor]

docs.title: Chain of Responsibility
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of handlers; each handler either handles it, rejects it, or passes it on. Use it for validation pipelines, approval escalations, middleware/filters and support routing, wherever "who deals with this?" depends on the request.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a checkout must check the delivery area, stock, coupon and payment limits. Writing it as one method with 40 lines of ifs makes it hard to reorder checks, reuse them in other flows (reorders, subscriptions), or add a new one (fraud). The sender shouldn't need to know which check will reject the order, or how many checks there are.

Formal definition (GoF):

Avoid coupling the sender of a request to its receiver by giving more than one object a chance to handle the request. Chain the receiving objects and pass the request along the chain until an object handles it.

Two flavours appear in practice:

Flavour Behavior Example Pure (GoF) Exactly one handler handles the request; the others pass it on Loan approval escalation (Example 2), support routing (challenge) Pipeline / filter chain Every handler gets a turn and may stop the chain Validation (Example 1), servlet filters / middleware (Example 3)

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Customer support escalation

Your question goes to the chatbot first. If it can't help, a level-1 agent. Then a specialist. Then engineering. You don't pick who answers; you just ask, and the request moves along until someone can deal with it.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Handler {
        <<abstract>>
        -Handler next
        +setNext(Handler) Handler
        +handle(request)
    }
    class ConcreteHandlerA {
        +handle(request)
    }
    class ConcreteHandlerB {
        +handle(request)
    }
    class Client
    Handler <|-- ConcreteHandlerA
    Handler <|-- ConcreteHandlerB
    Handler o--> Handler : next
    Client --> Handler : first in chain
Participant Responsibility Handler Interface for handling and a link to the next handler Concrete handler Handles what it's responsible for; otherwise forwards Client Builds the chain (or receives it) and sends requests to its head

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
String validate(Order o) {
    if (!PINCODES.contains(o.pincode())) return "not serviceable";
    if (stock.get(o.sku()) < o.qty()) return "out of stock";
    if (o.coupon() != null && !validCoupon(o)) return "bad coupon";
    if (o.amount() > 5000) return "COD limit";
    // fraud check? loyalty check? Insert somewhere in here and hope nothing breaks...
    return null;
}
  • One big method that changes for every new rule (violates Open/Closed).
  • Checks can't be reused or reordered per flow.
  • Hard to test rules in isolation.

docs.title: Example 1: Checkout Validation Chain (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce app validates every order before payment: is the pincode serviceable, is there enough stock in the nearest dark store, is the coupon valid, is the cash-on-delivery limit respected? Checks are ordered cheapest first (a pincode lookup is cheaper than a stock call). The same validators are reused in different combinations for scheduled orders and subscriptions. The customer must see the first problem in plain language.

Design:

flowchart LR
    O[Order] --> A[ServiceableArea] -->|ok| B[StockAvailable] -->|ok| C[CouponValid] -->|ok| D[CodLimit] -->|ok| P[Proceed to payment]
    A -->|problem| X[Reject with message]
    B -->|problem| X
    C -->|problem| X
    D -->|problem| X

Full Code:

CheckoutValidator.javaValidators.javaOrder.javaCheckoutDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout;

import java.util.Optional;

/** Handler: validates one thing, then passes the order to the next validator. */
public abstract class CheckoutValidator {

    private CheckoutValidator next;

    public CheckoutValidator then(CheckoutValidator next) { // (1)!
        this.next = next;
        return next;
    }

    public final Optional<String> validate(Order order) {
        Optional<String> problem = check(order);
        if (problem.isPresent()) {
            return problem; // (2)!
        }
        return next == null ? Optional.empty() : next.validate(order); // (3)!
    }

    protected abstract Optional<String> check(Order order);
}
  1. then(...) returns the next handler, so chains read left to right: a.then(b).then(c).
  2. Short-circuit: the first problem stops the chain. Later, more expensive checks never run.
  3. No problem here: hand the order to the next validator. The end of the chain means "all good".
package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.Set;

/** Concrete handlers, cheapest checks first. */
public final class Validators {

    private Validators() {
    }

    public static class ServiceableArea extends CheckoutValidator {
        private static final Set<String> PINCODES = Set.of("560034", "560038", "560102");

        protected Optional<String> check(Order o) {
            return PINCODES.contains(o.pincode()) ? Optional.empty()
                    : Optional.of("We don't deliver to " + o.pincode() + " yet");
        }
    }

    public static class StockAvailable extends CheckoutValidator {
        private final Map<String, Integer> stock = Map.of("MILK-1L", 40, "MANGO-1KG", 2);

        protected Optional<String> check(Order o) {
            int available = stock.getOrDefault(o.sku(), 0);
            return o.qty() <= available ? Optional.empty()
                    : Optional.of("Only " + available + " left of " + o.sku());
        }
    }

    public static class CouponValid extends CheckoutValidator {
        protected Optional<String> check(Order o) {
            if (o.coupon() == null) {
                return Optional.empty();
            }
            return o.coupon().equals("FRESH50") && o.amountInr() >= 299 ? Optional.empty()
                    : Optional.of("Coupon " + o.coupon() + " is not valid for this order");
        }
    }

    public static class CodLimit extends CheckoutValidator {
        protected Optional<String> check(Order o) {
            return o.amountInr() <= 5_000 ? Optional.empty()
                    : Optional.of("Cash on delivery is limited to INR 5000");
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout;

public record Order(String id, String pincode, String sku, int qty, String coupon, int amountInr) {
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout;

import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout.Validators.*;

import java.util.List;

public class CheckoutDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Checkout Validation Chain ===");
        CheckoutValidator chain = new ServiceableArea();
        chain.then(new StockAvailable()).then(new CouponValid()).then(new CodLimit());

        List<Order> orders = List.of(
                new Order("O-1", "560034", "MILK-1L", 2, null, 136),
                new Order("O-2", "110001", "MILK-1L", 2, null, 136),
                new Order("O-3", "560038", "MANGO-1KG", 5, null, 900),
                new Order("O-4", "560102", "MILK-1L", 3, "FRESH50", 204),
                new Order("O-5", "560034", "MILK-1L", 30, null, 6_000));

        for (Order o : orders) {
            System.out.println(o.id() + ": " + chain.validate(o).map(p -> "REJECTED - " + p).orElse("OK, proceed to payment"));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Checkout Validation Chain ===
O-1: OK, proceed to payment
O-2: REJECTED - We don't deliver to 110001 yet
O-3: REJECTED - Only 2 left of MANGO-1KG
O-4: REJECTED - Coupon FRESH50 is not valid for this order
O-5: REJECTED - Cash on delivery is limited to INR 5000

Why Chain of Responsibility here:

  • Each rule is one small class; adding a fraud check is one class plus one then(...).
  • Order is configuration: cheapest first, and different flows can build different chains.
  • The checkout screen only knows "the chain", not the rules.

docs.title: Example 2: Loan Approval Escalation (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank's loan workflow routes each application to the lowest authority that can decide it: loan officers up to INR 5 lakh, branch managers up to INR 25 lakh, the credit committee up to INR 2 crore. Each level has its own credit-score threshold. Anything larger goes to the board. Authority limits change with regulation, so they must be easy to adjust.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as Application (INR 1.5 crore)
    participant LO as Loan Officer (≤ 5 lakh)
    participant BM as Branch Manager (≤ 25 lakh)
    participant CC as Credit Committee (≤ 2 crore)
    App->>LO: decide()
    LO->>BM: escalate
    BM->>CC: escalate
    CC-->>App: APPROVED (score 780 ≥ 760)

Full Code:

Approver.javaApprovers.javaLoanDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.loan;

/** Handler: approves within its authority, otherwise escalates. */
public abstract class Approver {

    private final String title;
    private final long limitInr;
    private Approver escalateTo;

    protected Approver(String title, long limitInr) {
        this.title = title;
        this.limitInr = limitInr;
    }

    public Approver escalatesTo(Approver next) {
        this.escalateTo = next;
        return next;
    }

    public String decide(String applicant, long amountInr, int creditScore) {
        if (amountInr <= limitInr) {
            return title + " " + (approve(amountInr, creditScore) ? "APPROVED" : "DECLINED")
                    + " " + applicant + "'s loan of INR " + amountInr;
        }
        if (escalateTo == null) {
            return "No one can approve INR " + amountInr + "; refer to the board";
        }
        System.out.println("  " + title + " -> escalating INR " + amountInr);
        return escalateTo.decide(applicant, amountInr, creditScore);
    }

    protected abstract boolean approve(long amountInr, int creditScore);
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.loan;

public final class Approvers {

    private Approvers() {
    }

    public static class LoanOfficer extends Approver {
        public LoanOfficer() { super("Loan Officer", 500_000); }

        protected boolean approve(long amount, int score) { return score >= 700; }
    }

    public static class BranchManager extends Approver {
        public BranchManager() { super("Branch Manager", 2_500_000); }

        protected boolean approve(long amount, int score) { return score >= 730; }
    }

    public static class CreditCommittee extends Approver {
        public CreditCommittee() { super("Credit Committee", 20_000_000); }

        protected boolean approve(long amount, int score) { return score >= 760; }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.loan;

import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.loan.Approvers.*;

public class LoanDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Loan Approval Escalation ===");
        Approver chain = new LoanOfficer();
        chain.escalatesTo(new BranchManager()).escalatesTo(new CreditCommittee());

        System.out.println(chain.decide("Meena", 300_000, 720));
        System.out.println(chain.decide("Rahul", 1_800_000, 710));
        System.out.println(chain.decide("Acme Foods Pvt Ltd", 15_000_000, 780));
        System.out.println(chain.decide("Mega Infra Ltd", 90_000_000, 800));
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Loan Approval Escalation ===
Loan Officer APPROVED Meena's loan of INR 300000
  Loan Officer -> escalating INR 1800000
Branch Manager DECLINED Rahul's loan of INR 1800000
  Loan Officer -> escalating INR 15000000
  Branch Manager -> escalating INR 15000000
Credit Committee APPROVED Acme Foods Pvt Ltd's loan of INR 15000000
  Loan Officer -> escalating INR 90000000
  Branch Manager -> escalating INR 90000000
No one can approve INR 90000000; refer to the board

Why Chain of Responsibility here:

  • Pure GoF form: exactly one level decides; lower levels escalate.
  • The applicant (client) doesn't know the hierarchy; it just submits.
  • The end of the chain is handled explicitly ("refer to the board"): an unhandled request is a real outcome, not a silent null.

docs.title: Example 3: API Middleware (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: A SaaS invoicing API runs every request through logging, rate limiting (here, 2 requests per IP for the demo) and authentication before the endpoint. Any step can stop the request (401, 429). Logging must see the final status, so it wraps everything. This is how servlet filters, Spring Security's filter chain, Express/Koa middleware and API gateways work.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant L as logging
    participant R as rateLimit
    participant A as auth
    participant E as endpoint
    C->>L: GET /invoices
    L->>R: next.proceed()
    R->>A: next.proceed()
    A->>E: next.proceed()
    E-->>A: 200
    A-->>R: 200
    R-->>L: 200
    L->>L: log status 200
    L-->>C: 200

Full Code:

Middleware.javaApiGatewayDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.middleware;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Functional chain, like servlet filters / Spring WebFilter: each step may stop or continue. */
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Middleware {

    record Request(String path, Map<String, String> headers, String clientIp) {
    }

    record Response(int status, String body) {
    }

    interface Next {
        Response proceed(Request request);
    }

    Response handle(Request request, Next next);

    static Next chain(List<Middleware> middlewares, Next endpoint) { // (1)!
        Next current = endpoint;
        for (int i = middlewares.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            Middleware m = middlewares.get(i);
            Next downstream = current;
            current = req -> m.handle(req, downstream);
        }
        return current;
    }
}
  1. The chain is built back to front: each middleware is wrapped around the "rest of the chain". Calling the result runs them front to back. This is how jakarta.servlet.FilterChain and Spring's WebFilterChain work.
package com.handbook.behavioral.chain.middleware;

import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.middleware.Middleware.Request;
import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.middleware.Middleware.Response;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class ApiGatewayDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS API: Middleware Chain ===");
        Map<String, Integer> requestsPerIp = new HashMap<>();

        Middleware logging = (req, next) -> {
            Response res = next.proceed(req);
            System.out.println("  [log] " + req.path() + " -> " + res.status());
            return res;
        };
        Middleware rateLimit = (req, next) -> {
            int count = requestsPerIp.merge(req.clientIp(), 1, Integer::sum);
            return count > 2 ? new Response(429, "Too Many Requests") : next.proceed(req); // (1)!
        };
        Middleware auth = (req, next) ->
                "Bearer good-token".equals(req.headers().get("Authorization"))
                        ? next.proceed(req) : new Response(401, "Unauthorized");

        var api = Middleware.chain(List.of(logging, rateLimit, auth),
                req -> new Response(200, "{\"invoices\": 3}"));

        Map<String, String> ok = Map.of("Authorization", "Bearer good-token");
        System.out.println(api.proceed(new Request("/invoices", ok, "10.0.0.1")));
        System.out.println(api.proceed(new Request("/invoices", Map.of(), "10.0.0.2")));
        System.out.println(api.proceed(new Request("/invoices", ok, "10.0.0.1")));
        System.out.println(api.proceed(new Request("/invoices", ok, "10.0.0.1")));
    }
}
  1. Returning a response without calling next stops the chain.

Output:

=== SaaS API: Middleware Chain ===
  [log] /invoices -> 200
Response[status=200, body={"invoices": 3}]
  [log] /invoices -> 401
Response[status=401, body=Unauthorized]
  [log] /invoices -> 200
Response[status=200, body={"invoices": 3}]
  [log] /invoices -> 429
Response[status=429, body=Too Many Requests]

Why Chain of Responsibility here:

  • Cross-cutting request handling as independent, ordered steps.
  • Each middleware can act before and after the rest of the chain (logging sees the final status).
  • Lambdas make each step a few lines; order is a List, easy to change per route.
Unit Tests: ChainTest.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.chain;

import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout.CheckoutValidator;
import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout.Order;
import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.checkout.Validators.*;
import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.loan.Approver;
import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.loan.Approvers.*;
import com.handbook.behavioral.chain.middleware.Middleware;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ChainTest {

    @Test
    void firstFailingValidatorWins() {
        CheckoutValidator chain = new ServiceableArea();
        chain.then(new StockAvailable());
        assertThat(chain.validate(new Order("o", "999999", "NOPE", 99, null, 1))).hasValueSatisfying(
                m -> assertThat(m).contains("don't deliver"));
        assertThat(chain.validate(new Order("o", "560034", "MILK-1L", 1, null, 1))).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void loanEscalatesToTheRightLevel() {
        Approver chain = new LoanOfficer();
        chain.escalatesTo(new BranchManager());
        assertThat(chain.decide("a", 100, 800)).startsWith("Loan Officer APPROVED");
        assertThat(chain.decide("a", 1_000_000, 800)).startsWith("Branch Manager APPROVED");
        assertThat(chain.decide("a", 50_000_000, 800)).contains("refer to the board");
    }

    @Test
    void middlewareRunsInOrderAndCanShortCircuit() {
        List<String> trace = new ArrayList<>();
        Middleware a = (r, n) -> { trace.add("a"); return n.proceed(r); };
        Middleware stop = (r, n) -> { trace.add("stop"); return new Middleware.Response(403, "no"); };
        Middleware never = (r, n) -> { trace.add("never"); return n.proceed(r); };
        var res = Middleware.chain(List.of(a, stop, never), r -> new Middleware.Response(200, "ok"))
                .proceed(new Middleware.Request("/", Map.of(), "ip"));
        assertThat(res.status()).isEqualTo(403);
        assertThat(trace).containsExactly("a", "stop");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Linked handlers (next field) Classic GoF (Examples 1, 2) List of handlers + loop/stream Simpler to build and reorder: handlers.stream().map(h -> h.apply(t)).flatMap(Optional::stream).findFirst() (coding challenge) Wrapping chain (next.proceed()) Handlers act before and after (Example 3); also called "interceptor" Spring-assembled chains Inject List<Validator> with @Order on each bean; Spring sorts them Return type Optional<Problem>, a result type, or a sealed Decision (Approved / Rejected / Escalate) for clarity

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Chain Jakarta Servlet Filter + FilterChain.doFilter() Spring Security SecurityFilterChain (around 15 filters: CSRF, authentication, authorization...) Spring MVC HandlerInterceptor (preHandle/postHandle), HandlerExceptionResolver chain Spring WebFlux WebFilter / WebFilterChain Spring Cloud Gateway GatewayFilter chains per route JDK java.util.logging.Logger passes records to parent loggers' handlers OkHttp / Retrofit Interceptor chains Netty ChannelPipeline of ChannelHandlers

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Decouples sender from receivers A request may reach the end unhandled; you must design for that Add, remove or reorder handlers without changing others (OCP) Harder to debug: which handler did what? Each handler is small and testable Long chains add latency Different chains per flow from the same handlers Order dependencies between handlers are implicit and fragile

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Silent fall-through

A chain that ends without anyone handling the request, and returns null, hides bugs. Make the end of the chain explicit: a default handler, an exception, or a clear "unhandled" result.

Order-dependent handlers without documentation

Authentication must run before authorization; rate limiting usually before expensive auth calls. Write the order down and test it (see middlewareRunsInOrderAndCanShortCircuit).

Handlers that mutate the request

If handler 2 changes the order that handler 4 checks, reasoning becomes hard. Prefer immutable requests (records) and explicit enrichment steps.

Cycles in linked chains

a.then(b); b.then(a); loops forever. Build chains in one place, or use a list.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Configurable chains. In enterprise systems (SAP-style workflows, insurance claims), chains are often configured as data: a list of rule IDs per product or country. The code provides handlers; operations choose the chain. Version the configuration and log which chain version decided each request; auditors will ask.

Observability. Emit a span or log per handler (OpenTelemetry), and record which handler stopped a request. "Why was this order rejected?" should be answerable from logs in seconds.

Performance. Order handlers by cost and rejection probability: cheap, frequently failing checks first. Run independent, expensive checks in parallel when you need all results (e.g., collecting all validation errors for a form), rather than as a sequential chain.

Validation: first error vs. all errors. Customer-facing forms want all errors at once; a payment pipeline wants to stop at the first. Same handlers, different traversal: return a list instead of short-circuiting.

War story: the filter that ran too late

A team added an expensive "tenant lookup" filter that called a database on every request, and registered it before the rate limiter. During a bot attack, rejected-but-counted requests still hit the database 50,000 times per second, and the database went down, taking legitimate traffic with it. Fix: moved rate limiting to the edge (API gateway) and to the first position in the app's filter chain; cached tenant lookups; added a test asserting the filter order. Lesson: in a chain, position is policy. Cheap rejections go first.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Chain of Responsibility Decorator Command Observer Who handles? One (pure) or each in turn, and can stop the chain All layers, always forwarding One receiver All subscribers Shape Linear chain Linear wrappers Request object One-to-many Purpose Decide who handles Add behavior Encapsulate a request React to changes

Chain + Composite: in UI frameworks, events bubble up the component tree (child → parent → window), a chain built from parent links.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Pass the request along handlers until one handles it (or one stops it).
  • Pure (one handler decides) vs. pipeline (each may stop): know both.
  • Order is policy: cheap and likely rejections first; auth before authz.
  • Make unhandled requests explicit.
  • Real life: servlet FilterChain, Spring Security filters, interceptors, approval escalation.
chain = new ServiceableArea(); chain.then(new StockAvailable()).then(new CouponValid());
