docs.title: Observer
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🔴 Advanced Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Observer lets many objects subscribe to an object and get notified automatically when something happens to it. It's the basis of event listeners, pub/sub, reactive streams and event-driven microservices. The subject doesn't know who's listening, so you can add reactions without touching it.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: when an order is placed, the system must send an email, reserve inventory, record analytics and add loyalty points, and next month, notify the warehouse too. If OrderService.place() calls all of these directly, it depends on every one of them, a slow analytics call delays checkout, and every new reaction means editing the order code.

Formal definition (GoF):

Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A YouTube channel subscription

You subscribe to a channel. When a new video is published, every subscriber is notified. The creator doesn't call each subscriber; they don't even know who most subscribers are. You can unsubscribe at any time.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Subject {
        -List~Observer~ observers
        +subscribe(Observer)
        +unsubscribe(Observer)
        #notifyObservers(event)
    }
    class Observer {
        <<interface>>
        +update(event)
    }
    class ObserverA
    class ObserverB
    Subject o--> Observer : notifies
    Observer <|.. ObserverA
    Observer <|.. ObserverB
Participant Responsibility Subject (publisher) Keeps a list of observers; notifies them on change Observer (subscriber) Interface with an update/callback method Concrete observers React to notifications (send email, update UI, recalculate)

Push vs. pull: the subject either pushes the data with the notification (onPrice(symbol, price), used here) or just says "I changed" and observers pull what they need. Push is simpler; pull avoids sending data observers don't need.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public String place(Order order) {
    repository.save(order);
    emailService.sendConfirmation(order);       // OrderService knows about email...
    inventoryService.reserve(order);            // ...inventory...
    analyticsClient.track(order);               // ...analytics (slow, sometimes fails)...
    loyaltyService.addPoints(order);            // ...loyalty, and next month the warehouse
    return order.id();
}
  • Tight coupling: the core service depends on every reaction.
  • One failure breaks everything: analytics times out, so checkout fails.
  • Open/Closed violation: every new reaction edits place().

docs.title: Example 1: Price Alerts and Live Portfolio (Trading / Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A stock-trading app streams price ticks. A portfolio widget recalculates the user's holdings on every relevant tick, and users set one-shot price alerts ("tell me when ACME crosses INR 1,900"). Alerts must unsubscribe themselves after firing, during the notification, without crashing the feed.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant F as PriceFeed (subject)
    participant P as PortfolioTracker
    participant A as PriceAlert (ACME >= 1900)
    F->>P: onPrice(ACME, 1902.25)
    P->>P: recalculate value
    F->>A: onPrice(ACME, 1902.25)
    A->>A: notify user
    A->>F: unsubscribe()
    F->>P: onPrice(ACME, 1910.00)
    Note over A: no longer notified

Full Code:

PriceFeed.javaPriceAlert.javaPortfolioTracker.javaTradingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.trading;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Subject: publishes price ticks to whoever subscribed. */
public class PriceFeed {

    @FunctionalInterface
    public interface PriceListener { // (1)!
        void onPrice(String symbol, double price);
    }

    private final List<PriceListener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();

    public Runnable subscribe(PriceListener listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
        return () -> listeners.remove(listener); // (2)!
    }

    public void tick(String symbol, double price) {
        System.out.printf("TICK %s %.2f%n", symbol, price);
        List.copyOf(listeners).forEach(l -> l.onPrice(symbol, price)); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. A functional interface as the observer type, so observers can be lambdas.
  2. subscribe returns an unsubscribe handle. Callers don't need to keep the listener object around to remove it.
  3. Iterate over a copy of the list, so an observer can unsubscribe (or subscribe others) while being notified, without a ConcurrentModificationException.
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.trading;

/** Observer: fires once when a symbol crosses a target, then unsubscribes itself. */
public class PriceAlert implements PriceFeed.PriceListener {

    private final String user;
    private final String symbol;
    private final double target;
    private Runnable unsubscribe;

    public PriceAlert(String user, String symbol, double target) {
        this.user = user;
        this.symbol = symbol;
        this.target = target;
    }

    public void attachTo(PriceFeed feed) {
        unsubscribe = feed.subscribe(this);
    }

    @Override
    public void onPrice(String s, double price) {
        if (s.equals(symbol) && price >= target) {
            System.out.printf("  [alert] %s: %s crossed %.2f (now %.2f)%n", user, symbol, target, price);
            unsubscribe.run(); // one-shot alert
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.trading;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Observer: keeps a running portfolio value. */
public class PortfolioTracker implements PriceFeed.PriceListener {

    private final Map<String, Integer> holdings;
    private final Map<String, Double> lastPrice = new HashMap<>();

    public PortfolioTracker(Map<String, Integer> holdings) {
        this.holdings = holdings;
    }

    @Override
    public void onPrice(String symbol, double price) {
        if (holdings.containsKey(symbol)) {
            lastPrice.put(symbol, price);
            double value = holdings.entrySet().stream()
                    .mapToDouble(e -> e.getValue() * lastPrice.getOrDefault(e.getKey(), 0.0)).sum();
            System.out.printf("  [portfolio] value INR %,.2f%n", value);
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.trading;

import java.util.Map;

public class TradingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Trading App: Price Alerts and Live Portfolio ===");
        PriceFeed feed = new PriceFeed();
        feed.subscribe(new PortfolioTracker(Map.of("ACME", 10, "GLOBEX", 5)));
        new PriceAlert("asha", "ACME", 1_900).attachTo(feed);

        feed.tick("ACME", 1_875.50);
        feed.tick("GLOBEX", 4_120.00);
        feed.tick("ACME", 1_902.25);
        feed.tick("ACME", 1_910.00); // alert already fired and unsubscribed
    }
}

Output:

=== Trading App: Price Alerts and Live Portfolio ===
TICK ACME 1875.50
  [portfolio] value INR 18,755.00
TICK GLOBEX 4120.00
  [portfolio] value INR 39,355.00
TICK ACME 1902.25
  [portfolio] value INR 39,622.50
  [alert] asha: ACME crossed 1900.00 (now 1902.25)
TICK ACME 1910.00
  [portfolio] value INR 39,700.00

Why Observer here:

  • A stream of changes with many independent consumers.
  • Consumers come and go at runtime (alerts are created and removed by users).
  • The feed doesn't know about portfolios or alerts.

docs.title: Example 2: Reacting to OrderPlaced (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: After an order is saved, four teams want to react: email, inventory, analytics and loyalty. The analytics endpoint occasionally times out, and that must never stop the customer from getting their confirmation email or loyalty points. The order service should publish one event and know nothing about who listens.

Design:

flowchart LR
    O[OrderService.place] -->|publish OrderPlaced| E[(OrderEvents)]
    E --> M[Email]
    E --> I[Inventory]
    E --> A[Analytics]
    E --> L[Loyalty]
    A -. failure isolated .-> E

Full Code:

OrderEvents.javaOrderService.javaOrdersDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.orders;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/** In-process event publisher with failure isolation between listeners. */
public class OrderEvents {

    public record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String email, List<String> skus, int amountInr) {
    }

    private final List<Consumer<OrderPlaced>> listeners = new ArrayList<>();

    public void onOrderPlaced(Consumer<OrderPlaced> listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
    }

    public void publish(OrderPlaced event) {
        for (Consumer<OrderPlaced> l : listeners) {
            try {
                l.accept(event);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) { // (1)!
                System.out.println("  [events] listener failed: " + e.getMessage() + " (others continue)");
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. Failure isolation: one observer's exception is caught and logged; the rest still run. Without this, a buggy analytics listener would stop loyalty points from being added.
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.orders;

import java.util.List;

/** The subject's owner: places the order, then announces it. Knows nothing about email or analytics. */
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderEvents events;
    private int next = 1;

    public OrderService(OrderEvents events) {
        this.events = events;
    }

    public String place(String email, List<String> skus, int amountInr) {
        String id = "ORD-" + next++;
        System.out.println("Order " + id + " saved");
        events.publish(new OrderEvents.OrderPlaced(id, email, skus, amountInr)); // (1)!
        return id;
    }
}
  1. The service's only dependency is the event publisher. Adding a warehouse listener needs no change here.
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.orders;

import java.util.List;

public class OrdersDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Reacting to OrderPlaced ===");
        OrderEvents events = new OrderEvents();

        events.onOrderPlaced(e -> System.out.println("  [email] confirmation sent to " + e.email()));
        events.onOrderPlaced(e -> System.out.println("  [inventory] reserved " + e.skus()));
        events.onOrderPlaced(e -> {
            if (e.amountInr() > 50_000) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("analytics endpoint timed out");
            }
            System.out.println("  [analytics] revenue +" + e.amountInr());
        });
        events.onOrderPlaced(e -> System.out.println("  [loyalty] +" + e.amountInr() / 100 + " points"));

        OrderService orders = new OrderService(events);
        orders.place("asha@example.com", List.of("PHONE-CASE"), 499);
        orders.place("kabir@example.com", List.of("LAPTOP-14"), 72_000);
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Reacting to OrderPlaced ===
Order ORD-1 saved
  [email] confirmation sent to asha@example.com
  [inventory] reserved [PHONE-CASE]
  [analytics] revenue +499
  [loyalty] +4 points
Order ORD-2 saved
  [email] confirmation sent to kabir@example.com
  [inventory] reserved [LAPTOP-14]
  [events] listener failed: analytics endpoint timed out (others continue)
  [loyalty] +720 points

Why Observer here:

  • Open/Closed: new reactions are new listeners.
  • Failure isolation protects the core flow.
  • This is exactly Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher + @EventListener, and at system scale, publishing OrderPlaced to Kafka.

docs.title: Example 3: Live Delivery Tracking (Grocery Delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: While a grocery order is on the way, the rider's phone sends location pings. The customer app shows the distance; the ETA service recomputes the arrival time but only notifies on meaningful changes (no flood of "ETA 5 min" messages). When the order is delivered, all observers get a final notification and are detached, so a finished delivery doesn't keep references to them (a classic memory leak).

Design:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Tracking : observers attached
    Tracking --> Tracking : ping(km) / notify all
    Tracking --> Delivered : markDelivered() / notify all
    Delivered --> [*] : observers cleared

Full Code:

DeliveryTracker.javaTrackingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.tracking;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Subject: one per delivery. Observers are the customer app and the ETA service. */
public class DeliveryTracker {

    public interface Observer {
        void locationChanged(String orderId, double kmAway);

        void delivered(String orderId);
    }

    private final String orderId;
    private final List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<>();

    public DeliveryTracker(String orderId) {
        this.orderId = orderId;
    }

    public void attach(Observer o) { observers.add(o); }

    public void ping(double kmAway) {
        observers.forEach(o -> o.locationChanged(orderId, kmAway));
    }

    public void markDelivered() {
        observers.forEach(o -> o.delivered(orderId));
        observers.clear(); // (1)!
    }

    public int observerCount() { return observers.size(); }
}
  1. Detach on completion. Forgotten subscriptions (the "lapsed listener" problem) are the most common Observer memory leak.
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer.tracking;

public class TrackingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery Delivery: Live Tracking ===");
        DeliveryTracker tracker = new DeliveryTracker("GRO-981");

        tracker.attach(new DeliveryTracker.Observer() { // customer app
            public void locationChanged(String id, double km) {
                System.out.printf("  [app] rider is %.1f km away%n", km);
            }
            public void delivered(String id) { System.out.println("  [app] Delivered! Rate your order"); }
        });
        tracker.attach(new DeliveryTracker.Observer() { // ETA service, notifies only on meaningful change
            private int lastEta = -1;
            public void locationChanged(String id, double km) {
                int eta = (int) Math.ceil(km / 0.4); // 24 km/h in city traffic
                if (eta != lastEta) {
                    System.out.println("  [eta] " + id + " ETA " + eta + " min");
                    lastEta = eta;
                }
            }
            public void delivered(String id) { System.out.println("  [eta] closed tracking for " + id); }
        });

        for (double km : new double[] {2.4, 1.9, 1.8, 0.3}) {
            tracker.ping(km);
        }
        tracker.markDelivered();
        System.out.println("observers left: " + tracker.observerCount());
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery Delivery: Live Tracking ===
  [app] rider is 2.4 km away
  [eta] GRO-981 ETA 6 min
  [app] rider is 1.9 km away
  [eta] GRO-981 ETA 5 min
  [app] rider is 1.8 km away
  [app] rider is 0.3 km away
  [eta] GRO-981 ETA 1 min
  [app] Delivered! Rate your order
  [eta] closed tracking for GRO-981
observers left: 0

At 1.8 km the ETA is still 5 minutes, so the ETA observer stays quiet. Observers decide what matters to them.

Why Observer here:

  • One stream of pings, several consumers with different needs.
  • An observer interface with two events (locationChanged, delivered) models a lifecycle.
  • Explicit cleanup at the end of the lifecycle.
Unit Tests: ObserverTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.behavioral.observer;

import com.handbook.behavioral.observer.bus.EventBus;
import com.handbook.behavioral.observer.orders.OrderEvents;
import com.handbook.behavioral.observer.trading.PriceFeed;
import com.handbook.behavioral.observer.tracking.DeliveryTracker;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ObserverTest {

    @Test
    void unsubscribeStopsNotifications() {
        PriceFeed feed = new PriceFeed();
        List<Double> seen = new ArrayList<>();
        Runnable unsubscribe = feed.subscribe((s, p) -> seen.add(p));
        feed.tick("X", 1);
        unsubscribe.run();
        feed.tick("X", 2);
        assertThat(seen).containsExactly(1.0);
    }

    @Test
    void listenerMayUnsubscribeDuringNotification() {
        PriceFeed feed = new PriceFeed();
        Runnable[] holder = new Runnable[1];
        holder[0] = feed.subscribe((s, p) -> holder[0].run());
        feed.tick("X", 1); // no ConcurrentModificationException thanks to List.copyOf
    }

    @Test
    void failingListenerDoesNotBlockOthers() {
        OrderEvents events = new OrderEvents();
        AtomicInteger delivered = new AtomicInteger();
        events.onOrderPlaced(e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); });
        events.onOrderPlaced(e -> delivered.incrementAndGet());
        events.publish(new OrderEvents.OrderPlaced("1", "e", List.of(), 1));
        assertThat(delivered).hasValue(1);
    }

    @Test
    void trackerReleasesObserversAfterDelivery() {
        DeliveryTracker t = new DeliveryTracker("x");
        t.attach(new DeliveryTracker.Observer() {
            public void locationChanged(String id, double km) { }
            public void delivered(String id) { }
        });
        t.markDelivered();
        assertThat(t.observerCount()).isZero();
    }

    record Ping(int n) {
    }

    @Test
    void eventBusIsThreadSafe() {
        EventBus bus = new EventBus();
        AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();
        bus.subscribe(Ping.class, p -> count.incrementAndGet());
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                int n = i;
                ex.submit(() -> bus.publish(new Ping(n)));
            }
        }
        assertThat(count).hasValue(1_000);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Variation Notes Lambdas as observers (Examples 1, 2) Consumer<Event> or a custom functional interface Unsubscribe handles (Runnable, AutoCloseable) Easier and safer than removeListener(this) Typed event bus (coding challenge) Subscribe by event class; Guava EventBus, Spring events Async observers Notify on an executor so slow observers don't block the subject (Spring @Async @EventListener) Reactive streams java.util.concurrent.Flow (Publisher/Subscriber, SubmissionPublisher), Project Reactor, RxJava: Observer + back-pressure + operators Transactional events Spring @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT): notify only if the DB transaction committed

java.util.Observable is deprecated

Observable/Observer in java.util were deprecated in Java 9 (not thread-safe, class instead of interface, no event types). Use your own interfaces, PropertyChangeListener, Spring events, or Flow.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Observer JDK java.beans.PropertyChangeListener; Swing/AWT ActionListener, MouseListener; java.util.concurrent.Flow Spring ApplicationEventPublisher + @EventListener; ApplicationListener; @TransactionalEventListener Spring Boot Lifecycle events (ApplicationReadyEvent) JPA / Hibernate Entity listeners (@PostPersist, @PreUpdate) Reactive Project Reactor Flux/Mono (Spring WebFlux), RxJava Messaging Kafka consumer groups, RabbitMQ fan-out exchanges, AWS SNS: Observer across services Frontend DOM addEventListener, React state subscriptions, WebSockets

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Loose coupling: subject doesn't know concrete observers Hidden control flow: hard to see what happens when an event fires Add reactions without changing the subject (OCP) Ordering of notifications is usually unspecified Runtime subscribe/unsubscribe Memory leaks from forgotten subscriptions Natural fit for UIs, events, streams Cascades: observers triggering events that trigger more observers Synchronous observers can slow the subject; async ones complicate error handling

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Lapsed listener (memory leak)

A screen subscribes to a long-lived service and is never unsubscribed, so the screen (and everything it references) can never be garbage collected. Always unsubscribe (handles, try-with-resources, lifecycle hooks), or use weak references deliberately.

One observer breaks the others

Without try/catch per observer (Example 2), the first exception stops notification of the rest.

Side effects before commit

Sending "order confirmed" emails from an event published inside a DB transaction that later rolls back confirms an order that doesn't exist. Use after-commit events or a transactional outbox.

Concurrent modification

Observers subscribing or unsubscribing during notification. Iterate over a copy, or use CopyOnWriteArrayList.

Event storms and cycles

Observer A updates B, which notifies A... Detect re-entrance, debounce, or redesign the flow.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
In-process vs. distributed observers. In-process events (Spring) are fast but are lost if the process crashes after commit and before listeners run. For reliable reactions across services, use the transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, and a relay publishes it to Kafka. Consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

Choreography. Services reacting to each other's events (Observer at system scale) scale teams well but make end-to-end flows hard to see. Invest in event catalogs, schema registries (Avro/Protobuf with compatibility rules), and distributed tracing across async hops. Know when to switch to orchestration (Mediator).

Back-pressure. If the subject produces faster than observers consume, synchronous observers slow the subject and asynchronous ones build unbounded queues. Reactive streams (Flow, Reactor) make the subscriber request how many items it can handle.

Ordering and consistency. Kafka gives ordering per partition (key by entity ID); consumers see events eventually. Design UIs and APIs for eventual consistency ("Your order is being processed").

War story: the welcome email for users who never existed

A sign-up service published UserRegistered with Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher inside the @Transactional registration method. A synchronous listener sent the welcome email immediately. When a later step (duplicate phone number check) failed, the transaction rolled back, but the email was already sent. Thousands of "Welcome!" emails went to people whose accounts didn't exist, and support tickets piled up. Fix: @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) for in-process reactions, and a transactional outbox for cross-service events. Lesson: "when this changes, notify them" must mean "when this change is committed".

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Observer Mediator Pub/Sub (message broker) Chain of Responsibility Relationship Subject → many observers Colleagues ↔ one mediator Publishers → broker → subscribers Request along a chain Coupling Observers know the subject (to subscribe) Colleagues know the mediator Publishers and subscribers know only the topic Handlers know the next Who reacts All observers Mediator decides All subscribers (per group) One (or until stopped) Scope Usually in-process In-process or orchestrator Across processes In-process

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One-to-many: subject notifies all subscribed observers automatically.
  • Push vs. pull; unsubscribe handles; iterate over a copy when notifying.
  • Isolate failures, beware memory leaks, notify after commit.
  • Spring: @EventListener, @TransactionalEventListener. JDK: Flow. (java.util.Observable is deprecated.)
  • System scale: pub/sub (Kafka) + outbox + idempotent consumers.
Runnable unsubscribe = feed.subscribe((symbol, price) -> ...); unsubscribe.run();

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Make OrderEvents deliver to listeners asynchronously on virtual threads, keeping failure isolation.
  • Add supertype delivery to EventBus (a handler for Object receives everything).
  • Rewrite the price feed with java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher and a Flow.Subscriber that requests 1 item at a time.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Specification wraps a business rule ("is in stock", "credit score ≥ 700") in an object that can be combined with AND, OR and NOT, and reused for filtering, validation and querying. It comes from Domain-Driven Design (Eric Evans and Martin Fowler) and is what Spring Data JPA's Specification is built on.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a product search has many filters (in stock, under a price, brand, rating, COD), and customers combine them freely. Loan eligibility has a list of rules, and regulators require reasons for every rejection. Writing every combination as its own if or SQL query leads to duplicated, inconsistent rules ("in stock" means stock > 0 in search but stock >= 1 AND !blocked in checkout).

Definition (Evans & Fowler, Specifications):

A specification states a constraint on the state of another object. It can be combined with other specifications using logical operators, and used for validation, selection (querying) and creation (building to order).

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A job description's requirements

"3+ years of Java AND (Spring OR Micronaut) AND NOT requires visa sponsorship." Recruiters combine reusable criteria, apply the same criteria to every candidate, and can explain exactly which criterion a candidate didn't meet.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Specification~T~ {
        <<interface>>
        +isSatisfiedBy(T) boolean
        +and(Specification) Specification
        +or(Specification) Specification
        +not() Specification
    }
    class LeafSpec["Leaf rule (inStock, priceAtMost)"]
    class AndSpec
    class OrSpec
    class NotSpec
    Specification <|.. LeafSpec
    Specification <|.. AndSpec
    Specification <|.. OrSpec
    Specification <|.. NotSpec
    AndSpec o--> Specification : left, right
    OrSpec o--> Specification
    NotSpec o--> Specification
Participant Responsibility Specification isSatisfiedBy(candidate) plus combinators Leaf specifications Single named business rules Composite specifications AND / OR / NOT of other specifications (a Composite)

It's a code-built cousin of Interpreter: the same tree of rules, but built with Java method calls instead of parsed from text.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
List<Product> search(Filters f) {
    return products.stream().filter(p ->
            p.stock() > 0
            && (f.maxPrice() == null || p.price() <= f.maxPrice())
            && (f.brand() == null || p.brand().equals(f.brand()) || (f.minRating() != null && p.rating() >= f.minRating()))
            // ...the same rules re-typed in the SQL repository, the recommendations job and checkout
    ).toList();
}
  • Business rules duplicated in lambdas, SQL and services, and they drift.
  • Rules are anonymous: no names, no descriptions, no reasons.
  • Boolean soup that's hard to read and test.

docs.title: Example 1: Search Filters (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: An electronics store's search lets customers tick filters: in stock, maximum price, brand, minimum rating, cash on delivery. Filters combine with AND, and some with OR (brand or high rating). The same named rules (inStock, codAvailable) are reused by checkout and recommendations, so "in stock" means the same thing everywhere. The UI shows a readable description of the active filter.

Design:

flowchart TB
    A1[AND] --> A2[AND]
    A1 --> O[OR]
    A2 --> S1[in stock]
    A2 --> S2["price <= 2000"]
    O --> S3["brand = Pulse"]
    O --> S4["rating >= 4.5"]

Full Code:

Spec.javaProductSpecs.javaCatalogDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.specification.core;

import java.util.function.Predicate;

/** A named, composable business rule. */
public interface Spec<T> {

    boolean isSatisfiedBy(T candidate);

    String describe();

    static <T> Spec<T> of(String description, Predicate<T> rule) { // (1)!
        return new Spec<>() {
            public boolean isSatisfiedBy(T t) { return rule.test(t); }
            public String describe() { return description; }
        };
    }

    default Spec<T> and(Spec<T> other) { // (2)!
        return of("(" + describe() + " AND " + other.describe() + ")",
                t -> isSatisfiedBy(t) && other.isSatisfiedBy(t));
    }

    default Spec<T> or(Spec<T> other) {
        return of("(" + describe() + " OR " + other.describe() + ")",
                t -> isSatisfiedBy(t) || other.isSatisfiedBy(t));
    }

    default Spec<T> not() {
        return of("NOT " + describe(), t -> !isSatisfiedBy(t));
    }
}
  1. A factory turns a named predicate into a specification. The description travels with the rule.
  2. Combinators return new specifications, building a tree with readable descriptions. Specifications are immutable, so they're safe to share and reuse.
package com.handbook.behavioral.specification.catalog;

import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.core.Spec;

/** Reusable, named rules about products, the building blocks of every filter. */
public final class ProductSpecs {

    private ProductSpecs() {
    }

    public record Product(String name, String brand, int priceInr, double rating, int stock, boolean codAllowed) {
    }

    public static Spec<Product> inStock() {
        return Spec.of("in stock", p -> p.stock() > 0);
    }

    public static Spec<Product> priceAtMost(int max) {
        return Spec.of("price <= " + max, p -> p.priceInr() <= max);
    }

    public static Spec<Product> brand(String brand) {
        return Spec.of("brand = " + brand, p -> p.brand().equalsIgnoreCase(brand));
    }

    public static Spec<Product> ratingAtLeast(double r) {
        return Spec.of("rating >= " + r, p -> p.rating() >= r);
    }

    public static Spec<Product> codAvailable() {
        return Spec.of("COD available", Product::codAllowed);
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.specification.catalog;

import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.catalog.ProductSpecs.Product;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.core.Spec;

import java.util.List;

import static com.handbook.behavioral.specification.catalog.ProductSpecs.*;

public class CatalogDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Search Filters as Specifications ===");
        List<Product> catalog = List.of(
                new Product("Zing Buds 141", "Zing", 1_299, 4.1, 120, true),
                new Product("Pulse Buds VS104", "Pulse", 1_499, 4.6, 0, true),
                new Product("Sonix Wave 200", "Sonix", 2_999, 4.4, 35, false),
                new Product("Pulse Buds X Prime", "Pulse", 1_799, 4.5, 18, true),
                new Product("Aura Buds T300", "Aura", 2_299, 4.7, 60, true));

        // Customer ticked: in stock, under 2000, (Pulse OR rated 4.5+). A second shopper wants COD only.
        Spec<Product> filter = inStock().and(priceAtMost(2_000)).and(brand("Pulse").or(ratingAtLeast(4.5)));
        Spec<Product> codShopper = inStock().and(codAvailable()).and(brand("Sonix").not());

        for (Spec<Product> spec : List.of(filter, codShopper)) {
            System.out.println("Filter: " + spec.describe());
            catalog.stream().filter(spec::isSatisfiedBy).forEach(p -> System.out.println("  - " + p.name() + " INR " + p.priceInr()));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Search Filters as Specifications ===
Filter: ((in stock AND price <= 2000) AND (brand = Pulse OR rating >= 4.5))
  - Pulse Buds X Prime INR 1799
Filter: ((in stock AND COD available) AND NOT brand = Sonix)
  - Zing Buds 141 INR 1299
  - Pulse Buds X Prime INR 1799
  - Aura Buds T300 INR 2299

Why Specification here:

  • Named, reusable rules shared across search, checkout and recommendations.
  • Free combination with AND/OR/NOT, built at runtime from the user's choices.
  • Self-describing: the filter explains itself (useful for UI chips, logs and debugging).

docs.title: Example 2: Loan Eligibility with Reasons (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank's personal-loan journey checks age, KYC, credit score, income and existing EMIs (debt-to-income). Regulations and good customer service require telling applicants every reason they're not eligible, not just the first. The credit policy team updates thresholds quarterly. Each rule is a specification with a human-readable reason.

Design:

flowchart LR
    A[Applicant] --> R1{age 21-60}
    A --> R2{KYC done}
    A --> R3{score >= 700}
    A --> R4{"income >= 25k"}
    A --> R5{"EMI < 40% income"}
    R1 & R2 & R3 & R4 & R5 --> D["Result: eligible + list of failed reasons"]

Full Code:

Eligibility.javaLoanDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.specification.loan;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

/** Explainable specifications: every failed rule reports WHY (regulators require reasons). */
public final class Eligibility {

    private Eligibility() {
    }

    public record Applicant(String name, int age, long monthlyIncomeInr, int creditScore, long existingEmiInr, boolean kycDone) {
    }

    public record Rule(String reason, Predicate<Applicant> test) {
    }

    public record Result(boolean eligible, List<String> reasons) {
    }

    public static final List<Rule> PERSONAL_LOAN = List.of(
            new Rule("age must be 21-60", a -> a.age() >= 21 && a.age() <= 60),
            new Rule("KYC must be complete", Applicant::kycDone),
            new Rule("credit score must be at least 700", a -> a.creditScore() >= 700),
            new Rule("monthly income must be at least INR 25,000", a -> a.monthlyIncomeInr() >= 25_000),
            new Rule("existing EMIs must be under 40% of income", a -> a.existingEmiInr() * 100 < a.monthlyIncomeInr() * 40));

    public static Result check(Applicant a, List<Rule> rules) {
        List<String> failed = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Rule r : rules) {
            if (!r.test().test(a)) {
                failed.add(r.reason()); // (1)!
            }
        }
        return new Result(failed.isEmpty(), failed);
    }
}
  1. Explainable evaluation: all rules run and every failure is collected with its reason, instead of a single true/false.
package com.handbook.behavioral.specification.loan;

import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.loan.Eligibility.Applicant;

import java.util.List;

public class LoanDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Personal Loan Eligibility ===");
        List<Applicant> applicants = List.of(
                new Applicant("Meena", 32, 85_000, 752, 12_000, true),
                new Applicant("Rohit", 24, 30_000, 690, 14_000, true),
                new Applicant("Sara", 19, 20_000, 720, 0, false));

        for (Applicant a : applicants) {
            var result = Eligibility.check(a, Eligibility.PERSONAL_LOAN);
            System.out.println(a.name() + ": " + (result.eligible() ? "ELIGIBLE" : "NOT ELIGIBLE"));
            result.reasons().forEach(r -> System.out.println("  - " + r));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Personal Loan Eligibility ===
Meena: ELIGIBLE
Rohit: NOT ELIGIBLE
  - credit score must be at least 700
  - existing EMIs must be under 40% of income
Sara: NOT ELIGIBLE
  - age must be 21-60
  - KYC must be complete
  - monthly income must be at least INR 25,000

Why Specification here:

  • Rules are data-like objects with reasons: easy to review with the credit policy team.
  • Explainability is built in (reasons per rule), which is critical in lending.
  • Product variants (gold loan, two-wheeler loan) reuse rules in different lists.

docs.title: Example 3: Courier Selection (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A shipping aggregator decides which couriers can take each parcel. Requirements come from the shipment: weight within the courier's limit, destination pincode served, hazardous goods need certified couriers, cash on delivery needs couriers who collect cash. The specification is built per shipment and then applied to every courier. If none qualify, the parcel goes to manual booking.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Shipment (18 kg, hazardous, 411001)
    participant B as canCarry(shipment)
    participant C as Couriers
    S->>B: build spec
    B-->>S: weight AND pincode AND hazmat
    S->>C: filter(spec)
    C-->>S: [HeavyHaul]

Full Code:

CourierSelection.javaCourierDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.specification.courier;

import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.core.Spec;

import java.util.Set;

/** Specifications built from the SHIPMENT, applied to each courier. */
public final class CourierSelection {

    private CourierSelection() {
    }

    public record Courier(String name, int maxKg, boolean hazmat, boolean cod, Set<String> pincodes) {
    }

    public record Shipment(double kg, boolean hazardous, boolean cashOnDelivery, String pincode) {
    }

    public static Spec<Courier> canCarry(Shipment s) { // (1)!
        Spec<Courier> spec = Spec.of("max weight >= " + s.kg() + " kg", c -> c.maxKg() >= s.kg());
        spec = spec.and(Spec.of("serves " + s.pincode(), c -> c.pincodes().contains(s.pincode())));
        if (s.hazardous()) {
            spec = spec.and(Spec.of("hazmat certified", Courier::hazmat));
        }
        if (s.cashOnDelivery()) {
            spec = spec.and(Spec.of("collects COD", Courier::cod));
        }
        return spec;
    }
}
  1. Parameterized specifications: the shipment's needs decide which rules are included. Optional constraints (hazmat, COD) are only added when relevant.
package com.handbook.behavioral.specification.courier;

import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.core.Spec;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.courier.CourierSelection.Courier;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.courier.CourierSelection.Shipment;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

public class CourierDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Which Couriers Can Take This Parcel? ===");
        List<Courier> couriers = List.of(
                new Courier("SwiftShip", 10, false, true, Set.of("411001", "560034")),
                new Courier("HeavyHaul", 50, true, false, Set.of("411001", "110001")),
                new Courier("CityDash", 5, false, true, Set.of("560034")));

        List<Shipment> shipments = List.of(
                new Shipment(2.5, false, true, "560034"),
                new Shipment(18, true, false, "411001"),
                new Shipment(7, false, true, "110001"));

        for (Shipment s : shipments) {
            Spec<Courier> spec = CourierSelection.canCarry(s);
            List<String> ok = couriers.stream().filter(spec::isSatisfiedBy).map(Courier::name).toList();
            System.out.println(spec.describe());
            System.out.println("  -> " + (ok.isEmpty() ? "no courier available, flag for manual booking" : ok));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Which Couriers Can Take This Parcel? ===
((max weight >= 2.5 kg AND serves 560034) AND collects COD)
  -> [SwiftShip, CityDash]
((max weight >= 18.0 kg AND serves 411001) AND hazmat certified)
  -> [HeavyHaul]
((max weight >= 7.0 kg AND serves 110001) AND collects COD)
  -> no courier available, flag for manual booking

Why Specification here:

  • Requirements are assembled dynamically from the request.
  • The resulting rule is printable, so ops can see why a courier was excluded.
  • Courier filtering, pricing and SLA checks can share the same rule objects.
Unit Tests: SpecificationTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.behavioral.specification;

import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.catalog.ProductSpecs;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.catalog.ProductSpecs.Product;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.core.Spec;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.courier.CourierSelection;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.loan.Eligibility;
import com.handbook.behavioral.specification.sql.SqlSpec;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class SpecificationTest {

    private final Product p = new Product("x", "Pulse", 1_500, 4.0, 3, true);

    @Test
    void combinatorsAndDescriptions() {
        Spec<Product> s = ProductSpecs.inStock().and(ProductSpecs.brand("pulse").or(ProductSpecs.ratingAtLeast(4.5)));
        assertThat(s.isSatisfiedBy(p)).isTrue();
        assertThat(s.describe()).isEqualTo("(in stock AND (brand = pulse OR rating >= 4.5))");
        assertThat(ProductSpecs.inStock().not().isSatisfiedBy(p)).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void eligibilityListsEveryFailedRule() {
        var a = new Eligibility.Applicant("a", 19, 10_000, 600, 0, false);
        var r = Eligibility.check(a, Eligibility.PERSONAL_LOAN);
        assertThat(r.eligible()).isFalse();
        assertThat(r.reasons()).hasSize(4);
    }

    @Test
    void hazardousShipmentsNeedCertifiedCouriers() {
        var spec = CourierSelection.canCarry(new CourierSelection.Shipment(1, true, false, "1"));
        assertThat(spec.isSatisfiedBy(new CourierSelection.Courier("c", 10, false, true, Set.of("1")))).isFalse();
        assertThat(spec.isSatisfiedBy(new CourierSelection.Courier("c", 10, true, true, Set.of("1")))).isTrue();
    }

    @Test
    void sqlParamsStayInOrder() {
        SqlSpec s = SqlSpec.eq("a", 1).and(SqlSpec.eq("b", 2).or(SqlSpec.eq("c", 3)));
        assertThat(s.where()).isEqualTo("(a = ? AND (b = ? OR c = ?))");
        assertThat(s.params()).containsExactly(1, 2, 3);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Specification JDK Predicate with and/or/negate/not Spring Data JPA org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.Specification + JpaSpecificationExecutor Spring Data (Querydsl) QuerydslPredicateExecutor with BooleanExpression jOOQ Condition objects combined with and()/or() Hibernate Validator Constraint annotations (a declarative, per-field form of specification) Elasticsearch / OpenSearch Bool queries (must, should, must_not)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Named, reusable business rules (DDD ubiquitous language) In-memory filtering doesn't scale to large tables; you need query translation Composable (AND/OR/NOT) at runtime Two implementations (in-memory + SQL) can drift Testable rule by rule Overkill for one or two fixed conditions Self-describing and explainable Deep trees can be slow if leaves are expensive (order cheap rules first)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Filtering huge tables in memory

repository.findAll().stream().filter(spec::isSatisfiedBy) loads every row. For large data, specifications must translate to queries (Spring Data Specification, the coding challenge).

String-concatenated SQL

Building WHERE brand = ' + input + ' invites SQL injection. Always use bind parameters (see the challenge's injection attempt).

Rules that drift between layers

If "in stock" is a Java predicate in one place and SQL in another, they'll diverge. Keep one definition (e.g., JPA specs reused for both), or test both against the same cases.

Unexplainable rejections

A plain boolean result can't tell a customer why. Where people are affected (credit, insurance, hiring), collect reasons.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Specifications in DDD. Specifications express domain concepts ("overdue invoice", "eligible for free delivery") in the ubiquitous language. They live in the domain layer; repositories accept them (invoiceRepository.findAll(overdue())), keeping persistence details out of the domain.

Query translation strategies. (1) Implement each spec twice (in-memory and query) with shared tests; (2) express specs only as queries (JPA Criteria, QueryDSL) and evaluate in memory via an in-memory database in tests; (3) build a small AST (as in Interpreter) and write two visitors, one to evaluate and one to emit SQL.

Performance. Order AND operands by cost and selectivity (cheap, highly selective rules first). In SQL, make sure combined specs hit indexes; OR-heavy specs often defeat indexes, so check query plans.

Explainability and compliance. In lending and insurance, store the rules version and failed reasons with each decision. Regulators may ask "why was this customer rejected on 3 March?" months later.

War story: two definitions of 'eligible'

A bank's loan-offer emails used one eligibility query (in SQL, written by the marketing analytics team), while the application form used Java rules (written by the lending team). The SQL omitted the debt-to-income check. Thousands of customers received "You're pre-approved!" emails and were then rejected when applying, which led to complaints and a regulator inquiry. Fix: one set of eligibility specifications in the domain module, translated to SQL for campaigns and evaluated in memory for applications, with a shared test suite of 200 applicant profiles run against both. Lesson: a business rule should exist once. Specifications give it a home.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Specification Interpreter Strategy Chain of Responsibility Represents A business rule (boolean) A language (parsed) An algorithm A handler Combination AND / OR / NOT trees Grammar trees Usually not combined Sequential chain Built from Code Text Code Code/config Typical use Filtering, validation, querying User-written rules Swappable behavior Pipelines

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Business rule as an object: isSatisfiedBy, combined with AND / OR / NOT.
  • Named, reusable, testable, explainable (collect reasons where people are affected).
  • For big data, translate to queries (Spring Data JPA Specification), always with bind parameters.
  • One definition of each rule; shared tests if it has two implementations.
  • Predicate is the minimal Java version.
productRepository.findAll(inStock().and(priceAtMost(2000)).and(brand("Pulse").or(ratingAtLeast(4.5))));

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Make Spec.and report which side failed, producing a list of failed descriptions.
  • Rewrite ProductSpecs as Spring Data JPA Specifications and run them against H2.
  • Add an "express delivery available" rule to courier selection based on pincode tiers.
