docs.title: State
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

State lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes, by delegating to a state object. It's a clean way to build state machines. Use it for lifecycles (orders, trips, payments, documents), devices (ATMs, vending machines), and anything with "what's allowed depends on where we are".

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: an order can be cancelled when placed or packed, but not once the rider has left. Delivery is only possible when it's out for delivery. Without the pattern, every method becomes if (status == PLACED) ... else if (status == PACKED) ..., repeated in cancel(), dispatch(), deliver(), refunds and notifications. Adding a status ("READY_FOR_PICKUP") means editing every one of those switches.

Formal definition (GoF):

Allow an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object will appear to change its class.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A traffic light

Pressing the pedestrian button means something different on red (do nothing), green (shorten the cycle) and amber (ignore). The light is one device, but its behavior depends entirely on its current state, and each state knows which state comes next.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Context {
        -State state
        +request()
    }
    class State {
        <<interface>>
        +handle(Context) State
    }
    class StateA {
        +handle(Context) State
    }
    class StateB {
        +handle(Context) State
    }
    Context o--> State : current
    State <|.. StateA
    State <|.. StateB
    StateA ..> StateB : transitions to
Participant Responsibility Context Holds the current state; delegates actions to it State Interface with every action the context supports Concrete states Implement what each action means in that state, and which state comes next

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
void cancel() {
    switch (status) {
        case PLACED, PACKED -> { refund(); status = CANCELLED; }
        case OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> throw new IllegalStateException("rider on the way");
        case DELIVERED -> throw new IllegalStateException("already delivered");
        case CANCELLED -> throw new IllegalStateException("already cancelled");
    }
}
void dispatch() { switch (status) { /* the same five cases again */ } }
void deliver()  { switch (status) { /* ...and again */ } }
  • Rules for one state are spread across every method.
  • Adding a state touches every switch.
  • Easy to miss a case, which leaves an illegal transition open.

docs.title: Example 1: Order Lifecycle (Grocery) — classic state objects
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce order moves through PLACED → PACKED → OUT_FOR_DELIVERY → DELIVERED, or to CANCELLED. Cancelling is free before dispatch (with different side effects: refund only, or restock + refund) and not allowed once the rider has left. Delivered and cancelled orders accept no further actions. Support agents need clear messages when an action isn't allowed.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PLACED
    PLACED --> PACKED : pack
    PLACED --> CANCELLED : cancel / refund
    PACKED --> OUT_FOR_DELIVERY : dispatch
    PACKED --> CANCELLED : cancel / restock + refund
    OUT_FOR_DELIVERY --> DELIVERED : deliver (OTP)
    DELIVERED --> [*]
    CANCELLED --> [*]

Full Code:

OrderState.javaStates.javaOrder.javaOrderDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.state.order;

/** State interface: every action the order supports. Each state decides what each action means. */
public interface OrderState {

    default OrderState pack(Order o) { return o.reject("pack", this); } // (1)!

    default OrderState dispatch(Order o) { return o.reject("dispatch", this); }

    default OrderState deliver(Order o) { return o.reject("deliver", this); }

    default OrderState cancel(Order o) { return o.reject("cancel", this); }

    String name();
}
  1. Default methods reject every action. Each state overrides only what's legal in it, so illegal transitions are closed by default, which is the safe choice.
package com.handbook.behavioral.state.order;

/** Concrete states. Each overrides only the actions that are legal in it. */
public final class States {

    private States() {
    }

    public static final class Placed implements OrderState {
        public OrderState pack(Order o) { o.log("picker packed 6 items"); return new Packed(); }
        public OrderState cancel(Order o) { o.log("full refund issued"); return new Cancelled(); }
        public String name() { return "PLACED"; }
    }

    public static final class Packed implements OrderState {
        public OrderState dispatch(Order o) { o.log("rider assigned"); return new OutForDelivery(); }
        public OrderState cancel(Order o) { o.log("items restocked, full refund"); return new Cancelled(); }
        public String name() { return "PACKED"; }
    }

    public static final class OutForDelivery implements OrderState {
        public OrderState deliver(Order o) { o.log("OTP verified at door"); return new Delivered(); }
        public String name() { return "OUT_FOR_DELIVERY"; } // cancel not allowed: rider is on the way
    }

    public static final class Delivered implements OrderState {
        public String name() { return "DELIVERED"; }
    }

    public static final class Cancelled implements OrderState {
        public String name() { return "CANCELLED"; }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.state.order;

/** Context: delegates every action to its current state object. */
public class Order {

    private final String id;
    private OrderState state = new States.Placed();

    public Order(String id) {
        this.id = id;
    }

    public void pack() { state = state.pack(this); }         // (1)!

    public void dispatch() { state = state.dispatch(this); }

    public void deliver() { state = state.deliver(this); }

    public void cancel() { state = state.cancel(this); }

    public String status() { return state.name(); }

    void log(String message) {
        System.out.println("  " + id + " [" + state.name() + "] " + message);
    }

    OrderState reject(String action, OrderState current) {
        System.out.println("  " + id + " [" + current.name() + "] cannot " + action);
        return current; // stay in the same state
    }
}
  1. The context delegates and stores whatever state the current state returns. It contains no switch at all.
package com.handbook.behavioral.state.order;

public class OrderDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Order Lifecycle ===");
        Order happy = new Order("GRO-1");
        happy.pack();
        happy.dispatch();
        happy.cancel();   // too late
        happy.deliver();
        happy.deliver();  // already delivered
        System.out.println("GRO-1 final status: " + happy.status());

        Order changedMind = new Order("GRO-2");
        changedMind.pack();
        changedMind.cancel();
        changedMind.dispatch(); // cancelled orders go nowhere
        System.out.println("GRO-2 final status: " + changedMind.status());
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Order Lifecycle ===
  GRO-1 [PLACED] picker packed 6 items
  GRO-1 [PACKED] rider assigned
  GRO-1 [OUT_FOR_DELIVERY] cannot cancel
  GRO-1 [OUT_FOR_DELIVERY] OTP verified at door
  GRO-1 [DELIVERED] cannot deliver
GRO-1 final status: DELIVERED
  GRO-2 [PLACED] picker packed 6 items
  GRO-2 [PACKED] items restocked, full refund
  GRO-2 [CANCELLED] cannot dispatch
GRO-2 final status: CANCELLED

Why State here:

  • Each state's rules live together in one class (Packed: can dispatch or cancel).
  • New state (READY_FOR_PICKUP) = new class + transitions into it; other states are untouched.
  • Closed by default: forgetting to allow an action is safe, unlike forgetting to forbid one.

docs.title: Example 2: ATM Session (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: An ATM session has clear phases: no card, card inserted (PIN entry, max 3 attempts, then the card is retained), and authenticated (withdrawals in multiples of 100, within balance). The same buttons mean different things in each phase. Security auditors want to see exactly what's possible in each state.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NoCard
    NoCard --> CardInserted : insertCard
    CardInserted --> Authenticated : correct PIN
    CardInserted --> CardInserted : wrong PIN (attempts left)
    CardInserted --> NoCard : 3rd wrong PIN / retain card
    CardInserted --> NoCard : eject
    Authenticated --> Authenticated : withdraw
    Authenticated --> NoCard : eject

Full Code:

Atm.javaAtmDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.state.atm;

/** Context + states for an ATM session. States are inner classes so they can reach the context. */
public class Atm {

    private abstract class State { // inner (non-static) so states can use the ATM's fields
        void insertCard(String card) { say("card already inserted"); }
        void enterPin(String pin) { say("insert a card first"); }
        void withdraw(int amount) { say("enter your PIN first"); }
        void eject() { say("no card to eject"); }
    }

    private final String correctPin = "4321";
    private long balance = 12_000;
    private State state = new NoCard();

    public void insertCard(String card) { state.insertCard(card); }

    public void enterPin(String pin) { state.enterPin(pin); }

    public void withdraw(int amount) { state.withdraw(amount); }

    public void eject() { state.eject(); }

    private void say(String message) {
        System.out.println("  ATM: " + message);
    }

    private final class NoCard extends State {
        @Override
        public void withdraw(int amount) { say("insert a card first"); }

        @Override
        public void insertCard(String card) {
            say("card " + card + " read, enter PIN");
            state = new CardInserted();
        }
    }

    private final class CardInserted extends State {
        private int attemptsLeft = 3; // (1)!

        @Override
        public void enterPin(String pin) {
            if (pin.equals(correctPin)) {
                say("PIN ok");
                state = new Authenticated();
            } else if (--attemptsLeft > 0) {
                say("wrong PIN, " + attemptsLeft + " attempt(s) left");
            } else {
                say("card retained after 3 wrong PINs, please contact your branch");
                state = new NoCard();
            }
        }

        @Override
        public void eject() { say("card returned"); state = new NoCard(); }
    }

    private final class Authenticated extends State {
        @Override
        public void withdraw(int amount) {
            if (amount % 100 != 0) {
                say("amount must be a multiple of 100");
            } else if (amount > balance) {
                say("insufficient balance");
            } else {
                balance -= amount;
                say("dispensed INR " + amount + ", balance INR " + balance);
            }
        }

        @Override
        public void enterPin(String pin) { say("already authenticated"); }

        @Override
        public void eject() { say("card returned, thank you"); state = new NoCard(); }
    }
}
  1. State-specific data lives in the state object: the PIN attempt counter exists only while a card is inserted, and a new card starts with a fresh CardInserted and 3 attempts.
package com.handbook.behavioral.state.atm;

public class AtmDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: ATM Session ===");
        Atm atm = new Atm();
        System.out.println("Customer 1:");
        atm.withdraw(500);
        atm.insertCard("XXXX-1111");
        atm.enterPin("0000");
        atm.enterPin("4321");
        atm.withdraw(2_550);
        atm.withdraw(2_500);
        atm.eject();

        System.out.println("Customer 2 (forgot PIN):");
        atm.insertCard("XXXX-2222");
        atm.enterPin("1111");
        atm.enterPin("2222");
        atm.enterPin("3333");
        atm.withdraw(1_000);
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: ATM Session ===
Customer 1:
  ATM: insert a card first
  ATM: card XXXX-1111 read, enter PIN
  ATM: wrong PIN, 2 attempt(s) left
  ATM: PIN ok
  ATM: amount must be a multiple of 100
  ATM: dispensed INR 2500, balance INR 9500
  ATM: card returned, thank you
Customer 2 (forgot PIN):
  ATM: card XXXX-2222 read, enter PIN
  ATM: wrong PIN, 2 attempt(s) left
  ATM: wrong PIN, 1 attempt(s) left
  ATM: card retained after 3 wrong PINs, please contact your branch
  ATM: insert a card first

Why State here:

  • Behavior is driven entirely by state; the same input means different things.
  • State-local data (PIN attempts) is scoped naturally to its state.
  • Inner classes let states use the context's fields (balance, PIN) without exposing them publicly.

docs.title: Example 3: Trip State Machine (Ride-hailing) — functional style
docs.text:
Scenario: A ride-hailing trip goes from searching to driver assigned, driver arrived, in progress, and completed, or cancelled. Cancellation fees depend on the state (free while searching, INR 25 once a driver is assigned, INR 50 after arrival, INR 75 if the driver waited more than 5 minutes). Mobile apps send events that are sometimes out of order or duplicated, so invalid events must be rejected, not silently applied. The state is persisted and the transition function is used by several services.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Searching
    Searching --> DriverAssigned : Assign
    Searching --> Cancelled : RiderCancels (fee 0)
    DriverAssigned --> DriverArrived : Arrive
    DriverAssigned --> Cancelled : RiderCancels (fee 25)
    DriverArrived --> DriverArrived : Wait(min)
    DriverArrived --> InProgress : Start
    DriverArrived --> Cancelled : RiderCancels (fee 50 / 75)
    InProgress --> Completed : Finish(km)
    Completed --> [*]
    Cancelled --> [*]

Full Code:

Trip.javaTripDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.state.trip;

/**
 * Functional state machine: states and events are immutable sealed types;
 * a pure function computes the next state. Easy to test, persist and replay.
 */
public final class Trip {

    private Trip() {
    }

    public sealed interface State {
        record Searching() implements State { }
        record DriverAssigned(String driver) implements State { }
        record DriverArrived(String driver, int waitedMin) implements State { }
        record InProgress(String driver) implements State { }
        record Completed(String driver, int fareInr) implements State { }
        record Cancelled(String by, int feeInr) implements State { }
    }

    public sealed interface Event {
        record Assign(String driver) implements Event { }
        record Arrive() implements Event { }
        record Wait(int minutes) implements Event { }
        record Start() implements Event { }
        record Finish(int km) implements Event { }
        record RiderCancels() implements Event { }
    }

    public static State next(State state, Event event) { // (1)!
        return switch (state) {
            case State.Searching s -> switch (event) {
                case Event.Assign a -> new State.DriverAssigned(a.driver());
                case Event.RiderCancels c -> new State.Cancelled("rider", 0);
                default -> invalid(state, event);
            };
            case State.DriverAssigned s -> switch (event) {
                case Event.Arrive a -> new State.DriverArrived(s.driver(), 0);
                case Event.RiderCancels c -> new State.Cancelled("rider", 25); // driver already on the way
                default -> invalid(state, event);
            };
            case State.DriverArrived s -> switch (event) {
                case Event.Wait w -> new State.DriverArrived(s.driver(), s.waitedMin() + w.minutes());
                case Event.Start st -> new State.InProgress(s.driver());
                case Event.RiderCancels c -> new State.Cancelled("rider", s.waitedMin() > 5 ? 75 : 50);
                default -> invalid(state, event);
            };
            case State.InProgress s -> switch (event) {
                case Event.Finish f -> new State.Completed(s.driver(), 50 + 14 * f.km());
                default -> invalid(state, event);
            };
            case State.Completed s -> invalid(state, event);
            case State.Cancelled s -> invalid(state, event);
        };
    }

    private static State invalid(State state, Event event) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(event.getClass().getSimpleName() + " not allowed in "
                + state.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}
  1. A pure transition function (state, event) -> new state, using sealed types and nested pattern-matching switches. The compiler checks that every state is handled. States are immutable records, so they're trivial to persist, log and test.
package com.handbook.behavioral.state.trip;

import com.handbook.behavioral.state.trip.Trip.Event;
import com.handbook.behavioral.state.trip.Trip.State;

import java.util.List;

public class TripDemo {

    static State run(String title, List<Event> events) {
        System.out.println(title);
        State s = new State.Searching();
        for (Event e : events) {
            try {
                s = Trip.next(s, e);
                System.out.println("  " + e + " -> " + s);
            } catch (IllegalStateException ex) {
                System.out.println("  " + e + " rejected: " + ex.getMessage());
            }
        }
        return s;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: Trip State Machine ===");
        run("Normal trip:", List.of(new Event.Assign("Ramesh"), new Event.Arrive(), new Event.Start(), new Event.Finish(8)));
        run("Rider cancels after a long wait:", List.of(new Event.Assign("Sunita"), new Event.Arrive(), new Event.Wait(7), new Event.RiderCancels()));
        run("Bug in client app:", List.of(new Event.Start(), new Event.Assign("Imran"), new Event.Finish(3)));
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: Trip State Machine ===
Normal trip:
  Assign[driver=Ramesh] -> DriverAssigned[driver=Ramesh]
  Arrive[] -> DriverArrived[driver=Ramesh, waitedMin=0]
  Start[] -> InProgress[driver=Ramesh]
  Finish[km=8] -> Completed[driver=Ramesh, fareInr=162]
Rider cancels after a long wait:
  Assign[driver=Sunita] -> DriverAssigned[driver=Sunita]
  Arrive[] -> DriverArrived[driver=Sunita, waitedMin=0]
  Wait[minutes=7] -> DriverArrived[driver=Sunita, waitedMin=7]
  RiderCancels[] -> Cancelled[by=rider, feeInr=75]
Bug in client app:
  Start[] rejected: Start not allowed in Searching
  Assign[driver=Imran] -> DriverAssigned[driver=Imran]
  Finish[km=3] rejected: Finish not allowed in DriverAssigned

Why a functional state machine here:

  • Immutable states + a pure function means no hidden mutation: easy to test, replay and use in several services.
  • State carries data (driver, minutes waited, fare), so fees are computed from the state itself.
  • Invalid events from buggy clients are rejected loudly.
Unit Tests: StateTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.behavioral.state;

import com.handbook.behavioral.state.approval.DocumentStatus;
import com.handbook.behavioral.state.order.Order;
import com.handbook.behavioral.state.trip.Trip;
import com.handbook.behavioral.state.trip.Trip.Event;
import com.handbook.behavioral.state.trip.Trip.State;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class StateTest {

    @Test
    void orderCannotBeCancelledOnceDispatched() {
        Order o = new Order("X");
        o.pack();
        o.dispatch();
        o.cancel();
        assertThat(o.status()).isEqualTo("OUT_FOR_DELIVERY");
    }

    @Test
    void cancellationFeeDependsOnState() {
        State assigned = Trip.next(new State.Searching(), new Event.Assign("d"));
        assertThat(Trip.next(assigned, new Event.RiderCancels())).isEqualTo(new State.Cancelled("rider", 25));
        State waited = Trip.next(Trip.next(assigned, new Event.Arrive()), new Event.Wait(6));
        assertThat(Trip.next(waited, new Event.RiderCancels())).isEqualTo(new State.Cancelled("rider", 75));
    }

    @Test
    void finishedTripsRejectEvents() {
        State done = new State.Completed("d", 100);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Trip.next(done, new Event.Arrive())).isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void enumWorkflow() {
        assertThat(DocumentStatus.DRAFT.submit().approve().publish()).isEqualTo(DocumentStatus.PUBLISHED);
        assertThatThrownBy(DocumentStatus.DRAFT::publish).hasMessage("Cannot publish: document is DRAFT");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Style When State objects (Example 1) Each state has rich behavior; classic GoF Inner-class states (Example 2) States need the context's private data Sealed types + pure transition function (Example 3) Immutable, persisted, event-driven state (event sourcing, workflows) Enum with per-constant methods (coding challenge) Simple workflows with few actions and no state-specific data Transition table (Map<State, Map<Event, State>>) Large, data-driven state machines, possibly configured outside code Libraries Spring Statemachine, Squirrel; workflow engines (Temporal, Camunda) for long-running, persisted processes

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where State machine JDK Thread.State (NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, ...); java.util.concurrent.FutureTask states JDK Iterator implementations (states like "before first", "after last") Spring Statemachine Declarative states, events, guards and actions Spring Batch Job and step statuses (BatchStatus) TCP Connection states (LISTEN, SYN_SENT, ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT) Payments Payment intent lifecycles (requires_payment_method → processing → succeeded), as in Stripe-like APIs Kubernetes Pod phases (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Each state's behavior in one place (SRP) More classes than a switch for small machines New states without editing others (OCP) Transitions are spread across states; the full picture needs a diagram Illegal transitions are explicit (closed by default) Shared data between states needs care (context fields vs. state fields) Removes large conditional blocks Overkill for 2–3 states with trivial behavior

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Transitions without persistence discipline

In a database, two requests can read PACKED and both apply different transitions. Use optimistic locking (@Version) or a conditional update (UPDATE ... SET status='CANCELLED' WHERE id=? AND status='PACKED').

Silently ignoring invalid events

Returning "OK" for "deliver" on a cancelled order hides client bugs and corrupts reports. Reject loudly and log.

Boolean flags instead of states

isPaid, isShipped, isCancelled, isRefunded give 16 combinations, most of them nonsense ("cancelled and delivered"). One explicit state field makes impossible states impossible.

Side effects inside transition functions

Sending SMS from inside next(state, event) makes replays send it again. Compute the new state purely, then run side effects based on the transition (or emit events).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Persisted state machines. In real systems the state lives in a database row or an event log. Apply transitions atomically with concurrency control, record transition history (who, when, from, to, why) for audit and support, and publish events on transition (via outbox) so other services react.

Idempotency. Mobile and webhook clients retry. Treat "event already applied" as success (same target state), and reject truly invalid transitions. Include event IDs.

Long-running workflows. When states span days (loan approval, KYC, returns), add timeouts (escalate after 48 h) and compensation (refund after cancellation). This is where workflow engines (Temporal, Camunda) or sagas come in; they're state machines with durable timers.

Diagrams as documentation. Generate the state diagram from code or configuration (Spring Statemachine can export it) so docs never drift from behavior.

War story: the refund that happened twice

An e-commerce order service used flags and an if chain. "Cancel" checked !isShipped and issued a refund. The mobile app double-sent "Cancel" when the network hiccuped, and both requests passed the check before either saved. Two refunds per order, about 1,100 times on a sale day. Fix: an explicit status column with a State-pattern transition function, a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status IN ('PLACED','PACKED') (only one request wins), and idempotency keys on the cancel API. Lesson: a state machine is only as correct as the way its transitions are persisted.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
State Strategy Command Memento Object represents Current condition that changes itself An interchangeable algorithm A request A snapshot Who switches it States themselves (transitions) The client chooses N/A N/A Knows other variants? Yes: states know their successors No: strategies are independent No No

"State vs. Strategy" is a top interview question: same structure (context delegates to an interface), different intent. In State, the object changes itself based on events; in Strategy, the client picks a behavior.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Behavior depends on state; the context delegates to the current state object.
  • States implement only legal actions and return the next state (closed by default).
  • Styles: state objects, inner classes, sealed records + pure function, enums.
  • Persist with atomic transitions, history and idempotency.
  • State vs. Strategy: self-switching vs. client-chosen.
public void cancel() { state = state.cancel(this); }   // no switch in the context

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a READY_FOR_PICKUP state (for store pickup orders) to Example 1.
  • Add a daily withdrawal limit to the ATM's Authenticated state.
  • Write a test that checks every (state, event) pair of the trip machine against a table.
  • Persist Order state with a conditional SQL update (H2 in a test).

Observer Next: Strategy

docs.title: Strategy
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Strategy puts each variant of an algorithm behind a common interface, so the algorithm can be chosen and swapped at runtime. Use it whenever "how we calculate or decide this" varies: fees, pricing, matching, routing, sorting, validation, compression. In modern Java a strategy is often just a lambda.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: delivery fees depend on the customer: standard customers pay INR 30 below INR 199, express costs INR 49 (plus INR 10 beyond 3 km), pass members pay nothing, and late-night orders carry a surcharge. Writing all of this as one growing if/else inside checkout makes checkout change every time pricing changes, and the rules can't be tested or reused on their own.

Formal definition (GoF):

Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Getting to the airport

You can take a cab, the metro, or drive. Each is a different strategy for the same goal. You pick one based on time, budget and luggage, and you can switch at the last minute. The goal ("be at the airport by 6") doesn't change.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Context {
        -Strategy strategy
        +setStrategy(Strategy)
        +doWork()
    }
    class Strategy {
        <<interface>>
        +execute(data)
    }
    class StrategyA
    class StrategyB
    class StrategyC
    Context o--> Strategy
    Strategy <|.. StrategyA
    Strategy <|.. StrategyB
    Strategy <|.. StrategyC
Participant Responsibility Strategy Common interface for the algorithm Concrete strategies Different implementations (independent of each other) Context Uses a strategy; doesn't know which one Client / selector Chooses the strategy (from config, user, context)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
int deliveryFee(Customer c, int total, double km, int hour) {
    if (c.hasPass()) return 0;
    else if (c.wantsExpress()) return 49 + (km > 3 ? 10 : 0);
    else if (hour >= 23 || hour < 5) return (total >= 199 ? 0 : 30) + 25;
    else return total >= 199 ? 0 : 30;
    // Next sprint: rain surcharge, festival waiver, B2B pricing...
}
  • One method that changes for every pricing idea (violates Open/Closed).
  • Rules tangled with selection logic; hard to test each rule alone.
  • Can't switch behavior per city or A/B test without more ifs.

docs.title: Example 1: Delivery Fee Strategies (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery app has four delivery-fee rules: standard (free above INR 199), express (INR 49, +INR 10 beyond 3 km), member pass (always free) and late night (standard + INR 25). Pricing experiments add new rules monthly. Selection ("which rule applies to this customer right now?") is separate from the rules themselves.

Design:

flowchart LR
    C[Customer + time] --> S{chooseFor}
    S -->|pass| P[MEMBER_PASS]
    S -->|express| E[EXPRESS]
    S -->|23:00-05:00| N[LATE_NIGHT]
    S -->|otherwise| ST[STANDARD]
    P --> F["feeInr(total, km)"]
    E --> F
    N --> F
    ST --> F

Full Code:

DeliveryFeeStrategy.javaCheckout.javaDeliveryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.delivery;

/** Strategy: one way of computing a delivery fee. */
@FunctionalInterface
public interface DeliveryFeeStrategy {

    int feeInr(int cartTotalInr, double distanceKm);

    DeliveryFeeStrategy STANDARD = (total, km) -> total >= 199 ? 0 : 30; // (1)!
    DeliveryFeeStrategy EXPRESS = (total, km) -> 49 + (km > 3 ? 10 : 0);
    DeliveryFeeStrategy MEMBER_PASS = (total, km) -> 0;
    DeliveryFeeStrategy LATE_NIGHT = (total, km) -> STANDARD.feeInr(total, km) + 25;
}
  1. Strategies as lambdas on a functional interface. LATE_NIGHT even reuses STANDARD, so strategies compose.
package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.delivery;

/** Context: uses whichever strategy it is given. No if/else on customer type. */
public class Checkout {

    public record Customer(String name, boolean hasPass, boolean wantsExpress) {
    }

    public static DeliveryFeeStrategy chooseFor(Customer c, int hour) { // (1)!
        if (c.hasPass()) {
            return DeliveryFeeStrategy.MEMBER_PASS;
        }
        if (c.wantsExpress()) {
            return DeliveryFeeStrategy.EXPRESS;
        }
        return hour >= 23 || hour < 5 ? DeliveryFeeStrategy.LATE_NIGHT : DeliveryFeeStrategy.STANDARD;
    }

    public String total(Customer c, int cartTotal, double km, int hour) {
        DeliveryFeeStrategy strategy = chooseFor(c, hour);
        int fee = strategy.feeInr(cartTotal, km);
        return "%-6s cart INR %4d, %.1f km, %02d:00 -> fee INR %2d, pay INR %d"
                .formatted(c.name(), cartTotal, km, hour, fee, cartTotal + fee);
    }
}
  1. Selection is separate from the algorithms. The ifs that remain only choose; they don't calculate. In production this is often config- or experiment-driven.
package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.delivery;

import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.delivery.Checkout.Customer;

public class DeliveryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Delivery Fee Strategies ===");
        Checkout checkout = new Checkout();
        System.out.println(checkout.total(new Customer("Asha", false, false), 150, 2.0, 18));
        System.out.println(checkout.total(new Customer("Asha", false, false), 450, 2.0, 18));
        System.out.println(checkout.total(new Customer("Ravi", false, true), 450, 4.5, 18));
        System.out.println(checkout.total(new Customer("Meera", true, true), 90, 6.0, 18));
        System.out.println(checkout.total(new Customer("Kabir", false, false), 150, 1.0, 23));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Delivery Fee Strategies ===
Asha   cart INR  150, 2.0 km, 18:00 -> fee INR 30, pay INR 180
Asha   cart INR  450, 2.0 km, 18:00 -> fee INR  0, pay INR 450
Ravi   cart INR  450, 4.5 km, 18:00 -> fee INR 59, pay INR 509
Meera  cart INR   90, 6.0 km, 18:00 -> fee INR  0, pay INR 90
Kabir  cart INR  150, 1.0 km, 23:00 -> fee INR 55, pay INR 205

Why Strategy here:

  • A family of interchangeable calculations with the same inputs and output.
  • New pricing ideas are new strategies; checkout doesn't change.
  • Each rule is a one-line, independently testable function.

docs.title: Example 2: Driver Matching Policies (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: A ride-hailing company matches riders with drivers. The default is nearest driver; premium rides use best-rated within 2 km; in some cities regulators require fairness (the driver idle longest within 3 km gets the trip). Operations switch the policy per city and run experiments without deploying code. Same drivers, different decisions.

Design:

classDiagram
    class MatchingStrategy {
        <<interface>>
        +pick(List~Driver~) Optional~Driver~
        +name() String
    }
    class Nearest
    class BestRatedWithin {
        maxKm
    }
    class Fairness {
        maxKm
    }
    MatchingStrategy <|.. Nearest
    MatchingStrategy <|.. BestRatedWithin
    MatchingStrategy <|.. Fairness

Full Code:

MatchingStrategy.javaMatchingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.matching;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Strategy: how to pick a driver for a rider. Ops can switch it per city. */
public interface MatchingStrategy {

    record Driver(String name, double kmAway, double rating, int idleMinutes) {
    }

    Optional<Driver> pick(List<Driver> available);

    String name();

    static MatchingStrategy nearest() {
        return new MatchingStrategy() {
            public Optional<Driver> pick(List<Driver> d) { return d.stream().min(Comparator.comparingDouble(Driver::kmAway)); }
            public String name() { return "nearest"; }
        };
    }

    static MatchingStrategy bestRatedWithin(double maxKm) {
        return new MatchingStrategy() {
            public Optional<Driver> pick(List<Driver> d) {
                return d.stream().filter(x -> x.kmAway() <= maxKm).max(Comparator.comparingDouble(Driver::rating));
            }
            public String name() { return "best-rated within " + maxKm + " km"; }
        };
    }

    static MatchingStrategy fairness(double maxKm) {
        return new MatchingStrategy() {
            public Optional<Driver> pick(List<Driver> d) {
                return d.stream().filter(x -> x.kmAway() <= maxKm).max(Comparator.comparingInt(Driver::idleMinutes));
            }
            public String name() { return "longest-idle within " + maxKm + " km"; }
        };
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.matching;

import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.matching.MatchingStrategy.Driver;

import java.util.List;

public class MatchingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: Same Drivers, Different Matching Policies ===");
        List<Driver> available = List.of(
                new Driver("Ramesh", 0.6, 4.2, 3),
                new Driver("Sunita", 1.4, 4.9, 12),
                new Driver("Imran", 2.8, 4.7, 35));

        for (MatchingStrategy s : List.of(MatchingStrategy.nearest(),
                MatchingStrategy.bestRatedWithin(2.0), MatchingStrategy.fairness(3.0))) {
            System.out.printf("%-28s -> %s%n", s.name(), s.pick(available).map(Driver::name).orElse("no driver"));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: Same Drivers, Different Matching Policies ===
nearest                      -> Ramesh
best-rated within 2.0 km     -> Sunita
longest-idle within 3.0 km   -> Imran

Why Strategy here:

  • Policy is a business decision that changes per city and over time.
  • Strategies can be parameterized (max distance) through static factory methods.
  • Easy A/B testing: route 10% of requests to a new strategy and compare metrics.

docs.title: Example 3: Smart Gateway Routing (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payments platform can send each card payment through several gateways. The cheapest isn't always best: a failed payment costs a lost sale and a retry. The router supports lowest fee, highest success rate, and lowest expected cost (fee + failure rate × a penalty). During a bank outage, one gateway's success rate drops, and the expected-cost strategy moves traffic away automatically, using live metrics.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant P as Payment
    participant R as GatewayRouter
    participant S as Strategy (LOWEST_EXPECTED_COST)
    P->>R: route(gateways with live success rates)
    R->>S: score each gateway
    S-->>R: PayFast 2.50, SecurePay 2.25, ValueGate 2.10
    R-->>P: ValueGate
    Note over R: ValueGate success drops to 0.80
    R->>S: score again
    S-->>R: ValueGate 3.80 -> SecurePay wins

Full Code:

GatewayRouter.javaRoutingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.routing;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.ToDoubleFunction;

/** Context that routes each payment to a gateway using a pluggable scoring strategy. */
public class GatewayRouter {

    public record Gateway(String name, double feePercent, double successRate) {
    }

    /** Strategy as a function: lower score wins. */
    public enum Strategy {
        LOWEST_FEE(g -> g.feePercent()),
        HIGHEST_SUCCESS(g -> -g.successRate()),
        LOWEST_EXPECTED_COST(g -> g.feePercent() + (1 - g.successRate()) * 10); // (1)!

        private final ToDoubleFunction<Gateway> score;

        Strategy(ToDoubleFunction<Gateway> score) {
            this.score = score;
        }
    }

    private Strategy strategy;

    public GatewayRouter(Strategy strategy) {
        this.strategy = strategy;
    }

    public void setStrategy(Strategy strategy) { // (2)!
        this.strategy = strategy;
    }

    public Gateway route(List<Gateway> gateways) {
        return gateways.stream().min(Comparator.comparingDouble(strategy.score)).orElseThrow();
    }
}
  1. An enum of strategies, each holding a scoring function: a compact way to offer a fixed menu of algorithms that can be stored in config by name.
  2. The strategy can be swapped at runtime (by ops tooling or a feature flag).
package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.routing;

import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.routing.GatewayRouter.Gateway;
import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.routing.GatewayRouter.Strategy;

import java.util.List;

public class RoutingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Smart Gateway Routing ===");
        List<Gateway> gateways = List.of(
                new Gateway("PayFast", 1.6, 0.91),
                new Gateway("SecurePay", 2.1, 0.985),
                new Gateway("ValueGate", 1.8, 0.97));

        GatewayRouter router = new GatewayRouter(Strategy.LOWEST_FEE);
        for (Strategy s : Strategy.values()) {
            router.setStrategy(s);
            System.out.printf("%-20s -> %s%n", s, router.route(gateways).name());
        }

        System.out.println("ValueGate success rate drops to 0.80 during a bank outage:");
        List<Gateway> degraded = List.of(gateways.get(0), gateways.get(1), new Gateway("ValueGate", 1.8, 0.80));
        router.setStrategy(Strategy.LOWEST_EXPECTED_COST);
        System.out.printf("%-20s -> %s%n", Strategy.LOWEST_EXPECTED_COST, router.route(degraded).name());
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Smart Gateway Routing ===
LOWEST_FEE           -> PayFast
HIGHEST_SUCCESS      -> SecurePay
LOWEST_EXPECTED_COST -> ValueGate
ValueGate success rate drops to 0.80 during a bank outage:
LOWEST_EXPECTED_COST -> SecurePay

Why Strategy here:

  • Routing goals (cost, reliability, a mix) are business trade-offs that change.
  • The router stays the same; only the scoring changes.
  • The expected-cost strategy reacts to live data without code changes.
Unit Tests: StrategyTest.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.strategy;

import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.delivery.Checkout;
import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.delivery.DeliveryFeeStrategy;
import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.matching.MatchingStrategy;
import com.handbook.behavioral.strategy.routing.GatewayRouter;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class StrategyTest {

    @Test
    void eachFeeStrategyInIsolation() {
        assertThat(DeliveryFeeStrategy.STANDARD.feeInr(198, 1)).isEqualTo(30);
        assertThat(DeliveryFeeStrategy.STANDARD.feeInr(199, 1)).isZero();
        assertThat(DeliveryFeeStrategy.EXPRESS.feeInr(100, 3.5)).isEqualTo(59);
        assertThat(DeliveryFeeStrategy.LATE_NIGHT.feeInr(100, 1)).isEqualTo(55);
    }

    @Test
    void passHoldersAlwaysGetFreeDelivery() {
        var c = new Checkout.Customer("x", true, true);
        assertThat(Checkout.chooseFor(c, 2)).isSameAs(DeliveryFeeStrategy.MEMBER_PASS);
    }

    @Test
    void matchingReturnsEmptyWhenNoDriverQualifies() {
        var far = List.of(new MatchingStrategy.Driver("a", 9, 5, 1));
        assertThat(MatchingStrategy.bestRatedWithin(2).pick(far)).isEmpty();
        assertThat(MatchingStrategy.nearest().pick(far)).isPresent();
    }

    @Test
    void expectedCostAvoidsUnreliableCheapGateway() {
        var gws = List.of(new GatewayRouter.Gateway("cheap", 1.0, 0.5), new GatewayRouter.Gateway("solid", 2.0, 0.99));
        assertThat(new GatewayRouter(GatewayRouter.Strategy.LOWEST_FEE).route(gws).name()).isEqualTo("cheap");
        assertThat(new GatewayRouter(GatewayRouter.Strategy.LOWEST_EXPECTED_COST).route(gws).name()).isEqualTo("solid");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Form Example Lambda / functional interface DeliveryFeeStrategy (Example 1), Comparator, Predicate, Function Classes / anonymous classes When strategies have state, several methods, or names (Example 2) Enum of strategies Fixed menu, storable by name in config (Example 3) Map of strategies Map<String, Strategy> picked by a request parameter (coding challenge) Spring beans Each strategy is a @Component; inject Map<String, Strategy> or List<Strategy> and select at runtime Composed strategies comparing(...).thenComparing(...), predicate.and(...), LATE_NIGHT reusing STANDARD

java.util.Comparator is the most-used strategy in Java: list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Product::price)).

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Strategy JDK Comparator (for sort, TreeMap); RejectedExecutionHandler (thread-pool rejection policies); ThreadFactory JDK java.util.zip.Deflater levels; javax.crypto.Cipher algorithms (chosen by name) Spring PasswordEncoder (BCrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2); ResourceLoader; TaskExecutor; CacheManager Spring Security AuthenticationProviders; AccessDecisionVoters Spring Retry / Resilience4j BackOffPolicy (fixed, exponential); RetryPolicy Hibernate Dialect (SQL generation per database); ID generation strategies Jackson PropertyNamingStrategy (snake_case, camelCase)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Swap algorithms at runtime Clients (or a selector) must know which strategy to choose Open/Closed: new strategies without touching the context More objects/classes (lambdas reduce this) Each algorithm isolated and testable Strategies must share an interface even if some need less data Removes conditional logic from the context Overkill when there are only two stable variants

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Selection logic leaking back into the context

If the context still has if (strategy instanceof Express), you've gained nothing. All variant-specific behavior belongs in the strategy.

Strategies with hidden dependencies

A strategy that secretly calls a database or remote service makes the context's performance unpredictable. Pass data in, or make dependencies explicit.

Fat strategy interfaces

If each strategy implements 8 methods and most are no-ops, the abstraction is wrong. Split the interface or rethink it.

Stateful strategies shared between threads

Strategies are often shared singletons; keep them stateless or thread-safe.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Strategies + configuration + experiments. In production, the "client" choosing a strategy is often a feature-flag or experiment platform: strategy = flags.variant("matching", city). Log which strategy made each decision so you can compare outcomes (conversion, ETA, cost) across variants.

Policy engines. When strategies become data (pricing tables, routing weights), consider making parameters configurable (a parameterized strategy) rather than adding a class per variant. When rules become complex combinations, look at Specification or Interpreter.

Safety. Strategies that change money or matching need guardrails: limits (max fee), shadow mode (compute the new strategy's decision without using it), gradual rollout and fast rollback.

Performance. Strategy calls are interface calls the JIT handles well. With many strategies at one call site (megamorphic), hot loops can slow down slightly; rarely a concern outside of ultra-low-latency code.

War story: the cheapest gateway that cost the most

A merchant platform routed all card payments to the gateway with the lowest fee (a hard-coded min(fee)). One evening that gateway's issuing-bank connection degraded, and success rates fell from 95% to 60%. The router kept sending everything there because it was cheapest. Lost sales that evening were roughly 40× the fee savings of the whole month. Fix: routing became a Strategy; the default switched to expected cost using success rates from the last 5 minutes; a circuit breaker removed gateways below 80% success; every routing decision was logged with the strategy name. Lesson: make policies swappable, and make the default strategy reflect the real objective, not a proxy for it.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Strategy State Template Method Command Varies Whole algorithm Behavior per current state Steps of a fixed algorithm The request itself Chosen by Client States (self-transition) Subclass at compile time Client creates it Mechanism Composition Composition Inheritance Object as data Strategies know each other? No Yes (successor states) N/A No

Strategy vs. Template Method: composition (swap at runtime) vs. inheritance (fixed per subclass). Modern Java prefers Strategy with lambdas.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface; swap at runtime.
  • Context uses a strategy; a selector/config/DI chooses it.
  • Modern Java: lambdas, Comparator, enums of strategies, Map<String, Strategy>.
  • vs State: client-chosen vs. self-switching. vs Template Method: composition vs. inheritance.
  • Production: flags, shadow mode, decision logs.
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Product::rating).reversed().thenComparing(Product::reviews));
