docs.text:
• Add a RAIN_SURGE delivery strategy that adds INR 20 to whatever the base strategy returns (hint: wrap another strategy).
  • Make MatchingStrategy.nearest() break distance ties by rating.
  • Wire the gateway strategies as Spring beans and choose by a property.

State Next: Template Method

docs.title: Template Method
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class (a final method) and lets subclasses fill in specific steps. Use it when several variants share the same overall process and only some steps differ, and the order of steps must not be changed by subclasses.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: every data import does the same thing: read lines, parse, validate, reject bad rows, load good rows, report. CSV customers and fixed-width bank files differ only in parsing and validation. Copy-pasting the whole loop into each importer means the next fix (say, counting rejections) must be applied to every copy, and someone will forget one.

Formal definition (GoF):

Define the skeleton of an algorithm in an operation, deferring some steps to subclasses. Template Method lets subclasses redefine certain steps of an algorithm without changing the algorithm's structure.

Kinds of steps:

Step type Meaning Example Abstract Subclasses must implement parse(), validate() Hook Has a default; subclasses may override skipFirstLine() (default false), onRejected() Fixed (private/final) Subclasses can't change it load(), the order of steps

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Following a recipe card

"Making tea" is always: boil water, add the tea, steep, pour, add extras. Masala chai and green tea follow the same steps but differ in what you add and how long you steep. You don't reinvent the process each time; you fill in the blanks.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class AbstractClass {
        +templateMethod()$ final
        #step1()* abstract
        #step2()* abstract
        #hook() default
    }
    class ConcreteClassA {
        #step1()
        #step2()
    }
    class ConcreteClassB {
        #step1()
        #step2()
        #hook()
    }
    AbstractClass <|-- ConcreteClassA
    AbstractClass <|-- ConcreteClassB
Participant Responsibility Abstract class Defines the final template method (the order of steps) and shared steps Concrete classes Implement the abstract steps and optionally override hooks

The Hollywood Principle: "Don't call us, we'll call you." The base class calls subclass methods, not the other way around.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
class CsvImporter {
    String run(List<String> lines) {
        for (String line : lines.subList(1, lines.size())) { /* parse CSV, validate, load */ }
        return "...";
    }
}
class BankFileImporter {
    String run(List<String> lines) {
        for (String line : lines) { /* parse fixed width, validate, load */ }   // copied loop
        return "...";                                                         // forgot to count rejections
    }
}
  • Duplicated workflow that drifts between copies.
  • Nothing enforces the order of steps (validate before load).
  • Cross-cutting fixes must be repeated everywhere.

docs.title: Example 1: Nightly Data Imports (ERP)
docs.text:
Scenario: An ERP imports customers from a CRM (CSV with a header row) and transactions from banks (fixed-width files, the format banks have used for decades). Every import must parse, validate, reject bad rows, load good rows and report counts, in that order. Bank-file rejections go to a reconciliation queue instead of just being logged.

Design:

flowchart TB
    R["run(lines) — final"] --> H{"skipFirstLine()?<br/>hook"}
    H --> P["parse(line)<br/>abstract"]
    P --> V["validate(record)<br/>abstract"]
    V -->|problem| X["onRejected()<br/>hook"]
    V -->|ok| A[accepted]
    A --> L["load()<br/>fixed"]
    L --> S[summary]

Full Code:

DataImporter.javaCsvCustomerImporter.javaFixedWidthBankImporter.javaImportDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.template.importer;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Template: the import workflow is fixed; formats fill in the steps. */
public abstract class DataImporter {

    public final String run(List<String> lines) { // (1)!
        List<Map<String, String>> accepted = new ArrayList<>();
        int rejected = 0;
        List<String> data = skipFirstLine() ? lines.subList(1, lines.size()) : lines; // (2)!
        for (String line : data) {
            Map<String, String> record = parse(line);           // abstract step
            Optional<String> problem = validate(record);        // abstract step
            if (problem.isPresent()) {
                rejected++;
                onRejected(line, problem.get());                // hook with default behavior
            } else {
                accepted.add(record);
            }
        }
        load(accepted);                                          // shared step
        return "%s: %d loaded, %d rejected".formatted(name(), accepted.size(), rejected);
    }

    protected abstract String name();

    protected abstract Map<String, String> parse(String line);

    protected abstract Optional<String> validate(Map<String, String> record);

    protected boolean skipFirstLine() { // (3)!
        return false;
    }

    protected void onRejected(String line, String problem) {
        System.out.println("  rejected [" + line.strip() + "]: " + problem);
    }

    private void load(List<Map<String, String>> records) {
        records.forEach(r -> System.out.println("  load " + r));
    }
}
  1. final: subclasses can't change the order or skip validation. This is what makes it a template.
  2. A hook decides whether to skip the header; the template stays generic.
  3. Hooks have sensible defaults, so most subclasses don't override them.
package com.handbook.behavioral.template.importer;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Customers exported from a CRM as CSV with a header row. */
public class CsvCustomerImporter extends DataImporter {

    protected String name() { return "CRM customers (CSV)"; }

    @Override
    protected boolean skipFirstLine() { return true; } // header row

    protected Map<String, String> parse(String line) {
        String[] f = line.split(",", -1);
        Map<String, String> r = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        r.put("id", f[0]);
        r.put("name", f[1]);
        r.put("email", f[2]);
        return r;
    }

    protected Optional<String> validate(Map<String, String> r) {
        return r.get("email").contains("@") ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of("invalid email");
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.template.importer;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Bank statement file: fixed-width columns (account 10, date 8, amount 12, type 2). */
public class FixedWidthBankImporter extends DataImporter {

    protected String name() { return "Bank statement (fixed-width)"; }

    protected Map<String, String> parse(String line) {
        Map<String, String> r = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        r.put("account", line.substring(0, 10).strip());
        r.put("date", line.substring(10, 18));
        r.put("amountPaise", line.substring(18, 30).strip());
        r.put("type", line.substring(30, 32));
        return r;
    }

    protected Optional<String> validate(Map<String, String> r) {
        if (!r.get("type").equals("CR") && !r.get("type").equals("DR")) {
            return Optional.of("unknown type " + r.get("type"));
        }
        return r.get("amountPaise").matches("\\d+") ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of("bad amount");
    }

    @Override
    protected void onRejected(String line, String problem) { // bank files: rejections go to reconciliation
        System.out.println("  -> sent to reconciliation queue: " + problem);
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.template.importer;

import java.util.List;

public class ImportDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== ERP: Nightly Data Imports ===");
        System.out.println(new CsvCustomerImporter().run(List.of(
                "id,name,email",
                "C1,Asha Rao,asha@example.com",
                "C2,Ravi K,ravi-at-example.com",
                "C3,Li Wei,li@example.com")));

        System.out.println(new FixedWidthBankImporter().run(List.of(
                "SB0000100120261013000004500000CR",
                "SB0000100120261013000000129900DR",
                "SB0000100120261013000000050000XX")));
    }
}

Output:

=== ERP: Nightly Data Imports ===
  rejected [C2,Ravi K,ravi-at-example.com]: invalid email
  load {id=C1, name=Asha Rao, email=asha@example.com}
  load {id=C3, name=Li Wei, email=li@example.com}
CRM customers (CSV): 2 loaded, 1 rejected
  -> sent to reconciliation queue: unknown type XX
  load {account=SB00001001, date=20261013, amountPaise=000004500000, type=CR}
  load {account=SB00001001, date=20261013, amountPaise=000000129900, type=DR}
Bank statement (fixed-width): 2 loaded, 1 rejected

Why Template Method here:

  • Same process, different formats: subclasses supply only what differs.
  • The order is enforced (final), so no importer can load unvalidated data.
  • Shared improvements (rejection counts) happen once.

docs.title: Example 2: Payment Flows (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment platform supports cards and UPI. Compliance requires every payment to go through validate → (strong authentication if needed) → authorize → capture → notify, in that order. Cards need 3-D Secure above INR 5,000 and have separate authorize/capture steps (the bank places a hold, then captures). UPI authorizes and settles in one step. New methods (wallets, BNPL) must follow the same compliant sequence.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T as PaymentFlow.process (final)
    participant C as CardFlow
    T->>T: validate (fixed)
    T->>C: requiresStrongAuth(18000)? (hook)
    C-->>T: true
    T->>C: stepUp() (hook): 3-D Secure
    T->>C: authorize() (abstract): hold
    T->>C: capture() (abstract)
    T->>T: notifyCustomer (fixed)

Full Code:

PaymentFlow.javaFlows.javaPaymentDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.template.payment;

/** Template for every payment method: the order of steps is a compliance requirement. */
public abstract class PaymentFlow {

    public final String process(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        validate(orderId, amountInr);
        if (requiresStrongAuth(amountInr)) {        // hook
            stepUp(orderId);
        }
        String auth = authorize(orderId, amountInr); // abstract
        String capture = capture(auth, amountInr);   // abstract
        notifyCustomer(orderId, capture);            // fixed
        return capture;
    }

    private void validate(String orderId, int amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        }
        System.out.println("  [" + method() + "] validated " + orderId + " INR " + amount);
    }

    protected boolean requiresStrongAuth(int amountInr) { return false; }

    protected void stepUp(String orderId) { }

    protected abstract String method();

    protected abstract String authorize(String orderId, int amountInr);

    protected abstract String capture(String authorization, int amountInr);

    private void notifyCustomer(String orderId, String reference) {
        System.out.println("  [" + method() + "] receipt for " + orderId + ": " + reference);
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.template.payment;

public final class Flows {

    private Flows() {
    }

    public static class CardFlow extends PaymentFlow {
        protected String method() { return "card"; }

        @Override
        protected boolean requiresStrongAuth(int amount) { return amount > 5_000; } // step-up authentication for large amounts

        @Override
        protected void stepUp(String orderId) { System.out.println("  [card] 3-D Secure OTP verified"); }

        protected String authorize(String orderId, int amount) {
            System.out.println("  [card] authorization hold INR " + amount);
            return "AUTH-" + orderId;
        }

        protected String capture(String auth, int amount) {
            System.out.println("  [card] captured hold " + auth);
            return "CAP-" + auth;
        }
    }

    public static class UpiFlow extends PaymentFlow {
        protected String method() { return "upi"; }

        protected String authorize(String orderId, int amount) {
            System.out.println("  [upi] collect request approved in UPI app");
            return "UPI-" + orderId;
        }

        protected String capture(String auth, int amount) {
            return auth + "-SETTLED"; // UPI debits immediately; nothing extra to capture
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.template.payment;

import com.handbook.behavioral.template.payment.Flows.CardFlow;
import com.handbook.behavioral.template.payment.Flows.UpiFlow;

public class PaymentDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Same Steps, Different Methods ===");
        System.out.println("Card, INR 1,200:");
        new CardFlow().process("ORD-1", 1_200);
        System.out.println("Card, INR 18,000:");
        new CardFlow().process("ORD-2", 18_000);
        System.out.println("UPI, INR 18,000:");
        new UpiFlow().process("ORD-3", 18_000);
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Same Steps, Different Methods ===
Card, INR 1,200:
  [card] validated ORD-1 INR 1200
  [card] authorization hold INR 1200
  [card] captured hold AUTH-ORD-1
  [card] receipt for ORD-1: CAP-AUTH-ORD-1
Card, INR 18,000:
  [card] validated ORD-2 INR 18000
  [card] 3-D Secure OTP verified
  [card] authorization hold INR 18000
  [card] captured hold AUTH-ORD-2
  [card] receipt for ORD-2: CAP-AUTH-ORD-2
UPI, INR 18,000:
  [upi] validated ORD-3 INR 18000
  [upi] collect request approved in UPI app
  [upi] receipt for ORD-3: UPI-ORD-3-SETTLED

Why Template Method here:

  • The sequence is a compliance rule: encode it once and make it final.
  • Hooks express optional steps (strong authentication) without if (method == CARD) in the base class.
  • New payment methods inherit validation and notifications automatically.

docs.title: Example 3: Patient Admission (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital admits patients through a standard process: register, triage, insurance pre-authorization, bed assignment, billing. Emergency admissions skip pre-authorization and defer the deposit ("treat first, paperwork later"), with ICU beds. Planned admissions (surgery) require pre-authorization and a deposit. The process must be identical in structure for audit purposes.

Design:

flowchart LR
    A["admit() — final"] --> R[register]
    R --> T["triage()<br/>abstract"]
    T --> I{"needsInsurancePreAuth()<br/>hook"}
    I -->|yes| PA[request pre-auth]
    I -->|no| B
    PA --> B["assignBed()<br/>abstract"]
    B --> D["billing + depositInr()<br/>hook"]

Full Code:

Admission.javaAdmissions.javaAdmissionDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.template.admission;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Template for admitting a patient. Emergency and planned admissions differ in a few steps. */
public abstract class Admission {

    protected final List<String> steps = new ArrayList<>();

    public final List<String> admit(String patient) {
        steps.clear();
        register(patient);
        triage(patient);
        if (needsInsurancePreAuth()) { // hook
            steps.add("insurance pre-authorization requested");
        }
        steps.add("bed assigned: " + assignBed());
        steps.add("billing account opened" + (depositInr() > 0 ? ", deposit INR " + depositInr() : ", deposit deferred"));
        return List.copyOf(steps);
    }

    private void register(String patient) {
        steps.add("registered " + patient);
    }

    protected abstract void triage(String patient);

    protected abstract String assignBed();

    protected boolean needsInsurancePreAuth() { return true; }

    protected int depositInr() { return 20_000; }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.template.admission;

public final class Admissions {

    private Admissions() {
    }

    public static class Emergency extends Admission {
        protected void triage(String p) { steps.add("triage level 1 (critical), doctor paged"); }
        protected String assignBed() { return "ICU-04"; }
        @Override protected boolean needsInsurancePreAuth() { return false; } // treat first, paperwork later
        @Override protected int depositInr() { return 0; }
    }

    public static class Planned extends Admission {
        protected void triage(String p) { steps.add("pre-op checklist verified"); }
        protected String assignBed() { return "WARD-2B-17"; }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.template.admission;

public class AdmissionDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital: Patient Admission ===");
        System.out.println("Emergency (road accident):");
        new Admissions.Emergency().admit("P-7781").forEach(s -> System.out.println("  - " + s));
        System.out.println("Planned (knee surgery):");
        new Admissions.Planned().admit("P-1204").forEach(s -> System.out.println("  - " + s));
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital: Patient Admission ===
Emergency (road accident):
  - registered P-7781
  - triage level 1 (critical), doctor paged
  - bed assigned: ICU-04
  - billing account opened, deposit deferred
Planned (knee surgery):
  - registered P-1204
  - pre-op checklist verified
  - insurance pre-authorization requested
  - bed assigned: WARD-2B-17
  - billing account opened, deposit INR 20000

Why Template Method here:

  • One auditable process with controlled variation points.
  • Hooks (needsInsurancePreAuth, depositInr) express policy differences clearly.
  • Variants are small classes that read like policy documents.
Unit Tests: TemplateMethodTest.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.template;

import com.handbook.behavioral.template.admission.Admissions;
import com.handbook.behavioral.template.importer.CsvCustomerImporter;
import com.handbook.behavioral.template.payment.Flows;
import com.handbook.behavioral.template.payment.PaymentFlow;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class TemplateMethodTest {

    @Test
    void importerSkipsHeaderAndCountsRejections() {
        String result = new CsvCustomerImporter().run(List.of("h", "1,a,a@x", "2,b,bad"));
        assertThat(result).endsWith("1 loaded, 1 rejected");
    }

    @Test
    void templateValidatesForEveryMethod() {
        PaymentFlow upi = new Flows.UpiFlow();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> upi.process("O", 0)).hasMessageContaining("positive");
    }

    @Test
    void cardUsesStrongAuthOnlyAboveThreshold() {
        assertThat(new Flows.CardFlow().process("O", 100)).isEqualTo("CAP-AUTH-O");
    }

    @Test
    void emergencySkipsPreAuthAndDeposit() {
        List<String> steps = new Admissions.Emergency().admit("P");
        assertThat(steps).noneMatch(s -> s.contains("pre-authorization"));
        assertThat(steps).anyMatch(s -> s.contains("deposit deferred"));
        assertThat(new Admissions.Planned().admit("P")).anyMatch(s -> s.contains("pre-authorization"));
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Template Method with lambdas (composition instead of inheritance). You can pass the varying steps as functions instead of subclassing:

static String importLines(List<String> lines,
                          Function<String, Map<String, String>> parse,
                          Function<Map<String, String>, Optional<String>> validate) {
    // same skeleton; steps passed in
}

This is how Spring's JdbcTemplate works: the template handles connections, statements, exceptions and cleanup; you pass a RowMapper (a step) as a lambda.

Style Pros Cons Inheritance (classic) Hooks with defaults; clear named variants Tied to a class hierarchy; Java has single inheritance Callbacks/lambdas ("template + strategy") Flexible, no subclassing, easy to test Many parameters if there are many steps

Always make the template method final, and make steps protected (or package-private), not public, so clients call only the template.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Template JDK AbstractList (implement get and size, inherit the rest); AbstractMap; InputStream.read(byte[]) calls abstract read() JDK HttpServlet.service() calls doGet/doPost Spring JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, TransactionTemplate, JmsTemplate (callback style) Spring AbstractController, OncePerRequestFilter.doFilterInternal, AbstractRoutingDataSource.determineCurrentLookupKey Spring Batch AbstractItemCountingItemStreamItemReader JUnit Test lifecycle: @BeforeEach → test → @AfterEach (the framework is the template)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Removes duplication of the overall process Inheritance coupling: subclasses depend on base-class details Enforces order and invariants (final) Hard to understand when steps are spread across a deep hierarchy Hooks give controlled extension points Liskov risks: a subclass's step can break assumptions of the template Hollywood Principle keeps control in one place Single inheritance limits combining templates

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Non-final template methods

If subclasses can override run(), they can skip validation. Make it final.

Calling overridable methods from a constructor

The subclass isn't initialized yet when the base constructor runs. Call template steps from methods, never from constructors.

Deep hierarchies

AbstractImporter → AbstractCsvImporter → AbstractCustomerCsvImporter → ... becomes impossible to follow. Prefer one level of template plus composition (strategies) for further variation.

Too many hooks

15 optional hooks turn the template into a configuration maze. If variants differ a lot, use Strategy or separate classes.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Frameworks are templates. Spring, servlets and JUnit run the overall flow and call your code at defined points (inversion of control). When you design internal platforms (job frameworks, importers, payment SDKs), Template Method with few, well-documented hooks is a strong way to enforce company-wide rules (audit logging, metrics, security checks) while letting teams plug in business logic.

Favor "template + callbacks" in libraries. JdbcTemplate is the gold standard: it guarantees resource cleanup and exception translation, and you pass small lambdas. It avoids inheritance and works naturally with dependency injection and testing.

Observability and resilience in the template. Put metrics, tracing spans, retries and error handling in the template, not in each subclass, so every variant gets them (see the coding challenge: locking and cleanup for every job).

War story: the importer that loaded unvalidated rows

A team copied the CSV importer to create a supplier importer, and "temporarily" commented out validation to get a demo working. It shipped. Weeks later, 30,000 supplier records with malformed GST numbers were loaded, and tax filings failed at quarter-end. Fix: a base DataImporter with a final run() that always validates (with a validation step subclasses must implement), plus metrics on rejected rows per importer. Lesson: when a step is mandatory, don't rely on discipline. Put it in a final template.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Template Method Strategy Factory Method Hook-based frameworks Varies Steps of an algorithm The whole algorithm Which object to create Callbacks at lifecycle points Mechanism Inheritance Composition Inheritance (GoF) Inversion of control Bound when Compile time (subclass) Runtime Compile time Registration time

A Factory Method is often one step of a Template Method (see the logistics example on the Factory Method page).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Skeleton in a final base method; subclasses fill in steps.
  • Abstract steps (must), hooks (may), fixed steps (can't).
  • Hollywood Principle: the base class calls you.
  • Real life: HttpServlet, AbstractList, Spring JdbcTemplate (callback style).
  • vs Strategy: inheritance and steps vs. composition and whole algorithm.
public final String run(List<String> lines) { /* parse -> validate -> load, always in this order */ }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a JsonProductImporter that rejects products with negative prices.
  • Add a wallet payment flow that requires no capture step, with a test.
  • Rewrite DataImporter in callback style (importLines(lines, parse, validate)) and compare.

Strategy Next: Visitor

docs.title: Visitor
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Visitor lets you add new operations to a stable class hierarchy without changing those classes. Each operation is a "visitor" with one method per element type. In Java 21, sealed interfaces + pattern-matching switch often give the same benefit with far less code. Know both.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a cart has books, electronics and fresh produce. Finance wants GST per category, logistics wants shipping cost, marketing wants loyalty points, and next quarter someone wants carbon footprint. If each operation becomes a method on every item class (gst(), shipping(), points(), carbon()), item classes grow forever and mix tax rules with logistics rules. The item types rarely change; the operations keep coming.

Formal definition (GoF):

Represent an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure. Visitor lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates.

Double dispatch: item.accept(visitor) calls visitor.visit(this). The right visit method is chosen by both the element's runtime type (first dispatch, via accept) and the visitor's type (second dispatch). That's how Java, with only single dispatch, picks "GST rule for Electronics".

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Inspectors visiting a building

A building has flats, shops and a parking lot (stable element types). Different inspectors visit: fire safety, electrical, tax assessment. Each inspector knows what to check for each kind of unit. Adding a new kind of inspection doesn't require rebuilding the units; you just send a new inspector.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Visitor {
        <<interface>>
        +visit(ElementA)
        +visit(ElementB)
    }
    class ConcreteVisitor1
    class ConcreteVisitor2
    class Element {
        <<interface>>
        +accept(Visitor)
    }
    class ElementA {
        +accept(Visitor v) v.visit(this)
    }
    class ElementB {
        +accept(Visitor v) v.visit(this)
    }
    Visitor <|.. ConcreteVisitor1
    Visitor <|.. ConcreteVisitor2
    Element <|.. ElementA
    Element <|.. ElementB
    ElementA ..> Visitor
    ElementB ..> Visitor
Participant Responsibility Visitor One visit method per element type Concrete visitor One operation (GST, shipping, export) across all element types; may accumulate results Element accept(visitor) calls back the matching visit Object structure The collection or tree being visited (a cart, a document, an AST)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
double gst(Item item) {
    if (item instanceof Book) return 0;
    else if (item instanceof Electronics e) return e.price() * 0.18;
    else if (item instanceof FreshProduce) return 0;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();   // a new item type compiles fine and fails at runtime
}
int shipping(Item item) { /* the same instanceof chain again */ }
  • instanceof chains repeated per operation.
  • A new element type compiles fine and fails at runtime when a branch is missing.
  • Or, the alternative: every operation added as a method to every class, mixing unrelated concerns.

docs.title: Example 1: Tax and Shipping over a Mixed Cart (E-commerce) — classic double dispatch
docs.text:
Scenario: An Indian marketplace sells books (GST-exempt), electronics (18% GST, fragile items need careful packing) and fresh produce (exempt, chilled items need a cold-chain bag). Tax rules are owned by finance; shipping rules by logistics. Neither team should edit the item classes, which are shared by catalog, search and orders.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Cart loop
    participant E as Electronics (element)
    participant G as GstVisitor
    C->>E: accept(gst)
    E->>G: visit(this as Electronics)
    G->>G: gst += price * 0.18
    C->>E: accept(shipping)
    E->>G: (ShippingVisitor) visit(this): weight + fragile surcharge

Full Code:

CartItems.javaGstVisitor.javaShippingVisitor.javaCartDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart;

/** Element hierarchy (stable) + visitor interface (operations grow). Classic double dispatch. */
public final class CartItems {

    private CartItems() {
    }

    public interface CartVisitor { // (1)!
        void visit(Book b);
        void visit(Electronics e);
        void visit(FreshProduce f);
    }

    public interface Item {
        void accept(CartVisitor v); // (2)!
    }

    public record Book(String title, int priceInr, int grams) implements Item {
        public void accept(CartVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
    }

    public record Electronics(String name, int priceInr, int grams, boolean fragile) implements Item {
        public void accept(CartVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
    }

    public record FreshProduce(String name, int priceInr, int grams, boolean chilled) implements Item {
        public void accept(CartVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
    }
}
  1. One visit overload per element type. Adding an element type means adding a method here, and the compiler then forces every visitor to handle it.
  2. accept is identical in every element (v.visit(this)), but it must be written in each class: inside Book, this has static type Book, so the compiler picks visit(Book).
package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart.CartItems.*;

/** Operation 1: GST per category. Rates live here, not in the item classes. */
public class GstVisitor implements CartVisitor {

    private double gst;

    public void visit(Book b) { gst += 0; }                          // books exempt
    public void visit(Electronics e) { gst += e.priceInr() * 0.18; }
    public void visit(FreshProduce f) { gst += 0; }                  // unprocessed produce exempt

    public double total() { return gst; }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart.CartItems.*;

/** Operation 2: shipping cost. Each item type has its own rule. */
public class ShippingVisitor implements CartVisitor {

    private int grams;
    private int surcharges;

    public void visit(Book b) { grams += b.grams(); }

    public void visit(Electronics e) {
        grams += e.grams();
        if (e.fragile()) {
            surcharges += 40; // bubble wrap and careful handling
        }
    }

    public void visit(FreshProduce f) {
        grams += f.grams();
        if (f.chilled()) {
            surcharges += 25; // cold-chain bag
        }
    }

    public int costInr() {
        return 30 + (grams / 1000) * 10 + surcharges;
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart.CartItems.*;

import java.util.List;

public class CartDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Tax and Shipping over a Mixed Cart ===");
        List<Item> cart = List.of(
                new Book("Clean Code", 650, 700),
                new Electronics("Bluetooth Speaker", 2_999, 900, true),
                new FreshProduce("Alphonso Mangoes 1kg", 450, 1_100, true));

        GstVisitor gst = new GstVisitor();
        ShippingVisitor shipping = new ShippingVisitor();
        for (Item item : cart) {
            item.accept(gst);
            item.accept(shipping);
        }
        System.out.printf("GST      : INR %.2f%n", gst.total());
        System.out.println("Shipping : INR " + shipping.costInr() + " (2.7 kg + fragile + chilled)");
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Tax and Shipping over a Mixed Cart ===
GST      : INR 539.82
Shipping : INR 115 (2.7 kg + fragile + chilled)

Why Visitor here:

  • Stable element types, a growing list of operations owned by different teams.
  • Each operation's rules are together in one class (all GST rules in GstVisitor).
  • Visitors can accumulate results across the whole cart.

docs.title: Example 2: Claim Adjudication (Health Insurance) — sealed types + pattern matching
docs.text:
Scenario: A health insurer processes consultation, surgery and pharmacy claims. Two operations run on every claim: adjudication (approve, reject or review, with rules like "surgery needs pre-authorization" and "cap at sum insured") and fraud scoring. More operations (reserve estimation, reinsurance split) are planned. The claim types are fixed by regulation and rarely change.

Design:

flowchart LR
    C{{"sealed interface Claim"}} --> A[Consultation]
    C --> S[Surgery]
    C --> P[Pharmacy]
    O1["decide(Claim) — switch"] -.-> C
    O2["fraudScore(Claim) — switch"] -.-> C

Full Code:

Claim.javaClaimOperations.javaClaimsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.claims;

/** Sealed hierarchy: Java 21 pattern matching gives Visitor-style dispatch without accept(). */
public sealed interface Claim {

    String id();

    int amountInr();

    record Consultation(String id, int amountInr, String doctorRegNo) implements Claim { }

    record Surgery(String id, int amountInr, boolean preAuthorized, int daysAdmitted) implements Claim { }

    record Pharmacy(String id, int amountInr, boolean hasPrescription) implements Claim { }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.claims;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.claims.Claim.*;

/** Each operation is one method with an exhaustive switch: a "visitor" without boilerplate. */
public final class ClaimOperations {

    private ClaimOperations() {
    }

    public static String decide(Claim c) {
        return switch (c) { // (1)!
            case Consultation x when x.amountInr() <= 2_000 -> "AUTO-APPROVE";
            case Consultation x -> "REVIEW (consultation above INR 2000)";
            case Surgery s when !s.preAuthorized() -> "REJECT (no pre-authorization)";
            case Surgery s -> "APPROVE " + Math.min(s.amountInr(), 300_000) + " (sum insured cap)";
            case Pharmacy p when !p.hasPrescription() -> "REJECT (no prescription)";
            case Pharmacy p -> "AUTO-APPROVE";
        };
    }

    public static int fraudScore(Claim c) {
        return switch (c) {
            case Consultation x -> x.doctorRegNo().isBlank() ? 70 : 5;
            case Surgery s -> s.daysAdmitted() == 0 && s.amountInr() > 100_000 ? 60 : 10;
            case Pharmacy p -> p.amountInr() > 20_000 ? 40 : 5;
        };
    }
}
  1. The modern Visitor: a switch over a sealed type is checked for exhaustiveness (add Dental to Claim and both operations stop compiling, exactly like a visitor interface), with guards (when) for rule conditions. No accept() methods, no visitor interfaces.
package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.claims;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.claims.Claim.*;

import java.util.List;

public class ClaimsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Health Insurance: Claim Adjudication ===");
        List<Claim> claims = List.of(
                new Consultation("CL-1", 1_200, "KMC-55123"),
                new Consultation("CL-2", 3_500, ""),
                new Surgery("CL-3", 420_000, true, 4),
                new Surgery("CL-4", 150_000, false, 0),
                new Pharmacy("CL-5", 2_400, true),
                new Pharmacy("CL-6", 26_000, false));

        for (Claim c : claims) {
            System.out.printf("%s %-12s INR %,7d -> %-38s fraud score %d%n", c.id(), c.getClass().getSimpleName(),
                    c.amountInr(), ClaimOperations.decide(c), ClaimOperations.fraudScore(c));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Health Insurance: Claim Adjudication ===
CL-1 Consultation INR   1,200 -> AUTO-APPROVE                           fraud score 5
CL-2 Consultation INR   3,500 -> REVIEW (consultation above INR 2000)   fraud score 70
CL-3 Surgery      INR 420,000 -> APPROVE 300000 (sum insured cap)       fraud score 10
CL-4 Surgery      INR 150,000 -> REJECT (no pre-authorization)          fraud score 60
CL-5 Pharmacy     INR   2,400 -> AUTO-APPROVE                           fraud score 5
CL-6 Pharmacy     INR  26,000 -> REJECT (no prescription)               fraud score 40

Why this form here:

  • The hierarchy is closed (sealed) and owned by the same codebase, which is ideal for pattern matching.
  • Rules read like a decision table, which reviewers in insurance appreciate.
  • Same benefit as Visitor (new operations without touching claim classes), and the compiler still catches missing cases.

docs.title: Example 3: One Document, Many Exports (Docs SaaS) — visitor with return values
docs.text:
Scenario: A docs product stores documents as a list of elements: headings, paragraphs, images, tables. Users export to Markdown and HTML; the editor shows a word count; PDF and Google-Docs export are planned. Element classes are part of a stable, versioned document model; exporters are added by different teams.

Design:

classDiagram
    class Visitor~R~ {
        <<interface>>
        +heading(Heading) R
        +paragraph(Paragraph) R
        +image(Image) R
        +table(Table) R
    }
    class Markdown["Markdown : Visitor<String>"]
    class Html["Html : Visitor<String>"]
    class WordCount["WordCount : Visitor<Integer>"]
    Visitor <|.. Markdown
    Visitor <|.. Html
    Visitor <|.. WordCount

Full Code:

Doc.javaExporters.javaDocsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.docs;

import java.util.List;

/** Document elements with a generic visitor that returns a value. */
public final class Doc {

    private Doc() {
    }

    public interface Visitor<R> {
        R heading(Heading h);
        R paragraph(Paragraph p);
        R image(Image i);
        R table(Table t);
    }

    public interface Element {
        <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v);
    }

    public record Heading(int level, String text) implements Element {
        public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.heading(this); }
    }

    public record Paragraph(String text) implements Element {
        public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.paragraph(this); }
    }

    public record Image(String url, String alt) implements Element {
        public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.image(this); }
    }

    public record Table(List<String> header, List<List<String>> rows) implements Element {
        public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.table(this); }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.docs;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.docs.Doc.*;

import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** New operations = new visitors. The element classes never change. */
public final class Exporters {

    private Exporters() {
    }

    public static class Markdown implements Visitor<String> {
        public String heading(Heading h) { return "#".repeat(h.level()) + " " + h.text(); }
        public String paragraph(Paragraph p) { return p.text(); }
        public String image(Image i) { return "![" + i.alt() + "](" + i.url() + ")"; }
        public String table(Table t) {
            String head = "| " + String.join(" | ", t.header()) + " |";
            String sep = "|" + " --- |".repeat(t.header().size());
            String body = t.rows().stream().map(r -> "| " + String.join(" | ", r) + " |").collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
            return head + "\n" + sep + "\n" + body;
        }
    }

    public static class Html implements Visitor<String> {
        public String heading(Heading h) { return "<h%d>%s</h%d>".formatted(h.level(), h.text(), h.level()); }
        public String paragraph(Paragraph p) { return "<p>" + p.text() + "</p>"; }
        public String image(Image i) { return "<img src=\"" + i.url() + "\" alt=\"" + i.alt() + "\">"; }
        public String table(Table t) { return "<table>(" + t.rows().size() + " rows)</table>"; }
    }

    public static class WordCount implements Visitor<Integer> {
        private static int words(String s) { return s.isBlank() ? 0 : s.trim().split("\\s+").length; }
        public Integer heading(Heading h) { return words(h.text()); }
        public Integer paragraph(Paragraph p) { return words(p.text()); }
        public Integer image(Image i) { return 0; } // alt text doesn't count
        public Integer table(Table t) { return t.rows().stream().flatMap(r -> r.stream()).mapToInt(WordCount::words).sum(); }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.docs;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.docs.Doc.*;

import java.util.List;

public class DocsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Docs SaaS: One Document, Many Exports ===");
        List<Element> doc = List.of(
                new Heading(2, "Q3 Launch Plan"),
                new Paragraph("We launch in Pune and Jaipur on 1 November."),
                new Image("pune.png", "Pune dark store"),
                new Table(List.of("City", "Stores"), List.of(List.of("Pune", "12"), List.of("Jaipur", "7"))));

        System.out.println("--- Markdown ---");
        doc.forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.accept(new Exporters.Markdown())));
        System.out.println("--- HTML ---");
        doc.forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.accept(new Exporters.Html())));
        int words = doc.stream().mapToInt(e -> e.accept(new Exporters.WordCount())).sum();
        System.out.println("--- Word count: " + words + " ---");
    }
}

Output:

=== Docs SaaS: One Document, Many Exports ===
--- Markdown ---
## Q3 Launch Plan
We launch in Pune and Jaipur on 1 November.
![Pune dark store](pune.png)
| City | Stores |
| --- | --- |
| Pune | 12 |
| Jaipur | 7 |
--- HTML ---
<h2>Q3 Launch Plan</h2>
<p>We launch in Pune and Jaipur on 1 November.</p>
<img src="pune.png" alt="Pune dark store">
<table>(2 rows)</table>
--- Word count: 16 ---

Why Visitor here:

  • Generic Visitor<R> lets each operation return its own type (String for exports, Integer for counts) without casts or accumulator fields.
  • Exporters are independent plug-ins; the document model stays clean.
  • This is how compilers and document processors (ASTs, Markdown parsers) are typically structured.
Unit Tests: VisitorTest.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.visitor;

import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart.CartItems.*;
import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart.GstVisitor;
import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.cart.ShippingVisitor;
import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.claims.Claim;
import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.claims.ClaimOperations;
import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.docs.Doc;
import com.handbook.behavioral.visitor.docs.Exporters;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class VisitorTest {

    @Test
    void gstOnlyOnElectronics() {
        GstVisitor v = new GstVisitor();
        new Book("b", 100, 1).accept(v);
        new Electronics("e", 100, 1, false).accept(v);
        assertThat(v.total()).isEqualTo(18.0);
    }

    @Test
    void shippingAddsSurcharges() {
        ShippingVisitor v = new ShippingVisitor();
        new Electronics("e", 1, 500, true).accept(v);
        assertThat(v.costInr()).isEqualTo(70);
    }

    @Test
    void claimRulesWithGuards() {
        assertThat(ClaimOperations.decide(new Claim.Surgery("x", 500_000, true, 3))).isEqualTo("APPROVE 300000 (sum insured cap)");
        assertThat(ClaimOperations.decide(new Claim.Pharmacy("x", 10, false))).startsWith("REJECT");
    }

    @Test
    void wordCountIgnoresImages() {
        List<Doc.Element> doc = List.of(new Doc.Heading(1, "Two words"), new Doc.Image("a", "many alt words here"));
        assertThat(doc.stream().mapToInt(e -> e.accept(new Exporters.WordCount())).sum()).isEqualTo(2);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Form When to use Classic visitor (Example 1) Element types in another module/library you can't make sealed; visitors that keep state Generic Visitor<R> (Example 3, challenge) Operations that return values; no mutable accumulators Sealed + pattern-matching switch (Example 2) Closed hierarchies in your own code (Java 21+); usually the simplest choice today Reflective/dynamic visitors Avoid; you lose compile-time safety Visitor over a Composite Elements call accept on their children (tree traversal inside or outside the visitor)

The expression problem

OOP makes it easy to add types (new class) and hard to add operations (edit every class). Visitor flips that: easy to add operations, hard to add types (edit every visitor). Choose based on which side changes more often. This is a favourite senior-level discussion.

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Add operations without changing element classes (OCP for operations) Adding an element type breaks every visitor Related logic grouped per operation Boilerplate (accept everywhere, visitor interfaces) Visitors can accumulate state across a structure Visitors may need access to element internals (weaker encapsulation) Compile-time completeness (every type handled) Harder for beginners to follow (double dispatch)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Using Visitor on an unstable hierarchy

If new element types arrive every sprint, every visitor must change every sprint. Use plain polymorphic methods instead.

default branches that hide new types

A visitor base class with no-op defaults, or a switch with default, silently ignores new element types: the tax visitor returns 0 GST for a new "Jewellery" type. Prefer exhaustive handling.

Visitors with too much state

A visitor that both accumulates totals and mutates elements is hard to reason about. Keep visitors focused, or return values (Visitor<R>).

Reusing a stateful visitor

GstVisitor accumulates a total; reusing the same instance for two carts adds them together. Create one per traversal.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Where Visitor shines: ASTs. Compilers, query engines, rule engines and document processors have stable node types and many passes (type check, optimize, generate code, pretty-print). That's the textbook Visitor use case. The Interpreter page's ASTs could get a ToSqlVisitor this way.

Choosing in modern Java. Inside one codebase with a closed hierarchy, sealed + switch wins: less code, exhaustive, readable. Use classic visitors across module boundaries (public APIs where you can't seal types and want third parties to add operations), or when you need double dispatch over two hierarchies.

Traversal ownership. Decide whether the structure controls traversal (elements call children's accept) or the visitor does. For trees, letting the visitor control traversal enables pruning (skip a subtree) and different orders.

War story: the missing jewellery tax

A marketplace added a Jewellery item type. Their tax code used a visitor base class with no-op default methods "for convenience". GstVisitor didn't override visit(Jewellery), so jewellery was charged 0% GST instead of 3% for two months, and the company paid the shortfall plus interest. Fix: removed default implementations (every visitor must handle every type); migrated tax rules to a sealed hierarchy with an exhaustive switch; added a test that runs every visitor over one instance of every element type. Lesson: Visitor's main safety feature is the compiler forcing every case. Don't turn it off with defaults.
