docs.title: Concurrency Patterns
docs.text:
Concurrency patterns solve coordination between threads: sharing work, sharing data safely, and waiting for results, without races, deadlocks or wasted CPU. Every example in this section runs on Java 21 and uses virtual threads where they make sense.

Pattern Problem it solves Interview frequency Status Producer-Consumer Decouple work producers from workers with a buffer and back-pressure ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Thread Pool Reuse a bounded set of threads for many tasks ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Future / Promise Represent a result that will be available later; compose async steps ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Read-Write Lock Many concurrent readers, exclusive writers ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Immutable Object Share data between threads with no locks at all ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Double-Checked Locking Lazy, thread-safe initialization with minimal locking ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Virtual Threads Millions of cheap threads for blocking I/O (Java 21) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅

The three questions behind every concurrency bug

Visibility: will other threads see my write? Atomicity: can another thread see a half-done update? Ordering: can the JVM or CPU reorder my operations? The Java Memory Model's happens-before rules answer all three. Every pattern here is a way to get those guarantees right.

docs.title: Double-Checked Locking
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Double-checked locking (DCL) lazily initializes a field so that only the very first callers ever take a lock: check without the lock, lock, check again, create. In Java it is correct only with volatile. Often a simpler tool is better: the holder idiom (static), ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (per key), or a Lazy<T> helper.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a fraud model takes seconds to load and uses 400 MB. Loading it at start-up slows every deploy, even for instances that never score a payment. Loading it on first use is better, but 500 payments may arrive at the same instant, and you must load it exactly once. Making model() synchronized works, but then every call (millions per day) takes a lock forever, just to protect something that only matters for the first few milliseconds.

Definition:

Check whether initialization is needed without locking; if it is, acquire the lock and check again (another thread may have finished meanwhile) before initializing. The field must be volatile so that other threads never see a partially constructed object.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Turning on the office coffee machine

The first person in the morning glances at the machine (first check: is it on?). If it's off, they go to the switch, and before pressing it, look again (second check), because a colleague may have turned it on while they walked over. After that, everyone just glances and makes coffee; nobody walks to the switch again.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["get()"] --> B{"value != null?<br/>(volatile read, no lock)"}
    B -->|yes: fast path| R[return value]
    B -->|no| C["synchronized (lock)"]
    C --> D{"value != null?<br/>(second check)"}
    D -->|yes: another thread won| E[unlock, return value]
    D -->|no| F["value = create()<br/>(volatile write)"]
    F --> G[unlock, return value]

Why volatile is mandatory: value = new Model() is three steps (allocate, run constructor, assign the reference), and without a happens-before edge, the assignment can become visible to other threads before the constructor's writes. A thread on the fast path could then use a half-built object. volatile (Java 5+, JSR-133) forbids that reordering.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// (a) Broken: race. Two threads can both see null and load the model twice (or N times)
Model model() {
    if (model == null) model = new Model();
    return model;
}

// (b) Correct but slow forever: every call locks, long after initialization
synchronized Model model() { ... }

// (c) BROKEN DCL: no volatile. Readers may see a partially constructed Model
private Model model;
  • (a) duplicate expensive initialization, possibly inconsistent state.
  • (b) permanent lock contention on a hot path.
  • (c) the classic, very hard-to-reproduce memory-model bug.

docs.title: Example 1: Lazily Loaded Fraud Model (Payments) — instance-field DCL
docs.text:
Scenario: Each payment service instance has a FraudScorer. The model is loaded on the first payment, not at start-up, so deploys are fast and instances that only serve refunds never load it. The first burst after a deploy is 500 concurrent payments, and the model must be loaded once. After that, scoring must not take any lock.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T1 as Payment thread 1
    participant T2 as Payment thread 2..500
    participant S as FraudScorer
    T1->>S: model() sees null
    T2->>S: model() sees null
    T1->>S: synchronized: still null, load model
    T2->>S: waits for the lock
    T1->>S: volatile write: model ready
    T2->>S: synchronized: not null now, use it
    Note over S: all later calls: volatile read only, no lock

Full Code:

FraudScorer.javaFraudDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.dcl.fraud;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** The fraud model is 400 MB and takes seconds to load; load it once, on first use, per scorer. */
public class FraudScorer {

    static final class Model {
        static final AtomicInteger LOADS = new AtomicInteger();
        private final double threshold;

        Model() {
            LOADS.incrementAndGet();
            try {
                Thread.sleep(50); // reading weights from disk
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
            this.threshold = 0.8;
        }

        double score(int amountInr, boolean newDevice) {
            return Math.min(1.0, amountInr / 100_000.0 + (newDevice ? 0.5 : 0));
        }
    }

    private volatile Model model; // (1)!

    private Model model() {
        Model m = model; // (2)!
        if (m == null) { // first check, no lock
            synchronized (this) {
                m = model;
                if (m == null) { // second check, under the lock
                    model = m = new Model();
                }
            }
        }
        return m;
    }

    public boolean isFraud(int amountInr, boolean newDevice) {
        Model m = model();
        return m.score(amountInr, newDevice) >= m.threshold;
    }
}
  1. volatile is what makes DCL correct in Java.
  2. Read the volatile field once into a local: the fast path does a single volatile read (the form recommended in Effective Java, Item 83).
package com.handbook.concurrency.dcl.fraud;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class FraudDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Lazily Loaded Fraud Model ===");
        FraudScorer scorer = new FraudScorer();
        System.out.println("Service started; model loads so far: " + FraudScorer.Model.LOADS.get());

        AtomicInteger flagged = new AtomicInteger();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) { // the first burst of payments arrives at once
                int amount = (i % 10 == 0) ? 60_000 : 900;
                boolean newDevice = i % 10 == 0;
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    if (scorer.isFraud(amount, newDevice)) {
                        flagged.incrementAndGet();
                    }
                });
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Payments scored : 500");
        System.out.println("Flagged as fraud: " + flagged.get());
        System.out.println("Model loads     : " + FraudScorer.Model.LOADS.get() + " (despite 500 concurrent first calls)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Lazily Loaded Fraud Model ===
Service started; model loads so far: 0
Payments scored : 500
Flagged as fraud: 50
Model loads     : 1 (despite 500 concurrent first calls)

Why DCL here:

  • The field is an instance field (one model per scorer), so the static holder idiom doesn't apply.
  • Initialization is expensive and must happen once.
  • The steady-state path is hot, so it must be lock-free.

docs.title: Example 2: Per-Tenant Search Indexes (SaaS) — computeIfAbsent instead of DCL
docs.text:
Scenario: A multi-tenant SaaS opens a search index per tenant (expensive: files, caches) the first time that tenant searches. Thousands of requests across tenants arrive concurrently. Writing DCL by hand per key is error-prone (you'd need a lock per tenant). ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent gives "create at most once per key" with fine-grained locking.

Design:

flowchart LR
    R["3,000 concurrent requests"] --> M{"computeIfAbsent(tenant)"}
    M -->|first for acme| A[create acme index]
    M -->|first for globex| G[create globex index]
    M -->|first for initech| I[create initech index]
    M -->|all later calls| H[return existing index]

Full Code:

TenantResources.javaTenantsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.dcl.tenants;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Lazy, thread-safe creation PER KEY: the modern replacement for hand-written DCL. */
public class TenantResources {

    public record SearchIndex(String tenant) {
        static final AtomicInteger CREATED = new AtomicInteger();

        public SearchIndex {
            CREATED.incrementAndGet(); // expensive: opens index files, warms caches
        }
    }

    private final Map<String, SearchIndex> indexes = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public SearchIndex indexFor(String tenant) {
        return indexes.computeIfAbsent(tenant, SearchIndex::new); // (1)!
    }

    public int created() {
        return SearchIndex.CREATED.get();
    }
}
  1. Atomic per key: if two threads ask for "acme" at once, one creates and the other waits for that result. Different tenants don't block each other. Keep the creation function short and never call back into the same map from inside it.
package com.handbook.concurrency.dcl.tenants;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class TenantsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS: One Search Index per Tenant, Created on First Request ===");
        TenantResources resources = new TenantResources();
        String[] tenants = {"acme", "globex", "initech"};
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 3_000; i++) {
                String tenant = tenants[i % 3];
                ex.submit(() -> resources.indexFor(tenant));
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Requests        : 3000 across 3 tenants");
        System.out.println("Indexes created : " + resources.created());
        System.out.println("Same instance on repeat call: " + (resources.indexFor("acme") == resources.indexFor("acme")));
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS: One Search Index per Tenant, Created on First Request ===
Requests        : 3000 across 3 tenants
Indexes created : 3
Same instance on repeat call: true

Why this alternative here:

  • Lazy, once-per-key initialization without hand-written locking.
  • The JDK implementation is well tested; hand-rolled DCL per key is easy to get wrong.
  • In production, use a cache (Caffeine) if indexes must also be evicted.

docs.title: Example 3: Cached ETag for a Video Manifest (Streaming) — racy single-check
docs.text:
Scenario: A streaming service serves video manifests through a CDN, using a content hash (ETag) as the cache key. Manifests are immutable; the hash is cheap-ish to compute and always the same for a given manifest. Here even a lock on first use is unnecessary: if two threads compute the hash at the same moment, they get the same string, so computing it twice is harmless. This is the "racy single-check" idiom, the same trick String.hashCode() uses.

Design:

flowchart TD
    A["etag()"] --> B{"etag != null?<br/>(plain read)"}
    B -->|yes| R[return it]
    B -->|no| C["compute SHA-256<br/>(maybe in several threads at once)"]
    C --> D["etag = result<br/>(identical in every thread)"]
    D --> R

Full Code:

VideoManifest.javaManifestDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.dcl.manifest;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.security.NoSuchAlgorithmException;
import java.util.HexFormat;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/**
 * Immutable manifest with a lazily cached content hash (used as a CDN cache key).
 * "Racy single-check": no lock, no volatile. Safe ONLY because the value is
 * immutable, cheap to recompute and always the same; worst case it is computed twice.
 */
public final class VideoManifest {

    static final AtomicInteger COMPUTATIONS = new AtomicInteger();

    private final String titleId;
    private final List<String> renditions;
    private String etag; // (1)!

    public VideoManifest(String titleId, List<String> renditions) {
        this.titleId = titleId;
        this.renditions = List.copyOf(renditions);
    }

    public String etag() {
        String e = etag; // (2)!
        if (e == null) {
            e = computeEtag();
            etag = e;
        }
        return e;
    }

    private String computeEtag() {
        COMPUTATIONS.incrementAndGet();
        try {
            byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
                    .digest((titleId + renditions).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest, 0, 8); // a String is immutable: safe to publish racily
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException ex) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(ex);
        }
    }
}
  1. Not volatile, no lock. Safe only because the cached value is an immutable String (final-field semantics make it safe to publish through a data race), and every computation produces an equal value.
  2. Read the field once into a local. Reading it twice could see non-null, then null, under the memory model.
package com.handbook.concurrency.dcl.manifest;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class ManifestDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Cached ETag for a Video Manifest ===");
        VideoManifest manifest = new VideoManifest("MONSOON-EXPRESS-S1E1", List.of("480p", "720p", "1080p", "4k"));
        Set<String> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                ex.submit(() -> seen.add(manifest.etag()));
            }
        }
        System.out.println("ETag            : " + manifest.etag());
        System.out.println("Distinct values : " + seen.size() + " (every thread saw the same ETag)");
        System.out.println("Computed at least once, far fewer than 1000 times: "
                + (VideoManifest.COMPUTATIONS.get() >= 1 && VideoManifest.COMPUTATIONS.get() < 1_000));
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Cached ETag for a Video Manifest ===
ETag            : def9f56914337ef0
Distinct values : 1 (every thread saw the same ETag)
Computed at least once, far fewer than 1000 times: true

Know exactly when this is allowed

Racy single-check is only correct when: the value is immutable (or a primitive other than long/double), recomputing is cheap and side-effect free, and every computation returns an equal value. For anything else (models, connections, mutable objects), use real DCL with volatile or another safe idiom.

Why this idiom here:

  • The cheapest possible lazy cache for immutable, derivable values.
  • Same reasoning as the JDK's String.hashCode().
  • Shows interviewers you understand why DCL needs volatile, and when it doesn't.
Unit Tests: DclTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.dcl;

import com.handbook.concurrency.dcl.lazy.Lazy;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.RepeatedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class DclTest {

    @RepeatedTest(5)
    void lazyInitializesExactlyOnceUnderContention() throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
        Lazy<Object> lazy = Lazy.of(() -> { calls.incrementAndGet(); return new Object(); });
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
                ex.submit(() -> { start.await(); return lazy.get(); });
            }
            start.countDown(); // release all threads at once
        }
        assertThat(calls).hasValue(1);
    }

    @Test
    void nullResultsAreRejected() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Lazy.of(() -> null).get()).isInstanceOf(NullPointerException.class);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Need Best tool Lazy static singleton Initialization-on-demand holder idiom (or an enum); no locks, no volatile (see Singleton) Lazy instance field DCL with volatile (Example 1), or a reusable Lazy<T> (coding challenge) Lazy value per key ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (Example 2), or a Caffeine cache Lazy immutable derived value Racy single-check (Example 3) Library helpers Guava Suppliers.memoize, Vavr Lazy, Spring @Lazy beans Future JDK Stable values (JEP 502, preview in JDK 25): JVM-supported lazy constants

Virtual threads note: synchronized blocks pin the carrier thread in JDK 21–23 if the thread blocks inside them. DCL only holds the lock during one-time initialization, which is fine; if initialization does slow I/O on virtual threads, use a ReentrantLock instead of synchronized.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Lazy initialization JDK String.hashCode() (racy single-check); class initialization (the holder idiom relies on it); ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent Spring @Lazy beans; SingletonBeanRegistry (uses locking plus early references internally) Hibernate Lazy-loaded proxies and collections Guava Suppliers.memoize (DCL internally) Log4j2 / SLF4J Lazy logger initialization

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Lazy: pays the cost only if needed Subtle: broken without volatile; hard to review Lock taken only during initialization More code than the alternatives Works for instance fields with constructor arguments Holder idiom / computeIfAbsent / Lazy<T> are usually clearer Fast path is a single volatile read Exceptions during init must be handled (retry on next call?)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Missing volatile

The textbook bug: works on your laptop, fails rarely on many-core servers or other JVMs. Always declare the field volatile.

Reading the field twice

if (field != null) return field; reads twice; under races it can return null. Read once into a local.

DCL for statics

For static singletons, the holder idiom is simpler and faster. Reserve DCL for instance fields.

Initialization that fails

If creation throws, the field stays null and the next caller retries. Decide whether that's desired (transient failures) or whether to cache the failure (permanent misconfiguration).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
History. DCL was famously broken in Java before JSR-133 (Java 5) because volatile didn't prevent reordering of the constructor's writes. The "Double-Checked Locking is Broken" declaration (Pugh et al.) is why interviewers still ask. Since Java 5, volatile makes it correct.

Lazy vs. eager at service level. Lazy initialization moves cost from start-up to the first request, which can create cold-start latency spikes right after a deploy (exactly when everyone is watching dashboards). Many teams prefer eager warm-up during a readiness phase (Kubernetes readiness probe stays false until models and caches are loaded), and keep lazy loading for rarely used resources.

Memory model essentials to state in interviews: visibility (volatile write → volatile read creates happens-before), safe publication (volatile, final fields, locks, concurrent collections), and final-field semantics for immutable objects.

War story: the null pointer that only happened on Mondays

A pricing service used DCL without volatile for a lazily built rules engine. It worked in tests and on most days. On Monday mornings, when a scheduled deploy coincided with peak traffic on 64-core machines, a few requests failed with NullPointerException inside the rules engine: they had seen the reference before the constructor's field writes. The bug took weeks to find because it never reproduced locally. Fix: added volatile; later replaced it with eager initialization during the readiness phase, removing the lazy path from request handling. Lesson: memory-model bugs depend on hardware, load and timing. Use the established idioms exactly, and question whether laziness is needed at all.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: DCL (volatile) Holder idiom synchronized getter computeIfAbsent Racy single-check Scope Instance or static field Static only Any Per key Immutable derived values Lock after init None None Every call None for existing keys None Complexity Medium (subtle) Low Low Low Low, but strict conditions Computes once? Yes Yes Yes Yes No: may compute more than once (harmless)

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Check → lock → check again → create; the lock is used only during initialization.
  • volatile is mandatory (prevents seeing a half-built object).
  • Read the field once into a local.
  • Static: holder idiom. Per key: computeIfAbsent. Immutable derived values: racy single-check.
  • Consider eager warm-up to avoid post-deploy latency spikes.
private volatile Model model;
Model m = model; if (m == null) synchronized (this) { m = model; if (m == null) model = m = new Model(); }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Remove volatile from FraudScorer and explain, in writing, the exact failure scenario.
  • Add a reset() method to Lazy<T> for tests, and make it thread-safe.
  • Replace TenantResources with a Caffeine cache that evicts indexes idle for 30 minutes.

Immutable Object Next: Virtual Threads

docs.title: Future / Promise
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Future is a placeholder for a result that isn't ready yet; a Promise is the side that completes it. Java's CompletableFuture is both, and lets you compose async steps: run in parallel, chain, combine, time out and recover. Use it to call several services at once, to build async pipelines, and to add timeouts and fallbacks.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a fare search asks three airlines. Called one after another (60 ms + 120 ms + 2,000 ms), the customer waits over 2 seconds, and the slowest airline decides everyone's speed. Called in parallel, the wait is the slowest call, and with a timeout, at most 300 ms. You need a way to start work now, get the result later, combine results, and handle failures and timeouts.

Definition:

A Future represents the result of an asynchronous computation. A Promise is a writable, single-assignment container that completes that future. CompletableFuture<T> implements both: supplyAsync starts work; complete(...) / completeExceptionally(...) fulfill it manually; thenApply / thenCompose / thenCombine / allOf / anyOf compose it.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A token at a food court

You order, pay, and receive a token (the future). You don't stand at the counter; you find a table, chat, maybe order a drink elsewhere (other work). When the screen shows your number, you collect your meal. If the kitchen runs out, the token tells you that too (exceptional completion).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S1["supplyAsync(priceCall)"] --> C1["thenCombine"]
    S2["supplyAsync(stockCall)"] --> C1
    S3["supplyAsync(reviewsCall)"] --> E["exceptionally(empty list)"]
    C1 --> C2["thenCombine"]
    E --> C2
    C2 --> J["join() / thenAccept(render)"]
Method Use supplyAsync(supplier, executor) Start async work that returns a value thenApply(fn) Transform the result (like map) thenCompose(fn) Chain a step that itself returns a future (like flatMap) thenCombine(other, fn) Combine two independent futures allOf(...) / anyOf(...) Wait for all / the first to complete exceptionally(fn) / handle(fn) / whenComplete(fn) Recover from / inspect failures orTimeout(t) / completeOnTimeout(v, t) Fail / fall back after a timeout (Java 9+) join() / get() Block for the result (join throws unchecked CompletionException)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Quote a = skyIndia.quote();     // 60 ms
Quote b = blueJet.quote();      // 120 ms
Quote c = budgetAir.quote();    // 2,000 ms today: the customer waits for everything
// or raw threads + shared fields + manual joins + ad-hoc error handling...
  • Sequential calls add up latencies.
  • No timeouts: the slowest dependency sets your latency.
  • Hand-rolled threads make composition and error handling error-prone.

docs.title: Example 1: Fare Search with Timeouts (Travel)
docs.text:
Scenario: A travel site queries three airline APIs for BLR → DEL. Customers expect results in well under a second. Each airline gets 300 ms; airlines that don't answer in time are left out rather than delaying the page. The cheapest available quote is shown.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Search
    participant A as SkyIndia (60 ms)
    participant B as BlueJet (120 ms)
    participant C as BudgetAir (2000 ms)
    par
        S->>A: supplyAsync
        S->>B: supplyAsync
        S->>C: supplyAsync
    end
    A-->>S: 5840
    B-->>S: 5310
    Note over S,C: 300 ms: completeOnTimeout(empty)
    S->>S: cheapest = BlueJet 5310

Full Code:

FlightQuotesDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.future.flights;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

/** Ask three airlines at once; give each 300 ms; show the cheapest answer that arrived. */
public class FlightQuotesDemo {

    record Quote(String airline, int fareInr) {
    }

    static Optional<Quote> callAirline(String airline, int fare, long latencyMs) {
        try {
            Thread.sleep(latencyMs); // network + airline system
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
        return Optional.of(new Quote(airline, fare));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: BLR -> DEL Fare Search ===");
        try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>>> calls = List.of(
                    quote(io, "SkyIndia", 5_840, 60),
                    quote(io, "BlueJet", 5_310, 120),
                    quote(io, "BudgetAir", 4_990, 2_000)); // very slow today

            CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); // (1)!
            calls.forEach(c -> System.out.println("  " + c.join().map(Quote::toString).orElse("BudgetAir: no answer within 300 ms")));

            Quote best = calls.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).flatMap(Optional::stream)
                    .min(Comparator.comparingInt(Quote::fareInr)).orElseThrow();
            System.out.println("Cheapest shown to customer: " + best.airline() + " INR " + best.fareInr());
        }
    }

    static CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>> quote(ExecutorService io, String airline, int fare, long latency) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> callAirline(airline, fare, latency), io) // (2)!
                .completeOnTimeout(Optional.empty(), 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);           // (3)!
    }
}
  1. allOf waits for every future, but thanks to the timeouts, never longer than about 300 ms.
  2. Always pass an executor for blocking calls. Here it's virtual threads; without it, supplyAsync uses the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
  3. completeOnTimeout turns "too slow" into a fallback value (Optional.empty()). Use orTimeout when a timeout should be an error instead.

Output:

=== Travel: BLR -> DEL Fare Search ===
  Quote[airline=SkyIndia, fareInr=5840]
  Quote[airline=BlueJet, fareInr=5310]
  BudgetAir: no answer within 300 ms
Cheapest shown to customer: BlueJet INR 5310

Timeouts don't cancel the underlying work

completeOnTimeout completes the future, but BudgetAir's call keeps running in the background (the demo's executor waits for it when closing). Pass timeouts to the HTTP client as well (HttpClient request timeout), so the real call is abandoned too.

Why Future/Promise here:

  • Parallel fan-out reduces latency from the sum to the maximum.
  • Per-call timeouts with fallbacks keep the page fast when one provider is slow.
  • Results are combined with ordinary stream code once complete.

docs.title: Example 2: Product Page Composition (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: A product page needs price and stock (essential) and reviews (nice to have) from three services. They're independent, so they're fetched in parallel. If the reviews service fails, the page must still render, just without reviews; if price fails, the page should fail (you can't sell without a price).

Design:

flowchart LR
    P[price] --> C1{thenCombine}
    S[stock] --> C1
    R[reviews] -->|"503"| X["exceptionally -> []"]
    C1 --> C2{thenCombine}
    X --> C2
    C2 --> Page[render page]

Full Code:

ProductPageDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.future.productpage;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

/** Product page: price, stock and reviews fetched in parallel and combined; reviews may fail. */
public class ProductPageDemo {

    record Page(String sku, int priceInr, int stock, List<String> reviews) {
    }

    static int price(String sku) { sleep(50); return 1_299; }

    static int stock(String sku) { sleep(80); return 14; }

    static List<String> reviews(String sku) {
        sleep(30);
        throw new IllegalStateException("reviews service returned 503");
    }

    static void sleep(long ms) {
        try {
            Thread.sleep(ms);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Product Page Composition ===");
        String sku = "HEADPHONES-42";
        try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            CompletableFuture<Integer> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> price(sku), io);
            CompletableFuture<Integer> stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> stock(sku), io);
            CompletableFuture<List<String>> reviews = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> reviews(sku), io)
                    .exceptionally(e -> { // (1)!
                        System.out.println("  reviews unavailable (" + e.getCause().getMessage() + "), showing page without them");
                        return List.of();
                    });

            Page page = price.thenCombine(stock, (p, s) -> new Page(sku, p, s, List.of())) // (2)!
                    .thenCombine(reviews, (pg, r) -> new Page(pg.sku(), pg.priceInr(), pg.stock(), r))
                    .join();
            System.out.println("Rendered: " + page);
            System.out.println("Price and stock were essential; reviews were optional.");
        }
    }
}
  1. Recovery is attached only to the optional dependency. Price and stock failures still propagate.
  2. thenCombine joins independent futures as soon as both are ready, with no explicit waiting or locks.

Output:

=== E-commerce: Product Page Composition ===
  reviews unavailable (reviews service returned 503), showing page without them
Rendered: Page[sku=HEADPHONES-42, priceInr=1299, stock=14, reviews=[]]
Price and stock were essential; reviews were optional.

Why Future/Promise here:

  • Independent calls in parallel, combined declaratively.
  • Selective fallbacks: optional parts degrade gracefully; essential parts fail loudly.
  • This is the core of every Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) aggregation.

docs.title: Example 3: Async Payment Pipeline (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment goes through dependent async steps: validate, then fraud score, then charge. Each step is a call to another service. A high fraud score must stop the pipeline before charging. All failures (validation, fraud) must become clear "declined" results, not stack traces, and the original error must be visible (not wrapped in CompletionException).

Design:

flowchart LR
    V[validate] -->|thenCompose| F[fraudScore]
    F -->|"score <= 80: thenCompose"| C[charge]
    F -->|"score > 80"| X[FraudException]
    V -->|invalid| X2[IllegalArgumentException]
    C --> H[handle: CHARGED / DECLINED]
    X --> H
    X2 --> H

Full Code:

PaymentPipelineDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.future.payments;

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

/** Dependent async steps: validate -> fraud score -> charge. thenCompose chains steps that return futures. */
public class PaymentPipelineDemo {

    record Payment(String id, String card, int amountInr) {
    }

    static class FraudException extends RuntimeException {
        FraudException(String m) { super(m); }
    }

    private final ExecutorService io;

    PaymentPipelineDemo(ExecutorService io) {
        this.io = io;
    }

    CompletableFuture<Payment> validate(Payment p) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            if (p.amountInr() <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
            }
            return p;
        }, io);
    }

    CompletableFuture<Integer> fraudScore(Payment p) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> p.card().endsWith("0000") ? 92 : 12, io);
    }

    CompletableFuture<String> charge(Payment p) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "CHG-" + p.id(), io);
    }

    CompletableFuture<String> process(Payment p) {
        return validate(p)
                .thenCompose(valid -> fraudScore(valid).thenCompose(score -> { // (1)!
                    if (score > 80) {
                        throw new FraudException("fraud score " + score);
                    }
                    return charge(valid);
                }))
                .handle((chargeId, error) -> { // (2)!
                    if (error == null) {
                        return p.id() + ": CHARGED " + chargeId;
                    }
                    Throwable cause = error instanceof CompletionException ? error.getCause() : error; // (3)!
                    return p.id() + ": DECLINED (" + cause.getMessage() + ")";
                });
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Async Validation, Fraud Check and Charge ===");
        try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            PaymentPipelineDemo pipeline = new PaymentPipelineDemo(io);
            for (Payment p : new Payment[] {
                    new Payment("PAY-1", "4111-1111", 2_499),
                    new Payment("PAY-2", "4111-0000", 54_000),
                    new Payment("PAY-3", "4111-2222", 0)}) {
                System.out.println(pipeline.process(p).join());
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. thenCompose for steps that return futures. thenApply would give a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<...>>. It's flatMap for futures.
  2. handle sees both outcomes (result or error) and turns them into one value, the async version of try/catch.
  3. Exceptions thrown inside stages arrive wrapped in CompletionException. Unwrap to report the real cause.

Output:

=== Payments: Async Validation, Fraud Check and Charge ===
PAY-1: CHARGED CHG-PAY-1
PAY-2: DECLINED (fraud score 92)
PAY-3: DECLINED (amount must be positive)

Why Future/Promise here:

  • Dependent async steps without blocking threads between them.
  • Short-circuiting: an exception skips the remaining steps (no charge after a fraud hit).
  • One place (handle) maps every outcome to a business result.
Unit Tests: FutureTest.java (examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.concurrency.future;

import com.handbook.concurrency.future.mirrors.FirstSuccessful;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Timeout;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class FutureTest {

    @Test
    @Timeout(5)
    void completeOnTimeoutSuppliesFallback() {
        CompletableFuture<String> never = new CompletableFuture<>();
        assertThat(never.completeOnTimeout("fallback", 50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join()).isEqualTo("fallback");
    }

    @Test
    void exceptionallyRecovers() {
        CompletableFuture<Integer> f = CompletableFuture.<Integer>failedFuture(new RuntimeException("x")).exceptionally(e -> -1);
        assertThat(f.join()).isEqualTo(-1);
    }

    @Test
    void firstSuccessfulIgnoresEarlyFailures() {
        var failed = CompletableFuture.<String>failedFuture(new RuntimeException("down"));
        var ok = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("ok");
        assertThat(FirstSuccessful.of(List.of(failed, ok)).join()).isEqualTo("ok");
    }

    @Test
    void firstSuccessfulFailsWhenAllFail() {
        var a = CompletableFuture.<String>failedFuture(new RuntimeException("a"));
        var b = CompletableFuture.<String>failedFuture(new RuntimeException("b"));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> FirstSuccessful.of(List.of(a, b)).join())
                .isInstanceOf(CompletionException.class).hasMessageContaining("all 2 attempts failed");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
CompletableFuture vs. virtual threads (Java 21). With virtual threads, plain blocking code is cheap again. The product page could be written as:

try (var io = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<Integer> price = io.submit(() -> price(sku));
    Future<Integer> stock = io.submit(() -> stock(sku));
    Future<List<String>> reviews = io.submit(() -> reviews(sku));
    List<String> r;
    try { r = reviews.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { r = List.of(); }
    return new Page(sku, price.get(), stock.get(), r);
}

Readable, debuggable, with normal stack traces. Structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope, preview in Java 21–24) adds automatic cancellation of sibling tasks when one fails. CompletableFuture still shines for pipelines and composition (thenCompose, anyOf, timeouts) and for APIs that return futures.

Choice Best for CompletableFuture Composition, async APIs, non-blocking pipelines, timeouts Virtual threads + blocking code Simple fan-out/fan-in, readability, debugging Reactive (Reactor/RxJava) Streams of many values with back-pressure

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Futures JDK java.net.http.HttpClient.sendAsync returns CompletableFuture<HttpResponse> Spring @Async methods returning CompletableFuture; Spring MVC controllers returning CompletableFuture (async request processing) Spring Kafka KafkaTemplate.send() returns CompletableFuture<SendResult> AWS SDK v2 Async clients return CompletableFuture Reactor Mono.toFuture() / Mono.fromFuture() bridges JDBC alternatives R2DBC (reactive), Vert.x SQL client (futures)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Parallelism without managing threads Stack traces are fragmented; harder debugging Rich composition (chain, combine, race) Exception wrapping (CompletionException, ExecutionException) Built-in timeouts and fallbacks Easy to block accidentally (join() in the wrong place) Non-blocking pipelines save threads Default executor (common pool) is a trap for blocking calls Cancellation doesn't interrupt running work

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Blocking calls on the common pool

supplyAsync(() -> jdbcCall()) without an executor runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (sized to cores). A few slow calls starve every parallel stream and async task in the JVM. Always pass an executor for I/O.

Forgetting failures

A future that completes exceptionally and is never join()ed or handle()d fails silently. End every chain with handle/exceptionally/whenComplete (logging), or join it.

thenApply returning a future

thenApply(x -> callAsync(x)) gives CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>. Use thenCompose.

anyOf returns the first to complete, even if it failed

For "first successful", write a combinator (coding challenge).

join() inside a stage

Blocking inside a callback holds a pool thread while waiting, which can deadlock small pools. Compose instead.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Latency budgets and fan-out. For a page with a 300 ms budget calling 5 services in parallel, the page's p99 is driven by the slowest service's tail. Mitigations: per-call timeouts, fallbacks for optional parts, hedged requests (send a duplicate request after the p95 latency and take the first answer), and caching.

Deadline propagation. Pass a deadline (not a fixed timeout) down the call chain (gRPC does this) so inner calls don't keep working after the outer request has given up.

Cancellation. CompletableFuture.cancel(true) doesn't interrupt the running task. If work must be stopped, use executors and Future.cancel(true) (interrupts), structured concurrency, or client-level timeouts.

Context propagation. Async stages run on other threads, so ThreadLocal context (trace IDs, security context, MDC) is lost unless propagated (Micrometer Context Propagation, Spring's TaskDecorator, or ScopedValue with structured concurrency).

War story: the parallel stream that froze the service

A pricing service used CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> rulesRepository.load(...)) (a JDBC call) without an executor, and separately used parallelStream() for CPU-heavy discount calculations. On a slow-database day, the JDBC calls occupied every common-pool thread; the parallel streams queued behind them, and request latency went from 40 ms to 25 s. Thread dumps showed all ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker threads stuck in socket reads. Fix: a dedicated executor (later virtual threads) for I/O futures, a timeout on the JDBC queries, and an ArchUnit rule banning supplyAsync without an executor. Lesson: the common pool is for CPU work. I/O gets its own threads.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Future/Promise Callback Observer / Reactive stream Virtual threads Values One (eventually) One, via a function Many over time Any (blocking style) Composition Chain, combine, race Nested callbacks ("callback hell") Operators Plain code Back-pressure N/A N/A Yes (reactive) Through blocking Readability Good with care Poor at depth Steep learning curve Best

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Future = result later; Promise = who completes it; CompletableFuture = both.
  • Parallel: supplyAsync × N + allOf; combine: thenCombine; chain: thenCompose.
  • Errors: exceptionally / handle; unwrap CompletionException.
  • Timeouts: orTimeout / completeOnTimeout (they don't cancel the work).
  • Always pass an executor for I/O; consider virtual threads for simple fan-out.
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call(), io).completeOnTimeout(fallback, 300, MILLISECONDS);

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Rewrite the product page with virtual threads and blocking Future.get() calls; compare readability.
  • Make FirstSuccessful cancel the remaining attempts after the first success.
  • Add a 200 ms orTimeout to the fraud check and decide whether a timeout should decline or approve.

Thread Pool Next: Read-Write Lock

docs.title: Immutable Object
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An immutable object can't change after it's built. "Changes" create new objects. Immutable objects are automatically thread-safe, can be shared freely and cached, and make reasoning easy. In Java: records (with defensive copies), final fields, List.copyOf, java.time, BigDecimal, String.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: an order snapshot is shared with billing, the warehouse and the email service, each on its own thread. If the snapshot is mutable, any of them (or the cart UI that created it) can change it while others are reading, and you need locks everywhere. If it's immutable, nobody can change it, so nobody needs a lock. Every reader sees exactly what was agreed at checkout.

Definition:

An object whose state cannot be modified after construction. To "change" it, create a new object with the new state (a "wither" or copy-on-write).

The rules (from Java Concurrency in Practice and Effective Java Item 17):

  1. All fields final (records do this for you).
  2. No setters or other mutators.
  3. The class can't be subclassed in a way that adds mutability (final class or record).
  4. Defensive copies of mutable inputs (lists, arrays, Date) in the constructor, and never hand out internal mutable objects.
  5. this doesn't escape during construction.

Follow these and the Java Memory Model guarantees that any thread sees the fully constructed state (final-field semantics), even without synchronization.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A printed receipt

Once a receipt is printed, it doesn't change. Copies can go to the customer, the accountant and the auditor, and they'll always agree. If something needs correcting, you issue a new document (a credit note); you don't scribble on the old receipt.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Money {
        <<record, immutable>>
        +BigDecimal amount
        +Currency currency
        +plus(Money) Money
        +allocate(n) List~Money~
    }
    class Client
    Client ..> Money : operations return NEW instances
Technique Purpose record / final fields No reassignment after construction Compact constructor validation Invalid objects can't exist List.copyOf, Map.copyOf Defensive copy in, unmodifiable out Withers (withX(...)) Create modified copies AtomicReference<Immutable> Swap whole snapshots atomically

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class Order {
    private List<Line> lines;               // mutable list, shared
    public List<Line> getLines() { return lines; }        // caller can add lines
    public void setLines(List<Line> lines) { this.lines = lines; }  // caller keeps a reference
}
// Billing reads total while the cart UI is still adding lines -> invoice != charged amount.
  • Shared mutable state: races, locks everywhere.
  • Aliasing bugs: changing "my" list changes yours.
  • Objects can enter invalid states halfway through updates.

docs.title: Example 1: Money as an Immutable Value (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A banking app splits bills, sums transactions and converts currencies across many threads. Money must never lose a paisa: splitting INR 100 three ways must give 33.34 + 33.33 + 33.33, not 99.99. Amounts like INR 10.005 are invalid. A single Money instance (INR 1) is shared by a million parallel additions without any locks.

Design:

flowchart LR
    A["Money INR 100.00"] -->|"allocate(3)"| B["[33.34, 33.33, 33.33]"]
    B -->|"reduce(plus)"| C["Money INR 100.00 (new object)"]
    A -.->|unchanged| A

Full Code:

Money.javaMoneyDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.money;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Currency;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

/** Immutable value object: every operation returns a NEW Money. Safe to share across threads. */
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {

    public Money { // (1)!
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
        amount = amount.setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);
    }

    public static Money inr(String amount) {
        return new Money(new BigDecimal(amount), Currency.getInstance("INR"));
    }

    public Money plus(Money other) { // (2)!
        requireSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency);
    }

    /** Split into n parts that add back up EXACTLY: the extra paise go to the first parts. */
    public List<Money> allocate(int parts) {
        BigDecimal unit = BigDecimal.ONE.movePointLeft(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits()); // 0.01
        BigDecimal base = amount.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(parts), currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.DOWN);
        BigDecimal remainder = amount.subtract(base.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(parts)));
        int extra = remainder.divide(unit, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY).intValue();
        List<Money> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < parts; i++) {
            result.add(new Money(i < extra ? base.add(unit) : base, currency));
        }
        return List.copyOf(result);
    }

    private void requireSameCurrency(Money other) {
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot add " + other.currency + " to " + currency);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return currency.getCurrencyCode() + " " + amount.toPlainString();
    }
}
  1. The compact constructor validates and normalizes (scale to 2 for INR). An invalid Money can never exist, so no method needs to re-check.
  2. Every operation returns a new Money. Nothing is ever modified, so instances can be shared across threads with no locks.
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.money;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class MoneyDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Splitting a Bill and Summing in Parallel ===");
        Money dinner = Money.inr("100.00");
        List<Money> shares = dinner.allocate(3);
        System.out.println("INR 100 split 3 ways : " + shares);
        System.out.println("Shares add back up   : " + shares.stream().reduce(Money.inr("0"), Money::plus));

        Money oneRupee = Money.inr("1.00"); // shared by all threads, no locks needed
        Money total = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000).parallel()
                .mapToObj(i -> oneRupee)
                .reduce(Money.inr("0"), Money::plus); // (1)!
        System.out.println("1,000,000 x INR 1 in parallel: " + total);
        System.out.println("Original still INR 1.00      : " + oneRupee);

        try {
            Money.inr("10.005");
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected INR 10.005: fractions of a paisa are not money");
        }
    }
}
  1. A parallel reduction over a shared object: safe because plus never mutates. With a mutable accumulator this would be a race.

Output:

=== Banking: Splitting a Bill and Summing in Parallel ===
INR 100 split 3 ways : [INR 33.34, INR 33.33, INR 33.33]
Shares add back up   : INR 100.00
1,000,000 x INR 1 in parallel: INR 1000000.00
Original still INR 1.00      : INR 1.00
Rejected INR 10.005: fractions of a paisa are not money

Why immutability here:

  • Money is a value: two INR 5.00s are the same thing, so equals/hashCode by value (records give this).
  • Thread-safe by construction for parallel computations.
  • Validation in one place, the constructor, so invalid amounts can't exist.

docs.title: Example 2: Order Snapshot Shared by Services (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: At checkout, the order is frozen into a snapshot and handed to billing, warehouse, email and analytics, all running concurrently. The cart UI keeps its own mutable list (customers sometimes add items after paying, by mistake), and that must not change what was charged. Amendments (adding a screen guard after checkout) create a new snapshot.

Design:

flowchart LR
    Cart["Mutable cart list (UI)"] -->|"List.copyOf at construction"| S["OrderSnapshot (immutable)"]
    S --> B[Billing thread]
    S --> W[Warehouse thread]
    S --> E[Email thread]
    S --> A[Analytics thread]
    S -->|"withLine(...)"| S2["New amended snapshot"]

Full Code:

OrderSnapshot.javaOrderDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

/** What the customer agreed to at checkout. Shared with billing, warehouse and email threads. */
public record OrderSnapshot(String orderId, Instant placedAt, List<Line> lines) {

    public record Line(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInr) {
    }

    public OrderSnapshot {
        lines = List.copyOf(lines); // (1)!
    }

    public int totalInr() {
        return lines.stream().mapToInt(l -> l.qty() * l.unitPriceInr()).sum();
    }

    public OrderSnapshot withLine(Line extra) { // (2)!
        var copy = new java.util.ArrayList<>(lines);
        copy.add(extra);
        return new OrderSnapshot(orderId, placedAt, copy);
    }
}
  1. Defensive copy in, unmodifiable out: List.copyOf copies the caller's list (later cart changes can't leak in) and returns an unmodifiable list (callers can't modify it). Record components alone aren't enough: a record holding an ArrayList is shallowly immutable.
  2. A wither: the "change" produces a new snapshot; the original is untouched for everyone still using it.
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order;

import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order.OrderSnapshot.Line;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

public class OrderDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Order Snapshot Shared by Four Services ===");
        List<Line> cart = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Line("PHONE-CASE", 1, 499), new Line("CHARGER-65W", 1, 1_899)));
        OrderSnapshot snapshot = new OrderSnapshot("ORD-77", Instant.parse("2026-10-13T10:15:30Z"), cart);

        cart.add(new Line("SNEAKY-ADDON", 1, 9_999)); // the cart UI keeps changing after checkout...
        System.out.println("Cart changed after checkout; snapshot total still INR " + snapshot.totalInr());

        try {
            snapshot.lines().add(new Line("HACK", 1, 1));
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("Snapshot lines cannot be modified");
        }

        try (ExecutorService services = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<String>> results = List.of(
                    services.submit(() -> "billing  : invoice INR " + snapshot.totalInr()),
                    services.submit(() -> "warehouse: pick " + snapshot.lines().size() + " lines"),
                    services.submit(() -> "email    : receipt for " + snapshot.orderId()),
                    services.submit(() -> "analytics: revenue " + snapshot.totalInr()));
            for (Future<String> f : results) {
                System.out.println(f.get()); // no locks: nothing can change
            }
        }

        OrderSnapshot amended = snapshot.withLine(new Line("SCREEN-GUARD", 1, 299));
        System.out.println("Amended copy total INR " + amended.totalInr() + ", original still INR " + snapshot.totalInr());
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Order Snapshot Shared by Four Services ===
Cart changed after checkout; snapshot total still INR 2398
Snapshot lines cannot be modified
billing  : invoice INR 2398
warehouse: pick 2 lines
email    : receipt for ORD-77
analytics: revenue 2398
Amended copy total INR 2697, original still INR 2398

Why immutability here:

  • One agreed version of the order, shared by many threads without coordination.
  • No aliasing bugs from the cart UI.
  • Amendments are explicit new versions, which is good for auditing.

docs.title: Example 3: Lock-Free Config Snapshots (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: An API gateway enforces per-tenant rate limits read on every request (here 400,000 reads), while an admin tool updates the limits. The per-minute limit and burst must always be consistent with each other (burst = rpm / 10, and burst ≤ rpm). With an immutable snapshot inside an AtomicReference, readers never lock: they grab the current snapshot in one step and use it for the whole request.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as Request threads
    participant A as AtomicReference
    participant U as Admin update
    R->>A: get() snapshot v5 (600/60)
    U->>U: build snapshot v6 (1200/120) off to the side
    U->>A: updateAndGet (atomic swap)
    R->>A: get() snapshot v6
    Note over R: each request sees v5 or v6, never a mix

Full Code:

RateLimitConfig.javaConfigDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.config;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

/** Lock-free configuration: readers get an immutable snapshot; updates swap the whole snapshot. */
public final class RateLimitConfig {

    public record Snapshot(int version, int requestsPerMinute, int burst) { // (1)!
        public Snapshot {
            if (burst > requestsPerMinute) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("burst cannot exceed the per-minute limit");
            }
        }

        Snapshot withLimits(int rpm, int burst) {
            return new Snapshot(version + 1, rpm, burst);
        }
    }

    private final AtomicReference<Snapshot> current = new AtomicReference<>(new Snapshot(1, 600, 60));

    public Snapshot get() {
        return current.get(); // (2)!
    }

    public void update(int rpm, int burst) {
        current.updateAndGet(s -> s.withLimits(rpm, burst)); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. An immutable snapshot record with its invariant enforced in the constructor. An invalid config can't even be built, so it can't be published.
  2. Reading is a single volatile read: wait-free, no locks.
  3. updateAndGet applies the change atomically (retrying if another update raced). The update function must be side-effect free, because it may run more than once.
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.config;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class ConfigDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS API: Rate-Limit Config Updated While Serving Traffic ===");
        RateLimitConfig config = new RateLimitConfig();
        AtomicInteger reads = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger invalid = new AtomicInteger();

        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5)) {
            for (int r = 0; r < 4; r++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                        RateLimitConfig.Snapshot s = config.get(); // one consistent snapshot per request
                        if (s.burst() > s.requestsPerMinute() || s.burst() * 10 != s.requestsPerMinute()) {
                            invalid.incrementAndGet();
                        }
                        reads.incrementAndGet();
                    }
                });
            }
            ex.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 1; i <= 1_000; i++) {
                    int rpm = (i % 2 == 0) ? 600 : 1_200;
                    config.update(rpm, rpm / 10);
                }
            });
        }
        System.out.println("Requests served       : " + reads.get());
        System.out.println("Config versions       : " + config.get().version());
        System.out.println("Inconsistent configs  : " + invalid.get());
        System.out.println("Locks taken by readers: 0");
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS API: Rate-Limit Config Updated While Serving Traffic ===
Requests served       : 400000
Config versions       : 1001
Inconsistent configs  : 0
Locks taken by readers: 0

Why immutability here:

  • The read path is hot: no locks, no contention.
  • Consistency comes from swapping whole snapshots, not from locking fields.
  • Rollback is easy: keep the previous snapshot and swap it back.
Unit Tests: ImmutableTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable;

import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.config.RateLimitConfig;
import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.money.Money;
import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order.OrderSnapshot;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ImmutableTest {

    @Test
    void allocationNeverLosesPaise() {
        for (int parts = 1; parts <= 7; parts++) {
            Money total = Money.inr("100.00").allocate(parts).stream().reduce(Money.inr("0"), Money::plus);
            assertThat(total).isEqualTo(Money.inr("100.00"));
        }
    }

    @Test
    void moneyIsAValue() {
        assertThat(Money.inr("5")).isEqualTo(Money.inr("5.00")); // scale normalized in the constructor
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Money.inr("1").plus(new Money(java.math.BigDecimal.ONE, java.util.Currency.getInstance("USD"))))
                .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void snapshotIsIsolatedFromCallerList() {
        List<OrderSnapshot.Line> lines = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new OrderSnapshot.Line("A", 1, 10)));
        OrderSnapshot s = new OrderSnapshot("O", Instant.EPOCH, lines);
        lines.clear();
        assertThat(s.totalInr()).isEqualTo(10);
    }

    @Test
    void invalidConfigIsRejectedAndOldSnapshotKept() {
        RateLimitConfig c = new RateLimitConfig();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> c.update(10, 100)).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
        assertThat(c.get().version()).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Tool Notes Records (Java 16+) Final fields, value equals/hashCode, compact constructors for validation; shallowly immutable, so copy mutable components List.of/copyOf, Map.of/copyOf, Set.of Truly unmodifiable; null not allowed; copyOf returns the same instance if it's already immutable Collections.unmodifiableList(list) A view: if the original list changes, the view shows it. Not a copy java.time (LocalDate, Instant, Duration) Immutable replacements for Date/Calendar BigDecimal, String, wrapper types Immutable values Withers order.withLine(...); with many fields, builders with toBuilder() Persistent collections (Vavr, PCollections) Efficient "modified copies" via structural sharing

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Immutable JDK String, Integer and other wrappers, BigDecimal, java.time.*, Path, URI, Optional JDK collections List.of, Map.of, Set.of, Stream.toList() Spring HttpHeaders.readOnlyHttpHeaders, ResponseEntity, MediaType; immutable @ConfigurationProperties with constructor binding (records) Jackson Deserializes records and immutable classes via constructors Kafka Records sent are effectively immutable once handed to the producer Guava ImmutableList, ImmutableMap

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Thread-safe without locks New object per change: allocation and GC (usually cheap) Safe to share, cache, use as map keys Large objects copied on every change can be expensive Invariants checked once, at construction Deeply nested updates are verbose without lenses/withers Easy reasoning, no aliasing bugs Some frameworks (JPA entities) expect mutability

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Shallow immutability

record Order(List<Line> lines) is not immutable if lines is an ArrayList: callers can still change it. Copy in the compact constructor (List.copyOf).

Leaking mutable internals

Returning an internal Date, array or list lets callers change your "immutable" object (see the coding challenge). Return copies or immutable types.

Collections.unmodifiableList is a view, not a copy

If the backing list changes, so does the "unmodifiable" view. Use List.copyOf.

Escaping this in the constructor

Registering this with a listener inside the constructor lets other threads see a partially constructed object, voiding the final-field guarantee.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Final-field semantics. The JMM guarantees that once a constructor finishes, any thread that gets a reference to the object sees the correctly initialized values of its final fields, without synchronization, as long as this didn't escape. That's why immutable objects can be published through data races (e.g., a non-volatile field) and still be safe.

Immutability at architecture scale: event sourcing (events are immutable facts), Kafka logs, CRDTs, Git, and container images are all immutable data. Systems built on immutable data are easier to cache, replicate, audit and debug.

Performance reality. Short-lived small objects are almost free on modern JVMs (TLAB allocation, young-gen GC). Profile before introducing mutable "optimizations". For big structures with frequent small changes, use persistent data structures or confine mutation to one thread and publish immutable snapshots.

War story: the invoice that didn't match the charge

An e-commerce checkout passed the same mutable Order object to the payment thread and the invoice thread. A "recommended add-on" widget on the confirmation page added an item to the same object a few hundred milliseconds after payment. The payment charged the old total; the invoice, generated slightly later, included the add-on. About 0.3% of invoices didn't match the charged amount, and every one was a support ticket and a manual credit note. Fix: checkout now creates an immutable OrderSnapshot (record + List.copyOf) that payment, invoicing and email all receive; add-ons after payment create a separate order. Lesson: anything shared between threads, or meant to represent "what was agreed", should be immutable.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Immutable Object Read-Write Lock Prototype Flyweight Thread safety Inherent, no locks Locks N/A Requires immutability Changes New objects In place under a write lock Copy then modify Never (shared) Relationship Basis for safe sharing Alternative when mutation is needed Copying mutable objects Flyweights must be immutable

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Can't change after construction; changes create new objects.
  • Thread-safe for free; great keys, cache entries and shared snapshots.
  • Records are shallowly immutable: List.copyOf mutable components.
  • Don't leak internals; prefer java.time over Date.
  • Config pattern: immutable snapshot + AtomicReference swap.
record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) { Money plus(Money o) { return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency); } }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add minus and times(int) to Money, keeping exact paise.
  • Add a "previous snapshot" to RateLimitConfig and implement rollback().
  • Find a mutable DTO in your own project and make it a record with defensive copies.
