docs.title: Producer-Consumer
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Producers put work into a shared buffer (queue); consumers take work out and process it, at their own pace. The buffer decouples the two sides, smooths bursts, and, when it's bounded, applies back-pressure so fast producers can't overwhelm slow consumers. In Java, use a BlockingQueue.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: orders arrive at a dark store in bursts (a hundred at 7 pm, ten at 3 pm). Pickers work at a steady pace. If the order system hands each order directly to a picker, it has to wait when all pickers are busy, or orders get lost. A queue between them lets orders arrive at any rate and lets pickers take the next one when they're free. If the queue fills up, the system knows it's overloaded and can slow intake.

Definition:

Separate the code that produces work from the code that consumes it, connected by a thread-safe buffer. Producers block (or are rejected) when the buffer is full; consumers block when it's empty.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant's order rail

Waiters (producers) clip orders onto the rail. Cooks (consumers) take the next ticket when they're ready. If the rail is full, waiters stop taking new tables for a moment (back-pressure). Waiters never need to know which cook will cook the order.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P1[Producer 1] -->|put| Q[("Bounded BlockingQueue<br/>capacity N")]
    P2[Producer 2] -->|put| Q
    Q -->|take| C1[Consumer 1]
    Q -->|take| C2[Consumer 2]
    Q -->|take| C3[Consumer 3]
Participant Responsibility Producer Creates work items and puts/offers them Buffer Thread-safe queue; bounded to apply back-pressure Consumer takes/polls items and processes them Shutdown signal Poison pill, interrupt, or a "done" flag

BlockingQueue methods, the interview table:

Throws Returns special value Blocks Times out Insert add(e) offer(e) → false put(e) offer(e, t, unit) Remove remove() poll() → null take() poll(t, unit)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();          // not thread-safe
// producer
orders.add(order);
// consumer
while (true) {
    if (!orders.isEmpty()) {                     // busy-waiting burns CPU
        Order o = orders.remove(0);              // race: two consumers take the same order,
        pick(o);                                 // or one gets IndexOutOfBoundsException
    }
}
  • Races on an unsynchronized list.
  • Busy-waiting wastes CPU.
  • Unbounded growth: a burst eventually causes OutOfMemoryError.

docs.title: Example 1: Dark-Store Order Picking (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Order intake produces pick tasks; three pickers (consumers) collect items. The queue holds at most 5 waiting tasks; when it's full, intake blocks until a picker frees a slot, so the floor never has an ever-growing backlog. At closing time, the system must stop pickers cleanly after the last order.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant I as Order intake (producer)
    participant Q as ArrayBlockingQueue(5)
    participant P as Pickers x3 (consumers)
    I->>Q: put(ORD-1..ORD-5)
    I->>Q: put(ORD-6) blocks: queue full
    P->>Q: take() ORD-1
    Q-->>I: space available, ORD-6 queued
    I->>Q: put(STOP) x3 (poison pills)
    P->>Q: take() STOP, exit

Full Code:

PickingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.picking;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Dark store: the order intake produces pick tasks; 3 pickers consume them. */
public class PickingDemo {

    record PickTask(String orderId, int items) {
    }

    private static final PickTask POISON_PILL = new PickTask("STOP", 0); // (1)!

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery Dark Store: Order Picking ===");
        BlockingQueue<PickTask> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(5); // (2)!
        AtomicInteger maxDepth = new AtomicInteger();
        Map<String, Integer> pickedBy = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        AtomicInteger itemsPicked = new AtomicInteger();
        int pickers = 3;

        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int p = 1; p <= pickers; p++) {
                String picker = "picker-" + p;
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    while (true) {
                        PickTask task = queue.take(); // (3)!
                        if (task == POISON_PILL) {
                            return null;
                        }
                        Thread.sleep(5); // walking the aisles
                        itemsPicked.addAndGet(task.items());
                        pickedBy.merge(picker, 1, Integer::sum);
                    }
                });
            }

            for (int i = 1; i <= 30; i++) { // the producer: order intake
                queue.put(new PickTask("ORD-" + i, i % 4 + 1)); // blocks when 5 tasks are waiting
                maxDepth.accumulateAndGet(queue.size(), Math::max);
            }
            for (int p = 0; p < pickers; p++) {
                queue.put(POISON_PILL); // one pill per consumer
            }
        } // waits for all pickers to finish

        int orders = pickedBy.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
        System.out.println("Orders picked       : " + orders);
        System.out.println("Items picked        : " + itemsPicked.get());
        System.out.println("Queue never above 5 : " + (maxDepth.get() <= 5));
        System.out.println("All pickers worked  : " + (pickedBy.size() == pickers));
    }
}
  1. A poison pill: a special item that tells a consumer to stop. Send one per consumer. Compared with ==, so a real order can never be mistaken for it.
  2. Bounded to 5. This is what creates back-pressure; an unbounded queue just hides overload until memory runs out.
  3. take() blocks while the queue is empty: no busy-waiting. With virtual threads, a blocked consumer costs almost nothing.

Output:

=== Grocery Dark Store: Order Picking ===
Orders picked       : 30
Items picked        : 75
Queue never above 5 : true
All pickers worked  : true

The demo prints only what's guaranteed (totals, the queue bound). Which picker took which order varies from run to run, as it should.

Why Producer-Consumer here:

  • Arrival rate (bursty) and processing rate (steady) are decoupled.
  • The bound gives natural back-pressure on intake.
  • Adding a picker is adding a consumer; the producer doesn't change.

docs.title: Example 2: Batched GPS Ingestion (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: 200 delivery riders' phones send GPS pings constantly. Writing each ping with its own INSERT overwhelms the database. Instead, rider connections (many producers) put pings on a queue, and one writer (consumer) drains up to 100 at a time and writes them in a single batch insert. Under light load, batches are small and latency stays low; under heavy load, batches grow automatically.

Design:

flowchart LR
    R1[Rider 1] --> Q[(LinkedBlockingQueue)]
    R2[Rider 2] --> Q
    R3[... 200 riders] --> Q
    Q -->|"poll(20 ms) + drainTo(99)"| W[Batch writer]
    W -->|"1 INSERT with up to 100 rows"| DB[(Database)]

Full Code:

GpsIngestDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.gps;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Many riders' phones produce GPS pings; one writer batches them into the database. */
public class GpsIngestDemo {

    record Ping(String rider, double lat, double lng) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Batched GPS Ingestion ===");
        BlockingQueue<Ping> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10_000);
        AtomicBoolean producersDone = new AtomicBoolean();
        AtomicInteger written = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger batches = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger biggestBatch = new AtomicInteger();

        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            pool.submit(() -> { // single consumer: batch writer
                List<Ping> batch = new ArrayList<>(100);
                while (!producersDone.get() || !queue.isEmpty()) {
                    Ping first = queue.poll(20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // wait briefly for the first item
                    if (first == null) {
                        continue;
                    }
                    batch.add(first);
                    queue.drainTo(batch, 99); // (1)!
                    written.addAndGet(batch.size()); // one INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), ...
                    batches.incrementAndGet();
                    biggestBatch.accumulateAndGet(batch.size(), Math::max);
                    batch.clear();
                }
                return null;
            });

            try (ExecutorService riders = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                for (int r = 0; r < 200; r++) { // 200 riders x 25 pings
                    String rider = "R" + r;
                    riders.submit(() -> {
                        for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) {
                            queue.put(new Ping(rider, 12.9 + i * 0.0001, 77.6));
                        }
                        return null;
                    });
                }
            }
            producersDone.set(true);
        }

        System.out.println("Pings received      : 5000");
        System.out.println("Pings written       : " + written.get());
        System.out.println("Batch size <= 100   : " + (biggestBatch.get() <= 100));
        System.out.println("Fewer DB writes than pings: " + (batches.get() < 5_000));
    }
}
  1. drainTo grabs everything already waiting (up to a limit) in one call: the key to adaptive batching. Wait for the first item with a timeout, then take whatever else is ready.

Output:

=== Logistics: Batched GPS Ingestion ===
Pings received      : 5000
Pings written       : 5000
Batch size <= 100   : true
Fewer DB writes than pings: true

Why Producer-Consumer here:

  • Many producers, one consumer: a classic fan-in.
  • The consumer turns a stream of tiny writes into efficient batches.
  • Producers never wait for the database; the queue absorbs the difference.

docs.title: Example 3: Webhook Intake with Back-pressure (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment gateway sends webhooks (payment.captured, refund.created) to a merchant's server. The HTTP handler must respond fast, so it only enqueues the event and returns 202 Accepted; a worker processes events afterwards. If the queue is full (worker down or slow), the handler returns 503 within milliseconds, and the gateway retries later. That's back-pressure across a network boundary.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant G as Payment gateway
    participant H as HTTP handler (producer)
    participant Q as Queue (capacity 3)
    participant W as Worker (consumer)
    G->>H: POST evt_1..evt_3
    H->>Q: offer() ok
    H-->>G: 202 Accepted
    G->>H: POST evt_4
    H->>Q: offer(10 ms) fails: full
    H-->>G: 503 (retry later)
    W->>Q: poll() evt_1..evt_3
    G->>H: retry evt_4
    H-->>G: 202

Full Code:

WebhookDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.webhooks;

import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

/** Payment webhooks: accept fast, process later, and push back (HTTP 503) when the buffer is full. */
public class WebhookDemo {

    record Webhook(String id, String event) {
    }

    private final BlockingQueue<Webhook> inbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(3);

    int receive(Webhook w) throws InterruptedException { // the HTTP handler: producer
        boolean accepted = inbox.offer(w, 10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // (1)!
        return accepted ? 202 : 503;
    }

    void drain() { // the worker: consumer
        Webhook w;
        while ((w = inbox.poll()) != null) {
            System.out.println("  processed " + w.id() + " " + w.event());
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Webhook Intake with Back-pressure ===");
        WebhookDemo service = new WebhookDemo();
        String[] events = {"payment.captured", "payment.failed", "refund.created", "payment.captured", "dispute.opened"};
        for (int i = 0; i < events.length; i++) {
            Webhook w = new Webhook("evt_" + (i + 1), events[i]);
            int status = service.receive(w);
            System.out.println("POST " + w.id() + " -> " + status + (status == 503 ? " (gateway will retry later)" : " Accepted"));
        }
        System.out.println("Worker catches up:");
        service.drain();
        System.out.println("Retry of evt_4 -> " + service.receive(new Webhook("evt_4", "payment.captured")));
    }
}
  1. offer with a timeout never blocks an HTTP thread for long. A full queue becomes a fast, explicit "try again later" instead of a hung request.

Output:

=== Payments: Webhook Intake with Back-pressure ===
POST evt_1 -> 202 Accepted
POST evt_2 -> 202 Accepted
POST evt_3 -> 202 Accepted
POST evt_4 -> 503 (gateway will retry later)
POST evt_5 -> 503 (gateway will retry later)
Worker catches up:
  processed evt_1 payment.captured
  processed evt_2 payment.failed
  processed evt_3 refund.created
Retry of evt_4 -> 202

In-memory queues lose data on crash

Accepted-but-unprocessed webhooks are gone if the process dies. In production, persist them first (a database table or Kafka topic) and return 202 only after the write. The in-memory queue is fine for work you can afford to lose or rebuild.

Why Producer-Consumer here:

  • Fast acknowledgement, slow processing.
  • Explicit back-pressure (503) pushes the problem back to a sender that knows how to retry.
  • The worker can be restarted or scaled independently.
Unit Test: ProducerConsumerTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer;

import com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.buffer.BoundedBuffer;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Timeout;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ProducerConsumerTest {

    @Test
    @Timeout(10)
    void manyProducersAndConsumersLoseNothing() throws Exception {
        BoundedBuffer<Integer> buffer = new BoundedBuffer<>(8);
        Set<Integer> received = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 2_500; i++) {
                        received.add(buffer.take());
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }
            for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) {
                int base = p * 2_500;
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 2_500; i++) {
                        buffer.put(base + i);
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }
        }
        assertThat(received).hasSize(10_000);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Queue Bounded? Notes ArrayBlockingQueue Yes (fixed array) One lock; predictable memory; optional fairness LinkedBlockingQueue Optional (default unbounded!) Separate put/take locks: higher throughput. Always pass a capacity LinkedTransferQueue No transfer() waits until a consumer takes the item (hand-off) SynchronousQueue Zero capacity Direct hand-off; used by Executors.newCachedThreadPool() PriorityBlockingQueue No Consumers get the highest-priority item first (express orders) DelayQueue No Items become available after a delay (retries, scheduled reminders) LMAX Disruptor Ring buffer Lock-free, very high throughput (trading systems)

Virtual threads (Java 21): blocking take()/put() is cheap on virtual threads, so "one virtual thread per consumer" or "per producer" is fine even at large scale. Bound the queue (and the downstream resource), not the threads.

Shutdown options: poison pills (Example 1), a "done" flag plus a timed poll (Example 2), or interrupting consumers (executor.shutdownNow()), where consumers must handle InterruptedException by exiting.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Producer-Consumer JDK ThreadPoolExecutor (submitters produce tasks into a BlockingQueue; worker threads consume) Logback / Log4j2 AsyncAppender / async loggers: application threads produce log events, a background thread writes them Spring Batch ItemReader → chunk → ItemWriter Kafka / RabbitMQ / SQS The same pattern across processes; consumer groups are pools of consumers Netty Event loops consuming I/O events Reactive Streams Publisher/Subscriber with request(n) back-pressure

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Decouples production and consumption rates Extra latency (items wait in the buffer) Absorbs bursts In-memory buffers lose data on crash Back-pressure with bounded queues Shutdown and error handling need care Easy to scale consumers Ordering only per queue; parallel consumers process out of order Enables batching Unbounded queues hide overload until OOM

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Unbounded queues

new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() has a capacity of Integer.MAX_VALUE. Under sustained overload it grows until the JVM dies. Always bound and decide what happens when full (block, reject, drop oldest).

Swallowing InterruptedException

catch (InterruptedException e) {} inside a consumer loop makes it impossible to stop. Restore the flag (Thread.currentThread().interrupt()) and exit.

One poison pill for many consumers

Only one consumer gets it; the others block forever. Send one per consumer, or have the consumer that receives it put it back.

Slow consumers and ordering

With several consumers, items for the same entity (same order, same account) may be processed out of order. Partition by key (one queue per partition) if order matters.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Sizing. Little's Law again: queue length ≈ arrival rate × time in queue. Choose capacity from the latency you can tolerate, not from memory alone: a queue that holds 10 minutes of work means 10-minute-old results.

What to do when full: block the producer (in-process, trusted producers), reject with a retryable error (network edges, as in Example 3), drop (metrics, telemetry), or shed load by priority. Make the policy explicit and observable (queue depth, wait time, rejections).

From in-process to distributed. The same pattern at system scale is a message broker. Kafka adds durability, replay, partition-level ordering and consumer groups; SQS adds visibility timeouts and dead-letter queues. Consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

Batching trade-off. Bigger batches mean higher throughput and higher latency. Adaptive batching (Example 2) gives small batches under light load and large ones under heavy load. Add a max wait time so items never sit too long.

War story: the async logger that took down checkout

A team switched to an asynchronous log appender with an unbounded queue to "make logging free". During an incident, a downstream log collector slowed down; the queue grew to 9 GB of log events, triggered long GC pauses, and then an OutOfMemoryError on every checkout pod at once. Fix: a bounded queue (8,192 events) with "discard DEBUG/INFO when 80% full, never block on ERROR", plus a metric and alert on queue depth. Lesson: every queue is a decision about overload. "Unbounded" is a decision too: the decision to crash later.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Producer-Consumer Thread Pool Observer / Pub-Sub Pipeline Core idea Buffer between producers and consumers Workers consuming a task queue (a specific Producer-Consumer) Notify all subscribers Chain of producer-consumer stages Delivery Each item to one consumer One worker per task Every subscriber gets each event Each stage to the next Back-pressure Bounded queue Bounded queue + rejection policy Usually none (reactive streams add it) Bounded queues between stages

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Producers → bounded BlockingQueue → consumers.
  • put/take block; offer/poll with timeouts for back-pressure at edges.
  • Shutdown: poison pill per consumer or interrupts; never swallow InterruptedException.
  • drainTo for batching; partition by key for ordering.
  • wait() in a loop, prefer notifyAll().
BlockingQueue<Task> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100); q.put(task); Task t = q.take();

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Use a PriorityBlockingQueue so express orders are picked first.
  • Rewrite BoundedBuffer with ReentrantLock and two Conditions.
  • Add a max wait (50 ms) to the GPS writer so partial batches are flushed promptly.

docs.title: Read-Write Lock
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A read-write lock lets many readers proceed at the same time, but gives a writer exclusive access. Use it for read-mostly shared data that must be updated consistently (caches, configuration, positions). For extremely read-heavy data, consider StampedLock optimistic reads or immutable snapshots instead.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a feature-flag cache is read thousands of times per second and refreshed every few seconds. With a plain synchronized lock, readers block each other, though reading never conflicts with reading. With no lock, a reader can see a half-applied refresh: checkout-v2 on but payments-v2 still off, a combination that was never released. A read-write lock allows concurrent reads and exclusive, atomic writes.

Definition:

A read-write lock maintains a pair of locks: a read lock that any number of threads can hold at once (as long as no writer holds the write lock), and a write lock that is exclusive.

Another reader Another writer Reader holds the lock ✅ allowed ❌ waits Writer holds the lock ❌ waits ❌ waits

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A museum exhibit

Any number of visitors can look at an exhibit at the same time (readers). When staff need to rearrange it (a writer), they close the room, wait for visitors to leave, make all the changes, and reopen. Visitors never see a half-rearranged exhibit.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R1 as Reader 1
    participant R2 as Reader 2
    participant L as ReadWriteLock
    participant W as Writer
    R1->>L: readLock()
    R2->>L: readLock() (granted, shared)
    W->>L: writeLock() (waits for readers)
    R1->>L: unlock
    R2->>L: unlock
    L-->>W: write lock granted (exclusive)
    W->>L: update both fields, unlock
Java type Notes ReentrantReadWriteLock Reentrant, optional fairness, supports downgrading (write → read) StampedLock (Java 8) Adds optimistic reads (no locking at all if no write happened); not reentrant Immutable snapshot + AtomicReference Not a lock: readers never block; writers replace the whole snapshot

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// (a) No locking: readers may see a half-applied update
flags.put("checkout-v2", true);
flags.put("payments-v2", true);       // a reader between these two lines sees an invalid pair

// (b) synchronized everywhere: correct, but readers serialize behind each other
synchronized boolean[] read() { ... }  // 8 reader threads take turns doing something that could run in parallel
  • No lock: inconsistent reads (and visibility problems).
  • One exclusive lock: needless contention for read-mostly data.

docs.title: Example 1: Feature-Flag Cache (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: A SaaS platform releases "checkout v2" and "payments v2" together; the two flags must always be read as a consistent pair. Eight request threads read the flags constantly while a background job refreshes them. Readers must never see one flag on and the other off.

Design:

flowchart LR
    R1[Reader x8] -->|"readLock (shared)"| F[(flags map)]
    W[Refresher] -->|"writeLock (exclusive): set both"| F

Full Code:

FeatureFlags.javaFlagsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.flags;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReadWriteLock;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

/** Read-mostly cache: thousands of reads per second, a refresh every few seconds. */
public class FeatureFlags {

    private final ReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final Map<String, Boolean> flags = new HashMap<>(Map.of("checkout-v2", false, "payments-v2", false));
    private int version;

    /** Both flags must always be read together: the release turns them on as a pair. */
    public boolean[] checkoutAndPayments() {
        lock.readLock().lock(); // (1)!
        try {
            return new boolean[] {flags.get("checkout-v2"), flags.get("payments-v2")};
        } finally {
            lock.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    public void refresh(boolean enabled) {
        lock.writeLock().lock(); // (2)!
        try {
            flags.put("checkout-v2", enabled);
            Thread.onSpinWait(); // a reader sneaking in here would see a half-applied release
            flags.put("payments-v2", enabled);
            version++;
        } finally {
            lock.writeLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    public int version() {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try {
            return version;
        } finally {
            lock.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }
}
  1. Read lock: any number of readers at once. Always unlock in finally.
  2. Write lock: waits for all readers to leave, then excludes everyone while both flags change. Readers see the old pair or the new pair, never a mix.
package com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.flags;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class FlagsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS: Feature-Flag Cache (8 readers, 1 refresher) ===");
        FeatureFlags flags = new FeatureFlags();
        AtomicInteger reads = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger halfApplied = new AtomicInteger();

        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(9)) {
            for (int r = 0; r < 8; r++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) {
                        boolean[] pair = flags.checkoutAndPayments();
                        if (pair[0] != pair[1]) {
                            halfApplied.incrementAndGet();
                        }
                        reads.incrementAndGet();
                    }
                });
            }
            ex.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
                    flags.refresh(i % 2 == 0);
                }
            });
        }
        System.out.println("Reads                  : " + reads.get());
        System.out.println("Refreshes              : " + flags.version());
        System.out.println("Half-applied flag pairs: " + halfApplied.get());
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS: Feature-Flag Cache (8 readers, 1 refresher) ===
Reads                  : 160000
Refreshes              : 200
Half-applied flag pairs: 0

Why a read-write lock here:

  • Read-mostly data (160,000 reads vs. 200 writes).
  • Writes update several fields that must change atomically together.
  • Readers don't block each other.

docs.title: Example 2: Optimistic Reads of a Driver's Position (Ride-hailing) — StampedLock
docs.text:
Scenario: A driver's latitude and longitude are updated every second and read constantly by the matching and ETA services. Even a read lock has a cost under heavy contention (readers update a shared counter). StampedLock's optimistic read takes no lock at all: read the fields, then validate that no write happened; only if one did, retry under a real read lock. Reading lat and lng from two different updates (a "torn" read) would put the driver in the sea.

Design:

flowchart TB
    A["stamp = tryOptimisticRead()"] --> B[read lat, lng into locals]
    B --> C{"validate(stamp)?"}
    C -->|yes, no write happened| D[use values: no locking at all]
    C -->|no| E["readLock(), re-read, unlockRead()"]
    E --> D

Full Code:

DriverLocation.javaLocationDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.location;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock;

/** A driver's position, updated every second, read thousands of times by matching and ETA services. */
public class DriverLocation {

    private final StampedLock lock = new StampedLock();
    private double lat = 12.9300;
    private double lng = 77.6200;
    private final AtomicLong fallbacks = new AtomicLong(); // many readers can be in the read lock at once

    public void move(double newLat, double newLng) {
        long stamp = lock.writeLock();
        try {
            lat = newLat;
            lng = newLng;
        } finally {
            lock.unlockWrite(stamp);
        }
    }

    /** Optimistic read: no locking at all unless a write happened meanwhile. */
    public double[] position() {
        long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead(); // (1)!
        double la = lat;
        double ln = lng;
        if (!lock.validate(stamp)) { // (2)!
            stamp = lock.readLock();
            try {
                fallbacks.incrementAndGet();
                la = lat;
                ln = lng;
            } finally {
                lock.unlockRead(stamp);
            }
        }
        return new double[] {la, ln};
    }

    public long fallbacks() {
        return fallbacks.get();
    }
}
  1. Optimistic read: returns a stamp without blocking anyone, including writers.
  2. Validate: if a write happened since the stamp, the values read may be inconsistent, so fall back to a real read lock. Copy fields into locals before validating, and only use them afterwards.
package com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.location;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class LocationDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: Optimistic Reads of a Driver's Position ===");
        DriverLocation driver = new DriverLocation();
        AtomicInteger torn = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger reads = new AtomicInteger();

        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5)) {
            ex.submit(() -> { // GPS updates: lat and lng always move together (lng = lat + 64.69)
                for (int i = 1; i <= 5_000; i++) {
                    double lat = 12.93 + i * 0.00001;
                    driver.move(lat, lat + 64.69);
                }
            });
            for (int r = 0; r < 4; r++) { // ETA and matching services
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 50_000; i++) {
                        double[] p = driver.position();
                        if (p[1] - p[0] < 64.68 || p[1] - p[0] > 64.70) {
                            torn.incrementAndGet();
                        }
                        reads.incrementAndGet();
                    }
                });
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Position reads       : " + reads.get());
        System.out.println("Torn (mixed) reads   : " + torn.get());
        System.out.println("Most reads lock-free : " + (driver.fallbacks() < reads.get()));
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: Optimistic Reads of a Driver's Position ===
Position reads       : 200000
Torn (mixed) reads   : 0
Most reads lock-free : true

Why StampedLock here:

  • Very read-heavy, small state (two numbers), short critical sections.
  • Optimistic reads avoid even shared-lock contention.
  • Validation guarantees no torn reads.

docs.title: Example 3: Hospital Bed Board (Healthcare) — downgrading, and why upgrading fails
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital's bed board is read by nurses' stations all day and updated on admissions. After admitting a patient, the admission desk prints the board, and that printout must reflect the admission without another admission sneaking in between. That's lock downgrading: hold the write lock, acquire the read lock, then release the write lock. The opposite, upgrading a read lock to a write lock, isn't supported by ReentrantReadWriteLock, and trying it with lock() deadlocks the thread.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> WriteLocked : writeLock()
    WriteLocked --> BothHeld : readLock() (allowed)
    BothHeld --> ReadLocked : unlock write (downgrade)
    ReadLocked --> [*] : unlock read
    state "Read lock held" as R
    [*] --> R : readLock()
    R --> R : writeLock() blocks forever (no upgrade)

Full Code:

BedBoard.javaBedsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.beds;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

/** Hospital bed board: nurses read it constantly; admissions update it. Shows downgrading. */
public class BedBoard {

    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final Map<String, String> beds = new TreeMap<>(Map.of("ICU-1", "free", "ICU-2", "P-1001", "WARD-7", "free"));

    /** Admit, then print the board WITHOUT letting another writer change it in between. */
    public String admitAndSnapshot(String bed, String patient) {
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            if (!"free".equals(beds.get(bed))) {
                return bed + " is occupied";
            }
            beds.put(bed, patient);
            lock.readLock().lock(); // (1)!
        } finally {
            lock.writeLock().unlock(); // (2)!
        }
        try {
            return "after admitting " + patient + ": " + beds;
        } finally {
            lock.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    /** The trap: trying to upgrade a read lock to a write lock. */
    public boolean tryUpgradeWhileReading() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try {
            return lock.writeLock().tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // (3)!
        } finally {
            lock.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }
}
  1. Downgrade, step 1: while holding the write lock, take the read lock (allowed, the lock is reentrant).
  2. Downgrade, step 2: release the write lock. Other readers can now proceed, but no writer can change the board until we release the read lock.
  3. No upgrade: a thread holding the read lock can never get the write lock (the write lock waits for all readers, including itself). tryLock with a timeout shows it; lock() would hang.
package com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.beds;

public class BedsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital: Bed Board ===");
        BedBoard board = new BedBoard();
        System.out.println(board.admitAndSnapshot("ICU-1", "P-2042"));
        System.out.println(board.admitAndSnapshot("ICU-2", "P-3001"));
        System.out.println("Upgrade read lock -> write lock succeeded? " + board.tryUpgradeWhileReading()
                + " (with lock() instead of tryLock() this thread would wait forever)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital: Bed Board ===
after admitting P-2042: {ICU-1=P-2042, ICU-2=P-1001, WARD-7=free}
ICU-2 is occupied
Upgrade read lock -> write lock succeeded? false (with lock() instead of tryLock() this thread would wait forever)

Why a read-write lock here:

  • Shows the two subtle rules interviewers ask about: downgrade OK, upgrade deadlocks.
  • Read-mostly shared state with occasional consistent updates.
Unit Tests: ReadWriteLockTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock;

import com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.beds.BedBoard;
import com.handbook.concurrency.rwlock.custom.SimpleReadWriteLock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Timeout;

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ReadWriteLockTest {

    @Test
    @Timeout(5)
    void readersShareTheLock() throws Exception {
        ReentrantReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
        CountDownLatch bothInside = new CountDownLatch(2);
        Runnable reader = () -> {
            lock.readLock().lock();
            try {
                bothInside.countDown();
                bothInside.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {
            } finally {
                lock.readLock().unlock();
            }
        };
        Thread a = Thread.ofVirtual().start(reader);
        Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().start(reader);
        assertThat(bothInside.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue(); // both readers held it at once
        a.join();
        b.join();
    }

    @Test
    void upgradeIsNotPossible() throws Exception {
        assertThat(new BedBoard().tryUpgradeWhileReading()).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    @Timeout(5)
    void customLockExcludesWritersFromReaders() throws Exception {
        SimpleReadWriteLock lock = new SimpleReadWriteLock();
        lock.lockRead();
        Thread writer = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
            try {
                lock.lockWrite();
                lock.unlockWrite();
            } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {
            }
        });
        writer.join(100);
        assertThat(writer.isAlive()).isTrue(); // blocked while a reader holds the lock
        lock.unlockRead();
        writer.join();
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Option Readers block? Writers Best for synchronized / ReentrantLock Yes, on each other Exclusive Small, balanced read/write workloads ReentrantReadWriteLock No (with each other) Exclusive Read-mostly, longer reads, multi-field updates StampedLock optimistic Never (optimistically) Exclusive Very read-heavy, tiny state, short reads Immutable snapshot + AtomicReference Never Copy + swap Read-mostly config/caches; see Immutable Object ConcurrentHashMap No Fine-grained Independent keys (no multi-key consistency needed) CopyOnWriteArrayList No Copy the whole list Tiny, rarely changed lists (listeners)

Fairness: new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true) grants locks roughly in arrival order (no writer starvation, lower throughput). The default non-fair mode can starve writers under a constant stream of readers.

Virtual threads: ReentrantReadWriteLock and StampedLock don't pin virtual threads (unlike synchronized before JDK 24), so they're good choices in virtual-thread code.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Usage JDK ReentrantReadWriteLock, StampedLock; ConcurrentHashMap (lock striping, lock-free reads) Caffeine / Guava caches Fine-grained, mostly lock-free reads Spring ConcurrentReferenceHashMap; singleton registries with read-mostly access Databases Shared (S) and exclusive (X) row/table locks; MVCC (readers don't block writers at all) Linux kernel rwlock_t, RCU (read-copy-update: the extreme "readers never wait" design)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Concurrent readers More overhead than a simple lock for short critical sections Atomic multi-field updates Writer starvation (non-fair mode) Downgrading for consistent read-after-write No upgrade: a classic deadlock source StampedLock: lock-free optimistic reads StampedLock isn't reentrant; misuse is easy

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Upgrading read → write

readLock().lock(); ... writeLock().lock(); deadlocks the thread. Release the read lock first, then take the write lock and re-check the condition (another writer may have acted in between).

Forgetting to unlock

Always lock(); try { ... } finally { unlock(); }. A missed unlock blocks writers forever.

Using a read-write lock for tiny critical sections

For a counter or a single field, AtomicLong/volatile or a plain lock is faster. Read-write locks pay off when reads are frequent and non-trivial.

StampedLock mistakes

Using values read optimistically before validating; calling methods that could throw on inconsistent data inside the optimistic section; trying to reenter (not supported).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Measure before choosing. Under low contention, synchronized is often fastest (biased-lock removal in JDK 15+ notwithstanding). Use JMH and JFR lock profiling. Read-write locks shine at high read concurrency with meaningful work per read.

Prefer designs that avoid locks. For read-mostly configuration, an immutable snapshot behind an AtomicReference gives wait-free reads and simple reasoning: build the new snapshot off to the side, then swap. That's MVCC/RCU in miniature.

Distributed equivalents. Across processes, read-write semantics show up as database row locks (SELECT ... FOR SHARE vs. FOR UPDATE), MVCC snapshot reads (Postgres readers never block writers), and leases. Distributed read-write locks (Redis/ZooKeeper) are rarely worth their complexity; prefer versioned data and optimistic concurrency (@Version).

War story: the cache refresh that froze checkout

A pricing cache used ReentrantReadWriteLock. The refresh job took the write lock and then called a remote pricing service (2–3 s) while holding it. Every checkout request blocked on the read lock for the duration. Under load, refreshes every 30 s caused a 3-second checkout freeze every 30 s. Fix: fetch and build the new price table outside the lock, then take the write lock only to swap a reference (microseconds), and later replace the lock entirely with an AtomicReference to an immutable snapshot. Lesson: never do I/O while holding a write lock. Prepare outside, swap inside.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Read-Write Lock Immutable Object Copy-on-Write Mutex (synchronized) Readers block? Only during writes Never Never Yes Writers Exclusive, in place Create new objects Copy, then swap Exclusive Memory In-place New objects per change Full copy per change In-place Best for Read-mostly, in-place updates Values, snapshots Small, rarely changed collections Simple or write-heavy

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Shared reads, exclusive writes: ReentrantReadWriteLock.
  • Downgrade OK, upgrade deadlocks.
  • StampedLock: optimistic reads + validate; not reentrant.
  • Never do I/O while holding a write lock.
  • Often better: immutable snapshot + AtomicReference.
lock.readLock().lock(); try { return read(); } finally { lock.readLock().unlock(); }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Replace FeatureFlags' lock with an immutable Map in an AtomicReference and compare the code.
  • Make the flag refresh fetch new values from a (fake) slow service outside the write lock.
  • Benchmark synchronized vs ReentrantReadWriteLock vs StampedLock with JMH at 1, 4 and 16 reader threads.

Future / Promise Next: Immutable Object

docs.title: Thread Pool
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A thread pool keeps a fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue, instead of creating a thread per task. It caps concurrency, reuses threads, and gives you a policy for overload (queue, reject, or run in the caller). In Java: ThreadPoolExecutor. With Java 21, use pools for CPU-bound work and bulkheads, and virtual threads for blocking I/O.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: creating a platform thread costs memory (around 1 MB of stack) and time. A server that starts new Thread() for every request runs out of memory under load. Even with enough memory, 2,000 CPU-heavy threads on an 8-core machine just fight over the CPU. A pool limits how many tasks run at once and queues the rest.

Definition:

Maintain a pool of reusable worker threads consuming tasks from a shared queue. The pool's size, its queue, and its rejection policy determine behavior under load.

It's a specialized Producer-Consumer: submit() produces tasks; workers consume them.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A bank with four tellers

Customers take a token and wait in the lobby (the queue). Four tellers (worker threads) serve one customer at a time. The bank doesn't hire a new teller per customer. When the lobby is full, the guard asks new customers to come back later (rejection policy).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C1[Caller] -->|submit| Q[("Work queue<br/>(bounded)")]
    C2[Caller] -->|submit| Q
    Q --> W1[Worker 1]
    Q --> W2[Worker 2]
    Q --> W3[Worker N]
    Q -. full and max threads busy .-> R{{Rejection policy}}

How ThreadPoolExecutor decides what to do with a new task (a classic interview question):

flowchart TD
    S[submit task] --> A{running threads < corePoolSize?}
    A -->|yes| N1[start a new core thread]
    A -->|no| B{queue has space?}
    B -->|yes| QU[enqueue]
    B -->|no| C{running threads < maximumPoolSize?}
    C -->|yes| N2[start a non-core thread]
    C -->|no| R[RejectedExecutionHandler]
Rejection policy Behavior AbortPolicy (default) Throws RejectedExecutionException CallerRunsPolicy Runs the task on the submitting thread, which slows submitters (natural back-pressure) DiscardPolicy Silently drops the task (dangerous) DiscardOldestPolicy Drops the oldest queued task and retries

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
for (Request r : incoming) {
    new Thread(() -> handle(r)).start();   // 10,000 requests = 10,000 threads
}
// or the opposite mistake:
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);          // unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue inside!
Executors.newCachedThreadPool();           // unbounded number of threads!
  • Unbounded threads: memory exhaustion, context-switch thrashing.
  • Unbounded queues hidden in Executors factory methods: tasks pile up until OOM.
  • No overload policy, no names, no metrics.

docs.title: Example 1: Generating Thumbnails (E-commerce) — CPU-bound pool
docs.text:
Scenario: When sellers upload product photos, the catalog service generates thumbnails. Resizing is CPU-bound, so running more threads than cores only adds context switching. The pool is sized to the number of cores, has a bounded queue, named threads (so profilers and thread dumps make sense), and CallerRunsPolicy so that, if uploads outpace resizing, the uploading thread does some work itself and naturally slows down.

Design:

flowchart LR
    U[Upload handler] -->|invokeAll 40 jobs| P["ThreadPoolExecutor<br/>core = max = #cores<br/>queue = 100<br/>CallerRunsPolicy"]
    P --> T1[resizer-1]
    P --> T2[resizer-2]
    P --> TN[resizer-N]

Full Code:

ImageResizeDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.threadpool.images;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** CPU-bound work: a pool sized to the number of cores, with a bounded queue. */
public class ImageResizeDemo {

    static int resize(int width) { // stand-in for CPU-heavy pixel work
        long checksum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) {
            checksum += (i * 31L) ^ width;
        }
        return checksum != 0 ? width / 4 : 0; // the thumbnail width
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Generating Thumbnails for 40 Product Images ===");
        int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
        AtomicInteger threadNo = new AtomicInteger();
        ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                cores, cores,                                    // (1)!
                0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),                   // (2)!
                r -> new Thread(r, "resizer-" + threadNo.incrementAndGet()), // (3)!
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());      // (4)!

        List<Callable<Integer>> jobs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
            int width = 2_000 + i * 40;
            jobs.add(() -> resize(width));
        }
        int totalThumbWidth = 0;
        for (Future<Integer> f : pool.invokeAll(jobs)) { // waits for all
            totalThumbWidth += f.get();
        }
        pool.shutdown();
        System.out.println("Images resized          : " + jobs.size());
        System.out.println("Sum of thumbnail widths : " + totalThumbWidth);
        System.out.println("Threads never exceeded cores: " + (pool.getLargestPoolSize() <= cores));
        System.out.println("Pool terminated cleanly : " + pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
    }
}
  1. For CPU-bound work, threads ≈ number of cores. More threads don't make the CPU faster.
  2. A bounded queue, unlike Executors.newFixedThreadPool, which uses an unbounded one.
  3. A ThreadFactory that names threads. In a thread dump, "resizer-3" is far more useful than "pool-7-thread-3".
  4. CallerRunsPolicy: when saturated, the submitting thread runs the task, which throttles submission. No task is lost.

Output:

=== E-commerce: Generating Thumbnails for 40 Product Images ===
Images resized          : 40
Sum of thumbnail widths : 27800
Threads never exceeded cores: true
Pool terminated cleanly : true

Why a thread pool here:

  • CPU-bound work needs a cap equal to cores, not more threads.
  • invokeAll waits for a batch and returns results in submission order.
  • Explicit construction makes size, queue and overload policy visible in code review.

docs.title: Example 2: Report Generation Under Load (Banking) — saturation and rejection
docs.text:
Scenario: Customers download account statements as PDFs. Each report hits a slow reporting database. The service allows 2 concurrent reports and 2 waiting; beyond that it rejects quickly with HTTP 429 instead of queueing for minutes and timing out everywhere. The demo holds the first reports "in progress" with a latch so the saturation point is visible and deterministic.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Customers
    participant P as Pool (2 threads, queue 2, AbortPolicy)
    C->>P: STMT-1, STMT-2
    Note over P: both running
    C->>P: STMT-3, STMT-4
    Note over P: queued
    C->>P: STMT-5
    P-->>C: RejectedExecutionException, HTTP 429
    C->>P: STMT-6
    P-->>C: HTTP 429

Full Code:

ReportServiceDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.threadpool.reports;

import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Saturation made visible: 2 workers + 2 queue slots; the 5th and 6th requests are rejected. */
public class ReportServiceDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Statement Report Generation Under Load ===");
        CountDownLatch slowDatabase = new CountDownLatch(1); // holds the first reports "in progress"
        AtomicInteger finished = new AtomicInteger();
        ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2), new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); // (1)!

        for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
            String report = "STMT-" + i;
            try {
                pool.execute(() -> {
                    try {
                        slowDatabase.await();
                        finished.incrementAndGet();
                    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                    }
                });
                System.out.printf("%s accepted (running=%d, queued=%d)%n", report,
                        Math.min(pool.getPoolSize(), 2), pool.getQueue().size());
            } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
                System.out.println(report + " REJECTED -> HTTP 429, please retry in a minute"); // (2)!
            }
        }
        slowDatabase.countDown();
        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println("Reports completed: " + finished.get());
    }
}
  1. Fixed size + small bounded queue + AbortPolicy: the service promises a maximum amount of work in flight.
  2. Rejection becomes a fast, honest answer to the client. Failing fast protects the database and keeps latency predictable for accepted requests.

Output:

=== Banking: Statement Report Generation Under Load ===
STMT-1 accepted (running=1, queued=0)
STMT-2 accepted (running=2, queued=0)
STMT-3 accepted (running=2, queued=1)
STMT-4 accepted (running=2, queued=2)
STMT-5 REJECTED -> HTTP 429, please retry in a minute
STMT-6 REJECTED -> HTTP 429, please retry in a minute
Reports completed: 4

Why a thread pool here:

  • The pool size is the concurrency limit the slow database can handle.
  • The queue bound limits waiting time; the rejection policy defines overload behavior.
  • Everything is configurable and measurable (active count, queue size, rejections).

docs.title: Example 3: Per-Tenant Bulkheads (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: A B2B SaaS lets tenants export data. One tenant, "acme", schedules 10 huge exports at once. With a single shared pool, acme would fill every thread and the queue, and every other tenant's exports would wait or fail. With a small pool per tenant (a bulkhead, named after ship compartments), acme can only exhaust its own capacity; "globex" is unaffected.

Design:

flowchart LR
    A[acme: 10 huge exports] --> PA["acme pool<br/>2 threads + 2 queue"]
    PA -->|6 rejected| X[429]
    G[globex: 1 export] --> PG["globex pool<br/>2 threads + 2 queue"]
    PG --> OK[done immediately]

Full Code:

BulkheadDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.threadpool.bulkhead;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

/** One small pool per tenant: a noisy tenant can exhaust only its own capacity. */
public class BulkheadDemo {

    static ExecutorService tenantPool() {
        return new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS: Per-Tenant Bulkheads for Data Exports ===");
        Map<String, ExecutorService> pools = Map.of("acme", tenantPool(), "globex", tenantPool());
        CountDownLatch acmeHugeExports = new CountDownLatch(1);

        int acmeRejected = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { // acme floods the system with huge exports
            try {
                pools.get("acme").submit(() -> { acmeHugeExports.await(); return null; });
            } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
                acmeRejected++;
            }
        }
        System.out.println("acme: 10 huge exports requested, " + acmeRejected + " rejected (its bulkhead is full)");

        Future<String> globex = pools.get("globex").submit(() -> "invoice export done"); // (1)!
        System.out.println("globex: " + globex.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) + " (unaffected by acme)");

        acmeHugeExports.countDown();
        for (ExecutorService p : pools.values()) {
            p.shutdown();
            p.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        }
        System.out.println("all pools shut down");
    }
}
  1. globex's task runs on its own threads, so acme's saturation can't delay it.

Output:

=== SaaS: Per-Tenant Bulkheads for Data Exports ===
acme: 10 huge exports requested, 6 rejected (its bulkhead is full)
globex: invoice export done (unaffected by acme)
all pools shut down

Why a thread pool here:

  • Isolation: one tenant, endpoint or dependency can't starve the others.
  • This is the Bulkhead resilience pattern (Resilience4j has ThreadPoolBulkhead).
  • With many tenants, use pools per tier or semaphores per tenant instead of a pool each.
Unit Tests: ThreadPoolTest.java (examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.concurrency.threadpool;

import com.handbook.concurrency.threadpool.custom.SimpleThreadPool;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Timeout;

import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ThreadPoolTest {

    @Test
    @Timeout(5)
    void saturatedPoolRejectsWithAbortPolicy() throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch block = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(1, 1, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1));
        pool.execute(() -> { try { block.await(); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } });
        pool.execute(() -> { });
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> pool.execute(() -> { })).isInstanceOf(RejectedExecutionException.class);
        block.countDown();
        pool.shutdown();
        assertThat(pool.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue();
    }

    @Test
    @Timeout(5)
    void callerRunsPolicyRunsTaskOnSubmittingThread() throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch block = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(1, 1, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        pool.execute(() -> { try { block.await(); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } });
        pool.execute(() -> { });
        String[] ranOn = new String[1];
        pool.execute(() -> ranOn[0] = Thread.currentThread().getName());
        assertThat(ranOn[0]).isEqualTo(Thread.currentThread().getName());
        block.countDown();
        pool.shutdown();
    }

    @Test
    @Timeout(5)
    void simplePoolCompletesQueuedWorkBeforeShutdown() throws Exception {
        SimpleThreadPool pool = new SimpleThreadPool(2, 100);
        AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger();
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
            pool.execute(n::incrementAndGet);
        }
        pool.shutdownAndWait();
        assertThat(n).hasValue(100);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Executor Use for Watch out new ThreadPoolExecutor(...) Production pools: explicit size, bounded queue, policy, names More code, but every choice is visible Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) Quick demos Unbounded queue Executors.newCachedThreadPool() Short, bursty tasks Unbounded threads Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n) Delayed and periodic tasks Exceptions silently cancel periodic tasks; catch them ForkJoinPool / parallelStream() Divide-and-conquer CPU work Common pool is shared JVM-wide; don't block in it Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() (Java 21) Blocking I/O tasks: one cheap virtual thread per task Not a pool. Limit resources (connections, semaphores), not threads

Sizing rules of thumb:

  • CPU-bound: threads ≈ cores (maybe cores + 1).
  • I/O-bound (platform threads): threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait time / compute time). In Java 21, prefer virtual threads for this instead of huge pools.
  • Then measure: CPU utilization, queue wait time, latency percentiles.

Always shut down executors (or use try-with-resources: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since Java 19). Non-daemon pool threads keep the JVM alive.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Pool Tomcat / Jetty Request-handling thread pools (server.tomcat.threads.max); virtual threads with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true Spring ThreadPoolTaskExecutor for @Async; ThreadPoolTaskScheduler for @Scheduled Spring Boot Auto-configured task executor (spring.task.execution.pool.*) Resilience4j ThreadPoolBulkhead Kafka clients Consumer threads per partition assignment JDK ForkJoinPool.commonPool() behind parallel streams and CompletableFuture.*Async (default) Netty Event loop groups (a small, fixed number of threads)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Caps concurrency and memory Wrong sizing means idle CPUs or overload Reuses threads (no creation cost per task) Tasks queue up and latency grows when saturated Explicit overload policy Thread-local state leaks between tasks on reused threads Isolation via bulkheads Deadlocks if tasks wait for other tasks in the same full pool Metrics: active, queued, completed, rejected Platform threads blocked on I/O waste the pool (use virtual threads)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Unbounded queues from Executors factories

newFixedThreadPool and newSingleThreadExecutor use unbounded queues: overload becomes an OutOfMemoryError an hour later. Construct ThreadPoolExecutor explicitly with a bounded queue.

Thread-pool deadlock

A task submits a sub-task to the same bounded pool and waits for it. If all threads do this, none are free to run sub-tasks, and everything hangs. Use separate pools, ForkJoinPool for recursive work, or non-blocking composition.

Swallowed exceptions

Exceptions in tasks submitted with submit() are captured in the Future; if nobody calls get(), they vanish. Log inside tasks, or use execute() with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. For scheduled tasks, an exception cancels all future runs.

ThreadLocal leaks

Pool threads live forever; a ThreadLocal set by one task (a user ID, a tenant) is visible to the next task on that thread unless removed in finally.

Blocking the common pool

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> blockingCall()) without an executor runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which is sized for CPU work and shared by the whole JVM. Pass your own executor for blocking work (or use virtual threads).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Little's Law for pools. Required concurrency = throughput × latency. At 400 requests/s with 50 ms each, you need about 20 concurrent workers. If downstream latency jumps to 500 ms, you suddenly need 200, and if the pool has 20, the queue grows without bound. This is why timeouts on downstream calls matter as much as pool size.

Virtual threads change the picture. For I/O-bound request handling, Java 21 virtual threads remove the need for large platform-thread pools: create one per request and limit the scarce resources (DB connections, downstream concurrency) with pools and semaphores. Keep platform-thread pools for CPU-bound work and for bulkheads where you want a hard cap.

Observability. Export pool metrics (Micrometer ExecutorServiceMetrics): active threads, queue size, task wait time, rejections. Alert on queue wait time, not just queue length.

Graceful shutdown. On deploy: stop accepting new tasks (shutdown()), wait for in-flight work with a deadline (awaitTermination), then shutdownNow() and log what was dropped. Spring Boot's graceful shutdown coordinates this.

War story: the @Async that ate the heap

An order service sent confirmation emails with @Async. Spring's default executor at the time used an unbounded queue. The email provider slowed to 10 s per call during an outage; emails queued in memory, 1.2 million tasks and 6 GB later, the service died, and the queued emails were lost. Fix: an explicit ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (core 10, max 20, queue 1,000, CallerRunsPolicy), a 3 s timeout on the email client, and email moved to a durable queue (outbox + worker) so a crash loses nothing. Lesson: every executor has a queue. If you didn't choose its size, you chose "until OOM".

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Thread Pool Object Pool Producer-Consumer Virtual Threads Pools Threads (workers) Resources (connections) N/A (a queue between roles) Nothing: threads are cheap Caps Concurrent tasks Concurrent resource users Queue length Nothing by default; add semaphores Best for CPU-bound work, bulkheads Expensive, limited resources Decoupling rates Blocking I/O at high concurrency

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Reusable workers + task queue = capped concurrency.
  • Order: core threads → queue → extra threads up to max → rejection policy.
  • Production: explicit ThreadPoolExecutor, bounded queue, named threads, chosen policy, metrics.
  • CPU-bound: threads ≈ cores. Blocking I/O in Java 21: virtual threads.
  • Beware: unbounded queues, swallowed exceptions, same-pool deadlock, ThreadLocal leaks.
new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100), namedFactory, new CallerRunsPolicy());

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add Micrometer-style counters (submitted, completed, rejected) to the report pool.
  • Reproduce a thread-pool deadlock with a 2-thread pool, then fix it with a second pool.
  • Make the bulkhead per plan tier (free, pro, enterprise) instead of per tenant.

Producer-Consumer Next: Future / Promise

docs.title: Virtual Threads
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Virtual threads (Java 21, Project Loom) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM. You can have millions, and blocking one costs almost nothing. Write simple thread-per-task, blocking code for I/O-heavy workloads and get the scalability of async code. Limit scarce resources (connections, downstream calls) with semaphores and pools, not by limiting threads.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a checkout page checks delivery availability for 2,000 pincodes, each a 100 ms network call. With a pool of 50 platform threads, that's 40 rounds of 100 ms, about 4 seconds, while the CPU sits idle because threads are just waiting on the network. You could rewrite everything with CompletableFuture or reactive streams, but that code is harder to read, debug and profile. Virtual threads let blocking code scale: each call gets its own cheap thread, and the whole batch finishes in roughly 100 ms.

Definition (JEP 444, final in Java 21):

Virtual threads are lightweight threads that dramatically reduce the effort of writing, maintaining, and observing high-throughput concurrent applications. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier (platform) thread, which immediately runs another virtual thread.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Restaurant waiters and order tickets

Platform threads are like waiters who stand at the kitchen window waiting for each dish: you can only serve as many tables as you have waiters. Virtual threads are like order tickets: a few waiters (carrier threads) handle thousands of tickets, picking up whichever dish is ready. Waiting costs nothing because a ticket, not a person, does the waiting.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph JVM
        V1[Virtual thread 1] -.mounted.-> C1[Carrier thread 1]
        V2[Virtual thread 2] -.mounted.-> C2[Carrier thread 2]
        V3[Virtual thread 3<br/>blocked on I/O, unmounted, stack in heap]
        V4[Virtual thread 4<br/>waiting to run]
        V5[... 1,000,000 more]
    end
    C1 --> OS1[OS thread]
    C2 --> OS2[OS thread]
Concept Meaning Virtual thread A java.lang.Thread scheduled by the JVM; its stack lives on the heap and grows as needed Carrier thread A platform thread (from a ForkJoinPool, about one per core) that runs virtual threads Mount / unmount Blocking I/O, sleep, BlockingQueue.take, locks: the virtual thread is unmounted, freeing the carrier Pinning A virtual thread that can't unmount (inside synchronized before JDK 24, or native frames), which blocks its carrier

Creating them:

Thread.ofVirtual().name("worker-", 0).start(task);          // one thread
Thread.startVirtualThread(task);                           // shortcut
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { ex.submit(task); }  // one per task

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);   // 50 threads mostly waiting on the network
// to go faster: 2,000 platform threads? ~2 GB of stacks, heavy context switching.
// or rewrite everything as CompletableFuture/reactive chains: hard to read and debug.
  • Thread pools cap throughput for I/O-bound work (Little's Law: concurrency = throughput × latency).
  • Huge platform-thread pools waste memory and CPU on context switches.
  • Async rewrites fragment stack traces and complicate error handling.

docs.title: Example 1: Availability Fan-Out (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: A seller dashboard checks whether 2,000 pincodes are serviceable by calling an availability service (100 ms per call). The current implementation uses a fixed pool of 50 platform threads. Switching to virtual threads changes one line and the same blocking code finishes about 25× faster. Results must be identical.

Design:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Pool["Fixed pool: 50 platform threads"]
        P["2,000 tasks / 50 = 40 rounds x 100 ms = ~4 s"]
    end
    subgraph VT["Virtual thread per task"]
        V["2,000 virtual threads blocking at once = ~0.1-0.3 s"]
    end

Full Code:

AvailabilityDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.virtualthreads.fanout;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** 2,000 blocking calls to a pincode-availability service, 100 ms each. */
public class AvailabilityDemo {

    static boolean available(int pincode) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(100); // blocking I/O: an HTTP call to the availability service
        return pincode % 7 != 0;
    }

    static long run(ExecutorService executor, AtomicInteger availableCount) {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try (executor) { // (1)!
            for (int i = 0; i < 2_000; i++) {
                int pincode = 560_000 + i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    if (available(pincode)) {
                        availableCount.incrementAndGet();
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }
        }
        return Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - start).toMillis();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Checking Delivery Availability for 2,000 Pincodes ===");
        AtomicInteger platformCount = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger virtualCount = new AtomicInteger();

        long platformMs = run(Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50), platformCount);       // (2)!
        long virtualMs = run(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), virtualCount); // (3)!

        System.out.println("Serviceable pincodes (both runs agree): " + (platformCount.get() == virtualCount.get())
                + ", " + virtualCount.get() + " of 2000");
        System.out.println("50 platform threads took about 4 s       : " + (platformMs >= 3_500));
        System.out.println("Virtual threads finished in under 1.5 s  : " + (virtualMs < 1_500));
        System.out.println("Virtual threads at least 5x faster       : " + (platformMs >= 5 * virtualMs));
    }
}
  1. ExecutorService is AutoCloseable (Java 19+): leaving the try waits for all submitted tasks.
  2. 50 platform threads: at most 50 calls in flight.
  3. One virtual thread per task: all 2,000 calls in flight at once. Same task code.

Output:

=== E-commerce: Checking Delivery Availability for 2,000 Pincodes ===
Serviceable pincodes (both runs agree): true, 1714 of 2000
50 platform threads took about 4 s       : true
Virtual threads finished in under 1.5 s  : true
Virtual threads at least 5x faster       : true

(Timing results are printed as true/false checks so the output is stable across machines.)

Why virtual threads here:

  • I/O-bound work: threads spend almost all their time waiting.
  • The code stays blocking and simple; only the executor changes.
  • Throughput is bounded by the remote service, not by an artificial thread count.

docs.title: Example 2: Protecting the Core Banking System (Banking) — Semaphore
docs.text:
Scenario: A mobile banking backend serves 1,000 concurrent balance requests on virtual threads. The core banking system (a mainframe) accepts at most 20 concurrent connections from this service. With platform-thread pools, the pool size used to be the limit by accident; with virtual threads, there is no natural limit, so the limit must be explicit: a Semaphore with 20 permits.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant V as 1,000 virtual threads
    participant S as Semaphore(20)
    participant M as Core banking (max 20)
    V->>S: acquire()
    S-->>V: 20 granted, 980 wait (cheaply, unmounted)
    V->>M: balance calls (20 at a time)
    V->>S: release()
    S-->>V: next waiting thread proceeds

Full Code:

CoreBankingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.virtualthreads.semaphore;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Threads are cheap now; the core banking system is not. Limit the RESOURCE, not the threads. */
public class CoreBankingDemo {

    private static final Semaphore CORE_BANKING_SLOTS = new Semaphore(20); // (1)!
    private static final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger();
    private static final AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger();

    static long balance(String account) throws InterruptedException {
        CORE_BANKING_SLOTS.acquire(); // (2)!
        try {
            peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max);
            Thread.sleep(20); // mainframe round trip
            return 10_000 + account.hashCode() % 1_000;
        } finally {
            inFlight.decrementAndGet();
            CORE_BANKING_SLOTS.release();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: 1,000 Balance Checks, at Most 20 at the Core Banking System ===");
        AtomicInteger done = new AtomicInteger();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                String account = "SB-" + (1_000 + i);
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    balance(account);
                    done.incrementAndGet();
                    return null;
                });
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Virtual threads started  : 1000");
        System.out.println("Balance checks completed : " + done.get());
        System.out.println("Peak concurrent mainframe calls <= 20: " + (peak.get() <= 20));
        System.out.println("Limit was actually reached: " + (peak.get() == 20));
    }
}
  1. The resource limit, made explicit. With virtual threads, "limit concurrency" means semaphores, connection pools and bulkheads around the scarce thing.
  2. Waiting on a semaphore unmounts the virtual thread, so 980 waiting threads cost a few KB each, not 980 MB.

Output:

=== Banking: 1,000 Balance Checks, at Most 20 at the Core Banking System ===
Virtual threads started  : 1000
Balance checks completed : 1000
Peak concurrent mainframe calls <= 20: true
Limit was actually reached: true

Why virtual threads + semaphore here:

  • Many cheap threads for requests, few permits for the fragile downstream.
  • Back-pressure is explicit and easy to tune.
  • The same idea applies to JDBC: the connection pool (e.g. HikariCP with 20 connections) is the real limit.

docs.title: Example 3: 10,000 Live Tracking Sessions (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: During the evening peak, 10,000 customers watch their delivery on a tracking page. Each session waits for the next status update. With one virtual thread per session blocked on its own queue, the code is a simple loop ("wait for update, push it"), with no callbacks, and the JVM holds 10,000 blocked threads at negligible cost.

Design:

flowchart LR
    D[Dispatch system] -->|"put(update)"| Q1[inbox 1]
    D --> Q2[inbox 2]
    D --> QN[inbox 10,000]
    Q1 -->|"take() blocks cheaply"| S1[session thread 1]
    Q2 --> S2[session thread 2]
    QN --> SN[session thread 10,000]

Full Code:

TrackingSessionsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.virtualthreads.sessions;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** 10,000 customers watching their delivery: one blocked virtual thread per session. */
public class TrackingSessionsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: 10,000 Live Tracking Sessions ===");
        int sessions = 10_000;
        List<BlockingQueue<String>> inboxes = new ArrayList<>();
        CountDownLatch allWaiting = new CountDownLatch(sessions);
        AtomicInteger delivered = new AtomicInteger();

        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < sessions; i++) {
                BlockingQueue<String> inbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1);
                inboxes.add(inbox);
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    allWaiting.countDown();
                    String update = inbox.take(); // (1)!
                    if (update.startsWith("OUT_FOR_DELIVERY")) {
                        delivered.incrementAndGet(); // would push to the customer's WebSocket
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }
            allWaiting.await();
            System.out.println("Sessions blocked waiting for updates: " + sessions);
