            for (BlockingQueue<String> inbox : inboxes) {
                inbox.put("OUT_FOR_DELIVERY rider 1.2 km away");
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Sessions that received their update : " + delivered.get());
        System.out.println("Platform threads that would need    : " + sessions + " x ~1 MB stack");
    }
}
  1. A blocking take() in 10,000 threads at once. With platform threads that's around 10 GB of reserved stack; with virtual threads it's a few MB of heap.

Output:

=== Logistics: 10,000 Live Tracking Sessions ===
Sessions blocked waiting for updates: 10000
Sessions that received their update : 10000
Platform threads that would need    : 10000 x ~1 MB stack

Why virtual threads here:

  • Massive concurrency of mostly idle, waiting tasks.
  • Sequential, readable per-session logic instead of callback state machines.
  • Plays well with blocking APIs (BlockingQueue, sockets, JDBC).
Unit Tests: VirtualThreadsTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.virtualthreads;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Timeout;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class VirtualThreadsTest {

    @Test
    void virtualThreadsAreDaemonAndVirtual() throws Exception {
        Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-1").start(() -> { });
        t.join();
        assertThat(t.isVirtual()).isTrue();
        assertThat(t.isDaemon()).isTrue();
        assertThat(t.getName()).isEqualTo("vt-1");
    }

    @Test
    @Timeout(10)
    void tenThousandBlockingTasksFinishQuickly() {
        AtomicInteger done = new AtomicInteger();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
                ex.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(200); done.incrementAndGet(); return null; });
            }
        }
        assertThat(done).hasValue(10_000);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Feature Status Notes Virtual threads Final in Java 21 Thread.ofVirtual(), Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() synchronized pinning fixed JDK 24 (JEP 491) Before 24, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier; prefer ReentrantLock on 21–23 Structured concurrency Preview (JDK 21–25) StructuredTaskScope: fork subtasks, cancel siblings on failure, join as a unit Scoped values Preview (JDK 21–24), final in JDK 25 Immutable, inheritable context (a ThreadLocal replacement for virtual threads) Spring Boot 3.2+ spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true Tomcat/Jetty request handling and @Async on virtual threads

When NOT to use virtual threads: CPU-bound work (no benefit, use a pool sized to cores), code that relies heavily on ThreadLocal caches (each virtual thread gets its own, so millions of copies), and long blocking inside synchronized on JDK 21–23 (pinning).

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Support Spring Boot 3.2+ spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true for web servers, @Async, schedulers, Kafka/Rabbit listeners Tomcat / Jetty / Undertow / Helidon Níma Virtual-thread request handling (Helidon 4 is built on them) Quarkus @RunOnVirtualThread JDBC drivers Work unchanged; recent versions replaced synchronized to avoid pinning java.net.http.HttpClient, sockets, BlockingQueue, ReentrantLock Virtual-thread friendly (unmount on block)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Millions of threads; blocking is cheap No speed-up for CPU-bound work Simple blocking code with real stack traces Pinning (JDK 21–23 synchronized, native calls) can block carriers One-line migration from pools in many cases Unlimited concurrency can overwhelm downstreams: add explicit limits Great observability (jcmd Thread.dump_to_file shows virtual threads) ThreadLocal-heavy libraries can use lots of memory Works with existing APIs Pooling virtual threads is an anti-pattern (they're meant to be disposable)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Removing the only limit on a fragile downstream

A pool of 200 platform threads was an accidental cap on database load. With virtual threads, 10,000 requests can hit the database at once. Add explicit limits: connection pools, semaphores, bulkheads (Example 2).

Pinning on JDK 21–23

Blocking I/O inside synchronized keeps the carrier thread busy. With few carriers (one per core), a handful of pinned threads can stall the whole application. Use ReentrantLock, upgrade to JDK 24+, and detect with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full (JDK 21–23) or JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event.

Pooling virtual threads

Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) brings back the limits virtual threads were meant to remove. Create one per task; limit resources instead.

ThreadLocal caches

Libraries that cache expensive objects in ThreadLocal (formatters, buffers) assumed few long-lived threads. With a million short-lived virtual threads, those caches are recreated constantly and multiplied. Use shared thread-safe objects or ScopedValue.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Little's Law, revisited. Concurrency needed = throughput × latency. At 5,000 requests/s with 200 ms of I/O wait each, you need about 1,000 concurrent requests. Platform threads make that expensive; virtual threads make it trivial. The bottleneck moves to downstream capacity, which you must now manage explicitly (pools, semaphores, rate limiters, circuit breakers).

Migration strategy. (1) Upgrade to a recent JDK (24+ removes most pinning concerns). (2) Enable virtual threads in the web server. (3) Find and size resource limits (DB pool, HTTP client connection pool, semaphores per downstream). (4) Watch for pinning and ThreadLocal memory with JFR. (5) Load test; compare p99 latency and throughput against the old pools.

Virtual threads vs. reactive. Reactive stacks (WebFlux, Reactor) solved the same scalability problem with non-blocking I/O and back-pressure. With virtual threads, most request/response services can go back to blocking, imperative code. Reactive still makes sense for streaming with back-pressure and for teams already invested in it.

War story: virtual threads and the database meltdown

A team enabled virtual threads in a Spring Boot service and celebrated the load test: 6× throughput. In production, the first traffic spike opened 4,000 concurrent queries against Postgres. The old Tomcat pool (200 threads) had silently limited database concurrency; virtual threads removed that limit. The HikariCP pool was set to 500 connections "to be safe", so the database hit max_connections and started refusing everyone. Fix: HikariCP sized to what the database can handle (40 connections per pod, with a short connection timeout), a semaphore bulkhead around a heavy reporting query, and load tests against a production-sized database. Lesson: virtual threads remove the thread limit, so every other limit must now be deliberate.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Virtual threads Thread pool (platform) CompletableFuture / reactive Programming style Blocking, sequential Blocking, sequential Callbacks / operators Scales for I/O waits ✅ millions ❌ limited by pool size ✅ CPU-bound work No benefit ✅ sized to cores No benefit Debugging Normal stack traces Normal stack traces Fragmented traces Concurrency limit Must be explicit (semaphores, pools) Pool size Operators / back-pressure

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Cheap JVM-managed threads (Java 21): one per task, blocking is fine.
  • Great for I/O-bound concurrency; no benefit for CPU-bound work.
  • Limit resources, not threads: semaphores, connection pools, bulkheads.
  • Watch pinning (synchronized on JDK 21–23) and ThreadLocal memory.
  • Don't pool them. Spring Boot: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (var t : tasks) ex.submit(t); }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a JDBC-style connection pool (an ArrayBlockingQueue of 10 fake connections) to the banking example instead of a semaphore.
  • Reproduce pinning on JDK 21 with synchronized + Thread.sleep and observe it with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full.
  • Rewrite ProfilePageDemo with StructuredTaskScope (enable preview features).

Double-Checked Locking Next: Microservices

docs.title: Creational Patterns
docs.text:
Creational patterns answer one question: who creates an object, when, and how? They separate using an object from constructing it, so the rest of your code doesn't depend on concrete classes or complicated set-up steps.

Pattern Problem it solves Interview frequency Status Singleton Exactly one shared instance (config, ID generator, registry) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Factory Method Let subclasses or a method decide which class to instantiate ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Abstract Factory Create families of related objects that work together ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Builder Build complex or immutable objects step by step ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Prototype Create new objects by copying a configured one ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Object Pool Reuse expensive objects (connections, buffers) ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ 
flowchart TD
    Q1{Need exactly one<br/>shared instance?} -->|Yes| S[Singleton]
    Q1 -->|No| Q2{Object has many optional<br/>parameters or must be immutable?}
    Q2 -->|Yes| B[Builder]
    Q2 -->|No| Q3{Which concrete class<br/>is decided at runtime?}
    Q3 -->|One product| F[Factory Method]
    Q3 -->|A family of products| AF[Abstract Factory]
    Q3 -->|No| Q4{Creating is expensive and<br/>a copy would do?}
    Q4 -->|Copy a template| P[Prototype]
    Q4 -->|Reuse instances| OP[Object Pool]

docs.title: Abstract Factory
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Creational Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Abstract Factory creates whole families of related objects that are designed to work together, without naming their concrete classes. Use it when several objects must always match (same cloud, same country, same device) and you want to switch the whole family by changing one object.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a grocery checkout needs a tax policy, a price formatter and delivery rules. In India that's GST, INR 182.50 and 10-minute delivery. In Germany it's VAT (MwSt), 53,50 EUR and a 2-hour slot. If each piece is chosen separately, sooner or later someone combines German tax with Indian formatting, and customers see wrong prices.

Formal definition (GoF):

Provide an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.

The key word is families. Factory Method answers "which class?" for one product. Abstract Factory answers "which family?" for several products at once, and guarantees they're consistent.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
IKEA furniture collections

You furnish a room from one collection, say "Scandinavian Oak". You ask for a chair, a table and a sofa, and they all match. Switch to the "Industrial Metal" collection and you get a different chair, table and sofa that match each other. You never end up with an oak chair next to a metal table, because you choose the collection once, not each item.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class AbstractFactory {
        <<interface>>
        +createProductA() ProductA
        +createProductB() ProductB
    }
    class ConcreteFactory1
    class ConcreteFactory2
    class ProductA {
        <<interface>>
    }
    class ProductB {
        <<interface>>
    }
    class ProductA1
    class ProductA2
    class ProductB1
    class ProductB2
    class Client
    AbstractFactory <|.. ConcreteFactory1
    AbstractFactory <|.. ConcreteFactory2
    ProductA <|.. ProductA1
    ProductA <|.. ProductA2
    ProductB <|.. ProductB1
    ProductB <|.. ProductB2
    ConcreteFactory1 ..> ProductA1 : creates
    ConcreteFactory1 ..> ProductB1 : creates
    ConcreteFactory2 ..> ProductA2 : creates
    ConcreteFactory2 ..> ProductB2 : creates
    Client --> AbstractFactory
    Client --> ProductA
    Client --> ProductB
Participant Responsibility AbstractFactory Interface with one creation method per product in the family ConcreteFactory Implements all creation methods for one family (AWS, India, Smart TV) AbstractProduct Interface for each kind of product (ObjectStorage, TaxPolicy) ConcreteProduct One family's version of a product (S3 storage, GST policy) Client Uses only the abstract factory and abstract products

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class CheckoutCalculator {
    public String summary(String country, long subtotal) {
        long tax;
        if (country.equals("IN")) tax = subtotal * 5 / 100;
        else if (country.equals("DE")) tax = subtotal * 7 / 100;
        else throw new IllegalArgumentException(country);

        long fee;
        if (country.equals("IN")) fee = subtotal >= 19900 ? 0 : 2500;
        else fee = subtotal >= 4000 ? 0 : 299;

        String total;
        if (country.equals("IN")) total = "INR " + ...;
        else total = ... + " EUR";
        // ...and the same country checks again in invoices, emails, receipts
    }
}

What goes wrong:

  • Scattered if (country) checks. Launching Japan means finding and editing every one of them.
  • Inconsistent families. Nothing stops one check from saying "IN" while another falls through to the German branch.
  • Untestable. You can't test the checkout without real tax rules.

docs.title: Example 1: Multi-Cloud Invoice Archiving (SaaS / ERP)
docs.text:
Scenario: A SaaS ERP vendor (think SAP-style business software) sells to enterprises that each insist on their own cloud. Retail customers run on AWS; a pharma customer has an Azure-only policy. When an invoice is finalized, the ERP stores the PDF and publishes an "invoice archived" event for downstream systems. Mixing clouds (storing on S3 but notifying via Azure Service Bus) would break data-residency contracts, so storage and messaging must always come from the same cloud. The cloud is chosen once per tenant, from configuration.

Design:

classDiagram
    class CloudFactory {
        <<interface>>
        +objectStorage() ObjectStorage
        +messageQueue() MessageQueue
    }
    class AwsFactory
    class AzureFactory
    class ObjectStorage {
        <<interface>>
        +upload(key, sizeKb) String
    }
    class MessageQueue {
        <<interface>>
        +publish(topic, payload) String
    }
    class InvoiceArchiver {
        +archive(invoiceId, sizeKb) List~String~
    }
    CloudFactory <|.. AwsFactory
    CloudFactory <|.. AzureFactory
    InvoiceArchiver --> CloudFactory
    AwsFactory ..> ObjectStorage : S3
    AwsFactory ..> MessageQueue : SQS
    AzureFactory ..> ObjectStorage : Blob
    AzureFactory ..> MessageQueue : Service Bus

Full Code:

CloudFactory.javaAwsFactory.javaAzureFactory.javaInvoiceArchiver.javaProductsMultiCloudDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud;

/** Abstract factory: one method per product in the family. */
public interface CloudFactory {

    ObjectStorage objectStorage();

    MessageQueue messageQueue();
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud;

public class AwsFactory implements CloudFactory {

    private final String region;

    public AwsFactory(String region) {
        this.region = region;
    }

    @Override
    public ObjectStorage objectStorage() {
        return (key, sizeKb) -> "s3://erp-%s/%s (%d KB)".formatted(region, key, sizeKb);
    }

    @Override
    public MessageQueue messageQueue() {
        return (topic, payload) -> "SQS %s/%s <- %s".formatted(region, topic, payload);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud;

public class AzureFactory implements CloudFactory {

    private final String account;

    public AzureFactory(String account) {
        this.account = account;
    }

    @Override
    public ObjectStorage objectStorage() {
        return (key, sizeKb) -> "https://%s.blob.core.windows.net/erp/%s (%d KB)"
                .formatted(account, key, sizeKb);
    }

    @Override
    public MessageQueue messageQueue() {
        return (topic, payload) -> "ServiceBus %s/%s <- %s".formatted(account, topic, payload);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud;

import java.util.List;

/** Client. Depends only on the abstract factory and abstract products. */
public class InvoiceArchiver {

    private final ObjectStorage storage;
    private final MessageQueue queue;

    public InvoiceArchiver(CloudFactory cloud) { // (1)!
        this.storage = cloud.objectStorage();
        this.queue = cloud.messageQueue();
    }

    public List<String> archive(String invoiceId, int sizeKb) {
        String uri = storage.upload(invoiceId + ".pdf", sizeKb);
        String receipt = queue.publish("invoice-archived", invoiceId);
        return List.of(uri, receipt);
    }
}
  1. The client receives one object and pulls every product from it. Because there's a single source, the storage and the queue can't come from different clouds.
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud;

public interface ObjectStorage {

    /** Stores a file and returns its URI. */
    String upload(String key, int sizeKb);
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud;

public interface MessageQueue {

    /** Publishes a message and returns a delivery receipt. */
    String publish(String topic, String payload);
}

The products are functional interfaces, so the factories return lambdas. In production each would be a real class wrapping the AWS or Azure SDK client.

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud;

import java.util.Map;

public class MultiCloudDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS ERP: Invoice Archiving per Tenant Cloud ===");
        // Tenant -> cloud chosen once, from configuration
        Map<String, CloudFactory> tenants = Map.of(
                "acme-retail", new AwsFactory("ap-south-1"),
                "globex-pharma", new AzureFactory("globexprod"));

        archive("acme-retail", tenants.get("acme-retail"), "INV-1001", 120);
        archive("globex-pharma", tenants.get("globex-pharma"), "INV-2001", 85);
    }

    private static void archive(String tenant, CloudFactory cloud, String invoiceId, int sizeKb) {
        System.out.println("Tenant " + tenant + " (" + cloud.getClass().getSimpleName() + "):");
        new InvoiceArchiver(cloud).archive(invoiceId, sizeKb)
                .forEach(line -> System.out.println("  " + line));
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS ERP: Invoice Archiving per Tenant Cloud ===
Tenant acme-retail (AwsFactory):
  s3://erp-ap-south-1/INV-1001.pdf (120 KB)
  SQS ap-south-1/invoice-archived <- INV-1001
Tenant globex-pharma (AzureFactory):
  https://globexprod.blob.core.windows.net/erp/INV-2001.pdf (85 KB)
  ServiceBus globexprod/invoice-archived <- INV-2001

The same InvoiceArchiver code ran twice. Each tenant's storage and messaging came from its own cloud.

Why Abstract Factory here:

  • Two (and soon more: secrets, key management, CDN) products that must belong to the same provider.
  • The cloud is chosen once per tenant; business code is cloud-agnostic.
  • Adding GCP means one new factory class, not edits across the ERP.
  • Tests can pass an in-memory family (see the unit test) with no cloud SDK at all.
Unit Test: InvoiceArchiverTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory;

import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud.AwsFactory;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud.CloudFactory;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud.InvoiceArchiver;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud.MessageQueue;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.cloud.ObjectStorage;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class InvoiceArchiverTest {

    @Test
    void usesBothProductsFromTheSameFamily() {
        assertThat(new InvoiceArchiver(new AwsFactory("eu-west-1")).archive("INV-1", 10))
                .containsExactly("s3://erp-eu-west-1/INV-1.pdf (10 KB)",
                        "SQS eu-west-1/invoice-archived <- INV-1");
    }

    @Test
    void anInMemoryFamilyMakesTheClientEasyToTest() {
        List<String> calls = new ArrayList<>();
        CloudFactory inMemory = new CloudFactory() {
            public ObjectStorage objectStorage() {
                return (key, size) -> { calls.add("upload " + key); return "mem://" + key; };
            }
            public MessageQueue messageQueue() {
                return (topic, payload) -> { calls.add("publish " + payload); return "ok"; };
            }
        };
        new InvoiceArchiver(inMemory).archive("INV-9", 1);
        assertThat(calls).containsExactly("upload INV-9.pdf", "publish INV-9");
    }
}

docs.title: Example 2: Country-Specific Checkout (Grocery Delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce grocery company is expanding from India to Germany, with Japan next. Three things vary by country and must stay consistent with each other: the tax (GST 5% vs. the 7% reduced VAT rate for food), the price format (INR 182.50 vs. 53,50 EUR) and the delivery rules (minimum order, small-order fee, delivery promise). The checkout, receipt and email code must contain zero country checks, so a new country is a one-team change.

Design:

classDiagram
    class RegionFactory {
        <<interface>>
        +taxPolicy() TaxPolicy
        +priceFormatter() PriceFormatter
        +deliveryRules() DeliveryRules
    }
    class IndiaRegion
    class GermanyRegion
    class JapanRegion
    class CheckoutCalculator {
        +summary(subtotalMinor) String
    }
    RegionFactory <|.. IndiaRegion
    RegionFactory <|.. GermanyRegion
    RegionFactory <|.. JapanRegion
    CheckoutCalculator --> RegionFactory
    note for JapanRegion "Added in the coding challenge,<br>no change to CheckoutCalculator"

Full Code:

RegionFactory.javaIndiaRegion.javaGermanyRegion.javaCheckoutCalculator.javaProductsRegionDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

/** Abstract factory for everything that varies by country. */
public interface RegionFactory {

    TaxPolicy taxPolicy();

    PriceFormatter priceFormatter();

    DeliveryRules deliveryRules();

    /** Helper shared by tax policies: basis points, rounded half-up. */
    static long percentOf(long amountMinor, int basisPoints) {
        return (amountMinor * basisPoints + 5_000) / 10_000;
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

import java.util.Locale;

public class IndiaRegion implements RegionFactory {

    @Override
    public TaxPolicy taxPolicy() {
        return new TaxPolicy() {
            public String name() { return "GST 5%"; }
            public long taxOn(long amount) { return RegionFactory.percentOf(amount, 500); }
        };
    }

    @Override
    public PriceFormatter priceFormatter() {
        return paise -> String.format(Locale.ROOT, "INR %d.%02d", paise / 100, paise % 100);
    }

    @Override
    public DeliveryRules deliveryRules() {
        return new DeliveryRules() {
            public long minimumOrder() { return 99_00; }
            public long deliveryFee(long subtotal) { return subtotal >= 199_00 ? 0 : 25_00; }
            public String promise() { return "10-minute delivery"; }
        };
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

import java.util.Locale;

public class GermanyRegion implements RegionFactory {

    @Override
    public TaxPolicy taxPolicy() {
        return new TaxPolicy() {
            public String name() { return "MwSt 7%"; } // reduced VAT rate for food
            public long taxOn(long amount) { return RegionFactory.percentOf(amount, 700); }
        };
    }

    @Override
    public PriceFormatter priceFormatter() {
        return cents -> String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%d,%02d EUR", cents / 100, cents % 100);
    }

    @Override
    public DeliveryRules deliveryRules() {
        return new DeliveryRules() {
            public long minimumOrder() { return 25_00; }
            public long deliveryFee(long subtotal) { return subtotal >= 40_00 ? 0 : 2_99; }
            public String promise() { return "2-hour delivery slot"; }
        };
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

/** Client: no country-specific code anywhere in this class. */
public class CheckoutCalculator {

    private final TaxPolicy tax;
    private final PriceFormatter fmt;
    private final DeliveryRules delivery;

    public CheckoutCalculator(RegionFactory region) {
        this.tax = region.taxPolicy(); // (1)!
        this.fmt = region.priceFormatter();
        this.delivery = region.deliveryRules();
    }

    public String summary(long subtotalMinor) {
        if (subtotalMinor < delivery.minimumOrder()) {
            return "Minimum order is " + fmt.format(delivery.minimumOrder());
        }
        long taxAmount = tax.taxOn(subtotalMinor);
        long fee = delivery.deliveryFee(subtotalMinor);
        long total = subtotalMinor + taxAmount + fee;
        return "subtotal %s + %s %s + delivery %s = %s (%s)".formatted(
                fmt.format(subtotalMinor), tax.name(), fmt.format(taxAmount),
                fmt.format(fee), fmt.format(total), delivery.promise());
    }
}
  1. All three products come from the same region object, so tax, formatting and delivery rules always belong to the same country.
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

public interface TaxPolicy {

    String name();

    /** Tax on an amount in minor units (paise, cents, yen), rounded half-up. */
    long taxOn(long amountMinor);
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

public interface PriceFormatter {

    String format(long amountMinor);
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

public interface DeliveryRules {

    long minimumOrder();

    long deliveryFee(long subtotalMinor);

    String promise();
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region;

public class RegionDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: One Checkout, Many Countries ===");
        CheckoutCalculator india = new CheckoutCalculator(new IndiaRegion());
        CheckoutCalculator germany = new CheckoutCalculator(new GermanyRegion());

        System.out.println("IN: " + india.summary(150_00));
        System.out.println("IN: " + india.summary(250_00));
        System.out.println("IN: " + india.summary(50_00));
        System.out.println("DE: " + germany.summary(50_00));
        System.out.println("DE: " + germany.summary(30_00));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: One Checkout, Many Countries ===
IN: subtotal INR 150.00 + GST 5% INR 7.50 + delivery INR 25.00 = INR 182.50 (10-minute delivery)
IN: subtotal INR 250.00 + GST 5% INR 12.50 + delivery INR 0.00 = INR 262.50 (10-minute delivery)
IN: Minimum order is INR 99.00
DE: subtotal 50,00 EUR + MwSt 7% 3,50 EUR + delivery 0,00 EUR = 53,50 EUR (2-hour delivery slot)
DE: subtotal 30,00 EUR + MwSt 7% 2,10 EUR + delivery 2,99 EUR = 35,09 EUR (2-hour delivery slot)

Money is stored in minor units

Amounts are long paise or cents, never double. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in floating point, and rounding errors in tax are a compliance problem. In a real system use BigDecimal or a money library (JSR 354 / Moneta) and the country's legal rounding rule.

Why Abstract Factory here:

  • Tax, formatting and delivery rules form a family that must match.
  • CheckoutCalculator has no country logic; launching a country is one new class, as the coding challenge proves with Japan.
  • The country is decided once (from the user's store or domain) and flows everywhere.
Unit Test: CheckoutCalculatorTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory;

import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region.CheckoutCalculator;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region.GermanyRegion;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region.IndiaRegion;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.region.JapanRegion;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class CheckoutCalculatorTest {

    @Test
    void indiaAppliesGstAndSmallOrderFee() {
        assertThat(new CheckoutCalculator(new IndiaRegion()).summary(150_00))
                .contains("GST 5% INR 7.50", "delivery INR 25.00", "= INR 182.50");
    }

    @Test
    void germanyUsesEuroFormatAndReducedVat() {
        assertThat(new CheckoutCalculator(new GermanyRegion()).summary(50_00))
                .contains("MwSt 7% 3,50 EUR", "= 53,50 EUR");
    }

    @Test
    void minimumOrderIsEnforcedPerRegion() {
        assertThat(new CheckoutCalculator(new IndiaRegion()).summary(50_00))
                .isEqualTo("Minimum order is INR 99.00");
    }

    @Test
    void japanFamilyPlugsInWithoutChangingTheClient() {
        assertThat(new CheckoutCalculator(new JapanRegion()).summary(3_000))
                .contains("JPY 240", "= JPY 3,240");
    }
}

docs.title: Example 3: Device-Specific Playback (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: A video streaming service (Netflix/Prime-style) ships the same app logic to phones and smart TVs. Each device needs a video player tuned for it (720p adaptive bitrate on mobile networks vs. 4K HDR on TV) and a control scheme that fits the hardware (touch gestures vs. a remote's D-pad). A TV player with touch controls would be unusable, so the player and controls must always come as a pair. The device type is detected once at app start.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as App start-up
    participant F as DeviceUiFactory
    participant TV as SmartTvUiFactory
    participant S as PlaybackScreen
    App->>F: forDevice(SMART_TV)
    F-->>App: SmartTvUiFactory
    App->>S: new PlaybackScreen(factory)
    S->>TV: videoPlayer()
    S->>TV: controls()
    App->>S: render("The Monsoon Express")
    S-->>App: 4K HDR player + D-pad controls

Full Code:

DeviceUiFactory.javaMobileUiFactory.javaSmartTvUiFactory.javaPlaybackScreen.javaProductsStreamingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

public interface DeviceUiFactory {

    VideoPlayer videoPlayer();

    ControlScheme controls();

    /** A factory method that picks the right abstract factory. */
    static DeviceUiFactory forDevice(DeviceType type) { // (1)!
        return switch (type) {
            case MOBILE -> new MobileUiFactory();
            case SMART_TV -> new SmartTvUiFactory();
        };
    }
}
  1. A Factory Method that returns an Abstract Factory. This is very common: one static method picks the family; the family then creates the products.
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

public class MobileUiFactory implements DeviceUiFactory {

    @Override
    public VideoPlayer videoPlayer() {
        return title -> "Playing '%s' at 720p, adaptive bitrate for 4G".formatted(title);
    }

    @Override
    public ControlScheme controls() {
        return () -> "swipe=seek, double-tap=skip 10s, pinch=zoom";
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

public class SmartTvUiFactory implements DeviceUiFactory {

    @Override
    public VideoPlayer videoPlayer() {
        return title -> "Playing '%s' in 4K HDR with Dolby Atmos".formatted(title);
    }

    @Override
    public ControlScheme controls() {
        return () -> "D-pad=navigate, OK=play/pause, long-press=menu";
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

/** Client: renders a playback screen for whatever device it was given. */
public class PlaybackScreen {

    private final VideoPlayer player;
    private final ControlScheme controls;

    public PlaybackScreen(DeviceUiFactory ui) {
        this.player = ui.videoPlayer();
        this.controls = ui.controls(); // always from the same family as the player
    }

    public String render(String title) {
        return player.play(title) + "\n    controls: " + controls.describe();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

public interface VideoPlayer {

    String play(String title);
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

public interface ControlScheme {

    String describe();
}

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

public enum DeviceType { MOBILE, SMART_TV }

package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming;

public class StreamingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Device-Specific Playback ===");
        for (DeviceType device : DeviceType.values()) {
            PlaybackScreen screen = new PlaybackScreen(DeviceUiFactory.forDevice(device));
            System.out.println(device + ":");
            System.out.println("    " + screen.render("The Monsoon Express"));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Device-Specific Playback ===
MOBILE:
    Playing 'The Monsoon Express' at 720p, adaptive bitrate for 4G
    controls: swipe=seek, double-tap=skip 10s, pinch=zoom
SMART_TV:
    Playing 'The Monsoon Express' in 4K HDR with Dolby Atmos
    controls: D-pad=navigate, OK=play/pause, long-press=menu

Why Abstract Factory here:

  • The player and controls are a matched pair per device.
  • PlaybackScreen is written once and works for every device, including future ones (tablet, car display).
  • This is the classic GoF motivating example (cross-platform widget toolkits), in a modern setting.
Unit Test: DeviceUiFactoryTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory;

import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming.DeviceType;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming.DeviceUiFactory;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming.MobileUiFactory;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming.PlaybackScreen;
import com.handbook.creational.abstractfactory.streaming.SmartTvUiFactory;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DeviceUiFactoryTest {

    @Test
    void picksFactoryByDevice() {
        assertThat(DeviceUiFactory.forDevice(DeviceType.MOBILE)).isInstanceOf(MobileUiFactory.class);
        assertThat(DeviceUiFactory.forDevice(DeviceType.SMART_TV)).isInstanceOf(SmartTvUiFactory.class);
    }

    @Test
    void playerAndControlsAlwaysMatch() {
        String tv = new PlaybackScreen(new SmartTvUiFactory()).render("X");
        assertThat(tv).contains("4K HDR", "D-pad").doesNotContain("swipe");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Lambdas as products. When a product interface has a single method, the factory can return lambdas (all three examples do). That cuts the "class explosion" this pattern is criticized for. Promote to real classes once a product has state or several methods.

Records as factories. If a family is just data plus small behaviors, a record can be the factory:

record Region(TaxPolicy taxPolicy, PriceFormatter priceFormatter, DeliveryRules deliveryRules) {}

Region india = new Region(new GstPolicy(), paise -> "INR " + ..., new QuickCommerceRules());

Choosing the family:

Mechanism Example Static method DeviceUiFactory.forDevice(type) (Example 3) Map lookup per tenant Map<String, CloudFactory> (Example 1) Spring profiles @Profile("aws") @Configuration class AwsConfig { @Bean ObjectStorage ...; @Bean MessageQueue ...; } Spring Boot auto-configuration @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "cloud.provider", havingValue = "azure") ServiceLoader Each family ships as a plug-in JAR

Spring @Configuration is an Abstract Factory

A @Configuration class with several @Bean methods, switched on by @Profile or @ConditionalOnProperty, creates a consistent family of beans. Spring Boot's auto-configuration for DataSource, JdbcTemplate and TransactionManager works this way.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example Family JDK javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory, TransformerFactory, XPathFactory XML implementation (Xerces, Saxon) JDK java.sql.Connection Creates a matched Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement for one driver JDK javax.swing.UIManager + LookAndFeel Matching widgets per look-and-feel (the classic GoF example) JDK java.nio.file.FileSystem Path, PathMatcher, WatchService for the default disk, a ZIP file system, etc. Spring @Configuration + @Profile Beans per environment JPA EntityManagerFactory EntityManager, CriteriaBuilder, Metamodel for one persistence unit AWS / Azure SDKs Client builders per region/credentials Clients configured consistently

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text:
✅ Pros ❌ Cons Guarantees consistency: products from one family always match Adding a new product type (e.g. SecretsManager) means changing the interface and every factory Swap the entire family by changing one object Many classes and interfaces; heavy for small problems Client code free of if (provider) / if (country) Extra indirection to trace when debugging New family = one new class (OCP for families) Pointless if you only ever have one family Easy in-memory test families Family members can drift if teams own them separately; needs contract tests

The asymmetry interviewers love

Abstract Factory makes adding families easy (new JapanRegion) and adding product types hard (new method on RegionFactory means touching every region). If you expect more product types than families, reconsider. Default methods on the interface can soften the blow.

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Mixing families behind the factory's back

new CheckoutCalculator(region) plus a hard-coded new GstPolicy() somewhere else defeats the whole pattern. Code review rule: products of the family are only obtained from the factory.

Choosing the family per call

cloudFor(tenant).objectStorage() and later cloudFor(otherTenantVar).messageQueue() in the same flow can mix families. Resolve the family once at the edge (request filter, tenant context) and pass it in.

Abstract Factory for a single family

If there's only AwsFactory and no real plan for another, you've added interfaces for nothing. Start with concrete classes; extract the interfaces when the second family arrives.

Fat factory interfaces

A factory with 15 creation methods is usually several families glued together. Split it by bounded context (storage family, messaging family, security family).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Abstract Factory is a hexagonal-architecture tool. In Ports & Adapters, the ports are your product interfaces (ObjectStorage, MessageQueue) and each adapter family (AWS, Azure, in-memory) is a concrete factory. Domain code depends only on ports. That's how you get:

  • Cloud portability that is real, not theoretical: the domain compiles without any cloud SDK on the classpath.
  • Fast tests: the in-memory family runs in milliseconds; a separate contract test suite runs the same assertions against every family (in-memory, LocalStack, Azurite) so they behave identically.

Multi-tenancy. In SaaS, the family is often chosen per tenant: store a TenantContext (from the JWT or subdomain) and resolve the factory once per request in a filter. Cache factories per tenant (each holds expensive SDK clients), and evict on tenant config change.

Evolving the product set. When you must add a product type to an established family:

  1. Add the method to the interface as a default method that throws UnsupportedOperationException (or returns a no-op product).
  2. Roll out implementations family by family behind a feature flag.
  3. Remove the default once all families implement it, so the compiler enforces completeness again.

Know when to stop. Full multi-cloud abstraction has a cost: you can only use the lowest common denominator of features. Many teams pick one cloud and abstract only at a few strategic seams (storage, queues). Say this in a design review; it shows judgement.

War story: the cross-region data leak

A healthcare SaaS served EU and US customers. Storage clients were picked by tenant region, but the audit-event publisher was a global singleton bean pointing at a US queue. EU patient-access events (which contained patient IDs) flowed into US infrastructure for months, a GDPR data-residency breach found during an external audit. Fix: introduced a RegionInfrastructureFactory that creates storage, queue, cache and KMS clients together per region; banned direct injection of those clients through an ArchUnit rule; added a contract test asserting every product from a factory reports the same region. Lesson: when objects must match, don't let them be chosen independently. That's the whole reason Abstract Factory exists.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Abstract Factory Factory Method Builder Prototype Creates A family of products One product One complex product Copies of an existing object Main guarantee Products match each other The right class is picked Valid, fully built object Pre-configured clone Extension point New factory class (family) New subclass / registration New builder steps New prototype instance Structure Object composition (pass the factory in) Often inheritance (override createX()) Fluent API copy() / copy constructor

Often combined with: Factory Method (each creation method is a factory method; Example 3 also uses a factory method to choose the factory), Singleton (one factory instance per family), Prototype (factories that clone pre-configured products), Facade (a facade built on top of one family).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Families of matching products: one factory per family, one method per product.
  • Client depends only on interfaces; the family is chosen once and injected.
  • Easy: new family. Hard: new product type (touches every factory).
  • vs Factory Method: family vs one product; composition vs inheritance.
  • JDK: DocumentBuilderFactory, Connection, Swing LookAndFeel. Spring: @Configuration + @Profile.
interface RegionFactory { TaxPolicy taxPolicy(); PriceFormatter priceFormatter(); DeliveryRules deliveryRules(); }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a SecretsStore product to CloudFactory using a default method first, then implement it for both clouds.
  • Add a TABLET device family to Example 3.
  • Write a contract test class that runs the same assertions against IndiaRegion, GermanyRegion and JapanRegion.
  • Rebuild Example 1 with Spring @Profile("aws") / @Profile("azure") configuration classes.

Factory Method Next: Builder

docs.title: Builder
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Creational Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Builder constructs a complex object step by step and hands you a finished, valid, usually immutable object at the end. Use it when an object has many parameters (especially optional ones), needs validation across fields, or must be immutable.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: an order has a customer, an address, a list of items, a delivery slot, a coupon, instructions and a contactless flag. Most are optional. With constructors you end up with either 7-argument constructors where nobody remembers which null is which, or setters that leave the object half-built and mutable.

Formal definition (GoF):

Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation so that the same construction process can create different representations.

In modern Java "Builder" usually means Joshua Bloch's fluent builder (Effective Java, Item 2), which solves the telescoping constructor problem. The original GoF version (Director + Builder interface) is about building different representations from the same steps. You'll see both below.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Ordering a custom sandwich

At a sandwich counter you say: "Wheat bread, chicken, add cheese, no onions, toast it." You add choices one at a time, in any order, and skip what you don't want. Only when you say "that's it" does the staff check the order (no meat on the vegan bread) and hand you the finished sandwich. You never receive half a sandwich.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Product {
        -final fields
        -Product(Builder)
        +builder(required)$ Builder
    }
    class Builder {
        -required fields
        -optional fields with defaults
        +optionalA(value) Builder
        +optionalB(value) Builder
        +build() Product
    }
    class Client
    Product *-- Builder : static nested
    Client ..> Builder : chains calls
    Builder ..> Product : build() validates and creates
Participant Responsibility Product Immutable object with a private constructor that takes the builder Builder Collects values, applies defaults, validates in build() Director (GoF form only) Knows a recipe (the order of steps), not the concrete product Client Chains builder calls and calls build() once

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// Telescoping constructors
new GroceryOrder("CUST-7", "4 Park St", items, null, "WEEKLY50", null, true);
//                                              ^slot? ^coupon     ^note? ^contactless?

// JavaBeans setters
GroceryOrder o = new GroceryOrder();
o.setCustomerId("CUST-7");
o.setItems(items);
// forgot setAddress(): the object exists, is invalid, and is already in use
o.setContactless(true);  // mutable: another thread can change it later

What goes wrong:

  • Unreadable calls. Which null is the coupon? Swapping two String arguments compiles fine and ships a bug.
  • Inconsistent state. With setters, the object exists before it's valid.
  • No immutability. Setters make thread-safety and safe sharing much harder.
  • Validation is scattered. Nowhere is the right place to check "express delivery only for small orders".

docs.title: Example 1: Building Grocery Orders (Grocery Delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery app builds an order from what's in the cart, the chosen slot, an optional coupon and delivery notes. Orders are passed between threads (checkout, pricing, dispatch), so they must be immutable. Some rules involve several fields at once: an order needs at least one item, and 10-minute express delivery is only allowed up to INR 2,000 (bigger orders don't fit a scooter). Bad orders must be rejected before they exist.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Cart screen
    participant B as GroceryOrder.Builder
    participant O as GroceryOrder
    C->>B: builder("CUST-42", address)
    C->>B: item("MILK-1L", 2, 68)
    C->>B: item("BREAD-WW", 1, 55)
    C->>B: slot(EXPRESS_10_MIN)
    C->>B: build()
    B->>B: validate (items, express limit)
    B->>O: new GroceryOrder(this)
    O-->>C: immutable order

Full Code:

GroceryOrder.javaGroceryOrderDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.builder.grocery;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

/** Immutable order. The only way to create one is through {@link Builder}. */
public final class GroceryOrder {

    public record Item(String sku, int quantity, int unitPriceInr) {
        public int lineTotal() {
            return quantity * unitPriceInr;
        }
    }

    public enum Slot { EXPRESS_10_MIN, TODAY_6_TO_8_PM, TOMORROW_MORNING }

    private final String customerId;
    private final String address;
    private final List<Item> items;
    private final Slot slot;
    private final String couponCode;   // optional
    private final String instructions; // optional
    private final boolean contactless;

    private GroceryOrder(Builder b) { // (1)!
        this.customerId = b.customerId;
        this.address = b.address;
        this.items = List.copyOf(b.items); // (2)!
        this.slot = b.slot;
        this.couponCode = b.couponCode;
        this.instructions = b.instructions;
        this.contactless = b.contactless;
    }

    public static Builder builder(String customerId, String address) { // (3)!
        return new Builder(customerId, address);
    }

    public int subtotalInr() {
        return items.stream().mapToInt(Item::lineTotal).sum();
    }

    public List<Item> items() {
        return items;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Order[customer=%s, items=%d, subtotal=INR %d, slot=%s, coupon=%s, contactless=%s, note=%s]"
                .formatted(customerId, items.size(), subtotalInr(), slot,
                        couponCode == null ? "-" : couponCode, contactless,
                        instructions == null ? "-" : '"' + instructions + '"');
    }

    public static final class Builder {
        private final String customerId;
        private final String address;
        private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();
        private Slot slot = Slot.TODAY_6_TO_8_PM; // sensible default
        private String couponCode;
        private String instructions;
        private boolean contactless;

        private Builder(String customerId, String address) {
            this.customerId = Objects.requireNonNull(customerId, "customerId");
            this.address = Objects.requireNonNull(address, "address");
        }

        public Builder item(String sku, int quantity, int unitPriceInr) {
            items.add(new Item(sku, quantity, unitPriceInr));
            return this; // (4)!
        }

        public Builder slot(Slot slot) {
            this.slot = slot;
            return this;
        }

        public Builder coupon(String couponCode) {
            this.couponCode = couponCode;
            return this;
        }

        public Builder instructions(String instructions) {
            this.instructions = instructions;
            return this;
        }

        public Builder contactless() {
            this.contactless = true;
            return this;
        }

        public GroceryOrder build() { // (5)!
            if (items.isEmpty()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Order needs at least one item");
            }
            GroceryOrder order = new GroceryOrder(this);
            if (slot == Slot.EXPRESS_10_MIN && order.subtotalInr() > 2_000) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Express delivery is limited to orders up to INR 2000");
            }
            return order;
        }
    }
}
  1. The private constructor takes the builder. The builder is the only way in.
  2. List.copyOf makes a defensive, unmodifiable copy. Later item() calls on the builder can't change an order that's already built.
  3. Required parameters go into builder(...), so you can't forget them. Optional ones are chainable methods.
  4. Returning this is what makes the API fluent (chainable).
  5. build() is the single place for cross-field validation. If it throws, no invalid order ever exists.
package com.handbook.creational.builder.grocery;

import com.handbook.creational.builder.grocery.GroceryOrder.Slot;

public class GroceryOrderDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Building Orders ===");

        GroceryOrder quick = GroceryOrder.builder("CUST-42", "12 MG Road, Bengaluru")
                .item("MILK-1L", 2, 68)
                .item("BREAD-WW", 1, 55)
                .slot(Slot.EXPRESS_10_MIN)
                .build();
        System.out.println(quick);

        GroceryOrder weekly = GroceryOrder.builder("CUST-7", "4 Park Street, Kolkata")
                .item("RICE-5KG", 1, 420)
                .item("DAL-1KG", 2, 140)
                .item("OIL-1L", 2, 180)
                .coupon("WEEKLY50")
                .instructions("Leave with security")
                .contactless()
                .build();
        System.out.println(weekly);

        try {
            GroceryOrder.builder("CUST-9", "1 Marine Drive, Mumbai")
                    .item("TV-55IN", 1, 45_000)
                    .slot(Slot.EXPRESS_10_MIN)
                    .build();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        try {
            GroceryOrder.builder("CUST-9", "1 Marine Drive, Mumbai").build();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Building Orders ===
Order[customer=CUST-42, items=2, subtotal=INR 191, slot=EXPRESS_10_MIN, coupon=-, contactless=false, note=-]
Order[customer=CUST-7, items=3, subtotal=INR 1060, slot=TODAY_6_TO_8_PM, coupon=WEEKLY50, contactless=true, note="Leave with security"]
Rejected: Express delivery is limited to orders up to INR 2000
Rejected: Order needs at least one item

Why Builder here:

  • Seven fields, four optional. The builder call reads like a sentence, and defaults (the slot) live in one place.
  • Immutability makes orders safe to pass between threads and services.
  • Cross-field rules (express + amount) are enforced at the only point where all values are known: build().

docs.title: Example 2: Flight Search with a Step Builder (Travel Booking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A travel booking site sends flight searches to airline and aggregator APIs. A search must have an origin, a destination and a departure date, in that order. Return date, passengers, cabin and "non-stop only" are optional. With a normal builder, forgetting to(...) is a runtime error discovered in production logs. The team wants the compiler to enforce the required steps, so the IDE's autocomplete only offers the next valid step.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> FromStep : builder()
    FromStep --> ToStep : from()
    ToStep --> DepartingStep : to()
    DepartingStep --> OptionalStep : departing()
    OptionalStep --> OptionalStep : returning() / passengers() / cabin() / nonStopOnly()
    OptionalStep --> [*] : build()

Full Code:

FlightSearch.javaTravelDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.builder.travel;

import java.time.LocalDate;

/**
 * Flight search query built with a <b>step builder</b>: the compiler forces
 * from -> to -> departing, and only then exposes the optional settings and build().
 */
public record FlightSearch(String from, String to, LocalDate departing, LocalDate returning,
                           int adults, int children, CabinClass cabin, boolean nonStopOnly) {

    public enum CabinClass { ECONOMY, PREMIUM_ECONOMY, BUSINESS }

    public FlightSearch { // (1)!
        if (from.equals(to)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Origin and destination must differ");
        }
        if (returning != null && returning.isBefore(departing)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Return date is before departure");
        }
        if (adults < 1 || adults + children > 9) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("1-9 travellers, at least one adult");
        }
    }

    // ---- the steps: each interface exposes exactly one next move ----
    public interface FromStep { ToStep from(String airport); } // (2)!

    public interface ToStep { DepartingStep to(String airport); }

    public interface DepartingStep { OptionalStep departing(LocalDate date); }

    public interface OptionalStep { // (3)!
        OptionalStep returning(LocalDate date);
        OptionalStep passengers(int adults, int children);
        OptionalStep cabin(CabinClass cabin);
        OptionalStep nonStopOnly();
        FlightSearch build();
    }

    public static FromStep builder() {
        return new Steps();
    }

    private static final class Steps implements FromStep, ToStep, DepartingStep, OptionalStep { // (4)!
        private String from;
        private String to;
        private LocalDate departing;
        private LocalDate returning;
        private int adults = 1;
        private int children;
        private CabinClass cabin = CabinClass.ECONOMY;
        private boolean nonStopOnly;

        public ToStep from(String airport) { this.from = airport; return this; }
        public DepartingStep to(String airport) { this.to = airport; return this; }
        public OptionalStep departing(LocalDate date) { this.departing = date; return this; }
        public OptionalStep returning(LocalDate date) { this.returning = date; return this; }
        public OptionalStep passengers(int a, int c) { this.adults = a; this.children = c; return this; }
        public OptionalStep cabin(CabinClass cabin) { this.cabin = cabin; return this; }
        public OptionalStep nonStopOnly() { this.nonStopOnly = true; return this; }

        public FlightSearch build() {
            return new FlightSearch(from, to, departing, returning, adults, children, cabin, nonStopOnly);
        }
    }

    public String summary() {
        return "%s->%s %s%s | %d adult(s), %d child(ren) | %s%s".formatted(
                from, to, departing, returning == null ? " one-way" : " return " + returning,
                adults, children, cabin, nonStopOnly ? " | non-stop" : "");
    }
}
  1. The record's compact constructor holds the validation, so it runs however the record is created, by the builder or directly.
  2. Each step interface has exactly one method that returns the next step. After builder() the only thing you can call is from().
  3. Only the last step exposes the optional settings and build().
  4. One private class implements every step. Callers only ever see it through the narrow step interfaces.
package com.handbook.creational.builder.travel;

import com.handbook.creational.builder.travel.FlightSearch.CabinClass;

import java.time.LocalDate;

public class TravelDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: Flight Search Queries ===");

        FlightSearch oneWay = FlightSearch.builder()
                .from("BLR").to("DEL")
                .departing(LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 20))
                .build();
        System.out.println(oneWay.summary());

        FlightSearch family = FlightSearch.builder()
                .from("BOM").to("SIN")
                .departing(LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 22))
                .returning(LocalDate.of(2027, 1, 2))
                .passengers(2, 2)
                .cabin(CabinClass.PREMIUM_ECONOMY)
                .nonStopOnly()
                .build();
        System.out.println(family.summary());

        try {
            FlightSearch.builder().from("DEL").to("LHR")
                    .departing(LocalDate.of(2027, 3, 10))
                    .returning(LocalDate.of(2027, 3, 1))
                    .build();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Invalid search: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        // FlightSearch.builder().to("DEL")  <- does not compile: 'from' must come first
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: Flight Search Queries ===
BLR->DEL 2026-12-20 one-way | 1 adult(s), 0 child(ren) | ECONOMY
BOM->SIN 2026-12-22 return 2027-01-02 | 2 adult(s), 2 child(ren) | PREMIUM_ECONOMY | non-stop
Invalid search: Return date is before departure

Why a Step Builder here:

  • Required fields are enforced at compile time: FlightSearch.builder().to("DEL") doesn't compile.
  • Autocomplete guides the developer through the API, so there's no need to read docs to know what's required.
  • Records + compact constructors give immutability, equals/hashCode (useful as a cache key for search results) and validation for free.

docs.title: Example 3: Mobile Plans with a Director (Telecom)
docs.text:
Scenario: A telecom operator defines plans (Student Saver, Family Max) that appear in two places: the billing system needs a structured record, and the website needs marketing copy. Product managers change plan contents often, and in the past the website and billing drifted apart ("the site says 3 GB/day, my bill says 2"). The recipe for each plan must live in one place, with each output format produced from it.

Design:

classDiagram
    class PlanDirector {
        +studentPlan(PlanBuilder)
        +familyPlan(PlanBuilder)
    }
    class PlanBuilder {
        <<interface>>
        +name(String)
        +monthlyPriceInr(int)
        +data(int)
        +unlimitedCalls()
        +sms(int)
        +addOn(String)
    }
    class MobilePlanBuilder {
        +result() MobilePlan
    }
    class BrochureBuilder {
        +result() String
    }
    PlanDirector ..> PlanBuilder : drives steps
    PlanBuilder <|.. MobilePlanBuilder
    PlanBuilder <|.. BrochureBuilder

Full Code:

PlanDirector.javaPlanBuilder.javaMobilePlanBuilder.javaBrochureBuilder.javaTelecomDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom;

/** Director: owns the recipes. It knows the steps, not the representation. */
public class PlanDirector {

    public void studentPlan(PlanBuilder b) {
        b.name("Student Saver");
        b.monthlyPriceInr(199);
        b.data(1);
        b.unlimitedCalls();
        b.sms(100);
    }

    public void familyPlan(PlanBuilder b) {
        b.name("Family Max");
        b.monthlyPriceInr(999);
        b.data(3);
        b.unlimitedCalls();
        b.sms(100);
        b.addOn("OTT streaming bundle");
        b.addOn("International roaming 7 days");
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom;

/**
 * GoF Builder interface. Different builders turn the same construction steps
 * into different representations.
 */
public interface PlanBuilder {

    void name(String name);

    void monthlyPriceInr(int price);

    void data(int gbPerDay);

    void unlimitedCalls();

    void sms(int perDay);

    void addOn(String addOn);
}

package com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class MobilePlanBuilder implements PlanBuilder {

    private String name;
    private int price;
    private int data;
    private boolean calls;
    private int sms;
    private final List<String> addOns = new ArrayList<>();

    public void name(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void monthlyPriceInr(int price) { this.price = price; }
    public void data(int gbPerDay) { this.data = gbPerDay; }
    public void unlimitedCalls() { this.calls = true; }
    public void sms(int perDay) { this.sms = perDay; }
    public void addOn(String addOn) { addOns.add(addOn); }

    public MobilePlan result() {
        return new MobilePlan(name, price, data, calls, sms, addOns);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom;

import java.util.List;

/** Representation 1: the product the billing system stores. */
public record MobilePlan(String name, int monthlyPriceInr, int dataGbPerDay,
                         boolean unlimitedCalls, int smsPerDay, List<String> addOns) {

    public MobilePlan {
        addOns = List.copyOf(addOns);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom;

/** Representation 2: marketing text for the website, from the same steps. */
public class BrochureBuilder implements PlanBuilder {

    private final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();

    public void name(String name) { text.append("** ").append(name.toUpperCase()).append(" **\n"); }
    public void monthlyPriceInr(int price) { text.append("  Just INR ").append(price).append("/month\n"); }
    public void data(int gbPerDay) { text.append("  ").append(gbPerDay).append(" GB high-speed data every day\n"); }
    public void unlimitedCalls() { text.append("  Unlimited calls to any network\n"); }
    public void sms(int perDay) { text.append("  ").append(perDay).append(" SMS/day\n"); }
    public void addOn(String addOn) { text.append("  + FREE ").append(addOn).append('\n'); }

    public String result() {
        return text.toString().stripTrailing();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom;

public class TelecomDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Telecom: One Recipe, Two Representations ===");
        PlanDirector director = new PlanDirector();

        MobilePlanBuilder billing = new MobilePlanBuilder();
        director.familyPlan(billing);
        System.out.println("Billing record: " + billing.result());

        BrochureBuilder brochure = new BrochureBuilder();
        director.familyPlan(brochure);
        System.out.println("Website brochure:\n" + brochure.result());

        MobilePlanBuilder student = new MobilePlanBuilder();
        director.studentPlan(student);
        System.out.println("Billing record: " + student.result());
    }
}

Output:

=== Telecom: One Recipe, Two Representations ===
Billing record: MobilePlan[name=Family Max, monthlyPriceInr=999, dataGbPerDay=3, unlimitedCalls=true, smsPerDay=100, addOns=[OTT streaming bundle, International roaming 7 days]]
Website brochure:
** FAMILY MAX **
  Just INR 999/month
  3 GB high-speed data every day
  Unlimited calls to any network
  100 SMS/day
  + FREE OTT streaming bundle
  + FREE International roaming 7 days
Billing record: MobilePlan[name=Student Saver, monthlyPriceInr=199, dataGbPerDay=1, unlimitedCalls=true, smsPerDay=100, addOns=[]]

Why the GoF Builder here:

  • One recipe, many representations. Billing and marketing can't drift, because both come from familyPlan(...).
  • A new output (a PDF tariff sheet, a JSON feed for comparison sites) is one new builder with no change to the recipes.
  • The director is the "construction process"; the builders are the "representations". That's exactly the GoF intent.
Unit Tests: BuilderTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.creational.builder;

import com.handbook.creational.builder.api.ApiRequest;
import com.handbook.creational.builder.grocery.GroceryOrder;
import com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom.BrochureBuilder;
import com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom.MobilePlan;
import com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom.MobilePlanBuilder;
import com.handbook.creational.builder.telecom.PlanDirector;
import com.handbook.creational.builder.travel.FlightSearch;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Nested;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.LocalDate;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class BuilderTest {

    @Nested
    class GroceryOrderTest {
        @Test
        void buildsWithDefaultsAndCalculatesSubtotal() {
            GroceryOrder order = GroceryOrder.builder("C1", "addr").item("A", 2, 50).build();
            assertThat(order.subtotalInr()).isEqualTo(100);
            assertThat(order.toString()).contains("slot=TODAY_6_TO_8_PM", "coupon=-");
        }

        @Test
        void itemsCannotBeModifiedAfterBuild() {
            GroceryOrder order = GroceryOrder.builder("C1", "addr").item("A", 1, 10).build();
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> order.items().add(new GroceryOrder.Item("B", 1, 1)))
                    .isInstanceOf(UnsupportedOperationException.class);
        }

        @Test
        void rejectsInvalidCombinations() {
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> GroceryOrder.builder("C1", "addr").build())
                    .hasMessageContaining("at least one item");
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> GroceryOrder.builder("C1", "addr").item("TV", 1, 5000)
                    .slot(GroceryOrder.Slot.EXPRESS_10_MIN).build())
                    .hasMessageContaining("Express");
        }
    }

    @Nested
    class FlightSearchTest {
        @Test
        void stepBuilderFillsDefaults() {
            FlightSearch s = FlightSearch.builder().from("A").to("B").departing(LocalDate.of(2027, 1, 1)).build();
            assertThat(s.adults()).isEqualTo(1);
            assertThat(s.cabin()).isEqualTo(FlightSearch.CabinClass.ECONOMY);
        }

        @Test
        void validatesInCompactConstructor() {
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> FlightSearch.builder().from("A").to("A")
                    .departing(LocalDate.of(2027, 1, 1)).build())
                    .hasMessage("Origin and destination must differ");
        }
    }

    @Nested
    class TelecomTest {
        @Test
        void sameRecipeProducesDifferentRepresentations() {
            PlanDirector director = new PlanDirector();
            MobilePlanBuilder plan = new MobilePlanBuilder();
            BrochureBuilder text = new BrochureBuilder();
            director.familyPlan(plan);
            director.familyPlan(text);
            MobilePlan result = plan.result();
            assertThat(result.monthlyPriceInr()).isEqualTo(999);
            assertThat(result.addOns()).hasSize(2);
            assertThat(text.result()).contains("FAMILY MAX", "INR 999/month");
        }
    }

    @Nested
    class ApiRequestTest {
        @Test
        void toBuilderCopiesWithoutChangingOriginal() {
            ApiRequest base = ApiRequest.builder("https://x").header("A", "1").build();
            ApiRequest copy = base.toBuilder().header("B", "2").build();
            assertThat(base.headers()).containsOnlyKeys("A");
            assertThat(copy.headers()).containsOnlyKeys("A", "B");
        }

        @Test
        void enforcesIdempotencyKeyForRetriedPosts() {
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> ApiRequest.builder("https://x").post("{}").retries(1).build())
                    .hasMessageContaining("Idempotency-Key");
            assertThat(ApiRequest.builder("https://x").post("{}").retries(1)
                    .header("Idempotency-Key", "k").build().maxRetries()).isEqualTo(1);
        }

        @Test
        void rejectsPlainHttp() {
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> ApiRequest.builder("http://x").build()).hasMessageContaining("HTTPS");
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example JDK StringBuilder, Stream.builder(), Locale.Builder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), HttpClient.newBuilder() JDK Thread.ofVirtual().name("worker-", 0).start(task) (Java 21 thread builders) Spring UriComponentsBuilder, ResponseEntity.ok().header(..).body(..), RestClient.builder(), MockMvcRequestBuilders Spring Boot SpringApplicationBuilder, DataSourceBuilder Spring Security HttpSecurity DSL (http.authorizeHttpRequests(..).oauth2Login(..)) Others Lombok @Builder, Protobuf / gRPC message builders, Guava ImmutableList.builder(), OkHttp Request.Builder, AWS SDK v2 request builders

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Readable construction, like named parameters More code: a second class per product (Lombok or records reduce this) Products can be immutable and thread-safe Required fields aren't enforced unless you use a step builder or builder-constructor arguments One place for defaults and cross-field validation A small allocation for the builder (negligible except in very hot loops) Easy to add optional fields without breaking callers Easy to forget to copy a new field in toBuilder() or the product constructor GoF form: same steps, many representations Step builders need many small interfaces

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Exposing mutable collections

If the product stores the builder's ArrayList directly, later calls on the same builder silently change "immutable" objects. Always List.copyOf / Map.copyOf in the product constructor.

Validating in setters instead of build()

Field-by-field checks can't see combinations ("express and over INR 2,000"). Do cross-field validation in build() or the record's compact constructor.

Sharing a builder between threads

Builders are mutable and not thread-safe. Create one per object being built; never cache one in a static field.

Builder for a 2-field object

new Money(100, "INR") doesn't need a builder. Use builders when the parameter list is long or has several optional values.

Lombok @Builder on JPA entities

It skips no-arg constructors and field defaults unless you add @Builder.Default, and it bypasses invariants. Use builders for value objects and DTOs; be deliberate with entities.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Builders are API-evolution tools. In a public SDK, adding a constructor parameter is a breaking change; adding a builder method isn't. That's why the JDK's newer APIs (HttpClient, thread builders) and cloud SDKs use builders. When designing a library: builder for configuration, immutable product, and toBuilder() for "copy with changes".

Validation strategy. Put invariants (things that must always hold) in the product's constructor or compact constructor, so they hold however the object is created, including by deserialization frameworks. Put construction-only rules (defaults, "at least one item") in build(). Report all violations at once for user-facing input (collect errors, then throw one exception) and fail fast for programmer errors.

Performance. The builder is a short-lived object; escape analysis often removes it entirely. Don't avoid builders for speed without a profiler showing a problem. On the other hand, toBuilder() + build() in a tight loop copies collections every time, so batch the changes.

Serialization. Jackson can build immutable objects through builders with @JsonDeserialize(builder = X.Builder.class) + @JsonPOJOBuilder(withPrefix = ""), or directly with records (Jackson 2.12+). This keeps DTOs immutable at the API boundary.

Test data builders. In tests, a builder with valid defaults for every field (anOrder().withItems(3).build()) makes tests short and focused on what matters. This is one of the most effective uses of the pattern in large codebases.

War story: the retry storm that double-charged customers

A payments client was configured through a builder. A developer turned on retries(3) for a POST charge call to "improve reliability". The gateway timed out under load, the client retried, and the gateway processed the same charge up to 4 times. About 2,300 customers were double-charged in 40 minutes. Fix: the request builder's build() now refuses retried POSTs that lack an Idempotency-Key header (exactly the coding challenge below), and the gateway de-duplicates on that key. Lesson: build() is the right place for safety rules between options, not only for null checks.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Builder Factory Method Abstract Factory Prototype Focus How one complex object is assembled Which class to create Which family of objects Copy an existing object Steps Many, client-controlled One call One call per product One copy() Result Usually immutable, validated Any implementation of an interface Matching products A configured clone Typical sign Many optional params switch on type Products that must match Expensive setup reused

Often combined with: Factory Method (builder() is a static factory), Composite (builders that assemble trees, like UI or query builders), Prototype (toBuilder() is a "copy and modify" prototype).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Step-by-step construction, then build() returns a complete, validated, immutable object.
  • Fixes telescoping constructors and half-built JavaBeans.
  • Required fields in builder(...) or a step builder; cross-field validation in build().
  • GoF form: Director + Builder interface means the same steps give different representations.
  • JDK: StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Thread.ofVirtual(). Spring: UriComponentsBuilder, ResponseEntity.
Order o = Order.builder("CUST-1", addr).item("MILK", 2, 68).coupon("SAVE10").build();

  • Add a JsonFeedBuilder to Example 3 that outputs the plan as JSON.
  • Rewrite ApiRequest with Lombok @Builder(toBuilder = true) and compare what you lose.
