docs.title: Factory Method
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Creational Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Factory Method moves the new keyword out of your business code into one place that decides which concrete class to create. Use it when the exact class depends on input, configuration or a subclass, and you want to add new types without editing the code that uses them.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: your checkout code needs a payment processor. Today it's new UpiProcessor(). Tomorrow you add cards, then wallets, then net banking. If every caller writes if (method == UPI) new UpiProcessor() else if ..., each new payment method means editing (and re-testing) every one of those places.

Formal definition (GoF):

Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Factory Method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses.

In everyday Java the term covers three closely related forms. You'll meet all three in the examples:

Form What it looks like Example below Static factory method (a.k.a. Simple Factory) NotificationFactory.create(channel) Example 1 Classic GoF Factory Method abstract createTransport() overridden by subclasses Example 2 Registry-based factory Map<Type, Supplier<Product>> filled at start-up Example 3

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Ordering at a restaurant

You order "a pizza" from the menu. You don't walk into the kitchen and build it. The kitchen (the factory) decides whether it comes from the wood-fired oven or the electric one, and which chef makes it. You get a pizza either way. If the restaurant adds a new oven, your way of ordering doesn't change.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Creator {
        <<abstract>>
        +someOperation()
        #createProduct()* Product
    }
    class ConcreteCreatorA {
        #createProduct() Product
    }
    class ConcreteCreatorB {
        #createProduct() Product
    }
    class Product {
        <<interface>>
        +doStuff()
    }
    class ConcreteProductA
    class ConcreteProductB
    Creator <|-- ConcreteCreatorA
    Creator <|-- ConcreteCreatorB
    Product <|.. ConcreteProductA
    Product <|.. ConcreteProductB
    Creator ..> Product : uses
    ConcreteCreatorA ..> ConcreteProductA : creates
    ConcreteCreatorB ..> ConcreteProductB : creates
Participant Responsibility Product The interface every created object implements ConcreteProduct A real implementation (Truck, UpiProcessor) Creator Declares the factory method; often contains the business logic that uses the product ConcreteCreator Overrides the factory method to return a specific product

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class CheckoutService {
    public PaymentResult pay(String method, String orderId, int amount) {
        PaymentProcessor processor;
        if (method.equals("UPI")) {
            processor = new UpiProcessor();
        } else if (method.equals("CARD")) {
            processor = new CardProcessor();
        } else if (method.equals("WALLET")) {
            processor = new WalletProcessor();
        } else {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(method);
        }
        return processor.pay(orderId, amount);
    }
}
// The same if/else is copied into RefundService, ReconciliationJob, ...

What goes wrong:

  • Breaks Open/Closed. Every new payment method means editing working code in several places.
  • Tight coupling. CheckoutService depends on every concrete processor class.
  • Hard to test. You can't swap in a fake processor without changing the code under test.
  • Stringly typed. A typo like "UPl" is only caught at runtime.

docs.title: Example 1: Order Status Notifications (Food Delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A food delivery app (like Swiggy, Zomato or DoorDash) sends "out for delivery" updates. Each customer picks a channel: email, SMS or push. Each channel formats differently, and SMS has a strict length limit. On a Friday night the app sends hundreds of thousands of these, so the code that decides what to say must not care how it is sent. New channels (WhatsApp, in-app chat) are on the roadmap.

Design:

classDiagram
    class Notification {
        <<sealed interface>>
        +send(recipient, message) String
    }
    class EmailNotification
    class SmsNotification
    class PushNotification
    class NotificationFactory {
        +create(Channel)$ Notification
    }
    class OrderStatusNotifier {
        +notify(customer, orderId, status) String
    }
    Notification <|.. EmailNotification
    Notification <|.. SmsNotification
    Notification <|.. PushNotification
    OrderStatusNotifier ..> NotificationFactory : create(channel)
    NotificationFactory ..> Notification : returns

Full Code:

Notification.javaNotificationFactory.javaOrderStatusNotifier.javaProductsFoodDeliveryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

/** The product. Callers only ever see this interface. */
public sealed interface Notification
        permits EmailNotification, SmsNotification, PushNotification { // (1)!

    String send(String recipient, String message);
}
  1. sealed (Java 17+) lists every allowed implementation. The compiler then knows the full set, which is what makes the switch in the factory exhaustive.
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

/** Static factory method: the only place that knows the concrete classes. */
public final class NotificationFactory {

    private NotificationFactory() {
    }

    public static Notification create(Channel channel) {
        return switch (channel) { // (1)!
            case EMAIL -> new EmailNotification();
            case SMS -> new SmsNotification();
            case PUSH -> new PushNotification();
        };
    }
}
  1. A switch expression over an enum has no default. If someone adds WHATSAPP to Channel and forgets to handle it here, the code doesn't compile. That's much safer than an if/else chain.
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

public class OrderStatusNotifier {

    public record Customer(String name, Channel preferredChannel, String address) {
    }

    public String notify(Customer customer, String orderId, String status) {
        Notification notification = NotificationFactory.create(customer.preferredChannel()); // (1)!
        String message = "Hi %s, order %s is %s".formatted(customer.name(), orderId, status);
        return notification.send(customer.address(), message);
    }
}
  1. The only line that deals with creation. The notifier never mentions EmailNotification, SmsNotification or PushNotification.
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

public record EmailNotification() implements Notification {

    @Override
    public String send(String recipient, String message) {
        return "[EMAIL] to=%s subject=\"Order update\" body=\"%s\"".formatted(recipient, message);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

public record SmsNotification() implements Notification {

    private static final int MAX_LENGTH = 40; // short for the demo; real SMS allows 160

    @Override
    public String send(String recipient, String message) {
        String text = message.length() > MAX_LENGTH
                ? message.substring(0, MAX_LENGTH - 3) + "..."
                : message;
        return "[SMS]   to=%s text=\"%s\"".formatted(recipient, text);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

public record PushNotification() implements Notification {

    @Override
    public String send(String recipient, String message) {
        return "[PUSH]  device=%s title=\"Order update\" text=\"%s\"".formatted(recipient, message);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

public enum Channel { EMAIL, SMS, PUSH }

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification;

import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification.OrderStatusNotifier.Customer;

import java.util.List;

public class FoodDeliveryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Food Delivery: Order Status Notifications ===");
        OrderStatusNotifier notifier = new OrderStatusNotifier();

        List<Customer> customers = List.of(
                new Customer("Asha", Channel.EMAIL, "asha@example.com"),
                new Customer("Ravi", Channel.SMS, "+91-98450-00001"),
                new Customer("Meera", Channel.PUSH, "device-7f3a"));

        int orderNo = 501;
        for (Customer c : customers) {
            System.out.println(notifier.notify(c, "FD-" + orderNo++, "out for delivery"));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Food Delivery: Order Status Notifications ===
[EMAIL] to=asha@example.com subject="Order update" body="Hi Asha, order FD-501 is out for delivery"
[SMS]   to=+91-98450-00001 text="Hi Ravi, order FD-502 is out for deli..."
[PUSH]  device=device-7f3a title="Order update" text="Hi Meera, order FD-503 is out for delivery"

Same call, three different products. Note how the SMS product applies its own length limit, which the caller never has to know about.

Why Factory Method here:

  • The channel is only known at runtime (it's the customer's preference).
  • Creation logic lives in one place; adding WhatsApp means one new class and one new case.
  • sealed + switch gives compile-time exhaustiveness, so a forgotten channel is a build error, not a production bug.
Unit Test: NotificationFactoryTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod;

import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification.Channel;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification.EmailNotification;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification.NotificationFactory;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification.PushNotification;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.notification.SmsNotification;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.EnumSource;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class NotificationFactoryTest {

    @Test
    void createsTheRightProductForEachChannel() {
        assertThat(NotificationFactory.create(Channel.EMAIL)).isInstanceOf(EmailNotification.class);
        assertThat(NotificationFactory.create(Channel.SMS)).isInstanceOf(SmsNotification.class);
        assertThat(NotificationFactory.create(Channel.PUSH)).isInstanceOf(PushNotification.class);
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @EnumSource(Channel.class)
    void everyChannelIsSupported(Channel channel) {
        assertThat(NotificationFactory.create(channel).send("x", "hello")).contains("hello");
    }

    @Test
    void smsTruncatesLongMessages() {
        String sent = NotificationFactory.create(Channel.SMS).send("+91", "a".repeat(100));
        assertThat(sent).endsWith("...\"");
    }
}

docs.title: Example 2: Shipment Planning (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A logistics company plans shipments across India. Every plan follows the same steps: pick a vehicle, work out cost from distance, estimate arrival. Only the vehicle differs: trucks for short hauls, freight trains for long, cheap routes, and cargo planes for urgent medical supplies. The planning workflow is reviewed by finance and must not be copied per vehicle type. New modes (drones, ships) are expected.

Design:

classDiagram
    class LogisticsPlanner {
        <<abstract>>
        +plan(id, route, km) String
        #createTransport()* Transport
    }
    class RoadLogistics
    class RailLogistics
    class AirLogistics
    class Transport {
        <<interface>>
        +name() String
        +costPerKmInr() int
        +speedKmph() int
    }
    class Truck
    class FreightTrain
    class CargoPlane
    LogisticsPlanner <|-- RoadLogistics
    LogisticsPlanner <|-- RailLogistics
    LogisticsPlanner <|-- AirLogistics
    Transport <|.. Truck
    Transport <|.. FreightTrain
    Transport <|.. CargoPlane
    RoadLogistics ..> Truck : creates
    RailLogistics ..> FreightTrain : creates
    AirLogistics ..> CargoPlane : creates

Full Code:

LogisticsPlanner.javaCreatorsProductsLogisticsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

/**
 * Creator. Holds the shared planning workflow and defers the choice of
 * transport to subclasses through the factory method.
 */
public abstract class LogisticsPlanner {

    protected abstract Transport createTransport(); // (1)!

    public final String plan(String shipmentId, String route, int distanceKm) { // (2)!
        Transport transport = createTransport();
        int cost = transport.costPerKmInr() * distanceKm;
        int etaHours = Math.ceilDiv(distanceKm, transport.speedKmph());
        return "%s %-20s via %-5s | %4d km | cost INR %6d | ETA %2d h"
                .formatted(shipmentId, route, transport.name(), distanceKm, cost, etaHours);
    }
}
  1. This is the GoF Factory Method: an abstract, overridable method that returns the product. Subclasses decide the concrete class.
  2. final stops subclasses from changing the workflow. They may only change what is created. This is Factory Method working together with Template Method.
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class RoadLogistics extends LogisticsPlanner {

    @Override
    protected Transport createTransport() {
        return new Truck();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class RailLogistics extends LogisticsPlanner {

    @Override
    protected Transport createTransport() {
        return new FreightTrain();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class AirLogistics extends LogisticsPlanner {

    @Override
    protected Transport createTransport() {
        return new CargoPlane();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

/** Product interface. */
public interface Transport {

    String name();

    int costPerKmInr();

    int speedKmph();
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public record Truck() implements Transport {
    public String name() { return "Truck"; }
    public int costPerKmInr() { return 18; }
    public int speedKmph() { return 50; }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public record FreightTrain() implements Transport {
    public String name() { return "Train"; }
    public int costPerKmInr() { return 8; }
    public int speedKmph() { return 60; }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public record CargoPlane() implements Transport {
    public String name() { return "Plane"; }
    public int costPerKmInr() { return 95; }
    public int speedKmph() { return 700; }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class LogisticsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Shipment Planning ===");
        print(new RoadLogistics(), "SHP-1", "Bengaluru->Mysuru", 145);
        print(new RailLogistics(), "SHP-2", "Delhi->Mumbai", 1400);
        print(new AirLogistics(), "SHP-3", "Chennai->Guwahati", 2650);
    }

    private static void print(LogisticsPlanner planner, String id, String route, int km) {
        System.out.println(planner.plan(id, route, km)); // same call, different transport
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Shipment Planning ===
SHP-1 Bengaluru->Mysuru    via Truck |  145 km | cost INR   2610 | ETA  3 h
SHP-2 Delhi->Mumbai        via Train | 1400 km | cost INR  11200 | ETA 24 h
SHP-3 Chennai->Guwahati    via Plane | 2650 km | cost INR 251750 | ETA  4 h

One workflow (plan), three transports. The trade-off is visible in the numbers: the plane is about 22× the cost of the train for a 6× faster delivery.

Why Factory Method here:

  • The algorithm is fixed and the object it needs varies. That's the textbook GoF case.
  • Adding drones means one new subclass; plan() doesn't change. The unit test below proves it with an anonymous DroneLogistics.
  • Each subclass can be tested on its own.
Unit Test: LogisticsPlannerTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod;

import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.AirLogistics;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.LogisticsPlanner;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.RoadLogistics;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.Transport;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class LogisticsPlannerTest {

    @Test
    void subclassesDecideTheTransport() {
        assertThat(new RoadLogistics().plan("S", "A->B", 100)).contains("Truck", "cost INR   1800");
        assertThat(new AirLogistics().plan("S", "A->B", 1400)).contains("Plane", "ETA  2 h");
    }

    @Test
    void newTransportNeedsOnlyANewSubclass() {
        LogisticsPlanner drone = new LogisticsPlanner() {
            @Override
            protected Transport createTransport() {
                return new Transport() {
                    public String name() { return "Drone"; }
                    public int costPerKmInr() { return 40; }
                    public int speedKmph() { return 80; }
                };
            }
        };
        assertThat(drone.plan("S", "A->B", 10)).contains("Drone", "cost INR    400", "ETA  1 h");
    }
}

docs.title: Example 3: Pluggable Payment Processors (Banking / Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payments team runs checkout for a large e-commerce site. It supports UPI (no fee), cards (2% merchant fee) and wallets (regulatory limit of INR 10,000 per transaction). Net banking is being built by another team and isn't live yet. Payment methods are switched on per country and per merchant through configuration, so the factory can't be a hard-coded switch. It has to be a registry that's filled at start-up, and asking for a method that isn't registered must fail fast with a clear error.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Bootstrap / Config
    participant F as PaymentProcessorFactory
    participant C as Checkout
    participant P as CardProcessor
    B->>F: register(UPI, UpiProcessor::new)
    B->>F: register(CARD, CardProcessor::new)
    B->>F: register(WALLET, WalletProcessor::new)
    C->>F: create(CARD)
    F->>P: supplier.get()
    F-->>C: PaymentProcessor
    C->>P: pay("ORD-102", 2400)
    P-->>C: SUCCESS fee=48
    C->>F: create(NET_BANKING)
    F-->>C: UnsupportedPaymentMethodException

Full Code:

PaymentProcessorFactory.javaCheckoutDemo.javaProcessorsSupporting types 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Registry-based factory: new payment methods are added by registering a
 * supplier, not by editing a switch statement (Open/Closed Principle).
 */
public final class PaymentProcessorFactory {

    private final Map<PaymentMethod, Supplier<? extends PaymentProcessor>> registry =
            new EnumMap<>(PaymentMethod.class); // (1)!

    public PaymentProcessorFactory register(PaymentMethod method,
                                            Supplier<? extends PaymentProcessor> supplier) {
        registry.put(method, supplier);
        return this; // fluent registration
    }

    public PaymentProcessor create(PaymentMethod method) {
        Supplier<? extends PaymentProcessor> supplier = registry.get(method);
        if (supplier == null) {
            throw new UnsupportedPaymentMethodException(method); // (2)!
        }
        return supplier.get(); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. EnumMap is a compact, fast array-backed map for enum keys. Each value is a Supplier, which is a factory method passed as a value. UpiProcessor::new is a constructor reference.
  2. Fail fast with a domain exception. A null return would turn into a confusing NullPointerException far away from the cause.
  3. The supplier is called on every request, so each caller gets a new processor. Register a supplier that returns a shared instance if the processor is stateless and expensive to build.
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class CheckoutDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Checkout with Pluggable Processors ===");
        PaymentProcessorFactory factory = new PaymentProcessorFactory()
                .register(PaymentMethod.UPI, UpiProcessor::new)
                .register(PaymentMethod.CARD, CardProcessor::new)
                .register(PaymentMethod.WALLET, WalletProcessor::new);

        pay(factory, "ORD-101", PaymentMethod.UPI, 450);
        pay(factory, "ORD-102", PaymentMethod.CARD, 2400);
        pay(factory, "ORD-103", PaymentMethod.WALLET, 12000);
        pay(factory, "ORD-104", PaymentMethod.NET_BANKING, 999);
    }

    private static void pay(PaymentProcessorFactory factory, String orderId,
                            PaymentMethod method, int amountInr) {
        String prefix = "%s %-11s INR %5d -> ".formatted(orderId, method, amountInr);
        try {
            PaymentResult result = factory.create(method).pay(orderId, amountInr);
            System.out.println(prefix + (result.success()
                    ? "SUCCESS " + result.detail() + " fee=INR " + result.feeInr()
                    : "FAILED  " + result.detail()));
        } catch (UnsupportedPaymentMethodException e) {
            System.out.println(prefix + "ERROR   " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public interface PaymentProcessor {

    PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr);
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class UpiProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {

    @Override
    public PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        return PaymentResult.ok(0, "UPI-" + orderId); // UPI has no merchant fee
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class CardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {

    private static final int FEE_PERCENT = 2;

    @Override
    public PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        return PaymentResult.ok(amountInr * FEE_PERCENT / 100, "CARD-" + orderId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class WalletProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {

    private static final int WALLET_LIMIT_INR = 10_000;

    @Override
    public PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        if (amountInr > WALLET_LIMIT_INR) {
            return PaymentResult.failed("wallet limit INR " + WALLET_LIMIT_INR + " exceeded");
        }
        return PaymentResult.ok(0, "WAL-" + orderId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public enum PaymentMethod { UPI, CARD, WALLET, NET_BANKING }

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public record PaymentResult(boolean success, int feeInr, String detail) {

    public static PaymentResult ok(int feeInr, String reference) {
        return new PaymentResult(true, feeInr, "ref=" + reference);
    }

    public static PaymentResult failed(String reason) {
        return new PaymentResult(false, 0, reason);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class UnsupportedPaymentMethodException extends RuntimeException {

    public UnsupportedPaymentMethodException(PaymentMethod method) {
        super("No processor registered for " + method);
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Checkout with Pluggable Processors ===
ORD-101 UPI         INR   450 -> SUCCESS ref=UPI-ORD-101 fee=INR 0
ORD-102 CARD        INR  2400 -> SUCCESS ref=CARD-ORD-102 fee=INR 48
ORD-103 WALLET      INR 12000 -> FAILED  wallet limit INR 10000 exceeded
ORD-104 NET_BANKING INR   999 -> ERROR   No processor registered for NET_BANKING

Three outcomes worth noticing: a normal success, a business failure handled by the product itself (wallet limit), and a configuration failure caught by the factory (net banking isn't registered).

Why Factory Method here:

  • The set of products is decided by configuration, not by code, so a registry is the natural fit.
  • Open/Closed for real: the net-banking team adds register(NET_BANKING, NetBankingProcessor::new) and touches nothing else.
  • Tests can register a fake for any method (see canSwapInATestDouble below).
  • This is exactly how Spring injects Map<String, PaymentProcessor>; see section 6.
Unit Test: PaymentProcessorFactoryTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod;

import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.CardProcessor;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.PaymentMethod;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.PaymentProcessorFactory;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.PaymentResult;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.UnsupportedPaymentMethodException;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.UpiProcessor;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class PaymentProcessorFactoryTest {

    private final PaymentProcessorFactory factory = new PaymentProcessorFactory()
            .register(PaymentMethod.UPI, UpiProcessor::new)
            .register(PaymentMethod.CARD, CardProcessor::new);

    @Test
    void createsRegisteredProcessor() {
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.CARD)).isInstanceOf(CardProcessor.class);
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.CARD).pay("O1", 1000))
                .isEqualTo(new PaymentResult(true, 20, "ref=CARD-O1"));
    }

    @Test
    void returnsANewInstanceEachTime() {
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.UPI)).isNotSameAs(factory.create(PaymentMethod.UPI));
    }

    @Test
    void canSwapInATestDouble() {
        factory.register(PaymentMethod.UPI, () -> (orderId, amount) -> PaymentResult.failed("bank down"));
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.UPI).pay("O1", 10).success()).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void unknownMethodFailsFast() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> factory.create(PaymentMethod.NET_BANKING))
                .isInstanceOf(UnsupportedPaymentMethodException.class)
                .hasMessage("No processor registered for NET_BANKING");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Static factory methods on the type itself. Modern Java APIs prefer these to public constructors (Effective Java, Item 1):

List<String> names = List.of("a", "b");       // immutable list
Optional<User> user = Optional.ofNullable(u);
Path path = Path.of("/tmp", "x.txt");
Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(30);

Naming conventions: of, from, valueOf, getInstance, newInstance, create, getType / newType.

Factory method on an interface (Java 8+): the coding challenge below puts FareCalculator.of(type) right on the interface, with lambdas as the products.

Spring does the registry for you. Name each bean after the enum value and inject a map:

public interface PaymentProcessor { PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr); }

@Component("UPI")  class UpiProcessor  implements PaymentProcessor { /* ... */ }
@Component("CARD") class CardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { /* ... */ }

@Service
class PaymentProcessorFactory {
    private final Map<String, PaymentProcessor> processors; // bean name -> bean

    PaymentProcessorFactory(Map<String, PaymentProcessor> processors) {
        this.processors = processors;
    }

    PaymentProcessor create(PaymentMethod method) {
        PaymentProcessor p = processors.get(method.name());
        if (p == null) throw new UnsupportedPaymentMethodException(method);
        return p;
    }
}

Adding a payment method is now one new @Component class, and nothing else changes. Combine this with @ConditionalOnProperty to switch methods on per environment.

ServiceLoader for plug-ins. ServiceLoader.load(PaymentProcessor.class) discovers implementations on the classpath (from META-INF/services or module-info provides). It's how JDBC drivers and many JDK SPIs are found.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example Form JDK Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale) Static factory picks a subclass by locale JDK List.of, Map.of, EnumSet.of Static factory; EnumSet.of returns RegularEnumSet or JumboEnumSet depending on size JDK Collection.iterator() Classic GoF: each collection subclass creates its own iterator JDK URLStreamHandlerFactory, ThreadFactory Factory interfaces you plug in JDK DriverManager.getConnection(url), ServiceLoader Registry/discovery-based Spring FactoryBean<T>, @Bean methods, BeanFactory.getBean() The container is one big factory Spring RestClient.builder(), WebClient.create() Static factory methods Hibernate SessionFactory.openSession() Factory method on a long-lived factory SLF4J LoggerFactory.getLogger(...) Static factory with a pluggable back-end

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Callers depend on an interface, not on concrete classes More classes: one per product, plus creators in the GoF form New products without editing client code (OCP) A factory with a giant switch just moves the if/else, unless it's sealed/exhaustive or a registry Creation logic (validation, caching, pooling) in one place Indirection makes it harder to "jump to definition" in an IDE Easy to swap in test doubles The GoF subclass form uses inheritance, which is rigid. Prefer composition (pass a Supplier) when you can Static factories can have descriptive names and return cached instances or subtypes Static factories can't be overridden or mocked easily

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
The 'god factory'

One ObjectFactory.create(String type) that builds everything in the app is a service locator in disguise. Keep one factory per product family.

Returning null for unknown types

It turns a clear configuration error into a NullPointerException three layers away. Throw a domain exception with the bad key in the message (Example 3).

Stringly typed keys

create("upi") vs create("UPI") bugs. Use an enum (or sealed types) as the key, and convert external strings once at the boundary.

Factory for a single class

If there is, and will only ever be, one implementation, a factory is ceremony. YAGNI. Add it when the second implementation shows up.

Calling the factory method from a constructor

In the GoF form, if the base class constructor calls the abstract createX(), the subclass's fields aren't initialized yet. Call it lazily, or from a method (as plan() does).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Which form to pick:

Situation Choose Fixed, small set of types known at compile time Static factory + sealed + exhaustive switch Shared workflow, only one collaborator varies, a class hierarchy already exists GoF Factory Method (with a final template method) Types are switched on by config, tenant or feature flag, or contributed by other teams/modules Registry (Map<K, Supplier<T>>, Spring map injection, ServiceLoader) Several related products that must match Move up to Abstract Factory

Factories as a seam for operational concerns. Because every instance goes through one point, the factory is where you add metrics (processor.created{method=CARD}), circuit breakers (wrap the product in a Resilience4j-decorated proxy), feature flags (return the new implementation for 5% of traffic), and caching of stateless products.

Feature-flagged migrations. Migrating from an old payment provider to a new one? Register both and let the factory decide per request:

PaymentProcessor create(PaymentMethod m, String merchantId) {
    if (m == CARD && flags.isEnabled("new-card-gateway", merchantId)) {
        return newCardGateway.get();
    }
    return registry.get(m).get();
}

That's the Strangler Fig pattern at class level. Roll out per merchant, roll back instantly.

Testing strategy. Unit-test each product on its own; test the factory's mapping (every enum value maps to something, using @EnumSource as in Example 1's test); test the clients with a fake registry.

War story: the missing default that charged the wrong fee

A checkout service picked a fee calculator with an old-style switch statement that ended in default: return new StandardFeeCalculator();. A new BNPL (buy now, pay later) method was added to the enum. Nobody updated the switch, and BNPL silently fell through to the standard card fee calculator. For three weeks BNPL merchants were charged 2% instead of the contracted 3.5%, a revenue leak only found in a quarterly audit. Fix: replaced it with a switch expression with no default, so the compiler flags unhandled constants, and added a parameterized test over PaymentMethod.values() asserting each one maps to a calculator. Lesson: "silent default" in a factory is a bug waiting to happen. Make missing cases a compile error or a loud failure.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder Simple constructor Creates One product A family of related products One complex product, step by step One known class Decides Which class Which family How it's put together Nothing to decide Typical API create(type) / overridden createX() ui.button(), ui.checkbox() Order.builder().item(..).build() new Order(...) Use when Type varies at runtime Products must be consistent with each other Many optional params, immutability One implementation, simple setup

Works well with: Template Method (Example 2), Strategy (the products are often strategies), Singleton (cache stateless products), Prototype (factory clones a template instead of calling new).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Hide new behind a method; callers get an interface.
  • Three forms: static factory, GoF (subclass overrides createX()), registry (Map<K, Supplier<T>>).
  • OCP: new product = new class (+ registration), no edits to callers.
  • No silent default: use sealed/enum switch expressions, or throw on unknown keys.
  • JDK: List.of, Calendar.getInstance, Collection.iterator(). Spring: FactoryBean, map injection.
static Notification create(Channel c) { return switch (c) { case EMAIL -> new Email(); case SMS -> new Sms(); case PUSH -> new Push(); }; }

docs.text:
• Add a WHATSAPP channel to Example 1. Notice which line fails to compile first.
  • Add a DroneLogistics creator to Example 2 as a real class with its own test.
  • Rewrite Example 3 as a Spring Boot app using Map<String, PaymentProcessor> injection.
  • Make PaymentProcessorFactory cache stateless processors and prove it with a test.
