docs.title: Singleton
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🔴 Advanced Creational Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Singleton makes sure a class has exactly one instance and gives everyone a single global point of access to it. Use it for things that really are one-per-application, like configuration, an ID sequence or an audit trail. Prefer letting a DI container (Spring) manage the "one instance" rule whenever you can.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: some objects only make sense once. If two parts of your app each build their own configuration object, they might read different values. If two threads each create their own ID generator, they'll hand out duplicate IDs. If every service writes to its own audit log, auditors can't see one ordered trail.

Formal definition (GoF):

Ensure a class only has one instance, and provide a global point of access to it.

Two responsibilities:

  1. Control instantiation: nobody outside the class can call new.
  2. Provide access: a well-known way (getInstance() or INSTANCE) to reach the one object.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
The country's President

A country has exactly one sitting President at a time. You don't "create" a new President when you need one; you go through a well-known channel (the President's office) and reach the same person everyone else reaches. The constitution (the private constructor) stops anyone from appointing a second one.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Singleton {
        -static Singleton instance
        -Singleton()
        +static getInstance() Singleton
        +businessMethod()
    }
    class ClientA
    class ClientB
    ClientA ..> Singleton : getInstance()
    ClientB ..> Singleton : getInstance()
    Singleton --> Singleton : holds the only instance
Participant Responsibility Singleton Holds the single instance in a static field, hides its constructor, exposes getInstance() Client Never calls new; always asks the class for the shared instance

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class ConfigLoader {
    private final Map<String, String> settings;

    public ConfigLoader() {                 // anyone can call new
        settings = loadFromDisk();          // expensive I/O every time
    }
    // ...
}

// Somewhere in CheckoutService
ConfigLoader cfg1 = new ConfigLoader();     // reads file
// Somewhere in DeliveryService
ConfigLoader cfg2 = new ConfigLoader();     // reads file AGAIN; may see a different version

What goes wrong:

  • Wasted work. The file or remote config is read over and over.
  • Inconsistent state. Two copies can disagree if the file changes between reads.
  • Broken invariants. With a counter (an ID generator), two instances means duplicate IDs.

And the "obvious" lazy fix isn't thread-safe:

public static ConfigLoader getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {          // two threads can both see null here...
        instance = new ConfigLoader(); // ...and both create an instance
    }
    return instance;
}

docs.title: 5. Three Real-World Examples
docs.text: Each example uses a different Singleton implementation, so by the end you'll have seen the three you should know for interviews: enum, holder idiom and double-checked locking.

docs.title: Example 1: Store Configuration (Grocery Delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery delivery app (think Blinkit/Instacart) has a checkout service and a delivery-slot service. Both need the same business settings: the delivery fee (INR 30), the free-delivery threshold (INR 499) and feature flags such as express delivery. Loading the settings is expensive (in production it's a call to a config server), and every service must see the same values. Otherwise the cart page and the checkout page could show different delivery fees, which leads straight to customer complaints.

Design:

classDiagram
    class StoreConfig {
        <<enumeration>>
        INSTANCE
        -Map~String,String~ settings
        +getInt(key) int
        +isEnabled(feature) boolean
    }
    class CheckoutService {
        +deliveryFee(subtotal) int
        +checkout(cartId, subtotal) String
    }
    class DeliverySlotService {
        +expressAvailable() boolean
    }
    CheckoutService --> StoreConfig : INSTANCE
    DeliverySlotService --> StoreConfig : INSTANCE

Full Code:

StoreConfig.javaCheckoutService.javaDeliverySlotService.javaGroceryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Application-wide store configuration, loaded exactly once.
 * The enum form is the simplest thread-safe Singleton in Java and is
 * immune to reflection and serialization attacks.
 */
public enum StoreConfig {
    INSTANCE; // (1)!

    private final Map<String, String> settings;

    StoreConfig() { // (2)!
        System.out.println("[StoreConfig] Loading configuration (runs once)...");
        // In production this would come from a file, Spring Cloud Config or a DB.
        this.settings = Map.of(
                "delivery.fee.inr", "30",
                "free.delivery.above.inr", "499",
                "feature.express.delivery", "true");
    }

    public int getInt(String key) {
        String value = settings.get(key);
        if (value == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown config key: " + key);
        }
        return Integer.parseInt(value);
    }

    public boolean isEnabled(String feature) {
        return Boolean.parseBoolean(settings.getOrDefault("feature." + feature, "false"));
    }
}
  1. An enum with one constant is a Singleton. The JVM guarantees that INSTANCE is created exactly once, lazily (on first access to the enum class) and thread-safely.
  2. Enum constructors are implicitly private. Reflection cannot call them: Constructor.newInstance throws IllegalArgumentException: Cannot reflectively create enum objects.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

public class CheckoutService {

    private final StoreConfig config = StoreConfig.INSTANCE; // (1)!

    public int deliveryFee(int subtotalInr) {
        int freeAbove = config.getInt("free.delivery.above.inr");
        return subtotalInr >= freeAbove ? 0 : config.getInt("delivery.fee.inr");
    }

    public String checkout(int cartId, int subtotalInr) {
        int fee = deliveryFee(subtotalInr);
        return "Cart #%d subtotal=INR %d -> delivery fee=INR %d, total=INR %d"
                .formatted(cartId, subtotalInr, fee, subtotalInr + fee);
    }

    StoreConfig config() {
        return config;
    }
}
  1. The first line that touches StoreConfig triggers class initialization, and that's when the constructor runs and the "Loading configuration" line prints.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

public class DeliverySlotService {

    private final StoreConfig config = StoreConfig.INSTANCE;

    public boolean expressAvailable() {
        return config.isEnabled("express.delivery");
    }

    StoreConfig config() {
        return config;
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

public class GroceryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery Checkout Demo ===");

        CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService(); // first use triggers loading
        DeliverySlotService slots = new DeliverySlotService();

        System.out.println(checkout.checkout(1, 350));
        System.out.println(checkout.checkout(2, 620));
        System.out.println("Express delivery available: " + slots.expressAvailable());
        System.out.println("Same config instance in both services? "
                + (checkout.config() == slots.config()));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery Checkout Demo ===
[StoreConfig] Loading configuration (runs once)...
Cart #1 subtotal=INR 350 -> delivery fee=INR 30, total=INR 380
Cart #2 subtotal=INR 620 -> delivery fee=INR 0, total=INR 620
Express delivery available: true
Same config instance in both services? true

Notice that the loading message appears once, even though two services use the config, and only after the demo header. That shows the enum Singleton is lazy.

Why Singleton here:

  • Config is expensive to load and must be loaded once.
  • Every service must see identical values.
  • The enum form is the shortest correct implementation, and it's safe against reflection and serialization.
  • Joshua Bloch (Effective Java, Item 3): "a single-element enum type is often the best way to implement a singleton."
Unit Test: StoreConfigTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton;

import com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery.CheckoutService;
import com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery.StoreConfig;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class StoreConfigTest {

    @Test
    void enumSingletonIsTheSameInstance() {
        assertThat(StoreConfig.valueOf("INSTANCE")).isSameAs(StoreConfig.INSTANCE);
    }

    @Test
    void deliveryIsFreeAboveThreshold() {
        CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService();
        assertThat(checkout.deliveryFee(350)).isEqualTo(30);
        assertThat(checkout.deliveryFee(499)).isZero();
    }

    @Test
    void unknownKeyFailsFast() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> StoreConfig.INSTANCE.getInt("missing"))
                .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("missing");
    }
}

docs.title: Example 2: Transaction ID Generator (Banking / Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment switch for a bank's Bengaluru node issues an ID for every UPI/card transaction, such as TXN-BLR-0000001. At peak it processes thousands of payments per second on virtual threads. Two transactions with the same ID would be a serious reconciliation incident, so the sequence must be unique and gap-free within the node. There must be exactly one sequence per JVM, and it must be safe to use from thousands of threads at once.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T1 as Virtual Thread 1
    participant T2 as Virtual Thread 2
    participant G as TransactionIdGenerator<br/>(Holder.INSTANCE)
    participant A as AtomicLong
    T1->>G: getInstance().nextId()
    G->>A: incrementAndGet()
    A-->>G: 1
    G-->>T1: TXN-BLR-0000001
    T2->>G: getInstance().nextId()
    G->>A: incrementAndGet()
    A-->>G: 2
    G-->>T2: TXN-BLR-0000002

Full Code:

TransactionIdGenerator.javaPaymentsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.payments;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

/**
 * Issues unique, ordered transaction IDs for one payment node.
 * Uses the Initialization-on-demand Holder idiom: lazy, thread-safe, no locks.
 */
public final class TransactionIdGenerator {

    private final AtomicLong sequence = new AtomicLong(); // (1)!
    private final String branchCode;

    private TransactionIdGenerator(String branchCode) { // (2)!
        this.branchCode = branchCode;
    }

    private static final class Holder { // (3)!
        private static final TransactionIdGenerator INSTANCE = new TransactionIdGenerator("BLR");
    }

    public static TransactionIdGenerator getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE; // (4)!
    }

    public String nextId() {
        return "TXN-%s-%07d".formatted(branchCode, sequence.incrementAndGet());
    }
}
  1. The Singleton guarantees one object. AtomicLong makes that object's state thread-safe. You need both: a Singleton with a plain long++ would still hand out duplicates.
  2. The private constructor stops new TransactionIdGenerator(...) from outside.
  3. Initialization-on-demand holder idiom. The JVM doesn't initialize the nested Holder class until getInstance() first touches it, and class initialization is guaranteed thread-safe by the JLS (§12.4.2). You get lazy loading with no synchronized and no volatile.
  4. After the first call this is a plain static field read, about as fast as Java gets.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.payments;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class PaymentsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Transaction ID Generator ===");
        TransactionIdGenerator generator = TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance();
        System.out.println("First ID  : " + generator.nextId());
        System.out.println("Second ID : " + generator.nextId());

        int threads = 1_000;
        int idsPerThread = 10;
        Set<String> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

        System.out.println("Generating 10,000 IDs from 1,000 virtual threads...");
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < idsPerThread; i++) {
                        // every thread asks for "the" generator; all get the same object
                        ids.add(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance().nextId());
                    }
                });
            }
        } // close() waits for all tasks to finish

        System.out.println("Unique IDs : " + ids.size());
        System.out.println("Duplicates : " + (threads * idsPerThread - ids.size()));
        System.out.println("Next ID    : " + generator.nextId());
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Transaction ID Generator ===
First ID  : TXN-BLR-0000001
Second ID : TXN-BLR-0000002
Generating 10,000 IDs from 1,000 virtual threads...
Unique IDs : 10000
Duplicates : 0
Next ID    : TXN-BLR-0010003

10,000 concurrent requests, 0 duplicates, and the next ID continues exactly where the sequence left off (2 + 10,000 + 1 = 10,003).

Why Singleton here:

  • Uniqueness is a business invariant: two generators means two sequences means duplicate IDs.
  • The holder idiom gives lazy, lock-free access, so there's no contention even with thousands of threads.
  • The singleton is per JVM. Across nodes, the branch code (BLR) keeps IDs globally unique. (In a real cluster you'd use a Snowflake-style ID or a DB sequence. See the deep dive.)
Unit Test: TransactionIdGeneratorTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton;

import com.handbook.creational.singleton.payments.TransactionIdGenerator;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class TransactionIdGeneratorTest {

    @Test
    void getInstanceAlwaysReturnsSameObject() {
        assertThat(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance())
                .isSameAs(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance());
    }

    @Test
    void idsAreUniqueUnderConcurrency() {
        Set<String> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int t = 0; t < 500; t++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                        ids.add(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance().nextId());
                    }
                });
            }
        }
        assertThat(ids).hasSize(10_000);
        assertThat(ids).allMatch(id -> id.matches("TXN-BLR-\\d{7}"));
    }
}

docs.title: Example 3: Patient Record Audit Trail (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital information system must record every read and write of a patient record, as required by health-data regulations (for example HIPAA, or India's DPDP Act). Doctors view records, nurses update vitals, and the prescription module writes prescriptions. Compliance auditors need one ordered trail across all modules, not a separate log per module. The audit store is expensive to open, so it should only be created when first needed.

Design:

classDiagram
    class AuditLogger {
        -static volatile AuditLogger instance
        -List~String~ entries
        -AuditLogger()
        +static getInstance() AuditLogger
        +record(user, action, patientId)
        +entries() List~String~
    }
    class PatientRecordService {
        +view(user, patientId)
        +updateVitals(user, patientId)
    }
    class PrescriptionService {
        +prescribe(user, patientId)
    }
    PatientRecordService ..> AuditLogger
    PrescriptionService ..> AuditLogger

Full Code:

AuditLogger.javaPatientRecordService.javaPrescriptionService.javaHealthcareDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Central audit trail for access to patient records (compliance requirement:
 * every read/write must be recorded in one ordered log).
 * Implemented with lazy Double-Checked Locking.
 */
public final class AuditLogger {

    private static volatile AuditLogger instance; // (1)!

    private final List<String> entries = new ArrayList<>();

    private AuditLogger() {
        if (instance != null) { // (2)!
            throw new IllegalStateException("Use AuditLogger.getInstance()");
        }
        System.out.println("[AuditLogger] Opening audit store...");
    }

    public static AuditLogger getInstance() {
        AuditLogger local = instance; // (3)!
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (AuditLogger.class) {
                local = instance;
                if (local == null) {
                    instance = local = new AuditLogger();
                }
            }
        }
        return local;
    }

    public synchronized void record(String user, String action, String patientId) {
        entries.add("#%03d %-10s %-14s patient=%s"
                .formatted(entries.size() + 1, user, action, patientId));
    }

    public synchronized List<String> entries() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(entries));
    }
}
  1. volatile is mandatory. Without it, the JIT or CPU may publish the reference before the constructor finishes. Another thread could then see a non-null but half-built object. volatile creates a happens-before edge between the write and later reads.
  2. Reflection guard. If someone uses setAccessible(true) to call the constructor after the instance exists, it fails loudly instead of quietly creating a second audit trail.
  3. Reading the volatile field into a local means the common path (already initialized) does one volatile read instead of two. This is the form recommended in Effective Java, Item 83.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

public class PatientRecordService {

    public void view(String user, String patientId) {
        AuditLogger.getInstance().record(user, "VIEW_RECORD", patientId);
    }

    public void updateVitals(String user, String patientId) {
        AuditLogger.getInstance().record(user, "UPDATE_VITALS", patientId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

public class PrescriptionService {

    public void prescribe(String user, String patientId) {
        AuditLogger.getInstance().record(user, "PRESCRIBE", patientId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

public class HealthcareDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital: Patient Record Audit Trail ===");
        PatientRecordService records = new PatientRecordService();
        PrescriptionService prescriptions = new PrescriptionService();

        records.view("dr.mehta", "P-1001");
        records.updateVitals("nurse.anna", "P-1001");
        prescriptions.prescribe("dr.mehta", "P-1001");
        records.view("dr.khan", "P-2002");

        System.out.println("Audit trail:");
        AuditLogger.getInstance().entries().forEach(e -> System.out.println("  " + e));
        System.out.println("Single audit store? "
                + (AuditLogger.getInstance() == AuditLogger.getInstance()));
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital: Patient Record Audit Trail ===
[AuditLogger] Opening audit store...
Audit trail:
  #001 dr.mehta   VIEW_RECORD    patient=P-1001
  #002 nurse.anna UPDATE_VITALS  patient=P-1001
  #003 dr.mehta   PRESCRIBE      patient=P-1001
  #004 dr.khan    VIEW_RECORD    patient=P-2002
Single audit store? true

Two different services wrote into one ordered trail, with continuous sequence numbers.

Why Singleton here:

  • Regulations require one complete, ordered trail.
  • The store is expensive to open, so lazy creation (DCL) avoids paying for it in modules that never audit.
  • DCL is the version interviewers most often ask you to write and explain (volatile, two null checks).
  • The reflection guard shows you know how a Singleton can be broken.
Unit Test: AuditLoggerTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton;

import com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare.AuditLogger;
import com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare.PatientRecordService;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;
import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class AuditLoggerTest {

    @Test
    void servicesShareOneAuditTrail() {
        int before = AuditLogger.getInstance().entries().size();
        new PatientRecordService().view("dr.test", "P-9");
        assertThat(AuditLogger.getInstance().entries()).hasSize(before + 1);
    }

    @Test
    void reflectionCannotCreateSecondInstance() throws Exception {
        AuditLogger.getInstance(); // make sure the instance exists
        Constructor<AuditLogger> ctor = AuditLogger.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
        ctor.setAccessible(true);
        assertThatThrownBy(ctor::newInstance)
                .isInstanceOf(InvocationTargetException.class)
                .hasCauseInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example Notes JDK Runtime.getRuntime() Classic eager Singleton JDK java.awt.Desktop.getDesktop(), System.console() One per JVM JDK Collections.emptyList(), Comparator.naturalOrder() Shared immutable instances JDK Enum constants, Boolean.TRUE Built-in singletons Spring Default bean scope is singleton One instance per ApplicationContext, not per JVM, and without a private constructor Spring @Configuration classes CGLIB proxies make @Bean methods return the same instance Logging LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class) Cached per name (a Multiton) Hibernate SessionFactory Expensive; built once per app Kafka KafkaProducer Thread-safe; recommended to share one instance

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Guarantees one instance, so invariants hold (unique IDs, one config) Global state: hidden dependencies make code harder to reason about Lazy creation saves start-up time and memory Hard to unit-test: you can't easily swap in a mock; state leaks between tests Single point of access, no passing it around Violates Single Responsibility (manages its own lifecycle and does business work) Can be made lock-free (holder, enum) Becomes a bottleneck if it holds a contended lock Only "single" per class loader. In app servers or with multiple class loaders you can get several Doesn't scale across JVMs or pods; that needs a distributed solution

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Forgetting volatile in double-checked locking

Without volatile, another thread can see a partially constructed object. The code passes every test on your laptop and fails at 3 a.m. under load on a many-core server.

Reflection and serialization attacks

setAccessible(true) can call a private constructor. Deserializing creates a new object. Defend with a constructor guard and readResolve(), or just use an enum.

Mutable shared state

A Singleton holding a HashMap that many threads write to is a race condition with a global access point. Make its state immutable, or use concurrent structures (AtomicLong, ConcurrentHashMap).

Singleton as a service locator / god object

AppContext.getInstance().getOrderService().getRepo()... hides dependencies and couples everything to one class. Prefer constructor injection.

Thinking it's 'one per system'

In Kubernetes with 10 pods you have 10 singletons. A per-JVM AtomicLong sequence across pods produces duplicate IDs. That's exactly why Example 2 includes a node code.

Testing pain

Tests share the same instance, so test order changes results. Workarounds: inject the singleton through an interface, or let Spring manage the scope so you can use @MockitoBean.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Java Memory Model view. instance = new AuditLogger() is really three steps: allocate memory, run the constructor, publish the reference. Without a happens-before edge, steps 2 and 3 may be reordered. volatile (JSR-133, Java 5+) forbids that reordering. Class initialization (holder and enum) is protected by the JVM's initialization lock, which gives the same guarantee for free. That's why holder and enum are preferred.

Prefer container-managed singletons. In a Spring Boot service, write a plain class with a public constructor and let Spring make it a singleton bean:

@Service                       // singleton scope by default
public class TransactionIdService {
    private final AtomicLong sequence = new AtomicLong();
    public String nextId() { return "TXN-%07d".formatted(sequence.incrementAndGet()); }
}

You get one instance, constructor injection, easy mocking, and lifecycle hooks (@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy), without the downsides of global static state.

Distributed "singletons". When you need one of something across a cluster:

Need Tool Unique IDs across nodes Snowflake / ULID / UUIDv7, DB sequences, Redis INCR One scheduled job runner ShedLock, Quartz clustered mode, Kubernetes CronJob One leader Leader election (ZooKeeper, etcd, Kubernetes Lease, Spring Integration LockRegistryLeaderInitiator) One shared config Spring Cloud Config, Consul, AWS AppConfig, with refresh events

How to defend it in a design review: "This object enforces an invariant that only holds if there's one instance (a sequence or an ordered log). It's per-JVM by design, it's lock-free, it has no mutable state that can be seen from outside, and it's injected through an interface so tests can replace it. For cross-node uniqueness we rely on X."

When NOT to use it: to avoid passing parameters; for request- or user-specific data; for anything that needs different configurations in tests; for caches that should be bounded or evicted (use Caffeine instead).

War story: duplicate invoice numbers after scaling out

A billing service generated invoice numbers with a Singleton AtomicLong that was seeded from MAX(invoice_no) at start-up. It worked perfectly for two years on one VM. During a migration to Kubernetes, the service was scaled to 3 replicas. Each pod seeded from the same max and started issuing the same numbers. Finance found 1,200 duplicate invoices at month-end close. Fix: switched to a database sequence (nextval) with an allocation size of 50 per pod (Hibernate pooled optimizer) and added a unique constraint on invoice_no. Lesson: a Singleton is a per-process guarantee. Write down that assumption, and add a database constraint as the last line of defense.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Singleton Static utility class Spring singleton bean Monostate Instances 1 per class loader 0 1 per ApplicationContext Many objects, shared static state Can implement interfaces ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅ Polymorphism / mocking Hard ❌ ✅ Easy Hard Lazy init ✅ N/A ✅ (@Lazy) ❌ Holds state ✅ Should not ✅ ✅ Use for Real one-per-process invariants Pure functions (Math, Collections) Almost every service in a Spring app Rarely; legacy code

Patterns that often use Singleton: Abstract Factory (one factory per family), Facade (one entry point), Flyweight factory, Object Pool manager, State objects without fields.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One instance + global access. Private constructor, static holder, getInstance().
  • Best forms: enum (safest) or the holder idiom (lazy, lock-free).
  • DCL needs volatile. Say "happens-before" and "partially constructed object".
  • Breakers: reflection, serialization, cloning. Enum beats all three.
  • One per class loader / per JVM, never per cluster. In Spring, prefer singleton-scoped beans.
public enum Config { INSTANCE; public String get(String k) { return "..."; } }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Rewrite Example 1 using the holder idiom and compare the two.
  • Remove volatile from AuditLogger and explain, in writing, what could go wrong.
  • Add implements Serializable to TransactionIdGenerator, serialize and deserialize it, and show that you get a second instance. Then fix it with readResolve().
  • Turn TransactionIdGenerator into a Spring @Service and write a test that mocks it.

docs.title: How to Use This Handbook
docs.text:
This handbook is written for three readers at once. Pick the path that fits you; you can switch at any time.

Every pattern page has the same 13 sections

So once you've read one page, you know where everything is on every other page. Start with Singleton; it's the reference page.

docs.title: Beginner path
docs.text:
Who: students, freshers, engineers with 0–2 years of experience.

  1. Read OOP & SOLID Refresher first. Patterns are just SOLID applied to recurring problems.
  2. Skim the UML Cheat Sheet so the diagrams make sense.
  3. On each pattern page, read sections 1–5 (intent, analogy, structure, naive approach, the 3 examples) and section 13 (revision card).
  4. Run every example yourself. Change one thing and predict the new output before you run it.
  5. Do the 🟢 tab in the Interview Corner.

Suggested order: Singleton → Factory Method → Builder → Strategy → Observer → Decorator → Adapter → Facade → Template Method → State.

docs.title: Experienced path
docs.text:
Who: engineers with 5–15+ years, tech leads, architects.

  1. Skip the analogies. Go straight to section 5 and look at how each example is put together.
  2. Spend most of your time on sections 6–10: modern Java variants, framework internals, trade-offs, pitfalls, the senior deep dive and the war story.
  3. Use section 11 to sharpen how you explain the differences between similar patterns. This is where design reviews are won.
  4. Go through the microservices and architecture sections. That's where 10–15-year interviews spend most of their time.

docs.title: Interview path
docs.text:
Who: anyone with an interview in the next 2–6 weeks.

Target company type Focus on Typical rounds Service companies (Cognizant, TCS, Infosys, Accenture, Wipro, Capgemini) Definitions, Singleton/Factory/Builder/Strategy/Observer code, SOLID, differences between patterns Technical round 1–2, managerial, HR Product companies (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, SAP, Atlassian, Uber) Low-level design (LLD) problems, extensibility, concurrency, trade-offs, microservice patterns in system design Coding ×2–3, LLD/OOD, system design (senior), behavioral

4-week plan:

  • Week 1: Creational + SOLID. Write every Singleton variant from memory.
  • Week 2: Behavioral (Strategy, Observer, State, Command, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method).
  • Week 3: Structural + 5 LLD problems (Parking Lot, Elevator, Vending Machine, LRU Cache, Rate Limiter).
  • Week 4: Microservice patterns + mock interviews using the 🔴 tabs.

docs.title: Running the code
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/khiruashish/java-design-pattern.git
cd java-design-pattern/code
mvn test
java -cp creational/target/classes com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery.GroceryDemo

You need JDK 21+ and Maven 3.9+.

docs.title: Conventions used
docs.text: Marker Meaning 🟢 Beginner Safe for anyone who knows basic Java 🟡 Intermediate Needs collections, generics, some concurrency 🔴 Advanced Memory model, distributed systems, production concerns ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ How often the pattern comes up in interviews (1–5) (1) in code Click it to open the annotation for that line

docs.title: OOP & SOLID Refresher
docs.text: Design patterns are named, proven ways of applying these principles. If you understand why a principle exists, most patterns will feel obvious.

docs.title: The four pillars of OOP
docs.text: Pillar One-liner Java tool Encapsulation Hide state, expose behavior private fields, methods that protect invariants Abstraction Depend on what, not how interface, abstract class Inheritance Reuse via "is-a" extends (use sparingly) Polymorphism One call, many behaviors Overriding, interfaces, sealed + switch

docs.title: SOLID
Other principles you'll be asked about
docs.text:
Principle Meaning Interview sound bite DRY Don't Repeat Yourself "Every piece of knowledge has one authoritative place." KISS Keep It Simple "The simplest design that meets today's requirements." YAGNI You Aren't Gonna Need It "I don't add extension points until a second use case appears." Composition over inheritance Prefer "has-a" to "is-a" "Inheritance is the strongest coupling in Java; composition lets me swap behavior at runtime." Law of Demeter Talk only to your immediate friends "Avoid a.getB().getC().doX() chains."

Interview favourite

"Which SOLID principle does the Strategy pattern support?" Mainly Open/Closed (new strategies without editing the context) and Dependency Inversion (the context depends on the strategy interface). It also helps Single Responsibility, because each algorithm lives in its own class.

docs.title: UML Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Every diagram in this handbook is written in Mermaid, so it's plain text you can copy into your own notes, a GitHub README or Confluence.

docs.title: Class diagram relationships
docs.text:
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Animal {
        <<abstract>>
        #String name
        +speak()* String
    }
    class Dog
    class Owner
    class Leash
    class Kennel
    class Comparable~T~ {
        <<interface>>
        +compareTo(T other) int
    }
    Animal <|-- Dog : inheritance
    Comparable <|.. Dog : implements
    Owner --> Dog : association
    Dog o-- Leash : aggregation
    Kennel *-- Animal : composition
    Owner ..> Leash : dependency
Arrow Name Meaning Java <\|-- Inheritance is-a extends <\|.. Realization implements implements --> Association has a reference field o-- Aggregation has-a; the part can live on its own field passed in from outside *-- Composition owns; the part dies with the whole field created inside ..> Dependency uses temporarily method parameter or local variable

Visibility: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package-private. Members: * abstract, $ static.

docs.title: Sequence diagram
docs.text:
Used throughout the microservices section.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as Customer
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant O as Order Service
    participant P as Payment Service
    U->>G: POST /orders
    G->>O: createOrder()
    O->>P: charge(orderId, amount)
    alt payment ok
        P-->>O: CAPTURED
        O-->>G: 201 Created
    else payment failed
        P-->>O: DECLINED
        O-->>G: 402 Payment Required
    end
    G-->>U: response

docs.title: State diagram
docs.text:
Used for State, Saga and order lifecycles.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CREATED
    CREATED --> PAID : payment captured
    CREATED --> CANCELLED : payment failed
    PAID --> PACKED
    PACKED --> OUT_FOR_DELIVERY
    OUT_FOR_DELIVERY --> DELIVERED
    DELIVERED --> [*]
    CANCELLED --> [*]

In interviews

You don't need perfect UML. Interviewers want to see classes, their responsibilities, and the relationships between them (especially interface vs. implementation). Boxes and arrows on a whiteboard, labelled clearly, are enough.

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text:
This section turns the handbook into an interview plan. Pattern pages already end with an Interview Corner (beginner, mid-level, senior and a coding challenge) and a STAR story. The pages here add company-specific preparation, low-level design (LLD) problems with full code, system design patterns, and the top 100 questions in one place.

About company pages

Interview processes differ by team, level, country and year, and companies change them often. The company pages describe commonly reported formats and how design-pattern knowledge is typically tested there; they aren't official descriptions. Always check the company's own careers pages and ask your recruiter what your loop looks like.

docs.title: What you'll find here
docs.text:
• Company guides

    Google, Microsoft, Amazon, SAP, and service companies (TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro, Accenture, Capgemini and others): format, what's evaluated, 15 practice questions each, and a 4-week plan.

    Google · Microsoft · Amazon · SAP · Service companies

    12 classic machine-coding problems (Parking Lot, Elevator, Vending Machine, LRU Cache, Splitwise, BookMyShow-style booking and more), each with requirements, patterns, class diagram, runnable code and output.

    LLD problems

    System design patterns

docs.title: Which patterns matter at which level
docs.text: Level Expectation Must know Should know Fresher / 0–2 years Explain and code the classics; SOLID Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Adapter, Decorator, Template Method Facade, Proxy, Command, State, Iterator Mid / 3–7 years Choose patterns for LLD problems; Spring internals; basic microservices All GoF essentials + Chain of Responsibility, Composite, State, Producer-Consumer, Thread Pool Circuit Breaker, Saga, Outbox, API Gateway, CQRS Senior / 8–15 years Trade-offs, architecture, distributed systems, leading design reviews Hexagonal/Clean, modular monolith, all resilience and data-consistency patterns, observability Event sourcing, service mesh, migration strategies, anti-patterns and their cost

docs.title: A four-week plan (any company)
docs.text:
Week Focus Use these pages 1 OOP, SOLID, creational and structural patterns; code each example yourself OOP & SOLID, Creational, Structural 2 Behavioral and concurrency patterns; 4 LLD problems under time pressure (45 min each) Behavioral, Concurrency, LLD problems 3 Microservices and architecture; 2 system design mocks Microservices, Architecture, System design patterns 4 Company-specific prep, STAR stories, top 100 questions, revision Company page, Top 100, Cheat sheet

In every design interview

  1. Clarify requirements and constraints before drawing anything.
  2. Name the pattern only after describing the problem it solves ("the pricing rules change per campaign, so I'll isolate them behind a strategy").
  3. State the trade-off (what it costs) and an alternative you rejected.
  4. Write code that runs: small, tested pieces beat a big diagram.

docs.title: Amazon: Design Patterns in Interviews
docs.text:
Commonly reported, not official

Based on Amazon's public interview guidance and widely shared candidate experiences. Details vary by team and level. Confirm with your recruiter.

docs.title: What the process commonly looks like
docs.text:
• An online assessment (coding, sometimes work-style questions) or phone screen, then an interview loop (often 4–5 interviews).
  • Rounds cover coding, object-oriented / low-level design (common for SDE I/II), system design (SDE II and above), and behavioral questions in every round.
  • Amazon publishes its Leadership Principles (Customer Obsession, Ownership, Dive Deep, Bias for Action, and others) and its interview guidance says behavioral questions are based on them. One interviewer, often called the Bar Raiser, is from outside the hiring team.

docs.title: Where design patterns show up
docs.text: Situation Pattern knowledge that helps LLD: "design a locker system / parking lot / vending machine" State, Strategy, Factory Method, Singleton (and its pitfalls) Extensibility follow-ups ("now add a new payment type") Open/closed with Strategy/Factory, Decorator System design (orders, inventory, notifications) Saga, Outbox, Idempotent Consumer, CQRS, queues Operational excellence Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Rate Limiter, Tracing

docs.title: What interviewers look for
docs.text:
Signal What strong looks like LLD Clear entities and responsibilities, extensible where requirements will change, working code for the core flow System design Requirements and scale first, simple design that works, then bottlenecks, failure modes and cost Leadership Principles Specific STAR stories with your actions, data, and results; real trade-offs and mistakes Ownership Talks about operating what you build: monitoring, on-call, fixing root causes

Prepare two stories per Leadership Principle

Interviewers ask follow-ups ("what data did you use?", "what would you do differently?"). Each STAR tie-in at the end of the pattern pages in this handbook is a template; replace it with your own experience.

docs.title: 15 practice questions (with model answers)
docs.text:
1. Design an Amazon Locker-style package locker system.

Lockers with sizes (S/M/L), allocation Strategy (smallest fitting), codes with expiry, locker State (free/reserved/occupied), notifications via Observer; concurrency on allocation.

2. Design a vending machine.

State machine: Idle → HasMoney → Dispensing; coin handling; out-of-stock; refunds. See the Vending Machine LLD.

3. Your checkout calls payment, inventory and shipping. How do you keep them consistent?

Orchestrated Saga with compensations, Outbox for events, idempotent handlers, timeouts and PENDING states.

4. How do you avoid charging a customer twice when the client retries?

Idempotency-Key stored with the response; unique constraints; replay the stored response. See Idempotent Consumer.

5. Add a new discount type to a pricing engine without modifying existing code.

Each discount is a Strategy/Specification; a registry or chain applies them; new type = new class + registration. See the Discount Engine LLD.

6. Design a notification service for order updates (email, SMS, push).

Channel Strategy + Factory, templates (Template Method), preferences, retries and DLQ, dedupe keys, rate limits. See the Notification LLD.

7. Your service depends on a slow third-party API. How do you protect it?

Timeouts, Circuit Breaker with fallback, Bulkhead, caching, async processing via queues.

8. Design a system to show 'customers who bought this also bought'.

Event stream of orders → batch/stream job computing co-occurrence → read model per product (CQRS) in a key-value store, cached at the edge.

9. Singleton: when is it acceptable and what are the risks?

For truly single, stateless or immutable resources (config, registries) via DI; risks are hidden global state, testing pain, and false assumptions of uniqueness across JVMs. See Singleton.

10. Design an inventory service that never oversells during a flash sale.

Atomic conditional decrements (UPDATE ... SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0), reservations with TTL, a queue for the hottest SKUs, rate limits per user, and reconciliation.

11. How would you find the cause of rising p99 latency in production?

Metrics to find which endpoint, tracing to find the slow hop, logs for that trace; check recent deploys and dependencies (Dive Deep).

12. Observer vs. pub/sub messaging?

Observer is in-process and synchronous by default; pub/sub uses a broker for decoupled, asynchronous, durable delivery across services. See Event-Driven.

13. Design a parking garage pricing system that changes per hour, weekend and vehicle type.

Composable pricing rules (Strategy + Chain or Decorator), config-driven rates, injectable clock for tests.

14. Tell me about a time you disagreed with your team's design (Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit).

STAR: your data-driven argument, how you disagreed respectfully, the decision, how you committed, and the outcome either way.

15. Tell me about a production issue you owned end to end (Ownership, Dive Deep).

STAR: detection, mitigation first, root cause with evidence, long-term fix (tests, alarms, runbooks), and what you changed in the team's process.

docs.title: 4-week plan
docs.text:
Week Do 1 Coding fundamentals; 2 LLD problems (Parking Lot, Vending Machine) with working code 2 4 more LLD problems; patterns: State, Strategy, Observer, Factory, Decorator 3 System design: orders, inventory, notifications; Saga, Outbox, Idempotency, Circuit Breaker 4 2 STAR stories per Leadership Principle; mock loop with a "bar raiser" style interviewer

Microsoft Next: SAP

docs.title: Google: Design Patterns in Interviews
docs.text:
Commonly reported, not official

This page summarizes publicly shared candidate experiences and Google's own general hiring guidance. Formats vary by role, level and location and change over time. Confirm the details of your loop with your recruiter.

docs.title: What the process commonly looks like
docs.text:
• Coding interviews dominate for software engineers: data structures and algorithms, written in a shared doc or editor, with emphasis on correctness, complexity and clear code.
  • System design is commonly added for experienced (roughly L5+) candidates.
  • Behavioral / "Googleyness & leadership" conversations explore collaboration, ambiguity and impact.
  • Google's careers site describes evaluating general cognitive ability, role-related knowledge, leadership and "Googleyness". Feedback is typically reviewed by a hiring committee rather than decided by one interviewer.

docs.title: Where design patterns show up
docs.text:
Google interviews rarely ask "define the Visitor pattern". Patterns show up implicitly:

Situation Pattern knowledge that helps A coding problem with extensible rules ("now support a new type of discount") Strategy, Factory Method, open/closed design Iterating complex structures lazily Iterator, generators, Composite Designing an API or library Builder, Immutable Object, Facade Concurrency follow-ups Producer-Consumer, Thread Pool, Read-Write Lock System design Rate Limiter, caching, sharding, CQRS, Circuit Breaker

docs.title: What interviewers look for
docs.text:
Signal What strong looks like Problem solving Clarifies, explores examples, chooses a sound approach, states complexity Code quality Readable names, small functions, correct edge cases, no over-engineering Testing Walks through examples, finds own bugs, mentions test cases Communication Thinks aloud, takes hints well, explains trade-offs Design (senior) Requirements → API → data model → scaling → failure modes, with numbers

Pattern advice for Google-style coding rounds

Use patterns only when they simplify the solution. An interface plus two implementations for an extensibility follow-up is great; a factory of builders for a 30-line problem is not. Say why you chose the structure.

docs.title: 15 practice questions (with model answers)
docs.text:
1. Design an iterator that flattens a nested list of integers lazily.

Keep a stack of iterators; hasNext() advances until the top iterator yields an integer, pushing nested lists as you meet them. O(1) amortized per element, O(depth) memory. This is Iterator over a Composite.

2. Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. How would you make it thread-safe?

HashMap + doubly linked list (or LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true and removeEldestEntry). Thread safety: a single lock is simplest; for high concurrency, shard into N segments by key hash. See the LRU Cache LLD.

3. A pricing function grows a new if every sprint. Refactor it.

Extract each rule into a PricingRule Strategy (or Specification + action), register rules in a list or map, and test each independently. New rules don't touch existing code.

4. Design a rate limiter for an API used by millions of clients.

Token bucket per key, Redis with atomic Lua scripts for global limits, local buckets for hot paths, 429 with Retry-After. See Rate Limiter.

5. Make an expensive, immutable configuration object available everywhere, loaded once.

Lazy holder idiom or an enum singleton; better, dependency injection with a single instance. Immutable, so no locking after construction. See Singleton and Immutable Object.

6. Implement an event system where components subscribe to typed events.

Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<?>>>, type-safe subscribe/publish, copy-on-write lists for concurrent publishing, and unsubscribe handles to avoid leaks. See Observer.

7. Design a bounded blocking queue without java.util.concurrent collections.

Array + head/tail indices + ReentrantLock with two Conditions (notFull, notEmpty); always wait in a while loop. See Producer-Consumer.

8. Design a text editor's undo/redo.

Command objects with execute/undo on two stacks, or Memento snapshots for complex state; merge consecutive typing commands.

9. How would you parse and evaluate expressions like price > 100 AND category = 'fruit'?

Tokenize → recursive-descent parser → AST of composite nodes → evaluate with an Interpreter or Visitor. Discuss precedence and error messages.

10. Design a URL shortener. Which parts would you cache and how?

ID generation (counter + base62 or random with collision check), key-value store sharded by key, cache-aside for hot links with TTL, 301 vs 302 trade-off, analytics via async events. See System design patterns.

11. A service calls three backends; p99 latency is too high. What do you do?

Call in parallel (Future/Promise), add per-call timeouts and hedged requests for idempotent reads, cache, and make optional calls degradable. See BFF.

12. How do you guarantee only one instance runs a scheduled job across a cluster?

Leader election (lease in a DB/etcd/ZooKeeper with fencing tokens), or a DB row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), not a JVM singleton.

13. Builder vs. telescoping constructors vs. static factories: when each?

Static factories for simple named creation; builders for many optional parameters and validation across fields; avoid telescoping constructors. See Builder.

14. Design a thread-safe counter used by 64 threads at very high rate.

LongAdder (striped cells) beats AtomicLong under contention; reads sum the cells. Explain the trade-off (reads are not atomic snapshots).

15. Tell me about a time you simplified an over-engineered design.

STAR: what the abstraction cost (onboarding, bugs), the evidence you gathered, how you removed it safely (tests first), the measurable result. See the anti-patterns page: Anti-Patterns.

docs.title: 4-week plan
docs.text:
Week Do 1 30 algorithm problems (arrays, hashing, two pointers, trees, graphs); code cleanly with small helper classes 2 20 more problems + 4 design-flavoured coding problems (iterator, LRU, rate limiter, event bus) from this handbook 3 Concurrency patterns; 2 system design mocks (URL shortener, news feed) using System design patterns 4 Mock interviews with a timer; 5 STAR stories; revise the cheat sheet

docs.title: Low-Level Design (LLD) Problems
docs.text:
Machine-coding and object-oriented design rounds (common at Amazon, Microsoft, Flipkart, Uber, Swiggy, and in senior rounds at service companies) ask you to design and code a small system in 45–90 minutes. Below are 12 classic problems, each with requirements, the patterns that fit, a class diagram, complete runnable code, real output, and the follow-up questions interviewers usually ask.

A repeatable approach for any LLD round

  1. Clarify requirements (5 min): actors, use cases, what's out of scope. Write them down.
  2. Identify entities and their responsibilities (5 min): nouns become classes, verbs become methods.
  3. Find what varies and isolate it behind an interface (pricing, allocation, notifications): that's where patterns appear.
  4. Code the core flow first, then edge cases, then extensions. Keep it compiling and runnable.
  5. Talk about concurrency, testing and extensibility at the end.
# Problem Key patterns Interview frequency 1 Parking Lot Strategy (allocation, pricing), enums for types ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 2 Elevator System State, Strategy (dispatch), SCAN ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 3 Vending Machine State (sealed types) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 4 LRU Cache HashMap + doubly linked list; locking ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 5 Splitwise Strategy (split types), greedy settlement ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 6 Snake and Ladder Builder, Strategy (dice) ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 7 Library Management Strategy (fines), Observer (reservations) ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 8 Movie Ticket Booking Seat holds with expiry, atomic all-or-nothing ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 9 Notification System Strategy, Factory, Template Method, Decorator ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 10 Logging Framework Chain of Responsibility, Strategy, hierarchy ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 11 Grocery Discount Engine Specification, Strategy, combination policy ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 12 Tic-Tac-Toe O(1) win detection ⭐⭐⭐⭐

docs.title: 1. Parking Lot
docs.text:
Requirements: multiple floors; spot sizes small/medium/large; bikes, cars and trucks (a vehicle fits its size or larger); issue a ticket on entry; charge on exit (first 30 minutes free, then per started hour by vehicle type); show free spots; reject reused tickets. Patterns: Strategy for allocation and pricing, so rules can change per lot.

classDiagram
    class ParkingLot {
      +park(vehicle, time) Optional~Ticket~
      +exit(ticketId, time) Receipt
      +freeSpots(type) long
    }
    class AllocationStrategy {
      <<interface>>
      +choose(spots, vehicle) Optional~Spot~
    }
    class PricingStrategy {
      <<interface>>
      +feePaise(type, duration) long
    }
    class Spot {
      id
      floor
      size
      parked
    }
    class Ticket {
      id
      vehicle
      spotId
      entry
    }
    ParkingLot --> AllocationStrategy
    ParkingLot --> PricingStrategy
    ParkingLot "1" *-- "*" Spot
    ParkingLot --> Ticket

package com.handbook.lld.parkinglot;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * Parking lot LLD. Patterns: Strategy (spot allocation, pricing), Factory-style creation of spots
 * per floor, and a small state model per spot (free/occupied).
 */
public final class ParkingLot {

    public enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK }

    public enum SpotSize {
        SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE;

        boolean fits(VehicleType v) {
            return switch (v) {
                case BIKE -> true;
                case CAR -> this != SMALL;
                case TRUCK -> this == LARGE;
            };
        }
    }

    public record Vehicle(String plate, VehicleType type) {
    }

    public static final class Spot {
        final String id;
        final int floor;
        final SpotSize size;
        Vehicle parked;

        Spot(String id, int floor, SpotSize size) {
            this.id = id;
            this.floor = floor;
            this.size = size;
        }

        boolean isFree() {
            return parked == null;
        }
    }

    public record Ticket(String id, Vehicle vehicle, String spotId, Instant entry) {
    }

    public record Receipt(String ticketId, String plate, Duration parked, long feePaise) {
    }

    /** Strategy: which free spot to give a vehicle. */
    public interface AllocationStrategy {
        Optional<Spot> choose(List<Spot> spots, Vehicle vehicle);
    }

    /** Strategy: how much to charge. */
    public interface PricingStrategy {
        long feePaise(VehicleType type, Duration parked);
    }

    /** Nearest floor first, and the smallest spot that fits (keeps large spots for trucks). */
    public static AllocationStrategy nearestSmallestFit() {
        return (spots, v) -> spots.stream()
                .filter(Spot::isFree)
                .filter(s -> s.size.fits(v.type()))
                .min((a, b) -> a.floor != b.floor ? Integer.compare(a.floor, b.floor) : a.size.compareTo(b.size));
    }

    /** First 30 minutes free, then a per-hour rate by vehicle type, rounded up to whole hours. */
    public static PricingStrategy hourly(Map<VehicleType, Long> ratePerHourPaise) {
        return (type, parked) -> {
            if (parked.compareTo(Duration.ofMinutes(30)) <= 0) {
                return 0;
            }
            long hours = (parked.toMinutes() + 59) / 60;
            return hours * ratePerHourPaise.get(type);
        };
    }

    private final List<Spot> spots = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Spot> spotById = new HashMap<>();
    private final AllocationStrategy allocation;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private int nextTicket = 1;

    public ParkingLot(AllocationStrategy allocation, PricingStrategy pricing) {
        this.allocation = allocation;
        this.pricing = pricing;
    }

    public ParkingLot addFloor(int floor, int small, int medium, int large) {
        add(floor, SpotSize.SMALL, small);
        add(floor, SpotSize.MEDIUM, medium);
        add(floor, SpotSize.LARGE, large);
        return this;
    }

    private void add(int floor, SpotSize size, int count) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
            Spot s = new Spot("F" + floor + "-" + size.name().charAt(0) + i, floor, size);
            spots.add(s);
            spotById.put(s.id, s);
        }
    }

    public synchronized Optional<Ticket> park(Vehicle vehicle, Instant at) {
        return allocation.choose(spots, vehicle).map(spot -> {
            spot.parked = vehicle;
            Ticket t = new Ticket("T-" + nextTicket++, vehicle, spot.id, at);
            active.put(t.id(), t);
            return t;
        });
    }

    public synchronized Receipt exit(String ticketId, Instant at) {
        Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);
        if (t == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown or already used ticket " + ticketId);
        }
        spotById.get(t.spotId()).parked = null;
        Duration parked = Duration.between(t.entry(), at);
        return new Receipt(t.id(), t.vehicle().plate(), parked, pricing.feePaise(t.vehicle().type(), parked));
    }

    public synchronized long freeSpots(VehicleType type) {
        return spots.stream().filter(Spot::isFree).filter(s -> s.size.fits(type)).count();
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.parkinglot;

import com.handbook.lld.parkinglot.ParkingLot.Vehicle;
import com.handbook.lld.parkinglot.ParkingLot.VehicleType;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Map;

public class ParkingLotDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var lot = new ParkingLot(ParkingLot.nearestSmallestFit(), ParkingLot.hourly(Map.of(
                VehicleType.BIKE, 1_000L, VehicleType.CAR, 4_000L, VehicleType.TRUCK, 10_000L)))
                .addFloor(0, 1, 1, 0)
                .addFloor(1, 0, 1, 1);
        Instant nine = Instant.parse("2026-10-14T09:00:00Z");

        System.out.println("=== LLD: Parking lot ===");
        var bike = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-B-1", VehicleType.BIKE), nine).orElseThrow();
        var car1 = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-C-1", VehicleType.CAR), nine).orElseThrow();
        var car2 = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-C-2", VehicleType.CAR), nine).orElseThrow();
        var truck = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-T-1", VehicleType.TRUCK), nine.plusSeconds(600));
        System.out.println("bike  -> " + bike.spotId() + " (smallest fitting spot on the nearest floor)");
        System.out.println("car 1 -> " + car1.spotId());
        System.out.println("car 2 -> " + car2.spotId());
        System.out.println("truck -> " + truck.map(t -> t.spotId()).orElse("FULL"));
        System.out.println("free spots for cars now: " + lot.freeSpots(VehicleType.CAR));
        System.out.println("another car -> " + lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-C-3", VehicleType.CAR), nine)
                .map(t -> t.spotId()).orElse("FULL"));

        System.out.println(lot.exit(bike.id(), nine.plusSeconds(20 * 60)) + "  (first 30 min free)");
        System.out.println(lot.exit(car1.id(), nine.plusSeconds(2 * 3600 + 5 * 60)) + "  (3 started hours)");
        try {
            lot.exit(car1.id(), nine.plusSeconds(3 * 3600));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("re-using a ticket: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

=== LLD: Parking lot ===
bike  -> F0-S1 (smallest fitting spot on the nearest floor)
car 1 -> F0-M1
car 2 -> F1-M1
truck -> F1-L1
free spots for cars now: 0
another car -> FULL
Receipt[ticketId=T-1, plate=KA01-B-1, parked=PT20M, feePaise=0]  (first 30 min free)
Receipt[ticketId=T-2, plate=KA01-C-1, parked=PT2H5M, feePaise=12000]  (3 started hours)
re-using a ticket: unknown or already used ticket T-2

Follow-ups: concurrency at entry gates (synchronized here; per-floor locks or a DB row lock in a real system), electric-vehicle spots with chargers (a new SpotSize capability or a spot feature set), lost tickets, payments as a separate service, display boards (Observer).

docs.title: 2. Elevator System
docs.text:
Requirements: N elevators; hall calls (floor + direction) and car calls (button inside); serve requests efficiently; don't reverse while there are stops ahead. Patterns: State (direction per car), Strategy (dispatcher), SCAN scheduling.

classDiagram
    class ElevatorSystem {
      +hallCall(floor, dir)
      +carCall(car, floor)
      +tick()
    }
    class Car {
      id
      floor
      direction
      stops
      +step()
    }
    class Dispatcher {
      <<interface>>
      +choose(cars, floor, dir) Car
    }
    ElevatorSystem "1" *-- "*" Car
    ElevatorSystem --> Dispatcher
ElevatorSystem.javaElevatorDemo.java 
package com.handbook.lld.elevator;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/**
 * Elevator LLD. Patterns: State (each car's direction), Strategy (which car serves a hall call),
 * and the SCAN ("elevator") algorithm: keep moving in one direction while there are stops ahead.
 */
public final class ElevatorSystem {

    public enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }

    public static final class Car {
        final String id;
        int floor;
        Direction direction = Direction.IDLE;
        final TreeSet<Integer> stops = new TreeSet<>();

        Car(String id, int floor) {
            this.id = id;
            this.floor = floor;
        }

        /** One tick: move one floor toward the next stop in the current direction (SCAN). */
        String step() {
            if (stops.isEmpty()) {
                direction = Direction.IDLE;
                return id + "@" + floor + " idle";
            }
            if (direction == Direction.IDLE) {
                direction = stops.first() >= floor ? Direction.UP : Direction.DOWN;
            }
            if (direction == Direction.UP && stops.ceiling(floor) == null) {
                direction = Direction.DOWN; // nothing above: reverse
            } else if (direction == Direction.DOWN && stops.floor(floor) == null) {
                direction = Direction.UP;
            }
            if (stops.remove(floor)) {
                return id + "@" + floor + " doors open";
            }
            floor += direction == Direction.UP ? 1 : -1;
            if (stops.remove(floor)) {
                return id + "@" + floor + " doors open";
            }
            return id + "@" + floor + " moving " + direction;
        }
    }

    /** Strategy for assigning a hall call to a car. */
    public interface Dispatcher {
        Car choose(List<Car> cars, int floor, Direction wanted);
    }

    /** Prefer an idle car or one already heading toward the floor in the same direction; then nearest. */
    public static Dispatcher nearestSuitable() {
        return (cars, floor, wanted) -> cars.stream()
                .min((a, b) -> Integer.compare(cost(a, floor, wanted), cost(b, floor, wanted)))
                .orElseThrow();
    }

    private static int cost(Car c, int floor, Direction wanted) {
        int distance = Math.abs(c.floor - floor);
        boolean onTheWay = (c.direction == Direction.UP && wanted == Direction.UP && floor >= c.floor)
                || (c.direction == Direction.DOWN && wanted == Direction.DOWN && floor <= c.floor);
        if (c.direction == Direction.IDLE || onTheWay) {
            return distance;
        }
        return distance + 100; // busy in the other direction: last resort
    }

    private final List<Car> cars = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Dispatcher dispatcher;

    public ElevatorSystem(Dispatcher dispatcher, int... startFloors) {
        this.dispatcher = dispatcher;
        for (int i = 0; i < startFloors.length; i++) {
            cars.add(new Car("E" + (i + 1), startFloors[i]));
        }
    }

    public String hallCall(int floor, Direction wanted) {
        Car car = dispatcher.choose(cars, floor, wanted);
        car.stops.add(floor);
        return "hall call " + floor + " " + wanted + " -> " + car.id;
    }

    public void carCall(String carId, int floor) {
        cars.stream().filter(c -> c.id.equals(carId)).findFirst().orElseThrow().stops.add(floor);
    }

    public List<String> tick() {
        return cars.stream().map(Car::step).toList();
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.elevator;

import com.handbook.lld.elevator.ElevatorSystem.Direction;

public class ElevatorDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var building = new ElevatorSystem(ElevatorSystem.nearestSuitable(), 0, 8);

        System.out.println("=== LLD: Elevator system (2 cars, SCAN scheduling) ===");
        System.out.println(building.hallCall(3, Direction.UP));
        System.out.println(building.hallCall(7, Direction.DOWN));
        for (int t = 1; t <= 4; t++) {
            if (t == 2) {
                building.carCall("E1", 6); // passenger who got in at 3 presses 6
                System.out.println("   (passenger in E1 presses 6)");
            }
            System.out.println("t=" + t + " " + building.tick());
        }
        System.out.println(building.hallCall(5, Direction.UP) + "  (E1 is moving up past 5)");
        for (int t = 5; t <= 7; t++) {
            System.out.println("t=" + t + " " + building.tick());
        }
    }
}

=== LLD: Elevator system (2 cars, SCAN scheduling) ===
hall call 3 UP -> E1
hall call 7 DOWN -> E2
t=1 [E1@1 moving UP, E2@7 doors open]
   (passenger in E1 presses 6)
t=2 [E1@2 moving UP, E2@7 idle]
t=3 [E1@3 doors open, E2@7 idle]
t=4 [E1@4 moving UP, E2@7 idle]
hall call 5 UP -> E1  (E1 is moving up past 5)
t=5 [E1@5 doors open, E2@7 idle]
t=6 [E1@6 doors open, E2@7 idle]
t=7 [E1@6 idle, E2@7 idle]

Follow-ups: capacity/weight limits, express elevators serving certain floors, peak-hour strategies (up-peak in the morning), emergency mode (a state that overrides all), and making tick() driven by a scheduler thread.

docs.title: 3. Vending Machine
docs.text:
Requirements: accept ₹1/2/5/10 coins; select a product; dispense if paid enough and in stock; return change with the fewest coins; cancel and refund. Pattern: State, with sealed types and pattern matching so each state's behaviour is explicit.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> HasMoney: insert coin
    HasMoney --> HasMoney: insert coin / select (not enough, sold out)
    HasMoney --> Idle: select (dispense + change)
    HasMoney --> Idle: cancel (refund)
VendingMachine.javaVendingMachineDemo.java 
package com.handbook.lld.vending;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Vending machine LLD. Pattern: State. Each state decides how to react to the same events
 * (insert coin, select, cancel), which removes the big if/else on a status field.
 */
public final class VendingMachine {

    public record Product(String name, int priceRupees) {
    }

    sealed interface State permits Idle, HasMoney {
    }

    record Idle() implements State {
    }

    record HasMoney(int credit) implements State {
    }

    private static final int[] COINS = {10, 5, 2, 1};

    private final Map<String, Product> slots = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private State state = new Idle();

    public VendingMachine load(String slot, Product product, int quantity) {
        slots.put(slot, product);
        stock.put(slot, quantity);
        return this;
    }

    public String insert(int coin) {
        if (coin != 1 && coin != 2 && coin != 5 && coin != 10) {
            return "rejected coin ₹" + coin;
        }
        state = switch (state) {
            case Idle i -> new HasMoney(coin);
            case HasMoney m -> new HasMoney(m.credit() + coin);
        };
        return "credit ₹" + ((HasMoney) state).credit();
    }

    public String select(String slot) {
        return switch (state) {
            case Idle i -> "insert coins first";
            case HasMoney m -> {
                Product p = slots.get(slot);
                if (p == null) {
                    yield "no such slot " + slot;
                }
                if (stock.get(slot) == 0) {
                    yield p.name() + " sold out, credit ₹" + m.credit() + " kept";
                }
                if (m.credit() < p.priceRupees()) {
                    yield p.name() + " costs ₹" + p.priceRupees() + ", insert ₹" + (p.priceRupees() - m.credit()) + " more";
                }
                stock.merge(slot, -1, Integer::sum);
                state = new Idle();
                yield "dispensed " + p.name() + change(m.credit() - p.priceRupees());
            }
        };
    }

    public String cancel() {
        if (state instanceof HasMoney m) {
            state = new Idle();
            return "refunded" + change(m.credit());
        }
        return "nothing to refund";
    }

    /** Greedy change-making works for canonical coin systems like 10/5/2/1. */
    private static String change(int amount) {
        if (amount == 0) {
            return "";
        }
        List<Integer> coins = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int c : COINS) {
            while (amount >= c) {
                coins.add(c);
                amount -= c;
            }
        }
        return ", change " + coins;
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.vending;

import com.handbook.lld.vending.VendingMachine.Product;

        var vm = new VendingMachine()
                .load("A1", new Product("Masala chips", 20), 2)
                .load("B1", new Product("Mango juice", 35), 0);

        System.out.println("=== LLD: Vending machine (State pattern) ===");
        System.out.println("select A1       -> " + vm.select("A1"));
        System.out.println("insert ₹10      -> " + vm.insert(10));
        System.out.println("select A1       -> " + vm.select("A1"));
        System.out.println("insert ₹3       -> " + vm.insert(3));
        System.out.println("insert ₹10      -> " + vm.insert(10));
        System.out.println("insert ₹5       -> " + vm.insert(5));
        System.out.println("insert ₹2       -> " + vm.insert(2));

=== LLD: Vending machine (State pattern) ===
select A1       -> insert coins first
insert ₹10      -> credit ₹10

insert ₹10      -> credit ₹20
insert ₹5       -> credit ₹25
insert ₹2       -> credit ₹27

select A1       -> dispensed Masala chips, change [5, 2]
insert ₹10      -> credit ₹10
cancel          -> refunded, change [10]

Follow-ups: limited coin inventory for change (greedy may fail; use DP or refuse), UPI/card payments (a payment Strategy), maintenance mode, and audit logs per transaction.

docs.title: 4. LRU Cache
docs.text:
Requirements: fixed capacity; get and put in O(1); evict the least recently used entry; thread-safe. Design: HashMap<K, Node> + doubly linked list with sentinel head/tail; a lock around both.

flowchart LR
    H[head sentinel] <--> A["MANGO (MRU)"] <--> B[MILK] <--> C["RICE (LRU)"] <--> T[tail sentinel]
    M[(HashMap key → node)] -.-> A
    M -.-> B
    M -.-> C
LruCache.javaLruCacheDemo.java 
package com.handbook.lld.lrucache;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.StringJoiner;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

/**
 * LRU cache with O(1) get and put: a HashMap for lookup plus a doubly linked list for recency
 * (most recent at the head). A single lock makes it thread-safe; shard it for high concurrency.
 */
public final class LruCache<K, V> {

    private static final class Node<K, V> {
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K, V> prev;
        Node<K, V> next;

        Node(K key, V value) {
            this.key = key;
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, Node<K, V>> index = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node<K, V> head = new Node<>(null, null); // sentinels avoid null checks
    private final Node<K, V> tail = new Node<>(null, null);
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private int evictions;

    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity < 1) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be >= 1");
        }
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Node<K, V> n = index.get(key);
            if (n == null) {
                return null;
            }
            moveToHead(n);
            return n.value;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public void put(K key, V value) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Node<K, V> n = index.get(key);
            if (n != null) {
                n.value = value;
                moveToHead(n);
                return;
            }
            if (index.size() == capacity) {
                Node<K, V> lru = tail.prev;
                unlink(lru);
                index.remove(lru.key);
                evictions++;
            }
            n = new Node<>(key, value);
            index.put(key, n);
            linkAtHead(n);
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    private void moveToHead(Node<K, V> n) {
        unlink(n);
        linkAtHead(n);
    }

    private void unlink(Node<K, V> n) {
        n.prev.next = n.next;
        n.next.prev = n.prev;
    }

    private void linkAtHead(Node<K, V> n) {
        n.next = head.next;
        n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n;
        head.next = n;
    }

    public int evictions() {
        return evictions;
    }

    /** Most recently used first. */
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            StringJoiner j = new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]");
            for (Node<K, V> n = head.next; n != tail; n = n.next) {
                j.add(n.key + "=" + n.value);
            }
            return j.toString();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.lrucache;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

public class LruCacheDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        var cache = new LruCache<String, String>(3);

        System.out.println("=== LLD: LRU cache (capacity 3) for product details ===");
        cache.put("MANGO", "Alphonso ₹399");
        cache.put("RICE", "Basmati ₹649");
        cache.put("MILK", "Toned ₹56");
        System.out.println("after 3 puts      : " + cache);
        System.out.println("get MANGO         : " + cache.get("MANGO"));
        System.out.println("order now         : " + cache);
        cache.put("BREAD", "Whole wheat ₹45");
        System.out.println("put BREAD (evicts least recently used RICE): " + cache);
        System.out.println("get RICE          : " + cache.get("RICE"));

        var shared = new LruCache<Integer, Integer>(100);
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) {
            int offset = t * 1_000;
            threads.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
                try {
                    start.await();
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                }
                for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                    shared.put(offset + i, i);
                    shared.get(offset + i / 2);
                }
            }));
        }
        start.countDown();
        for (Thread t : threads) {
            t.join();
        }
        System.out.println("8 threads x 1,000 puts into capacity 100 -> evictions: " + shared.evictions()
                + " (exactly 8,000 - 100)");
    }
}

=== LLD: LRU cache (capacity 3) for product details ===
after 3 puts      : [MILK=Toned ₹56, RICE=Basmati ₹649, MANGO=Alphonso ₹399]
get MANGO         : Alphonso ₹399
order now         : [MANGO=Alphonso ₹399, MILK=Toned ₹56, RICE=Basmati ₹649]
put BREAD (evicts least recently used RICE): [BREAD=Whole wheat ₹45, MANGO=Alphonso ₹399, MILK=Toned ₹56]
get RICE          : null
8 threads x 1,000 puts into capacity 100 -> evictions: 7900 (exactly 8,000 - 100)

Follow-ups: the one-liner with LinkedHashMap(capacity, 0.75f, true) + removeEldestEntry; TTL expiry; LFU; sharding by key hash to reduce lock contention; Caffeine's W-TinyLFU in production.

docs.title: 5. Splitwise (Expense Sharing)
docs.text:
Requirements: groups of people; expenses paid by one person and split equally, by percentage or by exact amounts; show balances; settle up with few payments; never lose a paisa to rounding. Patterns: Strategy for split types; a greedy max-creditor/max-debtor settlement.

classDiagram
