docs.title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

CQRS splits a system into a write side (commands that enforce business rules) and one or more read sides (query models shaped for specific screens). The read models are updated from the write side's events, often asynchronously. Each side can use its own model, schema, database and scaling. The price is eventual consistency and more moving parts.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a single normalized products table must enforce pricing rules on writes and answer "cheapest organic fruit in Bengaluru, sorted by discount, with ratings" in 20 ms for millions of shoppers. The write model wants normalization and invariants; the read side wants denormalized, pre-joined, indexed data. One model serves both badly. In microservices it's worse: the data for one screen lives in several services.

Definition (Greg Young, building on Bertrand Meyer's CQS):

CQRS is simply the creation of two objects where there was previously only one. The separation occurs based upon whether the methods are a command or a query.

Levels of CQRS:

  1. Separate command and query classes in one service (same DB).
  2. Separate read tables/views in the same DB (materialized views).
  3. Separate read databases (Elasticsearch, Redis, Cassandra) fed by events, which is the microservices form.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant's kitchen and menu board

Orders go into the kitchen (write side), which enforces the rules: no dish without ingredients. The menu board (read side) is a separate, simplified display, updated when the kitchen runs out of something. For a few seconds the board may still show "Mango lassi" after the last mango is used (eventual consistency), and that's acceptable.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[Client] -->|commands| CMD[Command side<br/>validates, enforces rules]
    CMD --> W[(Write store)]
    CMD -->|events| BUS[[Event stream]]
    BUS --> P1[Projector] --> R1[(Search view<br/>Elasticsearch)]
    BUS --> P2[Projector] --> R2[(Dashboard view<br/>Redis/SQL)]
    U -->|queries| Q[Query side] --> R1
    Q --> R2
Participant Responsibility Command handler / write model Validates commands, enforces invariants, emits events Event stream Carries changes (outbox + Kafka, or an event store) Projector Updates read models from events; idempotent; tracks a checkpoint Read model Denormalized, query-shaped, disposable (rebuildable from events)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
-- Every page view runs this against the transactional database
SELECT p.*, AVG(r.stars), MIN(o.price), s.qty FROM products p
JOIN reviews r ON ... JOIN offers o ON ... JOIN stock s ON ...
WHERE p.category = 'fruit' GROUP BY ... ORDER BY MIN(o.price) LIMIT 20;
-- Reads slow down writes (locks, CPU); indexes for reads slow inserts;
-- and in microservices, reviews/offers/stock aren't even in this database.

docs.title: Example 1: Catalog Writes vs. Search Reads (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The write side validates product commands (no duplicates; price cuts over 50% need approval). The search view keeps denormalized rows answering "cheapest in a category". A price change is visible in search only after the projector catches up, a stale read that the demo shows on purpose.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Admin
    participant C as CatalogCommands
    participant V as CatalogSearchView
    participant S as Shopper
    A->>C: changePrice(APPLE, ₹59)
    C-->>V: PriceChanged (queued)
    S->>V: cheapest(fruit) → old price (stale)
    V->>V: catchUp()
    S->>V: cheapest(fruit) → new price

Full Code:

CatalogCommands.javaCatalogSearchView.javaCatalogCqrsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * The write side: validates commands against the current state and emits events.
 * It is optimised for correctness, not for queries; it can't even list products by category.
 */
public final class CatalogCommands {

    public sealed interface Event permits ProductAdded, PriceChanged {
    }

    public record ProductAdded(String sku, String name, String category, long pricePaise) implements Event {
    }

    public record PriceChanged(String sku, long oldPaise, long newPaise) implements Event {
    }

    private final Map<String, Long> prices = new HashMap<>();
    private final Consumer<Event> publish;

    public CatalogCommands(Consumer<Event> publish) {
        this.publish = publish;
    }

    public void addProduct(String sku, String name, String category, long pricePaise) {
        if (prices.containsKey(sku)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(sku + " already exists");
        }
        prices.put(sku, pricePaise);
        publish.accept(new ProductAdded(sku, name, category, pricePaise));
    }

    public void changePrice(String sku, long newPaise) {
        Long old = prices.get(sku);
        if (old == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown " + sku);
        }
        if (newPaise < old / 2) { // (1)!
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("price cut over 50% needs approval");
        }
        prices.put(sku, newPaise);
        publish.accept(new PriceChanged(sku, old, newPaise));
    }
}
  1. Invariants live on the write side only. The read side never needs to know about approval rules.
package com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog;

import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog.CatalogCommands.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog.CatalogCommands.PriceChanged;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog.CatalogCommands.ProductAdded;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Queue;

/**
 * The read side: a denormalised view shaped for "cheapest products in a category" (think an
 * Elasticsearch index or a Redis sorted set). It is updated asynchronously from events.
 */
public final class CatalogSearchView {

    public record Row(String sku, String name, String category, long pricePaise) {
    }

    private final Map<String, Row> rows = new HashMap<>();
    private final Queue<Event> inbox = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void enqueue(Event event) { // (1)!
        inbox.add(event);
    }

    /** The projector: applies queued events. In production this runs continuously off Kafka. */
    public int catchUp() {
        int applied = 0;
        for (Event e; (e = inbox.poll()) != null; applied++) {
            switch (e) { // (2)!
                case ProductAdded a -> rows.put(a.sku(), new Row(a.sku(), a.name(), a.category(), a.pricePaise()));
                case PriceChanged p -> rows.computeIfPresent(p.sku(),
                        (k, r) -> new Row(r.sku(), r.name(), r.category(), p.newPaise()));
            }
        }
        return applied;
    }

    public List<String> cheapest(String category, int limit) { // (3)!
        return rows.values().stream()
                .filter(r -> r.category().equals(category))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Row::pricePaise))
                .limit(limit)
                .map(r -> r.name() + " ₹" + r.pricePaise() / 100)
                .toList();
    }
}
  1. Events arrive asynchronously (here, an inbox queue; in production, a Kafka consumer).
  2. A sealed event hierarchy + pattern-matching switch: the compiler checks every event type is handled.
  3. The query is shaped for one screen; a real implementation would use a sorted index.
package com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog;

public class CatalogCqrsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var view = new CatalogSearchView();
        var commands = new CatalogCommands(view::enqueue);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: catalog writes vs. search reads ===");
        commands.addProduct("MANGO-1KG", "Alphonso mangoes 1 kg", "fruit", 39_900);
        commands.addProduct("BANANA-12", "Robusta bananas x12", "fruit", 6_900);
        commands.addProduct("APPLE-1KG", "Shimla apples 1 kg", "fruit", 9_900);
        System.out.println("applied " + view.catchUp() + " events -> cheapest fruit: " + view.cheapest("fruit", 2));

        commands.changePrice("APPLE-1KG", 5_900); // apple season sale
        System.out.println("Price changed, projection not yet caught up -> " + view.cheapest("fruit", 2) + "  (stale read)");
        System.out.println("applied " + view.catchUp() + " event  -> cheapest fruit: " + view.cheapest("fruit", 2));

        try {
            commands.changePrice("MANGO-1KG", 9_900);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Command rejected by the write model: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: catalog writes vs. search reads ===
applied 3 events -> cheapest fruit: [Robusta bananas x12 ₹69, Shimla apples 1 kg ₹99]
Price changed, projection not yet caught up -> [Robusta bananas x12 ₹69, Shimla apples 1 kg ₹99]  (stale read)
applied 1 event  -> cheapest fruit: [Shimla apples 1 kg ₹59, Robusta bananas x12 ₹69]
Command rejected by the write model: price cut over 50% needs approval

Why CQRS here:

  • Reads outnumber writes about 1000:1 in catalogs; the read side scales independently (search cluster, caches).
  • Write rules stay simple and consistent; search shape changes don't touch them.
  • The stale-read window is acceptable for browsing; checkout re-validates price on the write side.

docs.title: Example 2: One Write Model, Two Read Models (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The account write model enforces "no overdraft". Two projections serve two screens: a balance tile (one key lookup) and a mini statement (last 3 transactions, pre-formatted). Here they're updated synchronously in the same process, which shows CQRS doesn't require separate databases or async messaging.

Full Code:

AccountCqrs.javaAccountCqrsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.banking;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/** One write model, two read models, each shaped for one screen. */
public final class AccountCqrs {

    public record Transacted(String account, String description, long amountPaise, long balanceAfter) {
    }

    /** Write side: enforces the no-overdraft rule. */
    public static final class AccountCommands {
        private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>();
        private final List<Consumer<Transacted>> projections = new ArrayList<>();

        public void subscribe(Consumer<Transacted> projection) {
            projections.add(projection);
        }

        public void deposit(String account, long paise, String description) {
            apply(account, paise, description);
        }

        public void withdraw(String account, long paise, String description) {
            if (balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L) < paise) { // (1)!
                throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
            }
            apply(account, -paise, description);
        }

        private void apply(String account, long delta, String description) {
            long after = balances.merge(account, delta, Long::sum);
            Transacted event = new Transacted(account, description, delta, after);
            projections.forEach(p -> p.accept(event));
        }
    }

    /** Read model 1: the balance tile on the app home screen (one key lookup). */
    public static final class BalanceView implements Consumer<Transacted> {
        private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>();

        @Override
        public void accept(Transacted e) {
            balances.put(e.account(), e.balanceAfter());
        }

        public String balance(String account) {
            return String.format("₹%,.2f", balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L) / 100.0);
        }
    }

    /** Read model 2: the last N transactions, already formatted for the mini-statement. */
    public static final class MiniStatementView implements Consumer<Transacted> {
        private final Map<String, Deque<String>> lines = new HashMap<>();
        private final int size;

        public MiniStatementView(int size) {
            this.size = size;
        }

        @Override
        public void accept(Transacted e) {
            Deque<String> d = lines.computeIfAbsent(e.account(), k -> new ArrayDeque<>());
            d.addFirst(String.format("%-14s %+,10.2f", e.description(), e.amountPaise() / 100.0)); // (2)!
            if (d.size() > size) {
                d.removeLast();
            }
        }

        public List<String> statement(String account) {
            return List.copyOf(lines.getOrDefault(account, new ArrayDeque<>()));
        }
    }
}
  1. The rule is checked on the write side against authoritative state.
  2. The read model stores data already formatted for its screen.
package com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.banking;

import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.banking.AccountCqrs.AccountCommands;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.banking.AccountCqrs.BalanceView;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.banking.AccountCqrs.MiniStatementView;

public class AccountCqrsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var commands = new AccountCommands();
        var balance = new BalanceView();
        var statement = new MiniStatementView(3);
        commands.subscribe(balance);
        commands.subscribe(statement);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: one write model, two read models ===");
        commands.deposit("ACC-1", 5_000_000, "Salary");
        commands.withdraw("ACC-1", 1_250_000, "Rent");
        commands.withdraw("ACC-1", 89_900, "Groceries");
        commands.withdraw("ACC-1", 45_000, "Electricity");
        try {
            commands.withdraw("ACC-1", 9_999_900, "New laptop");
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Withdraw ₹99,999 rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("Balance tile   : " + balance.balance("ACC-1"));
        System.out.println("Mini statement :");
        statement.statement("ACC-1").forEach(line -> System.out.println("  " + line));
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: one write model, two read models ===
Withdraw ₹99,999 rejected: insufficient funds
Balance tile   : ₹36,151.00
Mini statement :
  Electricity       -450.00
  Groceries         -899.00
  Rent           -12,500.00

Why CQRS here:

  • The most frequent queries (balance, mini statement) become O(1) lookups.
  • New screens = new projections, without changing the write model.
  • Synchronous projections give read-your-writes where the UX needs it.

docs.title: Example 3: Patient Dashboard from Three Services (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: Appointments, lab results and prescriptions are owned by three services. The doctor's dashboard needs all three, instantly, during a consultation. A projection subscribes to events from all three and maintains one denormalized row per patient: next appointment, abnormal labs only, and active medications.

Full Code:

PatientDashboardView.javaPatientDashboardDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.healthcare;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * A read model fed by events from three services (appointments, lab, pharmacy). The doctor's
 * dashboard becomes one key lookup instead of three remote calls and an in-memory join.
 */
public final class PatientDashboardView {

    public sealed interface ClinicalEvent permits AppointmentBooked, LabResultReady, PrescriptionIssued, PrescriptionEnded {
        String patientId();
    }

    public record AppointmentBooked(String patientId, String when, String doctor) implements ClinicalEvent {
    }

    public record LabResultReady(String patientId, String test, double value, double upperLimit) implements ClinicalEvent {
    }

    public record PrescriptionIssued(String patientId, String drug) implements ClinicalEvent {
    }

    public record PrescriptionEnded(String patientId, String drug) implements ClinicalEvent {
    }

    public record Dashboard(String nextAppointment, List<String> abnormalLabs, List<String> activeMedications) {
    }

    private static final class Row {
        String nextAppointment = "none";
        final List<String> abnormalLabs = new ArrayList<>();
        final List<String> meds = new ArrayList<>();
    }

    private final Map<String, Row> rows = new HashMap<>();

    public void on(ClinicalEvent event) {
        Row row = rows.computeIfAbsent(event.patientId(), k -> new Row());
        switch (event) {
            case AppointmentBooked a -> row.nextAppointment = a.when() + " with " + a.doctor();
            case LabResultReady l -> {
                if (l.value() > l.upperLimit()) { // (1)!
                    row.abnormalLabs.add(l.test() + " " + l.value() + " (max " + l.upperLimit() + ")");
                }
            }
            case PrescriptionIssued p -> row.meds.add(p.drug());
            case PrescriptionEnded p -> row.meds.remove(p.drug());
        }
    }

    public Dashboard dashboard(String patientId) { // (2)!
        Row r = rows.getOrDefault(patientId, new Row());
        return new Dashboard(r.nextAppointment, List.copyOf(r.abnormalLabs), List.copyOf(r.meds));
    }
}
  1. The projection does work once, at write time (filtering abnormal results), not on every dashboard load.
  2. The query is a single lookup, with no calls to three services during the consultation.
package com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.healthcare;

import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.healthcare.PatientDashboardView.AppointmentBooked;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.healthcare.PatientDashboardView.LabResultReady;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.healthcare.PatientDashboardView.PrescriptionEnded;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.healthcare.PatientDashboardView.PrescriptionIssued;

public class PatientDashboardDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var view = new PatientDashboardView();

        System.out.println("=== Healthcare: doctor's dashboard built from three services' events ===");
        view.on(new PrescriptionIssued("PAT-5", "Metformin 500 mg"));        // pharmacy service
        view.on(new PrescriptionIssued("PAT-5", "Amoxicillin 250 mg"));      // pharmacy service
        view.on(new LabResultReady("PAT-5", "HbA1c %", 7.9, 6.5));           // lab service
        view.on(new LabResultReady("PAT-5", "TSH mIU/L", 2.1, 4.5));         // lab service (normal)
        view.on(new AppointmentBooked("PAT-5", "2026-10-20 10:30", "Dr. Iyer")); // appointments service
        view.on(new PrescriptionEnded("PAT-5", "Amoxicillin 250 mg"));       // course finished

        var d = view.dashboard("PAT-5");
        System.out.println("Next appointment  : " + d.nextAppointment());
        System.out.println("Abnormal labs     : " + d.abnormalLabs());
        System.out.println("Active medication : " + d.activeMedications());
        System.out.println("Unknown patient   : " + view.dashboard("PAT-404"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Healthcare: doctor's dashboard built from three services' events ===
Next appointment  : 2026-10-20 10:30 with Dr. Iyer
Abnormal labs     : [HbA1c % 7.9 (max 6.5)]
Active medication : [Metformin 500 mg]
Unknown patient   : Dashboard[nextAppointment=none, abnormalLabs=[], activeMedications=[]]

Why CQRS here:

  • Cross-service queries without API composition at request time (faster and more available).
  • The dashboard keeps working if the lab service is down (it shows the last known data).
  • In a clinical setting, show "last updated" timestamps so staleness is visible.
Unit Tests: CqrsTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog.CatalogCommands;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.catalog.CatalogSearchView;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.rebuild.TopSellersProjection;
import com.handbook.microservices.cqrs.rebuild.TopSellersProjection.OrderPlaced;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class CqrsTest {

    @Test
    void readModelIsEventuallyConsistent() {
        var view = new CatalogSearchView();
        var commands = new CatalogCommands(view::enqueue);
        commands.addProduct("A", "Apple", "fruit", 100);
        assertThat(view.cheapest("fruit", 5)).isEmpty();
        view.catchUp();
        assertThat(view.cheapest("fruit", 5)).containsExactly("Apple ₹1");
    }

    @Test
    void projectionIgnoresRedeliveredEvents() {
        var p = new TopSellersProjection();
        p.apply(new OrderPlaced(1, "X", 2));
        p.apply(new OrderPlaced(1, "X", 2));
        assertThat(p.top(1)).containsExactly("X=2");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
// Spring: a projector as a Kafka listener (reference)
@KafkaListener(topics = "catalog.events", groupId = "search-projection")
public void on(ProductEvent event, @Header(KafkaHeaders.OFFSET) long offset) {
    searchRepository.apply(event);          // idempotent upsert into Elasticsearch
}
Variation Notes Same DB, separate models Command and query services/classes over the same tables; simplest Materialized views DB-maintained read models (PostgreSQL materialized views, Oracle MVs) Separate read stores Elasticsearch for search, Redis for counters, Cassandra for timelines CQRS + Event Sourcing Write side stores events; projections build every read model (Axon) GraphQL on read models Query side exposed through GraphQL

Handling eventual consistency in the UI: return the new version from the command and poll the read model until it catches up; use optimistic UI updates; or route the user's own reads to the write side for a few seconds ("read-your-writes").

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where CQRS Axon Framework @CommandHandler, @EventHandler projections, @QueryHandler Spring Data Separate repositories / read-only replicas for queries Kafka Streams / ksqlDB Materialized views from event streams Elasticsearch + CDC Common read model for search

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Read and write sides scale and evolve independently Eventual consistency visible to users Fast, screen-shaped queries More infrastructure: event pipeline, projectors, read stores Cross-service queries without runtime joins Projection bugs require replays/rebuilds New read models added by replaying events Overkill for simple CRUD

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
CQRS everywhere

Most screens in most services are fine with simple CRUD. Apply CQRS to the parts with real read/write asymmetry or cross-service queries.

Validating commands against the read model

The read model is stale. "Is this username taken?" checked against a projection lets duplicates through. Enforce invariants on the write side (unique constraints).

Non-idempotent projectors

Events are redelivered. count = count + 1 on redelivery double counts. Track checkpoints or event IDs (see the coding challenge).

Ignoring rebuild time

If rebuilding a projection from 2 billion events takes 3 days, schema changes become impossible. Plan snapshots, parallel replays and blue/green projections.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Read models are caches with a contract. They're derived and disposable. Version them (search_v2), build the new one alongside the old by replaying, switch reads, then drop the old one: blue/green projections.

Consistency budgets. Agree on acceptable staleness per screen (search: seconds; balance after transfer: read-your-writes; analytics: minutes). Monitor projection lag (event time vs. applied time) and alert on it.

Ordering and partitioning. Projectors usually need per-aggregate ordering: key events by aggregate ID, process partitions independently, and handle cross-aggregate projections (e.g. totals) carefully.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Clear reason for CQRS (read/write asymmetry, cross-service views), not fashion.
  • Events published reliably (outbox) and keyed by aggregate.
  • Projectors idempotent, with checkpoints; dead-letter handling.
  • Projection lag metrics + alerts; "last updated" in sensitive UIs.
  • Rebuild procedure tested (blue/green projections).
  • Commands validated only against the write model.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Product writes go through the catalog service, which enforces pricing and stock rules in PostgreSQL and publishes events via the outbox. A projector consumes them and updates an Elasticsearch index shaped for search and listing pages, which take 99% of traffic and scale separately. Read models are rebuildable from Kafka (with compaction) or a full export. Staleness is a few hundred milliseconds; checkout re-validates price and stock against the write side, so stale reads can't cause wrong charges. We monitor projection lag."

War story: the leaderboard that counted twice

A fantasy-sports app built its leaderboard projection with points += event.points. After a Kafka consumer-group rebalance, a batch of events was reprocessed, and during the final minutes of a big match, thousands of users saw inflated scores. Prizes were almost paid on wrong rankings. Fix: the projection stores the last applied offset per partition in the same transaction as the score update and skips already-applied events; a nightly job recomputes scores from the event log and compares. Lesson: a projector must be idempotent before it's fast.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
CQRS Event Sourcing Cache-aside API Composition Purpose Separate write and read models Store state as events Speed up reads Join data at query time Consistency Eventual (usually) Strong in the stream Possibly stale Fresh, but depends on all services Good for Read-heavy, cross-service views Audit, temporal queries Hot keys Simple, low-volume joins

CQRS is often combined with Event Sourcing but doesn't require it. See Database per Service for API composition.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Commands (write, rules) vs. queries (read, shaped views).
  • Read models updated from events by idempotent projectors.
  • Eventual consistency; validate commands only on the write side.
  • Read models are disposable: replay to rebuild.
  • Use where reads and writes differ a lot, not everywhere.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a "products under ₹100" projection to Example 1 and rebuild it from the stored events.
  • Make CatalogSearchView report its lag (number of queued events) and print it in the demo.
  • Add "last updated" timestamps to the patient dashboard rows.

docs.title: Database per Service
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Each service owns its data, and no other service reads or writes it directly. Others go through the owner's API or its events. That makes services independently deployable and scalable, and lets each pick the right store. Cross-service queries then need API composition or CQRS read models, and cross-service consistency needs sagas.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: five "microservices" share one big database. The order team renames a column and the reporting service breaks. The catalog team can't move to a search engine because three other services join its tables. A long-running analytics query locks rows that checkout needs. You have a distributed monolith: all the costs of microservices, and none of the independence.

Definition (microservices.io):

Keep each microservice's persistent data private to that service and accessible only via its API. A service's transactions only involve its database.

What "private" can mean:

Level Isolation Notes Private tables in a shared server Weak Enforce with per-service DB users and grants Private schema per service Medium A common starting point; cheap Private database server per service Strong Independent scaling, tech choice, failure isolation

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Departments with their own filing cabinets

HR keeps personnel files; Finance keeps invoices. If Finance needs an employee's bank details, it asks HR (an API) or receives HR's "bank details changed" memo (an event). Finance never walks into HR's office and edits a file. HR can reorganize its cabinets any time without telling anyone.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    O[Order service] --> ODB[(orders_db<br/>PostgreSQL)]
    C[Customer service] --> CDB[(customers_db<br/>PostgreSQL)]
    S[Search service] --> SDB[(search index<br/>OpenSearch)]
    SE[Session service] --> RDB[(Redis)]
    O -. API / events .- C
    O -. events .-> S
    X[❌ Order service] -.->|direct SQL into customers_db| CDB
Need Solution Read another service's data now API composition (call the owner's API) Query across services fast CQRS read model fed by events Use another service's data offline Local replica updated by events Update across services consistently Saga Publish changes reliably Transactional outbox

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
-- order-service, running against the shared database:
SELECT o.id, c.name, c.phone FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- Customer team splits "name" into first_name/last_name → order-service breaks in production.
-- Nobody knows which services read which tables; every schema change is a coordination meeting.

docs.title: Example 1: Separate Databases + API Composition (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: orders_db and customers_db are two separate H2 databases. The SQL join that worked in the monolith now fails: the customers table simply isn't there. The order-history page uses API composition: get orders from the order service, ask the customer service for names, join in memory. The demo counts the API calls: one per order.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    participant UI
    participant H as OrderHistoryComposer
    participant O as Order service
    participant C as Customer service
    UI->>H: order history
    H->>O: recentOrders()
    loop each order
        H->>C: name(customerId)
    end
    H-->>UI: joined rows

Full Code:

OrderService.javaCustomerService.javaOrderHistoryComposer.javaDatabasePerServiceDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Owns the orders database. It stores customer IDs, never customer details. */
public final class OrderService {

    public record OrderRow(String id, String customerId, long totalPaise) {
    }

    private final DataSource db = Db.inMemory("orders_db",
            "CREATE TABLE orders (id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, customer_id VARCHAR, total_paise BIGINT)", // (1)!
            "INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('ORD-1', 'CUST-42', 79800), ('ORD-2', 'CUST-77', 64900),"
                    + " ('ORD-3', 'CUST-42', 12900), ('ORD-4', 'CUST-77', 39900)");

    public List<OrderRow> recentOrders() {
        return query("SELECT id, customer_id, total_paise FROM orders ORDER BY id");
    }

    /** What a monolith developer would try first. */
    public List<OrderRow> recentOrdersWithJoin() {
        return query("SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer_id, o.total_paise FROM orders o "
                + "JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id"); // (2)!
    }

    private List<OrderRow> query(String sql) {
        List<OrderRow> rows = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Connection c = db.getConnection(); Statement s = c.createStatement(); ResultSet rs = s.executeQuery(sql)) {
            while (rs.next()) {
                rows.add(new OrderRow(rs.getString(1), rs.getString(2), rs.getLong(3)));
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e.getMessage().split(";")[0], e);
        }
        return rows;
    }
}
  1. Orders store only the customer ID, a reference into another service's data.
  2. The monolith habit: a JOIN that can't work when data lives in another database.
package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Owns the customers database. Other services can only reach this data through its API. */
public final class CustomerService {

    private final DataSource db = Db.inMemory("customers_db",
            "CREATE TABLE customers (id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR, phone VARCHAR)",
            "INSERT INTO customers VALUES ('CUST-42', 'Asha Rao', '+91-98450-11111'),"
                    + " ('CUST-77', 'Vikram Singh', '+91-98450-22222')");
    private final AtomicInteger apiCalls = new AtomicInteger();

    /** GET /customers/{id}/name */
    public String name(String id) {
        apiCalls.incrementAndGet();
        return names(List.of(id)).getOrDefault(id, "?");
    }

    /** GET /customers?ids=a,b,c (batch endpoint) */
    public Map<String, String> namesBatch(Collection<String> ids) {
        apiCalls.incrementAndGet();
        return names(ids);
    }

    private Map<String, String> names(Collection<String> ids) {
        Map<String, String> result = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        String placeholders = String.join(",", Collections.nCopies(ids.size(), "?"));
        try (Connection c = db.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE id IN (" + placeholders + ")")) {
            int i = 1;
            for (String id : ids) {
                ps.setString(i++, id);
            }
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                while (rs.next()) {
                    result.put(rs.getString("id"), rs.getString("name"));
                }
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
        return result;
    }

    public int apiCalls() {
        return apiCalls.get();
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.grocery;

import java.util.List;

/** API composition: query the owning services and join the results in memory. */
public final class OrderHistoryComposer {

    private final OrderService orders;
    private final CustomerService customers;

    public OrderHistoryComposer(OrderService orders, CustomerService customers) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.customers = customers;
    }

    public List<String> history() {
        return orders.recentOrders().stream()
                .map(o -> o.id() + " " + customers.name(o.customerId()) + " ₹" + o.totalPaise() / 100) // (1)!
                .toList();
    }
}
  1. One remote call per order: the N+1 problem across the network. The coding challenge fixes it.
package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.grocery;

public class DatabasePerServiceDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var orders = new OrderService();
        var customers = new CustomerService();

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: orders_db and customers_db are separate databases ===");
        try {
            orders.recentOrdersWithJoin();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("SQL JOIN across services fails: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        System.out.println("API composition instead:");
        new OrderHistoryComposer(orders, customers).history().forEach(line -> System.out.println("  " + line));
        System.out.println("customer-service API calls: " + customers.apiCalls() + " (one per order, see the coding challenge)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: orders_db and customers_db are separate databases ===
SQL JOIN across services fails: Table "CUSTOMERS" not found
API composition instead:
  ORD-1 Asha Rao ₹798
  ORD-2 Vikram Singh ₹649
  ORD-3 Asha Rao ₹129
  ORD-4 Vikram Singh ₹399
customer-service API calls: 4 (one per order, see the coding challenge)

Why separate databases here:

  • The customer team can change its schema freely; only its API is a contract.
  • Each database scales, fails and is backed up independently.
  • The cost is visible: joins become application code.

docs.title: Example 2: Polyglot Persistence (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: Because each service owns its store, each can choose what fits its access pattern: sessions in a key-value store with TTL (Redis), product search in an inverted index (OpenSearch), payments in a relational database with ACID transactions (double-entry ledger that must always sum to zero).

Full Code:

PolyglotStores.javaPolyglotDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.polyglot;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/**
 * Database per service lets each service pick the store that fits its access pattern.
 * These in-memory stand-ins mimic the shape of each real store.
 */
public final class PolyglotStores {

    private PolyglotStores() {
    }

    /** Session service → key-value store with TTL (Redis): lookups by key, data expires. */
    public static final class SessionStore {
        private record Entry(String value, Instant expiresAt) {
        }

        private final Map<String, Entry> data = new HashMap<>();
        private final Clock clock;

        public SessionStore(Clock clock) {
            this.clock = clock;
        }

        public void put(String key, String value, Duration ttl) { // SET key value EX ttl
            data.put(key, new Entry(value, clock.instant().plus(ttl)));
        }

        public String get(String key) {
            Entry e = data.get(key);
            return e == null || !clock.instant().isBefore(e.expiresAt()) ? null : e.value();
        }
    }

    /** Search service → inverted index (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch): term → document IDs. */
    public static final class SearchIndex {
        private final Map<String, Set<String>> index = new TreeMap<>();
        private final Map<String, String> docs = new HashMap<>();

        public void index(String id, String text) {
            docs.put(id, text);
            for (String term : text.toLowerCase().split("\\W+")) {
                index.computeIfAbsent(term, t -> new TreeSet<>()).add(id);
            }
        }

        public List<String> search(String query) { // all terms must match
            return Arrays.stream(query.toLowerCase().split("\\s+"))
                    .map(t -> index.getOrDefault(t, Set.of()))
                    .reduce((a, b) -> {
                        Set<String> both = new TreeSet<>(a);
                        both.retainAll(b);
                        return both;
                    })
                    .orElse(Set.of()).stream().map(docs::get).toList();
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.polyglot;

import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.polyglot.PolyglotStores.SearchIndex;
import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.polyglot.PolyglotStores.SessionStore;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.time.Duration;

public class PolyglotDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: each service picks the store that fits ===");

        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T10:00:00Z");
        SessionStore sessions = new SessionStore(clock);
        sessions.put("sess-91", "CUST-42", Duration.ofMinutes(30));
        System.out.println("session-service (key-value + TTL): sess-91 -> " + sessions.get("sess-91"));
        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(31));
        System.out.println("                31 minutes later : sess-91 -> " + sessions.get("sess-91"));

        SearchIndex search = new SearchIndex();
        search.index("P1", "Organic Alphonso Mangoes 1 kg");
        search.index("P2", "Mango Pickle 500 g");
        search.index("P3", "Organic Basmati Rice 5 kg");
        System.out.println("search-service (inverted index)  : 'organic' -> " + search.search("organic"));
        System.out.println("                                   'organic mangoes' -> " + search.search("organic mangoes"));

        DataSource ledger = Db.inMemory("ledger_db",
                "CREATE TABLE entries (id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT, account VARCHAR, amount BIGINT CHECK (amount <> 0))");
        try (Connection c = ledger.getConnection(); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            s.executeUpdate("INSERT INTO entries (account, amount) VALUES ('customer:CUST-42', -79800)");
            s.executeUpdate("INSERT INTO entries (account, amount) VALUES ('merchant:FRESHCO', 79800)");
            c.commit(); // both legs of the double entry, atomically
        }
        System.out.println("payment-service (relational, ACID): ledger sums to "
                + Db.count(ledger, "SELECT SUM(amount) FROM entries") + " across "
                + Db.count(ledger, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM entries") + " entries");
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: each service picks the store that fits ===
session-service (key-value + TTL): sess-91 -> CUST-42
                31 minutes later : sess-91 -> null
search-service (inverted index)  : 'organic' -> [Organic Alphonso Mangoes 1 kg, Organic Basmati Rice 5 kg]
                                   'organic mangoes' -> [Organic Alphonso Mangoes 1 kg]
payment-service (relational, ACID): ledger sums to 0 across 2 entries

Why polyglot here:

  • Each workload gets the right data model: expiry, full-text search, transactions.
  • Caution: every new store type is something to operate, back up, secure and hire for. Choose deliberately.

docs.title: Example 3: Local Replica via Events (Food delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The shipping service needs customer addresses for every label. Calling the customer service each time couples their availability. Instead, shipping keeps a read-only replica of just the fields it needs, updated from CustomerAddressChanged events. A late-arriving older event (v2 after v3) is ignored thanks to a version check, and labels keep printing while the customer service is down.

Full Code:

ShippingService.javaReplicationDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.replication;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;

/**
 * Keeps a local, read-only copy of the customer data it needs (delivery address), updated from
 * CustomerAddressChanged events. Creating a shipping label needs no call to customer-service.
 */
public final class ShippingService {

    public record CustomerAddressChanged(String customerId, String address, long version) {
    }

    private final DataSource db = Db.inMemory("shipping_db",
            "CREATE TABLE customer_address_replica (customer_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, address VARCHAR, version BIGINT)"); // (1)!

    public void on(CustomerAddressChanged e) {
        try (Connection c = db.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
                     "MERGE INTO customer_address_replica r USING (VALUES (?, ?, ?)) v(id, addr, ver) "
                             + "ON r.customer_id = v.id "
                             + "WHEN MATCHED AND r.version < v.ver THEN UPDATE SET address = v.addr, version = v.ver " // (2)!
                             + "WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (v.id, v.addr, v.ver)")) {
            ps.setString(1, e.customerId());
            ps.setString(2, e.address());
            ps.setLong(3, e.version());
            ps.executeUpdate();
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(ex);
        }
    }

    public String createLabel(String orderId, String customerId) {
        try (Connection c = db.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
                     "SELECT address FROM customer_address_replica WHERE customer_id = ?")) {
            ps.setString(1, customerId);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                return rs.next() ? "LABEL " + orderId + " -> " + rs.getString(1) : "LABEL " + orderId + " -> address unknown";
            }
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(ex);
        }
    }
}
  1. The replica lives in shipping's own database and holds only the fields shipping needs.
  2. Version guard: out-of-order or duplicate events can't overwrite newer data.
package com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.replication;

import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.replication.ShippingService.CustomerAddressChanged;

public class ReplicationDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var shipping = new ShippingService();

        System.out.println("=== Food delivery: shipping keeps its own copy of addresses ===");
        shipping.on(new CustomerAddressChanged("CUST-42", "12 MG Road, Bengaluru", 1));
        System.out.println(shipping.createLabel("ORD-1", "CUST-42"));

        shipping.on(new CustomerAddressChanged("CUST-42", "7 Lake View, Bengaluru", 3));
        shipping.on(new CustomerAddressChanged("CUST-42", "Old flat (v2 arrived late)", 2));
        System.out.println("v3 then a late v2 event arrive -> " + shipping.createLabel("ORD-2", "CUST-42"));

        System.out.println("customer-service is down for maintenance...");
        System.out.println(shipping.createLabel("ORD-3", "CUST-42") + "   (no remote call needed)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Food delivery: shipping keeps its own copy of addresses ===
LABEL ORD-1 -> 12 MG Road, Bengaluru
v3 then a late v2 event arrive -> LABEL ORD-2 -> 7 Lake View, Bengaluru
customer-service is down for maintenance...
LABEL ORD-3 -> 7 Lake View, Bengaluru   (no remote call needed)

Why a replica here:

  • Runtime independence: shipping works when customer-service doesn't.
  • Lower latency (local query) and less load on the owner.
  • The owner is still the single writer; the replica is read-only and eventually consistent.
Unit Tests: DatabasePerServiceTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.batching.BatchedComposer;
import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.grocery.CustomerService;
import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.grocery.OrderService;
import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.replication.ShippingService;
import com.handbook.microservices.dbperservice.replication.ShippingService.CustomerAddressChanged;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DatabasePerServiceTest {

    @Test
    void batchedCompositionMakesOneCall() {
        var customers = new CustomerService();
        assertThat(new BatchedComposer(new OrderService(), customers).history()).hasSize(4);
        assertThat(customers.apiCalls()).isEqualTo(1);
    }

    @Test
    void replicaIgnoresOutOfOrderOlderVersions() {
        var shipping = new ShippingService();
        shipping.on(new CustomerAddressChanged("C", "new", 2));
        shipping.on(new CustomerAddressChanged("C", "old", 1));
        assertThat(shipping.createLabel("O", "C")).endsWith("new");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
# Each Spring Boot service has its own datasource and migrations (reference)
# order-service/application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db:5432/orders
    username: order_service          # this user has grants on the orders schema only
  flyway:
    locations: classpath:db/migration   # order-service owns its schema migrations
Variation Notes Schema per service on a shared cluster Cheaper; enforce isolation with DB users and grants Database per service Strongest isolation; higher cost Data mesh / analytics Services publish data products (events, CDC) to a lake/warehouse for cross-domain reporting Reference data Small, rarely changing data (countries, currencies) may be replicated to everyone via events

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Database per service Spring Boot + Flyway/Liquibase One datasource and migration set per service Kubernetes operators Per-service PostgreSQL clusters (CloudNativePG, Zalando operator) Cloud Managed DB instance per service (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure SQL) Debezium CDC from each service's DB into Kafka for replicas and analytics

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Loose coupling: schema changes are local No cross-service joins or transactions Independent scaling, tuning and failure isolation Data duplication and eventual consistency Right store per workload More databases to operate, back up and secure Clear data ownership Reporting across services needs a pipeline

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
The shared database

Two services writing the same tables is the most common reason microservices aren't independent. If you can't deploy one without the other, they share too much.

Reading another service's database 'just for reports'

A read-only connection still couples you to the schema. Use the owner's API, events, or a reporting pipeline (CDC → warehouse).

N+1 API calls

API composition with one call per row melts under load. Use batch endpoints, caching, or a CQRS read model (see the coding challenge).

Replicas that become a second source of truth

If shipping starts editing its address copy, the copies diverge forever. Replicas are read-only; changes go to the owner.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Migration path. Moving from a shared DB: (1) map which service reads and writes which tables; (2) assign an owner per table; (3) replace foreign readers with APIs or events; (4) separate schemas with per-service DB users; (5) move schemas to separate instances when needed. Each step is deployable on its own.

Reporting. Operational services shouldn't answer analytics queries. Stream changes (CDC/outbox) into a warehouse or lakehouse where cross-domain joins are cheap; that's the analytical side of the data mesh idea.

Uniqueness across services. Constraints like "username unique across tenants" belong to one owner. Cross-service invariants need a single owner, a reservation step in a saga, or a redesign of boundaries.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every table has exactly one owning service; DB credentials grant access only to it.
  • Schema migrations owned and run by that service (Flyway/Liquibase).
  • Cross-service reads via APIs (batched) or event-fed replicas/read models.
  • Cross-service writes via sagas; events via outbox.
  • Analytics via CDC/events into a warehouse, not direct reads.
  • Backups, restores and DR tested per database.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Each service owns its data: orders in its own PostgreSQL, catalog search in OpenSearch, sessions in Redis. No service touches another's database. For the order-history screen I'd use API composition with a batch customer endpoint, or a CQRS read model if it's hot. Shipping keeps a read-only replica of addresses fed by events, so it works when the customer service is down. Cross-service updates use sagas with an outbox, and analytics come from CDC into the warehouse, not from production databases."

War story: the column rename that took down checkout

At a retailer, the loyalty service quietly read the customers table owned by the account team "because it was faster than the API". The account team renamed mobile to phone_number in a routine migration. Loyalty's nightly job failed, and so did its real-time points lookup during checkout, which had no fallback. Checkout errors spiked for 45 minutes. Fix: revoked cross-service DB grants, added a batch customer API and CustomerChanged events, and loyalty built its own replica. A schema-access audit found 11 more hidden readers. Lesson: if someone else can read your tables, your schema is their API, whether you meant it or not.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Database per Service Shared Database API Composition CQRS Coupling Low High Runtime coupling to owners Low (async) Cross-service query Via APIs/events SQL joins Join in memory Pre-built read model Consistency Per service + sagas ACID Fresh Eventual

See Decomposition, Saga, CQRS and Transactional Outbox.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Each service owns its data; others use APIs or events.
  • Cross-service queries: API composition (batched) or CQRS read models.
  • Cross-service writes: sagas + outbox.
  • Replicas are read-only and version-checked.
  • Reporting via CDC → warehouse.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a cache with a 60 s TTL (FakeClock) to CustomerService.namesBatch callers.
  • Make BatchedComposer split IDs into batches of at most 2 and call the service in parallel.
  • Add a CustomerDeleted event to the replica and decide what labels should show.
