docs.title: Decomposition (by Business Capability / Subdomain)
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Split a system into services along business capabilities (what the business does) or DDD subdomains, so each service owns its data and can change and deploy independently. The test of a good boundary: most use cases write inside one service. If a common use case must update data in two services at once, the boundary is probably wrong.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a grocery monolith has catalog, inventory, orders, payments and delivery in one codebase and one database. Every team deploys together, a bad inventory query slows checkout, and a change to the products table breaks four teams. Microservices promise independent teams and deployments, but only if the boundaries are right. Split badly (by technical layer, or by today's org chart) and you get a distributed monolith: all the network problems, none of the independence.

Definitions (microservices.io / DDD):

  • Decompose by business capability: a service per thing the business does (catalog, inventory, ordering, billing), stable over time even as technology and org charts change.
  • Decompose by subdomain (DDD): model the domain, find bounded contexts where a term has one meaning ("Trip" in dispatch vs. billing), and align services with them.
Subdomain type Meaning Strategy Core Where you compete (pricing, matching, recommendations) Build in-house, best engineers Supporting Necessary, specific to you (catalog admin) Build simply, or customize Generic Same for everyone (auth, email, payments gateway) Buy or use a SaaS

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A hospital's departments

A hospital isn't organized by "people who use computers" and "people who use phones". It's organized by capability: emergency, radiology, pharmacy, billing. Each department has its own records and staff, and they coordinate through well-defined requests (a lab order, a discharge summary). A reorganization of managers doesn't move the pharmacy.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Monolith["Before: one deployable, one DB"]
        M[Catalog + Inventory + Orders + Payments] --> DB[(Shared DB)]
    end
    subgraph Services["After: services by business capability"]
        C[Catalog] --> CDB[(catalog DB)]
        I[Inventory] --> IDB[(inventory DB)]
        O[Ordering] --> ODB[(orders DB)]
        O -- "API: canFulfil?" --> I
        O -- "event: OrderPlaced" --> I
        I -- "event: StockLow" --> C
    end
Rule Why Each service owns its data No shared tables, so services can change their schema independently Integrate via APIs and events Explicit contracts instead of hidden coupling Most use cases write in one service Avoids distributed transactions A team owns each service end to end Conway's Law: the architecture mirrors communication paths

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Split by technical layer:      web-service, business-service, data-service    <- every feature touches all three
Split by current teams:        Registration, Doctors, Scheduling, Billing, Payments  <- org chart changes yearly
Split by entities (nouns):     CustomerService, ProductService, OrderService   <- "entity services": chatty, anemic
Shared database:               everyone reads/writes the same tables           <- distributed monolith
  • Every feature spans several services: coordinated deployments.
  • Distributed transactions for common use cases.
  • Chatty calls between services that should have been one.

docs.title: Example 1: Grocery Monolith Split by Business Capability (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce company splits its monolith into Catalog (what we sell and how it's shown), Inventory (units in each dark store) and Ordering (the order lifecycle). Ordering checks stock through Inventory's API, never its tables; Inventory announces events (StockLow) that Catalog uses to update the "only 1 left" badge. Each service could now be deployed, scaled and changed by its own team.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Ordering
    participant I as Inventory
    participant C as Catalog
    O->>I: canFulfil(MANGO-1KG, 2)? (API)
    I-->>O: yes
    O-)I: OrderPlaced (event)
    I->>I: reserve 2, 1 left
    I-)C: StockLow(left=1) (event)
    C->>C: badge "only 1 left"

Full Code:

GroceryServices.javaEventBus.java (support)GroceryDecompositionDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Three services split by BUSINESS CAPABILITY. Each owns its data (a private map standing in
 * for its own database) and talks to the others only through APIs and events.
 */
public final class GroceryServices {

    private GroceryServices() {
    }

    public record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String sku, int qty) {
    }

    public record StockLow(String sku, int left) {
    }

    /** Catalog: what we sell, how it's described, whether to show it as available. */
    public static class CatalogService {
        private final Map<String, String> products = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MANGO-1KG", "Alphonso mangoes, 1 kg"));
        private final Map<String, Boolean> showAsAvailable = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MANGO-1KG", true));

        public CatalogService(EventBus bus) {
            bus.<StockLow>subscribe("inventory.stock-low", e -> { // (1)!
                showAsAvailable.put(e.sku(), e.left() > 0);
                System.out.println("  [catalog] " + e.sku() + " badge -> " + (e.left() > 0 ? "only " + e.left() + " left" : "out of stock"));
            });
        }

        public String describe(String sku) {
            return products.get(sku) + (showAsAvailable.get(sku) ? "" : " (out of stock)");
        }
    }

    /** Inventory: how many units each dark store physically has. */
    public static class InventoryService {
        private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MANGO-1KG", 3));
        private final EventBus bus;

        public InventoryService(EventBus bus) {
            this.bus = bus;
            bus.<OrderPlaced>subscribe("orders.placed", e -> {
                int left = stock.merge(e.sku(), -e.qty(), Integer::sum);
                System.out.println("  [inventory] reserved " + e.qty() + " x " + e.sku() + ", " + left + " left");
                if (left <= 1) {
                    bus.publish("inventory.stock-low", new StockLow(e.sku(), left));
                }
            });
        }

        public boolean canFulfil(String sku, int qty) { // a synchronous API other services may call
            return stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0) >= qty;
        }
    }

    /** Ordering: the order lifecycle. It asks Inventory through its API, never reads its tables. */
    public static class OrderService {
        private final InventoryService inventoryApi;
        private final EventBus bus;
        private int next = 1;

        public OrderService(InventoryService inventoryApi, EventBus bus) {
            this.inventoryApi = inventoryApi;
            this.bus = bus;
        }

        public String place(String sku, int qty) {
            if (!inventoryApi.canFulfil(sku, qty)) { // (2)!
                return "rejected: not enough " + sku;
            }
            String id = "ORD-" + next++;
            bus.publish("orders.placed", new OrderPlaced(id, sku, qty)); // (3)!
            return "accepted " + id;
        }
    }

    public static List<String> ownership() {
        return List.of(
                "Catalog   owns: product names, descriptions, images, availability badge",
                "Inventory owns: units per dark store, reservations",
                "Ordering  owns: orders, order lifecycle");
    }
}
  1. Catalog reacts to Inventory's events instead of reading Inventory's tables. It keeps its own copy of what it needs (the badge).
  2. A synchronous API call for a question that needs a fresh answer before accepting the order.
  3. An event for something that already happened. Inventory decides what reservation means.
package com.handbook.microservices.support;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * A tiny, synchronous, in-memory stand-in for a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
 * Real brokers are asynchronous and at-least-once; the examples call that out where it matters.
 */
public final class EventBus {

    private final Map<String, List<Consumer<Object>>> subscribers = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final boolean log;

    public EventBus(boolean log) {
        this.log = log;
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <T> void subscribe(String topic, Consumer<T> handler) {
        subscribers.computeIfAbsent(topic, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e -> handler.accept((T) e));
    }

    public void publish(String topic, Object event) {
        if (log) {
            System.out.println("  [bus] " + topic + " <- " + event);
        }
        for (Consumer<Object> s : subscribers.getOrDefault(topic, List.of())) {
            s.accept(event);
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery.GroceryServices.*;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;

public class GroceryDecompositionDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Monolith Split by Business Capability ===");
        GroceryServices.ownership().forEach(System.out::println);
        EventBus bus = new EventBus(true);
        CatalogService catalog = new CatalogService(bus);
        InventoryService inventory = new InventoryService(bus);
        OrderService orders = new OrderService(inventory, bus);

        System.out.println("Customer 1 orders 2 mangoes:");
        System.out.println("  -> " + orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 2));
        System.out.println("Customer 2 orders 2 mangoes:");
        System.out.println("  -> " + orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 2));
        System.out.println("Customer 3 orders 1 mango:");
        System.out.println("  -> " + orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 1));
        System.out.println("Catalog page now shows: " + catalog.describe("MANGO-1KG"));
    }
}

Output (happy path and failure path):

=== Grocery: Monolith Split by Business Capability ===
Catalog   owns: product names, descriptions, images, availability badge
Inventory owns: units per dark store, reservations
Ordering  owns: orders, order lifecycle
Customer 1 orders 2 mangoes:
  [bus] orders.placed <- OrderPlaced[orderId=ORD-1, sku=MANGO-1KG, qty=2]
  [inventory] reserved 2 x MANGO-1KG, 1 left
  [bus] inventory.stock-low <- StockLow[sku=MANGO-1KG, left=1]
  [catalog] MANGO-1KG badge -> only 1 left
  -> accepted ORD-1
Customer 2 orders 2 mangoes:
  -> rejected: not enough MANGO-1KG
Customer 3 orders 1 mango:
  [bus] orders.placed <- OrderPlaced[orderId=ORD-2, sku=MANGO-1KG, qty=1]
  [inventory] reserved 1 x MANGO-1KG, 0 left
  [bus] inventory.stock-low <- StockLow[sku=MANGO-1KG, left=0]
  [catalog] MANGO-1KG badge -> out of stock
  -> accepted ORD-2
Catalog page now shows: Alphonso mangoes, 1 kg (out of stock)

Why this boundary:

  • Each capability has its own data and rules (reservation logic stays in Inventory).
  • Catalog stays fast and available even if Inventory is slow: it uses its own copy of the badge.
  • Teams map one-to-one to services.

docs.title: Example 2: One Word, Two Bounded Contexts (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: In a ride-hailing company, Dispatch thinks of a trip as a driver, a pickup location, an ETA and a status. Billing thinks of a trip as base fare, distance fare, time fare and surge. A single shared Trip class (and table) would grow 60 columns, couple both teams, and make every change risky. Instead, each bounded context has its own Trip model, and Dispatch publishes a small, stable TripCompleted event that Billing translates into its model.

Design:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Dispatch["Dispatch context"]
        DT["Trip: driverId, pickup lat/lng, etaMinutes, status"]
    end
    subgraph Billing["Billing context"]
        BT["Trip: baseFare, distanceFare, timeFare, surge, total"]
    end
    DT -- "TripCompleted(tripId, riderId, km, minutes, city)" --> BT

Full Code:

TripContexts.javaTripContextsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * The word "Trip" means different things in two bounded contexts. Each context has its OWN model;
 * they integrate through a published event, not a shared Trip class or shared table.
 */
public final class TripContexts {

    private TripContexts() {
    }

    // ---------- Dispatch context: moving cars around the city ----------
    public static final class Dispatch {
        public record Trip(String id, String driverId, double pickupLat, double pickupLng, int etaMinutes, String status) { // (1)!
        }

        /** The public contract Dispatch publishes. Deliberately small and stable. */
        public record TripCompleted(String tripId, String riderId, double distanceKm, int durationMin, String city) { // (2)!
        }

        private final List<Consumer<TripCompleted>> listeners = new ArrayList<>();

        public void onTripCompleted(Consumer<TripCompleted> l) {
            listeners.add(l);
        }

        public void complete(Trip trip, String riderId, double km, int minutes) {
            System.out.println("  [dispatch] " + trip.id() + " completed by driver " + trip.driverId() + " (ETA was " + trip.etaMinutes() + " min)");
            listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(new TripCompleted(trip.id(), riderId, km, minutes, "Bengaluru")));
        }
    }

    // ---------- Billing context: charging riders ----------
    public static final class Billing {
        public record Trip(String id, String riderId, int baseFare, int distanceFare, int timeFare, int surge, int totalInr) { // (3)!
        }

        private final List<Trip> invoiced = new ArrayList<>();

        public void handle(Dispatch.TripCompleted e) { // translate THEIR language into OURS
            int base = 50;
            int distance = (int) Math.round(e.distanceKm() * 14);
            int time = e.durationMin() * 2;
            int surge = e.city().equals("Bengaluru") ? 20 : 0;
            Trip t = new Trip(e.tripId(), e.riderId(), base, distance, time, surge, base + distance + time + surge);
            invoiced.add(t);
            System.out.println("  [billing] invoice " + t);
        }

        public List<Trip> invoiced() {
            return invoiced;
        }
    }
}
  1. Dispatch's model: what matters for moving cars.
  2. The published contract between contexts: small, explicit, versioned. It's not either side's internal model.
  3. Billing's model: what matters for charging money. Same word, different concept.
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing.TripContexts.Billing;
import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing.TripContexts.Dispatch;

public class TripContextsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: One Word, Two Bounded Contexts ===");
        Dispatch dispatch = new Dispatch();
        Billing billing = new Billing();
        dispatch.onTripCompleted(billing::handle);

        Dispatch.Trip trip = new Dispatch.Trip("TRIP-77", "DRV-12", 12.9352, 77.6245, 4, "IN_PROGRESS");
        dispatch.complete(trip, "RIDER-5", 8.4, 23);
        System.out.println("Dispatch's Trip has GPS + ETA; Billing's Trip has fare components. Neither knows the other's model.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: One Word, Two Bounded Contexts ===
  [dispatch] TRIP-77 completed by driver DRV-12 (ETA was 4 min)
  [billing] invoice Trip[id=TRIP-77, riderId=RIDER-5, baseFare=50, distanceFare=118, timeFare=46, surge=20, totalInr=234]
Dispatch's Trip has GPS + ETA; Billing's Trip has fare components. Neither knows the other's model.

Why bounded contexts here:

  • The ubiquitous language differs between teams; forcing one model makes both worse.
  • The event is the boundary: each side can evolve its internals freely.
  • Billing can add surge rules without touching Dispatch, and vice versa.

docs.title: Example 3: Checking Candidate Splits Against Use Cases (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital IT department wants to break up its patient-management system. One architect proposes splitting by current teams (Registration, Doctors, Scheduling, Billing, Payments); another by business capability (PatientRecords, Scheduling, Billing). Before writing code, they check each split against the real use cases: which ones would have to write data owned by two services in one transaction?

Design:

flowchart TB
    U[Use cases + tables they write/read] --> C{BoundaryChecker}
    S1[Split A: by teams] --> C
    S2[Split B: by capability] --> C
    C --> R1["Split A: 3 cross-service writes"]
    C --> R2["Split B: 1 cross-service write"]

Full Code:

BoundaryChecker.javaBoundaryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/**
 * Checks a proposed service split against the system's use cases: a use case that must WRITE
 * data owned by two services in one transaction is a warning sign (distributed transaction).
 */
public final class BoundaryChecker {

    public record UseCase(String name, Set<String> writes, Set<String> reads) {
    }

    private BoundaryChecker() {
    }

    public static Map<String, String> check(Map<String, String> tableOwner, List<UseCase> useCases) {
        Map<String, String> report = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (UseCase uc : useCases) {
            Set<String> writeOwners = new TreeSet<>();
            uc.writes().forEach(t -> writeOwners.add(tableOwner.get(t)));
            Set<String> readOwners = new TreeSet<>();
            uc.reads().forEach(t -> readOwners.add(tableOwner.get(t)));
            readOwners.removeAll(writeOwners);
            String verdict;
            if (writeOwners.size() > 1) {
                verdict = "WARN writes span " + writeOwners + " -> needs a saga or a different boundary"; // (1)!
            } else if (!readOwners.isEmpty()) {
                verdict = "ok   (reads from " + readOwners + ": API calls or a read model)";
            } else {
                verdict = "ok   (inside " + writeOwners + ")";
            }
            report.put(uc.name(), verdict);
        }
        return report;
    }
}
  1. The heuristic: writes across services in one use case mean a saga (complex) or a wrong boundary. Reads across services are normal (API calls or a local read model).
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare.BoundaryChecker.UseCase;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

public class BoundaryDemo {

    static final List<UseCase> USE_CASES = List.of(
            new UseCase("Book appointment", Set.of("appointments", "slots"), Set.of("patients", "doctors")),
            new UseCase("Check in patient", Set.of("appointments"), Set.of("patients")),
            new UseCase("Close consultation + bill", Set.of("appointments", "invoices"), Set.of("tariffs")),
            new UseCase("Pay invoice", Set.of("invoices", "payments"), Set.of()),
            new UseCase("Update allergies", Set.of("patients"), Set.of()));

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital: Checking Two Candidate Service Splits ===");
        Map<String, String> splitByTeam = Map.of( // split along today's org chart
                "patients", "Registration", "appointments", "Scheduling", "slots", "Doctors",
                "doctors", "Doctors", "invoices", "Billing", "payments", "Payments", "tariffs", "Billing");
        Map<String, String> splitByCapability = Map.of( // split along business capabilities
                "patients", "PatientRecords", "appointments", "Scheduling", "slots", "Scheduling",
                "doctors", "Scheduling", "invoices", "Billing", "payments", "Billing", "tariffs", "Billing");

        for (var split : List.of(Map.entry("Split A (by current teams)", splitByTeam),
                Map.entry("Split B (by business capability)", splitByCapability))) {
            System.out.println(split.getKey() + ":");
            BoundaryChecker.check(split.getValue(), USE_CASES)
                    .forEach((uc, verdict) -> System.out.printf("  %-26s %s%n", uc, verdict));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital: Checking Two Candidate Service Splits ===
Split A (by current teams):
  Book appointment           WARN writes span [Doctors, Scheduling] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Check in patient           ok   (reads from [Registration]: API calls or a read model)
  Close consultation + bill  WARN writes span [Billing, Scheduling] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Pay invoice                WARN writes span [Billing, Payments] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Update allergies           ok   (inside [Registration])
Split B (by business capability):
  Book appointment           ok   (reads from [PatientRecords]: API calls or a read model)
  Check in patient           ok   (reads from [PatientRecords]: API calls or a read model)
  Close consultation + bill  WARN writes span [Billing, Scheduling] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Pay invoice                ok   (inside [Billing])
  Update allergies           ok   (inside [PatientRecords])

The capability-based split leaves one warning, "Close consultation + bill". That's acceptable if Scheduling publishes ConsultationClosed and Billing creates the invoice asynchronously: the invoice doesn't need to exist in the same transaction. Making that decision explicitly is the point of the exercise.

Why this check:

  • Turns "where should the boundary be?" from opinion into evidence from use cases.
  • Splitting by org chart produced three cross-service writes: a distributed monolith in the making.
  • Cheap to run before writing any service code.
Unit Tests: DecompositionTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery.GroceryServices.*;
import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare.BoundaryChecker;
import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing.TripContexts;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DecompositionTest {

    @Test
    void servicesCollaborateOnlyThroughApisAndEvents() {
        EventBus bus = new EventBus(false);
        CatalogService catalog = new CatalogService(bus);
        OrderService orders = new OrderService(new InventoryService(bus), bus);
        assertThat(orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 3)).startsWith("accepted");
        assertThat(catalog.describe("MANGO-1KG")).endsWith("(out of stock)");
        assertThat(orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 1)).startsWith("rejected");
    }

    @Test
    void billingTranslatesDispatchEventIntoItsOwnModel() {
        var dispatch = new TripContexts.Dispatch();
        var billing = new TripContexts.Billing();
        dispatch.onTripCompleted(billing::handle);
        dispatch.complete(new TripContexts.Dispatch.Trip("T", "D", 0, 0, 1, "X"), "R", 10, 10);
        assertThat(billing.invoiced()).singleElement().extracting(TripContexts.Billing.Trip::totalInr).isEqualTo(50 + 140 + 20 + 20);
    }

    @Test
    void crossServiceWritesAreFlagged() {
        var report = BoundaryChecker.check(Map.of("a", "S1", "b", "S2"),
                List.of(new BoundaryChecker.UseCase("uc", Set.of("a", "b"), Set.of())));
        assertThat(report.get("uc")).startsWith("WARN");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Modular monolith first. Many teams start with one deployable split into strict modules (Java modules, Spring Modulith, ArchUnit rules), then extract services when a module needs independent scaling or deployment. See Modular Monolith.
  • Event storming workshops to discover domain events, aggregates and bounded contexts with domain experts.
  • Context mapping between bounded contexts: customer/supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, open-host service, published language.
  • Strangler fig to extract services from an existing monolith incrementally. See Strangler Fig.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Tool Helps with Spring Modulith Module boundaries inside one Spring Boot app, module events, verification tests ArchUnit Tests that fail when packages/modules depend on each other illegally Java Platform Module System module-info.java with exports/requires Spring Cloud / Kubernetes Running the resulting services (discovery, config, gateways) Kafka / RabbitMQ Integration events between services

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Independent deployment and scaling per capability Distributed system costs: network failures, latency, eventual consistency Team autonomy: one team, one service, one database Cross-service queries need API composition or read models Failures isolated to one capability Operational overhead: CI/CD, monitoring, on-call per service Each service can use the right technology Wrong boundaries are expensive to fix later

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Splitting by technical layer or by entity

ProductService, CustomerService, OrderService as CRUD wrappers ("entity services") create chatty, anemic services where every feature changes three of them.

Shared database

Services that share tables are one system with extra network hops. Each service must own its data; others get it through APIs or events.

Too many, too small

50 services for 8 engineers means more time on infrastructure than features. Size services to teams and capabilities, not to lines of code.

Splitting before understanding the domain

Boundaries are hardest to get right early. Start with a modular monolith and extract when the seams are clear.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Conway's Law and the Inverse Conway Maneuver. Systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Design team boundaries deliberately to get the architecture you want (Team Topologies: stream-aligned teams owning services end to end, platform teams providing paved roads).

Data ownership decides boundaries. Ask "who is allowed to change this data, and what invariants protect it?" An invariant that spans data in two services ("an appointment can't be booked unless the slot is free") belongs inside one service, or it needs a saga and accepts eventual consistency.

Migration path. Strangler fig: put a routing layer in front of the monolith, extract one capability at a time (start with one that has clear data and low coupling), replicate data with CDC during the transition, and delete the monolith code once traffic has moved.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Each service has one owning team and an on-call rotation.
  • Each service has its own database (or schema with enforced access control).
  • Integration contracts (APIs, events) are versioned and covered by contract tests.
  • The most common use cases write in a single service.
  • Cross-service flows have explicit consistency strategies (sagas, events, read models).
  • Observability: distributed tracing, per-service SLOs and dashboards.
  • Independent CI/CD pipelines; a service can deploy without others.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"I'd split by business capability: catalog, inventory, ordering, payments, delivery. Each owns its data; no shared tables. Ordering checks stock through Inventory's API for decisions that must be fresh, and publishes events like OrderPlaced that Inventory and Notifications consume. I'd validate the boundaries against core use cases: placing an order should write mostly within Ordering, with reservation and payment handled by a saga. I'd start as a modular monolith if the team is small, and extract services as scaling or team boundaries require."

War story: the twelve services that always deployed together

A fintech split its monolith into 12 services along its database tables (Customer, Account, Card, Transaction...). Every feature needed changes in 4–6 services, deployed in a strict order. Releases took a full day, and a failed deploy of one service broke the others. They had built a distributed monolith. Fix: re-drew boundaries around capabilities (Onboarding, Cards, Payments, Lending), merged services that always changed together, and introduced events for cross-capability flows. Deploys became independent and went from weekly to 30 per day. Lesson: services that change together belong together. Draw boundaries around change and data ownership, not nouns.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Decomposition by capability Decomposition by subdomain (DDD) Modular monolith Unit Business capability Bounded context Module inside one deployable Driver What the business does The domain model and language Code organization first, deployment later Deployable units Many Many One

Related patterns: Database per Service, Saga, API Gateway, Anti-Corruption Layer, Strangler Fig.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Split by business capability / bounded context, not by layer, entity or org chart.
  • Each service owns its data; integrate with APIs (fresh decisions) and events (facts).
  • Test: common use cases write inside one service.
  • Same word, different models across contexts; integrate with published events.
  • Small team or unclear domain? Start with a modular monolith.
Catalog | Inventory | Ordering | Payments | Delivery   — each with its own DB, team and pipeline

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a Payments service to Example 1 and decide what Ordering needs from it (API or event?).
  • Add a TripCancelled event and teach Billing to charge a cancellation fee.
  • Run the BoundaryChecker on a system you know and share the warnings with your team.

🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Give each request a trace ID at the edge, propagate it (with the current span ID) to every service it touches via headers such as W3C traceparent, and record a span per unit of work. A tracing backend assembles the spans into a tree showing where the time went and where it failed. Logs tell you what happened in one service; traces tell you where in the call chain it happened.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: checkout takes 1.5 s sometimes. The request touches the gateway, order, inventory, payment and an external bank. Each service's logs say "OK" and its average latency looks fine. Which hop is slow, for this request? Without a shared ID, correlating logs across five services by timestamp is guesswork.

Definition (OpenTelemetry):

Traces give us the big picture of what happens when a request is made to an application. A trace is made of one or more spans; each span represents a unit of work.

Concept Meaning Trace The whole journey of one request (one trace ID) Span One operation: name, start, duration, attributes, status, parent span ID Context propagation Passing trace ID + parent span ID across process boundaries (HTTP headers, message headers) traceparent W3C header: 00-<trace-id 32 hex>-<parent-id 16 hex>-<flags> Sampling Recording only a share of traces to control cost

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A parcel's tracking number

The parcel gets one tracking number at pickup. Every hub scans it on arrival and departure, so you can see it spent 14 hours stuck at the Pune sort centre. The tracking number is the trace ID; each scan pair is a span.

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> G[Gateway<br/>starts trace]
    G -->|traceparent| O[Order svc]
    O -->|traceparent| I[Inventory svc]
    O -->|traceparent| P[Payment svc]
    P -->|traceparent| K[[Kafka<br/>headers]] --> B[Billing svc]
    G & O & I & P & B -.->|spans via OTLP| COL[Collector] --> BE[(Jaeger / Tempo / Zipkin)]
Participant Responsibility Instrumentation (OTel agent, Micrometer) Creates spans for HTTP, DB, messaging; injects/extracts headers Propagator Serializes context into headers (W3C, B3) Collector Receives, batches, samples and exports spans Backend Stores and visualizes traces; links to logs and metrics

docs.title: 5. Three Real-World Examples
docs.text:
All examples use a small tracer and the W3C header format:

TraceContext.javaTracer.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core;

import java.util.Random;

/**
 * The W3C Trace Context carried between services in the {@code traceparent} header:
 * {@code 00-<32 hex trace-id>-<16 hex parent span-id>-<flags>} (flags 01 = sampled).
 */
public record TraceContext(String traceId, String spanId, boolean sampled) {

    public static TraceContext parse(String traceparent) {
        String[] parts = traceparent.split("-"); // (1)!
        if (parts.length != 4 || !parts[0].equals("00") || parts[1].length() != 32 || parts[2].length() != 16) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad traceparent: " + traceparent);
        }
        return new TraceContext(parts[1], parts[2], parts[3].equals("01"));
    }

    public String toTraceparent() {
        return "00-" + traceId + "-" + spanId + "-" + (sampled ? "01" : "00");
    }

    public static TraceContext newRoot(Random ids) {
        return new TraceContext(hex(ids, 16), hex(ids, 8), true);
    }

    public TraceContext newChild(Random ids) { // (2)!
        return new TraceContext(traceId, hex(ids, 8), sampled);
    }

    static String hex(Random ids, int bytes) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < bytes; i++) {
            sb.append(String.format("%02x", ids.nextInt(256)));
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
  1. Strict parsing: a malformed header should start a new trace rather than corrupt one.
  2. A child keeps the trace ID and gets a new span ID; the old span ID becomes its parent.
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** A tiny tracer: creates spans, records them when they end, and prints a trace as a tree. */
public final class Tracer {

    public record Span(String traceId, String spanId, String parentId, String service, String name,
                       long startMillis, long endMillis) {
        long duration() {
            return endMillis - startMillis;
        }
    }

    private final Clock clock;
    private final Random ids;
    private final List<Span> finished = new ArrayList<>(); // what a collector (Jaeger, Tempo) receives

    public Tracer(Clock clock, Random ids) {
        this.clock = clock;
        this.ids = ids;
    }

    /** Runs work inside a new span. {@code parent} may be null to start a new trace. */
    public <T> T inSpan(TraceContext parent, String service, String name,
                        Function<TraceContext, T> work) {
        TraceContext ctx = parent == null ? TraceContext.newRoot(ids) : parent.newChild(ids);
        long start = clock.millis();
        try {
            return work.apply(ctx);
        } finally {
            synchronized (finished) {
                finished.add(new Span(ctx.traceId(), ctx.spanId(), parent == null ? null : parent.spanId(),
                        service, name, start, clock.millis()));
            }
        }
    }

    public <T> T inSpan(TraceContext parent, String service, String name, Supplier<T> work) {
        return inSpan(parent, service, name, ctx -> work.get());
    }

    public List<Span> spans() {
        synchronized (finished) {
            return List.copyOf(finished);
        }
    }

    public void printTree(String traceId) {
        List<Span> trace = spans().stream().filter(s -> s.traceId().equals(traceId)).toList();
        long t0 = trace.stream().mapToLong(Span::startMillis).min().orElse(0);
        long t1 = trace.stream().mapToLong(Span::endMillis).max().orElse(t0);
        double msPerChar = Math.max(1, (t1 - t0) / 40.0); // the whole trace fits in 40 characters
        trace.stream().filter(s -> s.parentId() == null).forEach(root -> print(root, trace, t0, msPerChar, 0));
    }

    private void print(Span span, List<Span> trace, long t0, double msPerChar, int depth) {
        int offset = (int) ((span.startMillis() - t0) / msPerChar);
        int width = (int) Math.max(1, Math.round(span.duration() / msPerChar));
        System.out.printf("  %-50s %5d ms |%s%n", "  ".repeat(depth) + span.service() + ": " + span.name(),
                span.duration(), " ".repeat(offset) + "#".repeat(width));
        trace.stream().filter(s -> span.spanId().equals(s.parentId()))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Span::startMillis))
                .forEach(child -> print(child, trace, t0, msPerChar, depth + 1));
    }
}

docs.title: Example 1: Finding the Slow Hop in Checkout (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: One checkout request crosses the gateway, order, inventory and payment services. Each service parses the incoming traceparent, creates a child span and passes its own span ID downstream. The trace tree (with a timeline bar per span) makes the answer obvious: 1.4 s of the 1.5 s is the bank authorization call inside payment-service.

Full Code:

CheckoutTraceDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.Tracer;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Random;

/**
 * One checkout request crosses four services. Each service reads the incoming traceparent header,
 * creates a child span, and passes its own span ID downstream. The collector stitches the tree.
 */
public class CheckoutTraceDemo {

    static FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T19:00:00Z");
    static Tracer tracer = new Tracer(clock, new Random(7));

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: tracing one slow checkout across services ===");
        Request incoming = Request.get("/checkout", Map.of()); // no traceparent: the gateway starts the trace
        String traceId = tracer.inSpan(null, "api-gateway", "POST /checkout", gw -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(5);
            orderService(incoming.withHeader("traceparent", gw.toTraceparent())); // (1)!
            clock.advanceMillis(3);
            return gw.traceId();
        });
        System.out.println("trace-id " + traceId);
        tracer.printTree(traceId);
        System.out.println("The tree shows where the time went: payment-service waiting on the bank.");
    }

    static void orderService(Request req) {
        TraceContext parent = TraceContext.parse(req.header("traceparent")); // (2)!
        tracer.inSpan(parent, "order-service", "placeOrder", ctx -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(10);
            tracer.inSpan(ctx, "inventory-service", "reserve", () -> {
                clock.advanceMillis(40);
                return null;
            });
            paymentService(req.withHeader("traceparent", ctx.toTraceparent()));
            clock.advanceMillis(15);
            return null;
        });
    }

    static void paymentService(Request req) {
        TraceContext parent = TraceContext.parse(req.header("traceparent"));
        tracer.inSpan(parent, "payment-service", "charge", ctx -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(20);
            tracer.inSpan(ctx, "payment-service", "HTTP POST bank /authorize", () -> {
                clock.advanceMillis(1_400); // the slow external call
                return null;
            });
            return null;
        });
    }
}
  1. Inject: the gateway sends its context downstream in the traceparent header.
  2. Extract: each service continues the trace from the incoming header.

Output:

=== Grocery: tracing one slow checkout across services ===
trace-id bba3bf02597de5beb5915af31e40d9b2
  api-gateway: POST /checkout                         1493 ms |########################################
    order-service: placeOrder                         1485 ms |########################################
      inventory-service: reserve                        40 ms |#
      payment-service: charge                         1420 ms | ######################################
        payment-service: HTTP POST bank /authorize    1400 ms |  ######################################
The tree shows where the time went: payment-service waiting on the bank.

Why tracing here:

  • Latency is attributed to a specific hop for a specific request.
  • The tree also shows structure: inventory and payment run sequentially, so parallelizing them is a possible optimization.

docs.title: Example 2: Across Kafka (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: Completing a trip publishes TripCompleted; billing consumes it 2 seconds later on another machine. The producer puts traceparent into the message headers; the consumer extracts it and continues the same trace, so the invoice insert appears under the original HTTP request.

Full Code:

KafkaTracePropagationDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.async;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.Tracer;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Queue;
import java.util.Random;

/**
 * Traces cross asynchronous boundaries too: the producer puts traceparent into the message headers,
 * and the consumer, possibly seconds later on another machine, continues the same trace.
 */
public class KafkaTracePropagationDemo {

    record Message(String topic, Map<String, String> headers, String payload) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T22:00:00Z");
        Tracer tracer = new Tracer(clock, new Random(11));
        Queue<Message> topic = new ArrayDeque<>();

        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: trip completion -> async billing, one trace ===");
        String traceId = tracer.inSpan(null, "trip-service", "POST /trips/TRIP-5/complete", ctx -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(25);
            tracer.inSpan(ctx, "trip-service", "kafka send trips.completed", producer -> {
                topic.add(new Message("trips.completed",
                        Map.of("traceparent", producer.toTraceparent()), "TripCompleted TRIP-5")); // (1)!
                clock.advanceMillis(4);
                return null;
            });
            return ctx.traceId();
        });

        clock.advanceMillis(2_000); // consumer lag
        Message m = topic.poll();
        TraceContext fromHeaders = TraceContext.parse(m.headers().get("traceparent")); // (2)!
        tracer.inSpan(fromHeaders, "billing-service", "kafka receive " + m.topic(), consumer -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(30);
            tracer.inSpan(consumer, "billing-service", "INSERT invoice", () -> {
                clock.advanceMillis(12);
                return null;
            });
            return null;
        });

        System.out.println("message headers: " + m.headers());
        tracer.printTree(traceId);
        System.out.println("billing-service joined trace " + traceId.substring(0, 8) + "... 2 s after the HTTP request ended.");
    }
}
  1. Message headers carry the context just like HTTP headers do.
  2. The consumer extracts it; OpenTelemetry may model this as a child or as a span link for batch consumers.

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: trip completion -> async billing, one trace ===
message headers: {traceparent=00-bab66d36a16606e830490b8d6f70abfb-2d5a670a88b89bb4-01}
  trip-service: POST /trips/TRIP-5/complete             29 ms |#
    trip-service: kafka send trips.completed             4 ms |#
      billing-service: kafka receive trips.completed    42 ms |                                       #
        billing-service: INSERT invoice                 12 ms |                                       #
billing-service joined trace bab66d36... 2 s after the HTTP request ended.

Why propagate through messages:

  • Async flows (sagas, outbox relays) are where "where did it get stuck?" is hardest to answer.
  • Consumer lag becomes visible as a gap in the trace.

docs.title: Example 3: Keeping Context Across Threads (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: The home-screen service fetches three rows in parallel. The current trace lives in a ThreadLocal, so work on a plain executor loses it, and those spans become orphan traces. A context-propagating executor captures the context at submit time and restores it in the worker.

Full Code:

ContextPropagatingExecutor.javaThreadContextDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.threads;

import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;

import java.util.concurrent.Executor;

/**
 * The current trace context usually lives in a ThreadLocal. Work submitted to another thread loses
 * it unless the executor captures the context at submit time and restores it in the worker.
 */
public final class ContextPropagatingExecutor implements Executor {

    public static final ThreadLocal<TraceContext> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();

    private final Executor delegate;

    public ContextPropagatingExecutor(Executor delegate) {
        this.delegate = delegate;
    }

    @Override
    public void execute(Runnable task) {
        TraceContext captured = CURRENT.get(); // (1)!
        delegate.execute(() -> {
            TraceContext previous = CURRENT.get();
            CURRENT.set(captured); // (2)!
            try {
                task.run();
            } finally {
                CURRENT.set(previous); // (3)!
            }
        });
    }
}
  1. Capture on the submitting thread.
  2. Restore on the worker thread for the task's duration.
  3. Always restore the previous value. Pooled threads are reused, and leaking context into the next task corrupts traces.
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.threads;

import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.Executor;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class ThreadContextDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TraceContext request = TraceContext.newRoot(new Random(3));
        ContextPropagatingExecutor.CURRENT.set(request);

        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            System.out.println("=== Streaming: parallel home-screen fetches keep the trace ===");
            System.out.println("request thread trace: " + request.traceId().substring(0, 8) + "...");
            System.out.println("plain executor      : " + fetchAll(pool));
            System.out.println("propagating executor: " + fetchAll(new ContextPropagatingExecutor(pool)));
        } finally {
            ContextPropagatingExecutor.CURRENT.remove();
        }
    }

    private static List<String> fetchAll(Executor executor) {
        List<CompletableFuture<String>> rows = List.of("continue-watching", "trending", "for-you").stream()
                .map(row -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
                    TraceContext ctx = ContextPropagatingExecutor.CURRENT.get();
                    return row + "=" + (ctx == null ? "NO TRACE" : ctx.traceId().substring(0, 8));
                }, executor))
                .toList();
        return rows.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: parallel home-screen fetches keep the trace ===
request thread trace: bb8f12ce...
plain executor      : [continue-watching=NO TRACE, trending=NO TRACE, for-you=NO TRACE]
propagating executor: [continue-watching=bb8f12ce, trending=bb8f12ce, for-you=bb8f12ce]

Why this matters:

  • Async code (CompletableFuture, @Async, reactive) is the most common place traces break.
  • OpenTelemetry's Context.taskWrapping(executor) and Micrometer's ContextExecutorService do exactly this.
Unit Tests: DistributedTracingTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.sampling.RatioSampler;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Random;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class DistributedTracingTest {

    @Test
    void traceparentRoundTripsAndChildKeepsTraceId() {
        TraceContext root = TraceContext.newRoot(new Random(1));
        TraceContext parsed = TraceContext.parse(root.toTraceparent());
        assertThat(parsed).isEqualTo(root);
        TraceContext child = parsed.newChild(new Random(2));
        assertThat(child.traceId()).isEqualTo(root.traceId());
        assertThat(child.spanId()).isNotEqualTo(root.spanId());
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsMalformedHeaders() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> TraceContext.parse("00-abc-def-01")).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void samplingIsDeterministicPerTraceId() {
        RatioSampler sampler = new RatioSampler(0.5);
        String traceId = TraceContext.newRoot(new Random(9)).traceId();
        assertThat(sampler.shouldSampleRoot(traceId)).isEqualTo(sampler.shouldSampleRoot(traceId));
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Spring Boot 3 with Micrometer Tracing (compiled in the spring-reference module):

package com.handbook.springref.tracing;

import io.micrometer.observation.Observation;
import io.micrometer.observation.ObservationRegistry;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

/**
 * With micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel on the classpath, Spring Boot instruments incoming HTTP
 * requests and the auto-configured RestClient.Builder, so traceparent is propagated for free.
 * Custom spans for business steps use the Observation API.
 */
@Service
public class TracedCheckoutService {

    private final RestClient payments;
    private final ObservationRegistry observations;

    public TracedCheckoutService(RestClient.Builder builder, ObservationRegistry observations) {
        this.payments = builder.baseUrl("http://payment-service").build(); // builder carries tracing
        this.observations = observations;
    }

    public String checkout(String orderId) {
        long total = Observation.createNotStarted("checkout.price-cart", observations)
                .lowCardinalityKeyValue("channel", "app") // becomes a span tag and a metric dimension
                .observe(() -> priceCart(orderId));
        return payments.post().uri("/charges/{id}", orderId)
                .body(total)
                .retrieve()
                .body(String.class); // child span + traceparent header added automatically
    }

    private long priceCart(String orderId) {
        return 79_800;
    }
}

# application.yml (reference)
management:
  tracing:
    sampling.probability: 0.1          # 10% head sampling
  otlp:
    tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
logging.pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"  # IDs in every log line
Option Notes OpenTelemetry Java agent Zero-code instrumentation (-javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar) for HTTP, JDBC, Kafka and more Micrometer Tracing (Spring Boot 3) Observation API; bridges to OTel or Brave Head sampling Decide at the root (cheap; may miss rare errors) Tail sampling The collector decides after seeing the whole trace (keep errors and slow traces) Exemplars Link a metric spike to example trace IDs

docs.text: Where Tracing OpenTelemetry The standard API/SDK, OTLP protocol and collector Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Zipkin Open-source backends Spring Boot 3 Micrometer Tracing + ObservationRegistry auto-instrumentation Service meshes Proxies emit spans per hop (apps still forward headers) W3C Trace Context traceparent/tracestate header standard

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Pinpoints slow or failing hops per request Instrumentation gaps break traces Shows real dependency graphs Storage cost; requires sampling at scale Correlates logs, metrics and traces by ID Context propagation across async code needs care Standardized (W3C, OTel) Sensitive data can leak into span attributes

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Broken propagation

One service that doesn't forward traceparent (a hand-built HTTP client, a thread pool, a message without headers) splits every trace in two. Test propagation end to end.

High-cardinality or sensitive attributes

Putting card numbers, emails or full request bodies into span attributes leaks PII into the tracing backend. Use allow-lists for attributes.

Sampling inconsistently

If each service samples independently at 10%, only 1% of traces are complete. Use parent-based sampling (see the coding challenge).

Tracing without logs correlation

Put trace and span IDs in every log line (MDC), so you can jump from a trace to the exact logs.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Three pillars, one ID. Metrics tell you that something is wrong (error rate up), traces tell you where (which hop), logs tell you why (the exception). Wire them together: exemplars on metrics, trace IDs in logs, and service graphs from traces.

Sampling strategy. Head sampling at 1–10% for volume; tail sampling in the collector to always keep errors and slow traces; higher rates for low-traffic critical paths. Budget storage per day.

Baggage. W3C Baggage can carry business context (tenant ID, experiment) across services. It's sent on every hop and visible to every service, so keep it small and non-sensitive.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry agent or Micrometer Tracing in every service; W3C propagation everywhere (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka).
  • Context propagation through executors, @Async, reactive and virtual threads verified.
  • Trace/span IDs in logs (MDC); exemplars on latency metrics.
  • Parent-based head sampling + tail sampling for errors/slow requests.
  • Attribute allow-list; no PII in spans.
  • Collector deployed with batching and back-pressure; backend retention set.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Every service runs the OpenTelemetry agent. The gateway starts a trace and propagates W3C traceparent over HTTP, gRPC and Kafka headers, so a checkout produces one trace across all services and async consumers. Spans go via OTLP to a collector that does tail sampling (keep all errors and requests over 1 s, plus 5% of the rest) and exports to Tempo. Trace IDs are in every log line and metrics have exemplars, so from a latency spike we can click straight to a slow trace and then to its logs."

War story: the trace that ended at the thread pool

A payments team adopted tracing, but traces for refunds always stopped at refund-service. The refund flow used a custom ExecutorService for parallel ledger updates; the context stayed on the request thread. For months, slow refunds were blamed on the ledger database, which looked fine. Fix: wrapped the executor with context propagation; the now-complete traces showed the real culprit: a synchronous call to a fraud-scoring API inside the parallel tasks, with no timeout. Lesson: a trace that stops early hides the actual problem. Verify propagation across every async boundary.

  • Propagate traceparent over HTTP, gRPC and message headers.
  • Watch async boundaries (executors, @Async, reactive).

docs.title: Event Sourcing
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Instead of storing the current state and overwriting it, store every change as an immutable event in an append-only log. The current state is derived by replaying the events (sped up with snapshots). You get a complete audit trail, time travel ("what was the state on 1 March?"), and the ability to build new views from history, at the cost of more complexity (schema evolution, replays, eventual consistency of read models).

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a CRUD accounts table says the balance is ₹11,200. How did it get there? Which deposit was reversed? What was the balance at month-end for the regulator? The UPDATE destroyed that information. Bolting on audit tables later is error-prone (they drift from reality).

Definition (Martin Fowler):

Event Sourcing ensures that all changes to application state are stored as a sequence of events. Not just can we query these events, we can also use the event log to reconstruct past states.

Core mechanics:

Concept Meaning Event An immutable fact in the past tense: Deposited(₹100) Stream All events of one aggregate, in order (account-ACC-1) Rehydration Rebuilding state by applying events in order Snapshot Saved state at version N, so replay starts there Optimistic concurrency Append only if the stream is still at the expected version Projection A read model built from events (see CQRS)

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Your bank passbook vs. a whiteboard

A whiteboard shows only today's balance; erase and rewrite. A passbook lists every deposit and withdrawal; the balance is the sum. You can check any past balance, find a wrong entry, and correct it with a new entry (a reversal), never by tearing out a page. Accountants have worked this way for centuries.
