docs.title: Example 1: Event-Sourced Bank Account (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: An account stream with Opened, Deposited and Withdrawn events. The repository loads the latest snapshot (taken every 4 events) and replays only later events. Two tellers load version 6 at the same time; teller A withdraws first; teller B's append is rejected by optimistic concurrency, reloads, and the rule check now correctly refuses the withdrawal: no double spend.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Teller A
    participant B as Teller B
    participant S as Event store
    A->>S: load (v6)
    B->>S: load (v6)
    A->>S: append Withdrawn(10000), expected v6 ✔ → v7
    B->>S: append Withdrawn(10000), expected v6 ✘ (now v7)
    B->>S: reload v7 → balance 1200 → insufficient funds

Full Code:

Account.javaEventStore.javaAccountRepository.javaAccountEventSourcingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import java.util.List;

/**
 * An event-sourced aggregate. State is never stored directly: it is the result of applying every
 * event in order. Commands check rules against that state and return NEW events.
 */
public final class Account {

    public sealed interface Event permits Opened, Deposited, Withdrawn {
    }

    public record Opened(String owner) implements Event {
    }

    public record Deposited(long paise) implements Event {
    }

    public record Withdrawn(long paise) implements Event {
    }

    /** A snapshot: the state as of a version, so replay can start there. */
    public record Snapshot(long version, String owner, long balance) {
    }

    private String owner;
    private long balance;
    private long version;

    public static Account replay(Snapshot snapshot, List<Event> laterEvents) {
        Account a = new Account();
        if (snapshot != null) {
            a.owner = snapshot.owner();
            a.balance = snapshot.balance();
            a.version = snapshot.version();
        }
        laterEvents.forEach(a::apply); // (1)!
        return a;
    }

    private void apply(Event e) { // (2)!
        switch (e) {
            case Opened o -> owner = o.owner();
            case Deposited d -> balance += d.paise();
            case Withdrawn w -> balance -= w.paise();
        }
        version++;
    }

    public List<Event> deposit(long paise) { // (3)!
        if (paise <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        }
        return List.of(new Deposited(paise));
    }

    public List<Event> withdraw(long paise) {
        if (paise > balance) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        }
        return List.of(new Withdrawn(paise));
    }

    public Snapshot snapshot() {
        return new Snapshot(version, owner, balance);
    }

    public long version() {
        return version;
    }

    public long balance() {
        return balance;
    }
}
  1. State = fold of events, starting from a snapshot if there is one.
  2. apply only changes state; it never validates (past events are facts, even if today's rules differ).
  3. Commands validate and return new events; they don't mutate state directly.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * An append-only store of events per stream (one stream per aggregate). Appends carry the version
 * the writer last saw; if someone else appended first, the write is rejected (optimistic locking).
 */
public final class EventStore<E> {

    public static final class ConcurrencyException extends RuntimeException {
        ConcurrencyException(String stream, long expected, long actual) {
            super(stream + ": expected version " + expected + " but was " + actual);
        }
    }

    private final Map<String, List<E>> streams = new HashMap<>();
    private int reads;

    public synchronized void append(String stream, long expectedVersion, List<E> events) {
        List<E> existing = streams.computeIfAbsent(stream, k -> new ArrayList<>());
        if (existing.size() != expectedVersion) { // (1)!
            throw new ConcurrencyException(stream, expectedVersion, existing.size());
        }
        existing.addAll(events);
    }

    /** Events with version greater than {@code afterVersion} (versions start at 1). */
    public synchronized List<E> read(String stream, long afterVersion) {
        List<E> all = streams.getOrDefault(stream, List.of());
        reads += all.size() - (int) afterVersion;
        return List.copyOf(all.subList((int) afterVersion, all.size()));
    }

    public synchronized int eventsReadSoFar() {
        return reads;
    }
}
  1. Optimistic concurrency: the append fails if someone else appended since we loaded.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Snapshot;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Loads aggregates from snapshot + later events, and saves new events with optimistic locking. */
public final class AccountRepository {

    private final EventStore<Event> store;
    private final Map<String, Snapshot> snapshots = new HashMap<>();
    private final int snapshotEvery;

    public AccountRepository(EventStore<Event> store, int snapshotEvery) {
        this.store = store;
        this.snapshotEvery = snapshotEvery;
    }

    public Account load(String id) {
        Snapshot snap = snapshots.get(id);
        return Account.replay(snap, store.read(id, snap == null ? 0 : snap.version()));
    }

    /** Load, run the command, append its events at the version we loaded. */
    public void execute(String id, Function<Account, List<Event>> command) {
        Account account = load(id);
        List<Event> events = command.apply(account);
        store.append(id, account.version(), events);
        Account after = Account.replay(account.snapshot(), events);
        if (after.version() / snapshotEvery > account.version() / snapshotEvery) { // (1)!
            snapshots.put(id, after.snapshot());
        }
    }
}
  1. Take a snapshot when the version crosses a multiple of snapshotEvery.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Opened;

import java.util.List;

public class AccountEventSourcingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EventStore<Event> store = new EventStore<>();
        var repo = new AccountRepository(store, 4);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: an event-sourced account ===");
        store.append("ACC-1", 0, List.of(new Opened("Asha")));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.deposit(10_000));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.withdraw(2_500));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.deposit(4_000));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.withdraw(1_000));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.deposit(700));

        System.out.println("Event stream : " + store.read("ACC-1", 0));
        int before = store.eventsReadSoFar();
        Account loaded = repo.load("ACC-1");
        System.out.println("Balance " + loaded.balance() + " at version " + loaded.version()
                + ", rebuilt by replaying " + (store.eventsReadSoFar() - before) + " event(s) after the snapshot at v4");

        System.out.println("-- two tellers load v6 at the same time --");
        Account tellerA = repo.load("ACC-1");
        Account tellerB = repo.load("ACC-1");
        store.append("ACC-1", tellerA.version(), tellerA.withdraw(10_000));
        System.out.println("Teller A withdrew 10000 -> balance " + repo.load("ACC-1").balance());
        try {
            store.append("ACC-1", tellerB.version(), tellerB.withdraw(10_000));
        } catch (EventStore.ConcurrencyException e) {
            System.out.println("Teller B rejected: " + e.getMessage() + " -> reload and retry");
            try {
                repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.withdraw(10_000));
            } catch (IllegalStateException retryFailed) {
                System.out.println("Retry on fresh state: " + retryFailed.getMessage() + " (no double spend)");
            }
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: an event-sourced account ===
Event stream : [Opened[owner=Asha], Deposited[paise=10000], Withdrawn[paise=2500], Deposited[paise=4000], Withdrawn[paise=1000], Deposited[paise=700]]
Balance 11200 at version 6, rebuilt by replaying 2 event(s) after the snapshot at v4
-- two tellers load v6 at the same time --
Teller A withdrew 10000 -> balance 1200
Teller B rejected: ACC-1: expected version 6 but was 7 -> reload and retry
Retry on fresh state: insufficient funds (no double spend)

Why event sourcing here:

  • The ledger is the history; audits and disputes read it directly.
  • Concurrency is handled per stream without row locks.
  • Snapshots keep loading fast as streams grow.

docs.title: Example 2: What the Cart Table Forgets (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: A CRUD cart table shows only what's in each cart now. The event log also knows what was added and removed. Replaying it reveals that avocados are removed right before checkout in carts that still get bought, a signal about price or stock reliability that CRUD would have deleted.

Full Code:

CartEvents.javaCartHistoryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** Cart events, the current cart derived from them, and an insight a CRUD table would have lost. */
public final class CartEvents {

    public sealed interface Event permits ItemAdded, ItemRemoved, CheckedOut {
        String cartId();
    }

    public record ItemAdded(String cartId, String sku) implements Event {
    }

    public record ItemRemoved(String cartId, String sku) implements Event {
    }

    public record CheckedOut(String cartId) implements Event {
    }

    private CartEvents() {
    }

    /** Current state: what a CRUD "cart_items" table would hold. */
    public static Map<String, List<String>> currentCarts(List<Event> log) {
        Map<String, List<String>> carts = new TreeMap<>();
        for (Event e : log) {
            switch (e) {
                case ItemAdded a -> carts.computeIfAbsent(a.cartId(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(a.sku());
                case ItemRemoved r -> carts.get(r.cartId()).remove(r.sku());
                case CheckedOut c -> { }
            }
        }
        return carts;
    }

    /** History-based insight: items removed from carts that were later checked out anyway. */
    public static Map<String, Integer> removedBeforeCheckout(List<Event> log) {
        Map<String, List<String>> removedPerCart = new HashMap<>();
        Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>();
        for (Event e : log) {
            switch (e) {
                case ItemRemoved r -> removedPerCart.computeIfAbsent(r.cartId(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(r.sku());
                case CheckedOut c -> removedPerCart.getOrDefault(c.cartId(), List.of())
                        .forEach(sku -> counts.merge(sku, 1, Integer::sum)); // (1)!
                case ItemAdded a -> { }
            }
        }
        return counts;
    }
}
  1. A new question asked of old data: no schema change, just a new fold over the events.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.CheckedOut;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.ItemAdded;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.ItemRemoved;

import java.util.List;

public class CartHistoryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Event> log = List.of(
                new ItemAdded("C1", "MANGO-1KG"), new ItemAdded("C1", "AVOCADO-2"), new ItemRemoved("C1", "AVOCADO-2"),
                new CheckedOut("C1"),
                new ItemAdded("C2", "AVOCADO-2"), new ItemAdded("C2", "RICE-5KG"), new ItemRemoved("C2", "AVOCADO-2"),
                new CheckedOut("C2"),
                new ItemAdded("C3", "MILK-1L"), new ItemAdded("C3", "BREAD"), new ItemRemoved("C3", "BREAD"));

        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: what the cart table shows vs. what the events know ===");
        System.out.println("Current carts (CRUD view)          : " + CartEvents.currentCarts(log));
        System.out.println("Removed, yet the cart was bought   : " + CartEvents.removedBeforeCheckout(log));
        System.out.println("Insight: avocados are dropped at checkout. Is the price too high, or is stock unreliable?");
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: what the cart table shows vs. what the events know ===
Current carts (CRUD view)          : {C1=[MANGO-1KG], C2=[RICE-5KG], C3=[MILK-1L]}
Removed, yet the cart was bought   : {AVOCADO-2=2}
Insight: avocados are dropped at checkout. Is the price too high, or is stock unreliable?

Why event sourcing here:

  • Business questions nobody thought of at design time can be answered retroactively.
  • Analytics and ML features come from the same source of truth as the app.

docs.title: Example 3: Temporal Queries on a Shipment (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A customer disputes a late delivery and blames the courier. Replaying the shipment's scans up to a point in time shows exactly what the system knew then: at 14:00 the parcel was in transit at Pune; by midnight it was flagged with a weather delay.

Full Code:

ShipmentHistory.javaShipmentTemporalDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.shipment;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

/** Shipment events with timestamps support "what did we know at time T?" queries. */
public final class ShipmentHistory {

    public record Scanned(Instant at, String location, String status) {
    }

    public record State(String location, String status) {
    }

    private final List<Scanned> events;

    public ShipmentHistory(List<Scanned> events) {
        this.events = List.copyOf(events);
    }

    public State current() {
        return stateAt(Instant.MAX);
    }

    public State stateAt(Instant when) { // (1)!
        State state = new State("-", "CREATED");
        for (Scanned e : events) {
            if (e.at().isAfter(when)) {
                break;
            }
            state = new State(e.location(), e.status());
        }
        return state;
    }
}
  1. Time travel: replay only events up to when.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.shipment;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.shipment.ShipmentHistory.Scanned;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

public class ShipmentTemporalDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var history = new ShipmentHistory(List.of(
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T06:10:00Z"), "Mumbai hub", "PICKED_UP"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T13:45:00Z"), "Pune sort centre", "IN_TRANSIT"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T18:20:00Z"), "Pune sort centre", "DELAYED_WEATHER"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-13T09:05:00Z"), "Bengaluru hub", "IN_TRANSIT"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-13T15:30:00Z"), "Koramangala", "DELIVERED")));

        System.out.println("=== Logistics: temporal queries on a shipment ===");
        System.out.println("Now                         : " + history.current());
        System.out.println("At 2026-10-12 14:00 UTC     : " + history.stateAt(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T14:00:00Z")));
        System.out.println("At 2026-10-12 23:59 UTC     : " + history.stateAt(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T23:59:00Z")));
        System.out.println("Customer says: \"the delay was the courier's fault\" -> the history shows a weather delay at Pune, 18:20.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: temporal queries on a shipment ===
Now                         : State[location=Koramangala, status=DELIVERED]
At 2026-10-12 14:00 UTC     : State[location=Pune sort centre, status=IN_TRANSIT]
At 2026-10-12 23:59 UTC     : State[location=Pune sort centre, status=DELAYED_WEATHER]
Customer says: "the delay was the courier's fault" -> the history shows a weather delay at Pune, 18:20.

Why event sourcing here:

  • "As of" queries are natural; with CRUD they need bitemporal tables.
  • Dispute resolution and SLA penalties rely on exact history.
Unit Tests: EventSourcingTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Deposited;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Opened;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.AccountRepository;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.EventStore;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.upcasting.Upcaster;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class EventSourcingTest {

    @Test
    void stateIsRebuiltFromEventsWithOrWithoutSnapshots() {
        EventStore<Event> store = new EventStore<>();
        store.append("A", 0, List.of(new Opened("x")));
        var repo = new AccountRepository(store, 2);
        repo.execute("A", a -> a.deposit(100));
        repo.execute("A", a -> a.deposit(50));
        assertThat(repo.load("A").balance()).isEqualTo(150);
        assertThat(Account.replay(null, store.read("A", 0)).balance()).isEqualTo(150);
    }

    @Test
    void staleWriterIsRejected() {
        EventStore<Event> store = new EventStore<>();
        store.append("A", 0, List.of(new Opened("x")));
        store.append("A", 1, List.of(new Deposited(1)));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> store.append("A", 1, List.of(new Deposited(1))))
                .isInstanceOf(EventStore.ConcurrencyException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void upcasterConvertsRupeeStringsToPaise() {
        Map<String, Object> v1 = new java.util.LinkedHashMap<>(Map.of("type", "PriceSet", "version", 1, "price", "1.05"));
        assertThat(Upcaster.upcast(v1)).containsEntry("amountPaise", 105L).containsEntry("version", 2);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
// Axon Framework (reference): an event-sourced aggregate
@Aggregate
class AccountAggregate {
    @AggregateIdentifier String id;
    long balance;

    @CommandHandler
    void handle(WithdrawCommand cmd) {
        if (cmd.amount() > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        AggregateLifecycle.apply(new Withdrawn(cmd.accountId(), cmd.amount())); // stored + applied
    }

    @EventSourcingHandler
    void on(Withdrawn e) { balance -= e.amount(); }  // used for rehydration
}
Option Notes EventStoreDB (Kurrent) Purpose-built event store: streams, subscriptions, optimistic concurrency Axon Framework + Axon Server Java CQRS/ES framework with snapshots and sagas PostgreSQL table events(stream_id, version, type, payload, PRIMARY KEY(stream_id, version)): the unique key enforces concurrency Kafka Great for distributing events, but weak as the store for per-aggregate loads and optimistic concurrency Java records + sealed interfaces Ideal for events: immutable, exhaustive switch in apply

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Event sourcing Axon Framework @EventSourcingHandler, snapshots, upcasters EventStoreDB Streams with expected-version appends Git Commits are events; a checkout is a replay Database WAL / Kafka log compaction Log-first storage underneath many systems Accounting ledgers Double-entry bookkeeping is event sourcing on paper

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Complete audit trail by design Steep learning curve; unfamiliar to most teams Temporal queries and debugging by replay Event schema evolution is hard (events are forever) New read models from old data Queries need projections (CQRS) Natural fit with event-driven integration GDPR "right to be forgotten" in an immutable log needs crypto-shredding No lost updates (optimistic concurrency per stream) Replays can be slow without snapshots

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Event sourcing the whole system

Use it for aggregates where history matters (ledgers, orders, workflows), not for user profiles or reference data. Mixing styles per service is normal.

Using events as a message bus between services without contracts

Internal domain events (fine-grained, private) are different from integration events (public, stable). Publishing internal events couples other services to your internals.

Validating in apply

If rules change, old events would fail to replay. apply must accept every historical event; validate in command handlers.

Changing or deleting stored events

Fix mistakes with compensating events (DepositReversed). For schema changes, use upcasting (see the coding challenge) or copy-and-transform migrations.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Schema evolution strategies. Weak schemas (tolerant readers ignoring unknown fields), upcasters that convert old versions on read, versioned event types, or copy-transform migrations of whole streams. Keep events small and business-focused to limit change.

GDPR and immutability. Encrypt personal data in events with a per-subject key and delete the key on erasure (crypto-shredding), or keep PII out of events and reference it.

Snapshot policy. Snapshot every N events or when load time exceeds a threshold; snapshots are a cache, so they can be discarded and rebuilt after model changes.

When it pays off. Domains with inherent history (finance, logistics, compliance), complex workflows, or heavy analytics needs. When it doesn't: CRUD-heavy domains, small teams, tight deadlines.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Clear reason (audit, temporal queries, complex domain), scoped to specific aggregates.
  • Event store with per-stream optimistic concurrency (unique (stream, version)).
  • Snapshot policy; replay performance measured.
  • Versioned events + upcasters; tolerant readers.
  • Separate internal domain events from published integration events.
  • PII strategy (crypto-shredding); retention and archival plan.
  • Projections idempotent with checkpoints; rebuild procedure tested.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"For the wallet ledger I'd use event sourcing: each wallet is a stream of Credited/Debited/Reversed events in a PostgreSQL events table with a unique (wallet_id, version) constraint for optimistic concurrency. Commands load a snapshot plus recent events, check the balance rule and append. Events go to Kafka via the outbox and feed projections: balance, statements and fraud features. Corrections are new events, never updates. Snapshots every 100 events keep loads fast, upcasters handle schema changes, and personal data is encrypted per user for erasure."

War story: the event nobody could replay

A logistics company renamed a field in ParcelScanned and deployed. Old events still had the old field name; the next projection rebuild failed halfway through 400 million events, and the tracking page served stale data for 9 hours while engineers wrote an emergency upcaster. Fix: schema-compatibility checks in CI (every historical event version must deserialize), upcasters registered for every change, and a nightly replay of a sample of old streams. Lesson: in event sourcing, old events are part of your API forever. Test them like an API.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Event Sourcing CRUD + audit table Transactional Outbox Memento Source of truth Events Current state Current state Current state History Complete, by design Partial, can drift Published events only Explicit snapshots Temporal queries Natural Hard No Snapshots only

See CQRS (projections), Transactional Outbox, and the in-process Memento and Command patterns.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • State = replay of immutable events; snapshots for speed.
  • Commands validate → new events; apply never validates.
  • Optimistic concurrency per stream (expected version).
  • Corrections are new events; upcasters for schema changes.
  • Pair with CQRS projections for queries.

docs.text:
• Add a DepositReversed event and make the account handle it.
  • Add stateAt(version) to Account (replay only the first N events).
  • Write an upcaster chain v1 → v2 → v3 where v3 adds a region field defaulting to "IN".

docs.title: Idempotent Consumer
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Message brokers and clients deliver at-least-once, so the same message or request will arrive more than once. An idempotent consumer makes processing a duplicate harmless, typically by recording processed message IDs (or idempotency keys) in the same transaction as the side effect. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives an exactly-once effect.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a Kafka consumer credits ₹199 to a wallet and crashes before committing its offset; on restart it gets the message again and credits again. A mobile app's "Pay" request times out on a bad network; the app retries; the customer is charged twice. A courier app sends "out for delivery" twice; the customer gets two SMS. Duplicates are normal in distributed systems:

Source of duplicates Example Consumer crash/rebalance before offset commit Kafka redelivers the batch Producer retries Outbox relay republishes after a crash Client retries after a timeout The first request actually succeeded Upstream bugs Partner sends the same webhook twice

Definition (microservices.io):

Implement an idempotent consumer, which is a message consumer that can handle duplicate messages correctly.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A doorman with a guest list

Each guest's invitation has a number. When a guest arrives, the doorman ticks the number off. If someone arrives again with the same invitation (they stepped out and came back), the doorman sees the tick and doesn't hand them a second welcome gift.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    B[[Broker / client]] -->|message id=501| C[Consumer]
    C --> TX{{One local transaction}}
    TX --> P[(processed_messages<br/>PRIMARY KEY message_id)]
    TX --> S[(Business tables)]
    P -->|duplicate key| SKIP[Skip: already processed]
Technique How Processed-message table Insert message ID with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect Idempotency key (APIs) Client sends a unique key; server stores the response and replays it for retries Natural idempotency Design operations to be idempotent: "set status = SHIPPED" vs. "add 1" Version / sequence checks Apply only if the event's version is newer than the stored one TTL dedupe cache Remember keys for a window (Redis SET NX EX) when occasional duplicates are tolerable

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@KafkaListener(topics = "refunds")
void on(RefundIssued e) {
    if (!processedIds.contains(e.id())) {   // check...
        wallet.credit(e.customer(), e.amount());
        processedIds.add(e.id());           // ...then act, in memory, outside the DB transaction
    }
}
// Crash between credit and add → duplicate credit after restart.
// Two instances processing concurrently → both pass the check.

docs.title: Example 1: Wallet Credits with a Processed-Messages Table (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Refund messages credit a customer's wallet. Each message's ID is inserted into processed_messages (primary key) in the same JDBC transaction as the credit (real H2 database). A redelivered message violates the key, the transaction rolls back, and the duplicate is acknowledged without effect.

Full Code:

WalletCreditConsumer.javaWalletDedupeDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.wallet;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;

/**
 * Credits a wallet for each RefundIssued message. The message ID is inserted into
 * processed_messages in the SAME transaction as the credit; a duplicate violates the primary key,
 * the whole transaction rolls back, and the duplicate is acknowledged without effect.
 */
public final class WalletCreditConsumer {

    public static final String[] SCHEMA = {
            "CREATE TABLE wallets (customer VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, balance BIGINT)",
            "CREATE TABLE processed_messages (message_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, processed_at TIMESTAMP)" // (1)!
    };

    private final DataSource db;

    public WalletCreditConsumer(DataSource db) {
        this.db = db;
    }

    /** Returns true if the message had an effect, false if it was a duplicate. */
    public boolean onRefundIssued(String messageId, String customer, long paise) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = db.getConnection()) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (PreparedStatement dedupe = c.prepareStatement(
                    "INSERT INTO processed_messages VALUES (?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)");
                 PreparedStatement credit = c.prepareStatement(
                         "MERGE INTO wallets w USING (VALUES (?, ?)) v(c, amt) ON w.customer = v.c "
                                 + "WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET balance = balance + v.amt "
                                 + "WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (v.c, v.amt)")) {
                dedupe.setString(1, messageId);
                dedupe.executeUpdate(); // (2)!
                credit.setString(1, customer);
                credit.setLong(2, paise);
                credit.executeUpdate();
                c.commit(); // (3)!
                return true;
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                c.rollback();
                if ("23505".equals(e.getSQLState())) { // unique violation: already processed
                    return false;
                }
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. The unique constraint is the guard: the database enforces it even across instances and threads.
  2. Inserting the ID first means a duplicate fails before any business change.
  3. ID and effect commit together. A crash before commit means neither happened, so the redelivery is processed normally.
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.wallet;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class WalletDedupeDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        DataSource db = Db.inMemory("wallet", WalletCreditConsumer.SCHEMA);
        var consumer = new WalletCreditConsumer(db);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: refund messages credited to the wallet exactly once ===");
        String[][] deliveries = {
                {"msg-501", "CUST-42", "19900"},
                {"msg-502", "CUST-42", "4500"},
                {"msg-501", "CUST-42", "19900"}, // redelivered after a consumer rebalance
                {"msg-502", "CUST-42", "4500"},  // redelivered again
        };
        for (String[] d : deliveries) {
            boolean applied = consumer.onRefundIssued(d[0], d[1], Long.parseLong(d[2]));
            System.out.println(d[0] + " ₹" + Long.parseLong(d[2]) / 100 + " -> " + (applied ? "credited" : "duplicate, skipped"));
        }
        System.out.println("Wallet balance: ₹" + Db.count(db, "SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE customer = 'CUST-42'") / 100
                + " (expected ₹244)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: refund messages credited to the wallet exactly once ===
msg-501 ₹199 -> credited
msg-502 ₹45 -> credited
msg-501 ₹199 -> duplicate, skipped
msg-502 ₹45 -> duplicate, skipped
Wallet balance: ₹244 (expected ₹244)

Why this design:

  • Correct under crashes, rebalances and multiple instances.
  • Cheap: one extra insert per message; old IDs can be purged after the broker's redelivery window.

docs.title: Example 2: Idempotency-Key for a Transfer API (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The mobile app sends POST /transfers with an Idempotency-Key. The response is lost on a flaky network; the app retries with the same key and gets the same response (TX-1001), so only one transfer is executed. Reusing the key with a different amount is a client bug and returns 422.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant API as Transfer API
    participant S as Key store
    App->>API: POST /transfers (key-7f3a)
    API->>S: new key → execute → store response
    API--xApp: 201 (lost on network)
    App->>API: retry POST /transfers (key-7f3a)
    API->>S: key exists, same body → stored response
    API-->>App: 201 TX-1001 (no second transfer)

Full Code:

IdempotencyKeyStore.javaTransferApiDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Server side of the Idempotency-Key header (as used by payment APIs): the first request with a key
 * is executed and its response stored; retries with the same key get the stored response. Reusing a
 * key with a different request body is a client bug and is rejected.
 * Simplified for one thread: in production, first insert the key as IN_PROGRESS with a unique
 * constraint, so a concurrent retry gets 409 Conflict instead of executing the operation twice.
 */
public final class IdempotencyKeyStore {

    public record StoredResponse(String requestFingerprint, int status, String body) {
    }

    private final Map<String, StoredResponse> responses = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public StoredResponse execute(String key, String requestBody, Supplier<StoredResponse> operation) {
        String fingerprint = Integer.toHexString(requestBody.hashCode()); // (1)!
        StoredResponse previous = responses.get(key);
        if (previous != null) {
            if (!previous.requestFingerprint().equals(fingerprint)) {
                return new StoredResponse(fingerprint, 422, "Idempotency-Key reused with a different request"); // (2)!
            }
            return previous; // (3)!
        }
        StoredResponse fresh = operation.get();
        StoredResponse stored = new StoredResponse(fingerprint, fresh.status(), fresh.body());
        responses.put(key, stored);
        return stored;
    }
}
  1. A fingerprint of the request detects key reuse with a different body. Production code uses SHA-256 of the canonical body.
  2. Same key, different request: reject (422) rather than guessing.
  3. A retry gets the original response, including the original transfer ID.
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey;

import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey.IdempotencyKeyStore.StoredResponse;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class TransferApiDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var store = new IdempotencyKeyStore();
        AtomicInteger transfersExecuted = new AtomicInteger();

        System.out.println("=== Banking: POST /transfers with an Idempotency-Key ===");
        String body = "{from: A-100, to: B-200, amount: 5000}";
        StoredResponse first = store.execute("key-7f3a", body,
                () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "transfer TX-" + (1000 + transfersExecuted.incrementAndGet()) + " created"));
        System.out.println("1st attempt (response lost on a flaky mobile network): " + first.status() + " " + first.body());

        StoredResponse retry = store.execute("key-7f3a", body,
                () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "transfer TX-" + (1000 + transfersExecuted.incrementAndGet()) + " created"));
        System.out.println("App retries with the same key                          : " + retry.status() + " " + retry.body());

        StoredResponse misuse = store.execute("key-7f3a", "{from: A-100, to: B-200, amount: 9000}",
                () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "should not run"));
        System.out.println("Same key, different amount                             : " + misuse.status() + " " + misuse.body());
        System.out.println("Transfers actually executed: " + transfersExecuted.get());
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: POST /transfers with an Idempotency-Key ===
1st attempt (response lost on a flaky mobile network): 201 transfer TX-1001 created
App retries with the same key                          : 201 transfer TX-1001 created
Same key, different amount                             : 422 Idempotency-Key reused with a different request
Transfers actually executed: 1

Why idempotency keys here:

  • Clients can safely retry POSTs, which is essential on mobile networks.
  • Payment providers (Stripe, Adyen and others) expose exactly this contract.

docs.title: Example 3: Time-Window Dedupe for SMS (Food delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Status updates arrive from courier apps, sometimes twice within seconds. The notification service remembers orderId:status keys for 24 hours (Redis SET key 1 NX EX 86400), so customers get one SMS per status. Memory stays bounded because keys expire.

Full Code:

SmsDeduplicator.javaSmsDedupeDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.notifications;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Remembers recently sent notification keys for a limited time, like Redis
 * {@code SET key 1 NX EX 86400}. Memory stays bounded because old keys expire; duplicates arriving
 * later than the window are rare and, for notifications, acceptable.
 */
public final class SmsDeduplicator {

    private final Map<String, Instant> seen = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Duration window;
    private final Clock clock;

    public SmsDeduplicator(Duration window, Clock clock) {
        this.window = window;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    /** Atomically "set if absent": true means this key is new and the SMS should be sent. */
    public synchronized boolean firstTime(String dedupeKey) {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        seen.values().removeIf(expiry -> !now.isBefore(expiry)); // (1)!
        return seen.putIfAbsent(dedupeKey, now.plus(window)) == null; // (2)!
    }

    public synchronized int size() {
        return seen.size();
    }
}
  1. Expire old keys, so memory is bounded by traffic within the window.
  2. Set-if-absent is atomic, so concurrent duplicates can't both pass.
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.notifications;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;

public class SmsDedupeDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T07:00:00Z");
        var dedupe = new SmsDeduplicator(Duration.ofHours(24), clock);

        System.out.println("=== Food delivery: \"Your order is out for delivery\" SMS ===");
        send(dedupe, "ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(4));
        send(dedupe, "ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY"); // the courier app sent the status twice
        send(dedupe, "ORD-9:DELIVERED");
        send(dedupe, "ORD-10:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY");
        System.out.println("keys remembered: " + dedupe.size());
        clock.advance(Duration.ofHours(25));
        send(dedupe, "ORD-11:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY");
        System.out.println("keys remembered after 25 h: " + dedupe.size() + " (old keys expired)");
    }

    private static void send(SmsDeduplicator dedupe, String key) {
        System.out.println(key + " -> " + (dedupe.firstTime(key) ? "SMS sent" : "duplicate, not sent"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Food delivery: "Your order is out for delivery" SMS ===
ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> SMS sent
ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> duplicate, not sent
ORD-9:DELIVERED -> SMS sent
ORD-10:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> SMS sent
keys remembered: 3
ORD-11:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> SMS sent
keys remembered after 25 h: 1 (old keys expired)

Why a TTL window here:

  • A duplicate SMS a day later is unlikely and harmless; a permanent table of every notification key isn't worth it.
  • Choose the window from how late duplicates can realistically arrive.
Unit Tests: IdempotentConsumerTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey.IdempotencyKeyStore;
import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey.IdempotencyKeyStore.StoredResponse;
import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.wallet.WalletCreditConsumer;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import javax.sql.DataSource;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class IdempotentConsumerTest {

    @Test
    void duplicateMessageHasNoEffect() throws Exception {
        DataSource db = Db.inMemory("t_wallet", WalletCreditConsumer.SCHEMA);
        var consumer = new WalletCreditConsumer(db);
        assertThat(consumer.onRefundIssued("m1", "C", 100)).isTrue();
        assertThat(consumer.onRefundIssued("m1", "C", 100)).isFalse();
        assertThat(Db.count(db, "SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE customer = 'C'")).isEqualTo(100);
    }

    @Test
    void idempotencyKeyReturnsStoredResponse() {
        var store = new IdempotencyKeyStore();
        int[] runs = {0};
        StoredResponse a = store.execute("k", "body", () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "run " + ++runs[0]));
        StoredResponse b = store.execute("k", "body", () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "run " + ++runs[0]));
        assertThat(b.body()).isEqualTo(a.body());
        assertThat(store.execute("k", "other", () -> null).status()).isEqualTo(422);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
// Spring Kafka + JDBC (reference): the dedupe insert and the effect share @Transactional
@KafkaListener(topics = "payments.refunds", groupId = "wallet")
@Transactional
public void on(ConsumerRecord<String, String> record) {
    String messageId = new String(record.headers().lastHeader("message-id").value(), UTF_8);
    try {
        jdbc.update("INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id) VALUES (?)", messageId);
    } catch (DuplicateKeyException duplicate) {
        return;                                     // already processed: ack and move on
    }
    jdbc.update("UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + ? WHERE customer = ?", amount, customer);
}
Variation Notes Kafka exactly-once (EOS) Transactions across consume → produce within Kafka; doesn't cover external DB side effects Upsert by business key INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on (order_id, event_type) Version check UPDATE ... WHERE version < :eventVersion (see the replica in Database per Service) Transactional inbox Store incoming messages first, process from the inbox table

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Idempotency Stripe, Adyen, PayPal APIs Idempotency-Key headers on POST Spring Integration IdempotentReceiverInterceptor with a MetadataStore Apache Camel Idempotent Consumer EIP with JDBC/Redis repositories Kafka Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) prevents producer-side duplicates AWS Lambda Powertools Idempotency utility backed by DynamoDB

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Exactly-once effect on at-least-once infrastructure Extra storage and write per message Safe retries everywhere (clients, relays, consumers) Requires a stable message ID / key from producers Simple, database-enforced correctness Dedupe tables need retention/purging Enables aggressive retry policies TTL-based dedupe can miss very late duplicates

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Dedupe outside the transaction

Recording the ID in Redis and the effect in Postgres (or in memory) creates a crash window between them. Store the ID in the same database transaction as the effect, or make the effect itself idempotent.

Using the payload hash as the ID

Two legitimate refunds of ₹199 to the same customer have identical payloads. Use a producer-assigned unique ID.

Check-then-act in application code

if (!exists(id)) process() races between concurrent consumers. Let a unique constraint or atomic SET NX decide (see the coding challenge).

Idempotent handler, non-idempotent side calls

The handler dedupes, but it also calls an email API before the commit. On retry after a crash, the email is sent again. Move side effects to the outbox or make them idempotent too.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Exactly-once is a property of the whole pipeline. Producer: idempotent producer or outbox with stable IDs. Broker: at-least-once. Consumer: dedupe in the same transaction as effects; external calls with idempotency keys. Any non-idempotent link breaks the chain.

Retention. Keep processed IDs at least as long as duplicates can arrive: broker retention plus your maximum replay window. For replays of months of history, use version checks instead of ID tables.

API idempotency at scale. Store keys with status (IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED + response), scope them per client, expire after 24–72 h, and return 409 for concurrent in-progress requests with the same key.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every message has a unique, stable ID assigned by the producer.
  • Consumers insert the ID with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect.
  • POST APIs that create money movements accept Idempotency-Key; responses are stored and replayed.
  • Side effects (emails, partner calls) go through the outbox or carry idempotency keys.
  • Retention/purge policy for dedupe tables; metrics on duplicate rate.
  • Tests that deliver every message twice, and concurrently.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"I assume at-least-once delivery everywhere. Producers give every event a unique ID through the outbox. Each consumer, in the same database transaction as its side effect, inserts that ID into a processed_messages table with a primary key, so duplicates fail the insert and are skipped, even across instances. Client-facing POST endpoints that move money accept an Idempotency-Key; we store the response and replay it on retries, and reject reuse with a different body. Where possible, operations are naturally idempotent: set-state and versioned upserts instead of increments."

War story: the double payout

A gig-economy platform paid drivers via a Kafka consumer that called the bank's payout API and then committed offsets. A deploy restarted consumers mid-batch; 2,300 payouts were sent again. Drivers were happy; finance spent three weeks recovering the money. Fix: payouts recorded in a payouts table with a unique (driver_id, period) key before calling the bank; the bank call uses the payout ID as its idempotency key; the consumer skips periods already recorded. Lesson: "we'll commit the offset right after" is not a strategy. Make the effect idempotent.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Idempotent Consumer Transactional Outbox Kafka EOS Saga Side Consumer Producer Kafka-to-Kafka Workflow Solves Duplicate processing Lost/phantom events Duplicates within Kafka Cross-service consistency Combined as Outbox + idempotent consumer = exactly-once effect Saga steps must be idempotent

See Transactional Outbox, Saga and Retry / Timeout / Bulkhead.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Delivery is at-least-once; make effects idempotent.
  • Message ID + unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect.
  • APIs: Idempotency-Key, stored response, 422 on mismatch, 409 while in progress.
  • Prefer naturally idempotent operations (set state, versioned upserts).
  • Outbox (producer) + idempotent consumer = exactly-once effect.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add an IN_PROGRESS state to IdempotencyKeyStore and return 409 for concurrent requests with the same key.
  • Purge processed_messages rows older than 7 days in WalletCreditConsumer.
  • Rewrite the wallet credit as a naturally idempotent operation keyed by refund ID (a wallet_entries table).
