Capability negotiation. Example 3's maxLength() is a simple version of capability negotiation. In larger systems, implementors expose a capability set (Set<Feature>), and the abstraction degrades gracefully (no image support, so post a link).

Testing. Test the abstraction with a fake implementor (records calls) and test each implementor with a shared contract test (every renderer escapes special characters; every device clamps volume).

Bridge vs. Strategy, honestly. Structurally they're nearly identical (an object delegating to an interface). The difference is intent and scale: Strategy swaps an algorithm for one context; Bridge separates two whole hierarchies that both keep growing. In interviews, saying that clearly is worth more than a diagram.

War story: 54 notification classes

A fintech's notification module started with OtpSms and OtpEmail. Two years later it had 9 notification types × 6 channels = 54 classes, each with copied formatting and retry code. A WhatsApp channel meant 9 new classes; a retry bug had to be fixed 54 times (they found 51). Fix: split into Notification (abstraction: what to say, with refined types) and Channel (implementor: send, with capability flags like supportsRichText). 54 classes became 15; retries moved into a single channel decorator. Lesson: when class names are two nouns glued together (OtpSms, SalesCsv), look for a Bridge.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Bridge Strategy Adapter Abstract Factory Intent Let two hierarchies vary independently Swap one algorithm Make incompatible interfaces fit Create a family of matching objects When designed Up front Up front After the fact Up front Structure Abstraction has-a implementor; both sides subclassed Context has-a strategy Adapter has-a adaptee Factory creates products

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Two dimensions that vary independently become two hierarchies joined by a reference.
  • Fixes class explosion: M × N becomes M + N.
  • Abstraction = what (high level); implementor = how (primitives).
  • vs Strategy: two growing hierarchies vs. one swappable algorithm. vs Adapter: up front vs. after the fact.
  • Real life: JDBC, SLF4J, AWT peers, Handler + Formatter.
abstract class Report { protected final ReportRenderer renderer; String generate() { return renderer.render(title(), columns(), rows()); } }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a MarkdownRenderer and a PayrollReport; count how many classes you touched.
  • Add a Soundbar device that has no open(content) support, and design a capability check.
  • Add a supportsImages() capability to SocialPlatform and degrade ImagePost to a link when it's false.

Adapter Next: Composite

docs.title: Composite
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Structural Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Composite lets you build trees of objects and treat a single object and a whole group of objects in exactly the same way. Use it for part–whole hierarchies: bundles of products, departments of employees, roles of permissions, folders of files, UI components.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a shop sells products, but also bundles, and bundles can contain other bundles. The cart wants to ask "what's your price?" without caring whether it's holding a mouse or a "Home Office Combo" with a nested "Accessories Pack". Without Composite, every caller needs if (item instanceof Bundle) { loop... recurse... }.

Formal definition (GoF):

Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
An army's chain of command

A general orders "advance". The order goes to divisions, which pass it to brigades, then platoons, then individual soldiers. The general doesn't care whether "Division 3" is one person or ten thousand: they give the same order to a unit and the unit handles its own members.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Component {
        <<interface>>
        +operation()
    }
    class Leaf {
        +operation()
    }
    class Composite {
        -List~Component~ children
        +add(Component)
        +operation()
    }
    Component <|.. Leaf
    Component <|.. Composite
    Composite o--> "0..*" Component : children
Participant Responsibility Component The common interface (priceInr(), headcount(), grants()) Leaf An individual object with no children (Product, Employee, Permission) Composite Holds children (leaves or composites) and implements the operation by delegating to them and combining the results Client Works with Component only

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
int price(Object item) {
    if (item instanceof Product p) return p.getPrice();
    if (item instanceof Bundle b) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (Object child : b.getItems()) sum += price(child);   // recursion lives in the CLIENT
        return sum - sum * b.getDiscount() / 100;
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();
}
// ...and the same type checks again in describe(), weight(), taxCategory(), isInStock()...
  • Type checks and recursion in every client.
  • A new node type (gift card) means editing every one of those methods.

docs.title: Example 1: Nested Product Bundles (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: An electronics marketplace sells "Home Office Combo" bundles at 10% off, and a bundle can contain another bundle (an "Accessories Pack" at 5% off). Discounts apply at each level. Cart, checkout, invoices and recommendations all need the price of "an item" without special-casing bundles, and merchandisers create new bundles from the admin UI every week.

Design:

flowchart TB
    HO["+ Home Office Combo (10% off)"] --> L["- Laptop 14in"]
    HO --> AP["+ Accessories Pack (5% off)"]
    HO --> C["- Ergonomic Chair"]
    AP --> M["- Wireless Mouse"]
    AP --> K["- Mechanical Keyboard"]

Full Code:

Bundle.javaCatalogItem.javaProduct.javaBundleDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.composite.ecommerce;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Composite: contains products AND other bundles, and is priced the same way. */
public final class Bundle implements CatalogItem {

    private final String name;
    private final int discountPercent;
    private final List<CatalogItem> children = new ArrayList<>(); // (1)!

    public Bundle(String name, int discountPercent) {
        this.name = name;
        this.discountPercent = discountPercent;
    }

    public Bundle add(CatalogItem item) {
        children.add(item);
        return this;
    }

    @Override
    public String name() {
        return name;
    }

    @Override
    public int priceInr() {
        int sum = children.stream().mapToInt(CatalogItem::priceInr).sum(); // (2)!
        return sum - sum * discountPercent / 100;
    }

    @Override
    public String describe(String indent) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("%s+ %s (%d%% off): INR %,d".formatted(indent, name, discountPercent, priceInr()));
        children.forEach(c -> sb.append('\n').append(c.describe(indent + "    "))); // (3)!
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
  1. Children are typed as the component interface, so a bundle can hold products and bundles.
  2. The composite delegates to its children and combines their results. Recursion happens naturally: a child bundle computes its own discounted price first.
  3. Same idea for display: each level indents its children.
package com.handbook.structural.composite.ecommerce;

/** Component: products and bundles are both catalog items. */
public sealed interface CatalogItem permits Product, Bundle {

    String name();

    int priceInr();

    String describe(String indent);
}

package com.handbook.structural.composite.ecommerce;

/** Leaf. */
public record Product(String name, int priceInr) implements CatalogItem {

    @Override
    public String describe(String indent) {
        return "%s- %s: INR %,d".formatted(indent, name, priceInr);
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.composite.ecommerce;

import java.util.List;

public class BundleDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Nested Product Bundles ===");
        Bundle accessories = new Bundle("Accessories Pack", 5)
                .add(new Product("Wireless Mouse", 799))
                .add(new Product("Mechanical Keyboard", 1_499));

        Bundle homeOffice = new Bundle("Home Office Combo", 10)
                .add(new Product("Laptop 14in", 55_000))
                .add(accessories)
                .add(new Product("Ergonomic Chair", 8_999));

        System.out.println(homeOffice.describe(""));

        System.out.println("\nCart (client treats every item the same way):");
        List<CatalogItem> cart = List.of(homeOffice, new Product("USB-C Cable", 349));
        int total = 0;
        for (CatalogItem item : cart) {
            System.out.printf("  %-18s INR %,7d%n", item.name(), item.priceInr());
            total += item.priceInr();
        }
        System.out.printf("  %-18s INR %,7d%n", "TOTAL", total);
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Nested Product Bundles ===
+ Home Office Combo (10% off): INR 59,565
    - Laptop 14in: INR 55,000
    + Accessories Pack (5% off): INR 2,184
        - Wireless Mouse: INR 799
        - Mechanical Keyboard: INR 1,499
    - Ergonomic Chair: INR 8,999

Cart (client treats every item the same way):
  Home Office Combo  INR  59,565
  USB-C Cable        INR     349
  TOTAL              INR  59,914

The cart loop treats the 5-product bundle and the single cable identically.

Why Composite here:

  • Bundles are a part–whole tree of arbitrary depth.
  • Clients call priceInr() on anything. No instanceof, no recursion in client code.
  • sealed lists the node types, so the compiler knows every kind of CatalogItem.

docs.title: Example 2: Org Chart Cost Roll-up (HR SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: An HR and finance SaaS shows managers their org's headcount and annual salary cost, rolled up through any depth of departments and teams. Finance asks questions like "what share of Engineering's budget is the Payments team?". Re-orgs happen quarterly, so the tree is data, not code.

Design:

classDiagram
    class OrgUnit {
        <<sealed interface>>
        +name() String
        +headcount() int
        +annualCostInr() long
    }
    class Employee {
        <<record>>
        +salaryInr
    }
    class Department {
        -List~OrgUnit~ members
        +add(OrgUnit...)
    }
    OrgUnit <|.. Employee
    OrgUnit <|.. Department
    Department o--> OrgUnit

Full Code:

OrgUnit.javaOrgChartDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.composite.org;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Component + both implementations in one place, using a sealed interface. */
public sealed interface OrgUnit permits OrgUnit.Employee, OrgUnit.Department {

    String name();

    int headcount();

    long annualCostInr();

    record Employee(String name, String title, long salaryInr) implements OrgUnit {
        public int headcount() { return 1; }
        public long annualCostInr() { return salaryInr; }
    }

    final class Department implements OrgUnit {
        private final String name;
        private final List<OrgUnit> members = new ArrayList<>();

        public Department(String name) {
            this.name = name;
        }

        public Department add(OrgUnit... units) {
            members.addAll(List.of(units));
            return this;
        }

        public String name() { return name; }

        public int headcount() {
            return members.stream().mapToInt(OrgUnit::headcount).sum();
        }

        public long annualCostInr() {
            return members.stream().mapToLong(OrgUnit::annualCostInr).sum();
        }

        public List<OrgUnit> members() {
            return List.copyOf(members);
        }
    }

    /** Pattern matching over the sealed hierarchy: an alternative to a describe() method. */
    static void print(OrgUnit unit, String indent) {
        switch (unit) { // (1)!
            case Employee e -> System.out.printf("%s%s, %s%n", indent, e.name(), e.title());
            case Department d -> {
                System.out.printf("%s[%s] headcount=%d cost=INR %.1f lakh%n",
                        indent, d.name(), d.headcount(), d.annualCostInr() / 100_000.0);
                d.members().forEach(m -> print(m, indent + "  "));
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. With a sealed component, Java 21 pattern matching for switch can replace a polymorphic print() method. The switch is exhaustive with no default, so a new node type is a compile error here. Use methods for core behavior, and pattern matching for operations that don't belong on the nodes (rendering, export).
package com.handbook.structural.composite.org;

import com.handbook.structural.composite.org.OrgUnit.Department;
import com.handbook.structural.composite.org.OrgUnit.Employee;

public class OrgChartDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== HR SaaS: Org Chart Cost Roll-up ===");
        Department payments = new Department("Payments Team").add(
                new Employee("Neha", "Engineering Manager", 4_800_000),
                new Employee("Arjun", "Senior Engineer", 3_600_000),
                new Employee("Li", "Engineer", 2_400_000));
        Department search = new Department("Search Team").add(
                new Employee("Fatima", "Staff Engineer", 5_200_000),
                new Employee("Rohan", "Engineer", 2_300_000));
        Department engineering = new Department("Engineering").add(
                new Employee("Priya", "VP Engineering", 9_000_000), payments, search);

        OrgUnit.print(engineering, "");
        System.out.println("Budget check, Payments vs Engineering share: "
                + (100 * payments.annualCostInr() / engineering.annualCostInr()) + "%");
    }
}

Output:

=== HR SaaS: Org Chart Cost Roll-up ===
[Engineering] headcount=6 cost=INR 273.0 lakh
  Priya, VP Engineering
  [Payments Team] headcount=3 cost=INR 108.0 lakh
    Neha, Engineering Manager
    Arjun, Senior Engineer
    Li, Engineer
  [Search Team] headcount=2 cost=INR 75.0 lakh
    Fatima, Staff Engineer
    Rohan, Engineer
Budget check, Payments vs Engineering share: 39%

Why Composite here:

  • An org is a textbook part–whole hierarchy: a department contains employees and departments.
  • Roll-ups (headcount, cost) are written once and work at every level.
  • Records for leaves + a sealed interface keep the model small and safe.

docs.title: Example 3: Nested Roles and Permissions (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A core banking system controls who can do what. A Teller can view accounts, take deposits and make small withdrawals. A Branch Manager includes everything a Teller and a Loan Officer can do, plus large withdrawals and loan approvals. Security asks two questions: "can this user do X?" (checked on every request) and "list everything this role allows" (for audits). Roles must never include themselves through a chain, which would cause infinite recursion in production.

Design:

flowchart TB
    BM[Role: BranchManager] --> T[Role: Teller]
    BM --> LO[Role: LoanOfficer]
    BM --> P1([cash.withdraw.large])
    BM --> P2([loan.approve])
    T --> P3([account.view])
    T --> P4([cash.deposit])
    T --> P5([cash.withdraw.small])
    LO --> P6([account.view])
    LO --> P7([loan.create])

Full Code:

Role.javaAccessRight.javaPermission.javaAccessDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.composite.banking;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

/** Composite. Roles can include roles, e.g. BranchManager includes Teller. */
public final class Role implements AccessRight {

    private final String name;
    private final List<AccessRight> rights = new ArrayList<>();

    public Role(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public Role include(AccessRight right) {
        if (right == this || (right instanceof Role r && r.contains(this))) { // (1)!
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cycle: " + right.name() + " already includes " + name);
        }
        rights.add(right);
        return this;
    }

    private boolean contains(Role target) {
        return rights.stream().anyMatch(r -> r == target || (r instanceof Role role && role.contains(target)));
    }

    public String name() {
        return name;
    }

    public boolean grants(String permission) {
        return rights.stream().anyMatch(r -> r.grants(permission)); // (2)!
    }

    public void collect(Set<String> into) {
        rights.forEach(r -> r.collect(into));
    }
}
  1. Cycle protection. A tree must stay a tree. If Teller included BranchManager, which includes Teller, grants() would recurse forever. Reject cycles when the tree is built, not when it's used.
  2. anyMatch short-circuits: it stops at the first child that grants the permission.
package com.handbook.structural.composite.banking;

import java.util.Set;

/** Component: a single permission or a role made of permissions and other roles. */
public interface AccessRight {

    String name();

    boolean grants(String permission);

    void collect(Set<String> into);
}

package com.handbook.structural.composite.banking;

import java.util.Set;

/** Leaf. */
public record Permission(String name) implements AccessRight {

    public boolean grants(String permission) {
        return name.equals(permission);
    }

    public void collect(Set<String> into) {
        into.add(name);
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.composite.banking;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;

public class AccessDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Core Banking: Nested Roles ===");
        Role teller = new Role("Teller")
                .include(new Permission("account.view"))
                .include(new Permission("cash.deposit"))
                .include(new Permission("cash.withdraw.small"));
        Role loanOfficer = new Role("LoanOfficer")
                .include(new Permission("account.view"))
                .include(new Permission("loan.create"));
        Role branchManager = new Role("BranchManager")
                .include(teller)
                .include(loanOfficer)
                .include(new Permission("cash.withdraw.large"))
                .include(new Permission("loan.approve"));

        for (Role role : new Role[] {teller, branchManager}) {
            Set<String> all = new TreeSet<>();
            role.collect(all);
            System.out.println(role.name() + " -> " + all);
        }
        System.out.println("Teller can approve loans? " + teller.grants("loan.approve"));
        System.out.println("BranchManager can deposit cash (via Teller)? " + branchManager.grants("cash.deposit"));

        try {
            teller.include(branchManager);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Core Banking: Nested Roles ===
Teller -> [account.view, cash.deposit, cash.withdraw.small]
BranchManager -> [account.view, cash.deposit, cash.withdraw.large, cash.withdraw.small, loan.approve, loan.create]
Teller can approve loans? false
BranchManager can deposit cash (via Teller)? true
Rejected: Cycle: BranchManager already includes Teller

Why Composite here:

  • Roles contain permissions and roles: the same interface answers "does it grant X?" at any level.
  • Two different operations, search (grants) and collect (collect), both follow the tree naturally.
  • Shows the production concern most tutorials skip: cycles.
Unit Tests: CompositeTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.structural.composite;

import com.handbook.structural.composite.banking.Permission;
import com.handbook.structural.composite.banking.Role;
import com.handbook.structural.composite.ecommerce.Bundle;
import com.handbook.structural.composite.ecommerce.Product;
import com.handbook.structural.composite.filesystem.Node;
import com.handbook.structural.composite.org.OrgUnit;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class CompositeTest {

    @Test
    void bundlePriceAppliesDiscountsAtEachLevel() {
        Bundle inner = new Bundle("inner", 50).add(new Product("a", 100));
        Bundle outer = new Bundle("outer", 10).add(inner).add(new Product("b", 50));
        assertThat(inner.priceInr()).isEqualTo(50);
        assertThat(outer.priceInr()).isEqualTo(90);
    }

    @Test
    void emptyBundleCostsNothing() {
        assertThat(new Bundle("empty", 10).priceInr()).isZero();
    }

    @Test
    void departmentsRollUpHeadcountAndCost() {
        var team = new OrgUnit.Department("t").add(new OrgUnit.Employee("a", "x", 10), new OrgUnit.Employee("b", "y", 20));
        var org = new OrgUnit.Department("o").add(team, new OrgUnit.Employee("c", "z", 5));
        assertThat(org.headcount()).isEqualTo(3);
        assertThat(org.annualCostInr()).isEqualTo(35);
    }

    @Test
    void rolesInheritNestedPermissionsAndRejectCycles() {
        Role a = new Role("A").include(new Permission("p1"));
        Role b = new Role("B").include(a);
        Role c = new Role("C").include(b);
        assertThat(c.grants("p1")).isTrue();
        assertThat(c.grants("p2")).isFalse();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> a.include(c)).hasMessageContaining("Cycle");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> a.include(a)).hasMessageContaining("Cycle");
    }

    @Test
    void folderSizeIsSumOfDescendants() {
        var root = new Node.Folder("r", new Node.File("a", 1), new Node.Folder("s", new Node.File("b", 2)));
        assertThat(root.sizeBytes()).isEqualTo(3);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Where do add/remove live? (Transparency vs. safety)

Option Pros Cons On the Component (GoF "transparent") Clients treat everything the same, even for building Leaves must throw on add(), which fails at runtime On the Composite only ("safe"), as in all examples here Compiler stops you adding children to a leaf Builders must know they hold a composite

Modern Java leans to safe: sealed interfaces + records for leaves + pattern matching where needed.

Other variations:

  • Parent references for walking upward (breadcrumbs, "which department is this person in?"). Keep them consistent when moving nodes.
  • Caching expensive aggregates (cost of a huge org) and invalidating up the tree on change.
  • Iteration with an external iterator (depth-first, breadth-first) or a Visitor for many different operations over the same tree.
  • Immutable trees built with builders, safe to share between threads.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Composite Leaf JDK AWT/Swing Container (JPanel, JFrame) JButton, JLabel JavaFX Parent / Group Node leaves (Text, Shape) DOM / XML Element with child Nodes Text nodes JDK NIO Directories in Files.walk() Regular files Spring CompositeCacheManager, CompositePropertySource, CompositeHealthContributor (Actuator) Individual managers, sources, health indicators Spring Security Role hierarchies (RoleHierarchyImpl: ROLE_ADMIN > ROLE_USER) Authorities JUnit 5 Test containers (classes, @Nested) Test methods

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Clients treat single items and groups uniformly Hard to restrict what a composite can contain (a "Bundle that only contains electronics") with types alone New node types without changing clients (OCP) Generic interfaces can be too general for some leaves Recursive operations are natural and short Deep trees can mean deep recursion (stack overflow) and slow roll-ups Matches how the domain is described ("contains") Cycles, if you allow arbitrary graphs

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Cycles

A node that (indirectly) contains itself makes recursive operations loop forever. Validate on insert (Example 3) or detect with a visited set.

Very deep trees and recursion

A user-built hierarchy 10,000 levels deep can overflow the stack. Limit depth, or use an explicit stack (iterative traversal) for operations on untrusted trees.

Expensive roll-ups on every call

Recomputing the cost of a 50,000-person org on every page view is slow. Cache aggregates per node and invalidate on change, or pre-compute in the database (materialized path, closure tables).

Forcing a hierarchy that isn't one

If items can belong to several parents (a product in many bundles is fine; a department reporting to two VPs isn't a tree), you have a graph. Model it as one.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Trees in databases. Composites in memory usually come from relational or document stores. Know the options: adjacency list (parent_id, simple, recursive CTE queries), materialized path (/1/4/9/, fast subtree reads), nested sets (fast reads, slow writes), closure table (all ancestor–descendant pairs, flexible and fast, more storage). Interviewers at product companies love this follow-up.

Authorization at scale. Example 3 is a mini RBAC. Real systems flatten role trees into effective permission sets (cached per user, invalidated on role change) because grants() runs on every request. Some move to relationship-based access control (Google Zanzibar style: OpenFGA, SpiceDB), which generalizes the tree to a graph.

Composite + Visitor + Iterator. When many unrelated operations run over the same stable tree (price, tax, export to PDF, validate), put the operations in visitors instead of growing the component interface. Java 21's sealed + pattern matching is often a lighter alternative to a classic Visitor (Example 2).

Concurrency. Shared, mutable trees need care: copy-on-write subtrees, or build immutable trees and swap the root atomically (AtomicReference<Node>).

War story: the role that included itself

An admin UI let customers build custom roles from other roles. One enterprise customer created "Ops" including "Support", then edited "Support" to include "Ops". The next login evaluated permissions recursively, hit a StackOverflowError, and the error was cached as "no permissions". Every user in that tenant was locked out on a Monday morning. Fix: cycle detection on save (with a clear error in the UI), an iterative permission resolver with a visited set as defence in depth, and effective-permission caching that never caches failures. Lesson: any tree editable by users is a graph until you prove otherwise.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Composite Decorator Chain of Responsibility Visitor Shape Tree: many children Chain: one wrapped object Chain of handlers Operation over a structure Purpose Treat parts and wholes alike Add behavior Pass a request until handled Add operations without changing nodes Combines results? Yes (sum, any, all) Wraps one result Usually one handler answers Accumulates in the visitor

Often used with: Iterator (traverse the tree), Visitor (operations on the tree), Builder (assemble trees), Flyweight (share identical leaves), Chain of Responsibility (events bubbling up parent links, as in UI frameworks).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Tree of parts and wholes; leaves and composites share one interface.
  • The composite delegates to its children and combines results (sum, any, all).
  • Safe vs. transparent: put add() on the composite only (modern preference).
  • Watch for cycles, deep recursion and slow roll-ups.
  • Real life: Swing Container, DOM, file systems, Spring Composite* classes, role hierarchies.
int priceInr() { int sum = children.stream().mapToInt(CatalogItem::priceInr).sum(); return sum - sum * discount / 100; }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a weightGrams() operation to the catalog and see how many classes change.
  • Rewrite Role.grants iteratively with a stack and a visited set.
  • Add a parent reference to OrgUnit.Department and print an employee's reporting chain.
  • Add a GiftCard leaf type to CatalogItem and follow the compiler errors.

Bridge Next: Decorator

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Structural Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Decorator wraps an object in another object with the same interface, adding behavior before or after delegating to it. Wrappers can be stacked. Use it to add cross-cutting features (logging, retries, caching, encryption, pricing rules) without subclassing and without touching the original class.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a payment processor needs logging, retries and fraud checks, but not always all of them, and not always in the same order. Subclassing gives you LoggingRetryingFraudCheckedProcessor, LoggingProcessor, RetryingFraudCheckedProcessor... one subclass per combination. With decorators you write each feature once and compose them at runtime.

Formal definition (GoF):

Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators provide a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Dressing for the weather

You're still you. On a cold day you put on a sweater, then a jacket, then a raincoat. Each layer adds something (warmth, wind protection, waterproofing) and you can add or remove layers in any combination. Nobody needs to manufacture a "you-with-sweater-and-raincoat" person.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Component {
        <<interface>>
        +operation()
    }
    class ConcreteComponent {
        +operation()
    }
    class Decorator {
        <<abstract>>
        #Component inner
        +operation()
    }
    class DecoratorA {
        +operation()
    }
    class DecoratorB {
        +operation()
    }
    Component <|.. ConcreteComponent
    Component <|.. Decorator
    Decorator o--> Component : wraps
    Decorator <|-- DecoratorA
    Decorator <|-- DecoratorB
Participant Responsibility Component The interface clients use (PaymentProcessor) Concrete component The real work (FlakyGatewayProcessor) Decorator Implements Component and holds a Component; forwards by default Concrete decorators Add behavior before/after forwarding, or instead of it (RetryingProcessor, FraudCheckProcessor)

The key trick: a decorator is-a Component and has-a Component, so decorators can wrap decorators.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
class PaymentProcessor { String pay(...) { /* gateway call */ } }
class LoggingPaymentProcessor extends PaymentProcessor { ... }
class RetryingPaymentProcessor extends PaymentProcessor { ... }
class LoggingRetryingPaymentProcessor extends RetryingPaymentProcessor { ... }       // logging copied
class FraudLoggingRetryingPaymentProcessor extends LoggingRetryingPaymentProcessor { ... }
// 3 features = up to 7 subclasses; a 4th feature doubles it. Order is fixed at compile time.
  • Subclass explosion (2ⁿ combinations).
  • Fixed at compile time: can't turn retries on for one merchant only.
  • Code duplication of each feature across subclasses.

docs.title: Example 1: Stacking Payment Concerns (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment gateway call sometimes times out under load. The payments team wants fraud screening (block orders above a limit before calling the gateway at all), retries (up to 3 attempts on timeouts), and logging of every attempt for incident analysis. Different merchants get different stacks (some have no fraud rule), so the composition must be decided at runtime, from configuration.

Design:

flowchart LR
    C[Checkout] --> F[FraudCheckProcessor<br/>limit INR 50,000]
    F --> R[RetryingProcessor<br/>3 attempts]
    R --> L[LoggingProcessor]
    L --> G[FlakyGatewayProcessor<br/>real gateway call]

Full Code:

PaymentDecorator.javaFraudCheckProcessor.javaRetryingProcessor.javaLoggingProcessor.javaComponentPaymentsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments;

/** Base decorator: implements the interface and forwards to the wrapped processor. */
public abstract class PaymentDecorator implements PaymentProcessor {

    protected final PaymentProcessor inner; // (1)!

    protected PaymentDecorator(PaymentProcessor inner) {
        this.inner = inner;
    }

    @Override
    public String pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        return inner.pay(orderId, amountInr);
    }
}
  1. The decorator implements the interface and holds an instance of it. Because the field's type is the interface, it can hold the real processor or another decorator.
package com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments;

public class FraudCheckProcessor extends PaymentDecorator {

    private final int limitInr;

    public FraudCheckProcessor(PaymentProcessor inner, int limitInr) {
        super(inner);
        this.limitInr = limitInr;
    }

    @Override
    public String pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        if (amountInr > limitInr) {
            return "BLOCKED " + orderId + " (fraud rule: amount > INR " + limitInr + ")"; // (1)!
        }
        return super.pay(orderId, amountInr);
    }
}
  1. A decorator can short-circuit: it answers without calling inner at all. That's why fraud screening sits outermost: blocked orders never reach the gateway.
package com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments;

public class RetryingProcessor extends PaymentDecorator {

    private final int maxAttempts;

    public RetryingProcessor(PaymentProcessor inner, int maxAttempts) {
        super(inner);
        this.maxAttempts = maxAttempts;
    }

    @Override
    public String pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                return super.pay(orderId, amountInr);
            } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                if (attempt == maxAttempts) {
                    throw e;
                }
                System.out.println("  [retry] attempt " + attempt + " failed (" + e.getMessage() + "), retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments;

public class LoggingProcessor extends PaymentDecorator {

    public LoggingProcessor(PaymentProcessor inner) {
        super(inner);
    }

    @Override
    public String pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        System.out.println("  [log] -> pay " + orderId + " INR " + amountInr);
        try {
            String result = super.pay(orderId, amountInr);
            System.out.println("  [log] <- " + result);
            return result;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("  [log] <- FAILED: " + e.getMessage());
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments;

public interface PaymentProcessor {

    String pay(String orderId, int amountInr);
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments;

/** Concrete component: the real gateway call. Fails the first N attempts to simulate timeouts. */
public class FlakyGatewayProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {

    private int failuresLeft;

    public FlakyGatewayProcessor(int failuresBeforeSuccess) {
        this.failuresLeft = failuresBeforeSuccess;
    }

    @Override
    public String pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        if (failuresLeft-- > 0) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("gateway timeout");
        }
        return "PAID " + orderId;
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments;

public class PaymentsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Stacking Cross-Cutting Concerns ===");

        PaymentProcessor processor =
                new FraudCheckProcessor(                // outermost: cheapest check first
                        new RetryingProcessor(
                                new LoggingProcessor(   // logs every attempt
                                        new FlakyGatewayProcessor(2)),
                                3),
                        50_000);

        System.out.println("Order 1:");
        System.out.println("Result: " + processor.pay("ORD-1", 1_200));
        System.out.println("Order 2:");
        System.out.println("Result: " + processor.pay("ORD-2", 75_000));
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Stacking Cross-Cutting Concerns ===
Order 1:
  [log] -> pay ORD-1 INR 1200
  [log] <- FAILED: gateway timeout
  [retry] attempt 1 failed (gateway timeout), retrying
  [log] -> pay ORD-1 INR 1200
  [log] <- FAILED: gateway timeout
  [retry] attempt 2 failed (gateway timeout), retrying
  [log] -> pay ORD-1 INR 1200
  [log] <- PAID ORD-1
Result: PAID ORD-1
Order 2:
Result: BLOCKED ORD-2 (fraud rule: amount > INR 50000)

Because logging sits inside the retry decorator, every attempt is logged. Put it outside and you'd see one log line per order. Order is a design decision.

Why Decorator here:

  • Each concern is one small class, testable on its own.
  • Stacks are composed at runtime, per merchant, from config.
  • The checkout code sees only PaymentProcessor; it doesn't know what's stacked.

docs.title: Example 2: Patient Record Storage Pipeline (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital stores ECG traces and clinical notes in object storage. Regulations require encryption at rest and an audit trail of every read and write; ECG traces are long and repetitive, so compression cuts storage cost. Some record types (small notes) skip compression; test environments skip encryption. Each concern must be pluggable, and the order matters: compress before encrypting, because encrypted data looks random and doesn't compress.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as Doctor app
    participant A as AuditingStore
    participant C as CompressingStore
    participant E as EncryptingStore
    participant S as Storage
    D->>A: write("P-1001/ecg", 93 chars)
    A->>A: audit "dr.mehta WRITE"
    A->>C: write(...)
    C->>C: run-length encode
    C->>E: write(compressed)
    E->>E: encrypt + Base64
    E->>S: write(44 chars)

Full Code:

CompressingStore.javaEncryptingStore.javaAuditingStore.javaComponentRecordsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare;

import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** Decorator: run-length encoding, e.g. "AAAB" <-> "3A1B". Real code would use GZIP. */
public class CompressingStore implements RecordStore {

    private static final Pattern RUN = Pattern.compile("(\\d+)(\\D)");
    private final RecordStore inner;

    public CompressingStore(RecordStore inner) {
        this.inner = inner;
    }

    @Override
    public void write(String key, String data) {
        if (data.chars().anyMatch(Character::isDigit)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("demo RLE does not support digits");
        }
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < data.length(); ) {
            int j = i;
            while (j < data.length() && data.charAt(j) == data.charAt(i)) {
                j++;
            }
            out.append(j - i).append(data.charAt(i));
            i = j;
        }
        inner.write(key, out.toString());
    }

    @Override
    public String read(String key) {
        Matcher m = RUN.matcher(inner.read(key));
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        while (m.find()) {
            out.append(m.group(2).repeat(Integer.parseInt(m.group(1))));
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Base64;

/** Decorator: toy XOR cipher + Base64 to keep the demo readable. Use AES-GCM in real systems. */
public class EncryptingStore implements RecordStore {

    private final RecordStore inner;
    private final byte[] key;

    public EncryptingStore(RecordStore inner, String key) {
        this.inner = inner;
        this.key = key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }

    @Override
    public void write(String id, String data) {
        inner.write(id, Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(xor(data.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))));
    }

    @Override
    public String read(String id) {
        return new String(xor(Base64.getDecoder().decode(inner.read(id))), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }

    private byte[] xor(byte[] in) {
        byte[] out = new byte[in.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < in.length; i++) {
            out[i] = (byte) (in[i] ^ key[i % key.length]);
        }
        return out;
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Decorator: records who touched which record, then delegates. */
public class AuditingStore implements RecordStore {

    private final RecordStore inner;
    private final String user;
    private final List<String> auditLog;

    public AuditingStore(RecordStore inner, String user, List<String> auditLog) {
        this.inner = inner;
        this.user = user;
        this.auditLog = auditLog;
    }

    public void write(String key, String data) {
        auditLog.add(user + " WRITE " + key);
        inner.write(key, data);
    }

    public String read(String key) {
        auditLog.add(user + " READ " + key);
        return inner.read(key);
    }

    public static List<String> newLog() {
        return new ArrayList<>();
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare;

public interface RecordStore {

    void write(String key, String data);

    String read(String key);
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Concrete component: stores exactly what it is given (think: object storage). */
public class InMemoryRecordStore implements RecordStore {

    private final Map<String, String> data = new HashMap<>();

    public void write(String key, String value) { data.put(key, value); }

    public String read(String key) { return data.get(key); }

    public String raw(String key) { return data.get(key); }
}

package com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare;

import java.util.List;

public class RecordsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Healthcare: Patient Record Storage Pipeline ===");
        InMemoryRecordStore disk = new InMemoryRecordStore();
        List<String> audit = AuditingStore.newLog();

        // audit -> compress -> encrypt -> disk  (compress BEFORE encrypt: encrypted data does not compress)
        RecordStore store = new AuditingStore(
                new CompressingStore(new EncryptingStore(disk, "k3y")), "dr.mehta", audit);

        String ecg = "ECG:" + "N".repeat(40) + "V" + "N".repeat(40) + ";BP:high"; // long runs, like real traces
        store.write("P-1001/ecg", ecg);

        System.out.println("Original      (" + ecg.length() + " chars): " + ecg);
        System.out.println("Stored on disk(" + disk.raw("P-1001/ecg").length() + " chars): " + disk.raw("P-1001/ecg"));
        System.out.println("Read back     : " + store.read("P-1001/ecg"));
        System.out.println("Round trip OK : " + ecg.equals(store.read("P-1001/ecg")));
        System.out.println("Audit log     : " + audit);
    }
}

Output:

=== Healthcare: Patient Record Storage Pipeline ===
Original      (93 chars): ECG:NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNVNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN;BP:high
Stored on disk(44 chars): WnZIKAI+WglNW31IPQdJJQJCWnFIOwJDWltIAgIeWls=
Read back     : ECG:NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNVNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN;BP:high
Round trip OK : true
Audit log     : [dr.mehta WRITE P-1001/ecg, dr.mehta READ P-1001/ecg, dr.mehta READ P-1001/ecg]

Toy algorithms on purpose

The run-length encoding and XOR cipher keep the output readable. In production use GZIPOutputStream (or Zstandard) and AES-GCM via javax.crypto with keys from a KMS. The structure stays exactly the same.

Why Decorator here:

  • This is exactly how java.io works: new GZIPOutputStream(new CipherOutputStream(new FileOutputStream(...))).
  • Each concern is a separate, certifiable unit, which auditors like.
  • Bidirectional decorators: write transforms on the way in, read reverses on the way out, in mirror order.

docs.title: Example 3: Pricing Rules (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery app applies a member discount (10%), a festival offer (INR 100 off above INR 500) and GST (5%). Marketing changes the active rules weekly. Finance has one firm requirement: GST is charged on the discounted price. In an earlier version someone applied rules in the wrong order, and customers were charged INR 5 too much per order. Here each rule is a functional decorator built with Java default methods.

Design:

flowchart LR
    S["Subtotal<br/>INR 1000"] --> M["Member -10%<br/>INR 900"] --> F["Festival -INR 100<br/>INR 800"] --> G["GST +5%<br/>INR 840"]

Full Code:

PriceCalculator.javaPricingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.decorator.pricing;

/** Component. Amounts in paise to avoid floating-point money. */
@FunctionalInterface
public interface PriceCalculator {

    long price(long subtotalPaise);

    static PriceCalculator base() {
        return subtotal -> subtotal;
    }

    // ---- decorators as small functions that wrap another calculator ----

    default PriceCalculator thenMemberDiscount(int percent) { // (1)!
        return subtotal -> {
            long p = price(subtotal);
            return p - p * percent / 100;
        };
    }

    default PriceCalculator thenFlatOff(long paiseOff, long minimumPaise) {
        return subtotal -> {
            long p = price(subtotal);
            return p >= minimumPaise ? p - paiseOff : p;
        };
    }

    default PriceCalculator thenGst(int percent) {
        return subtotal -> {
            long p = price(subtotal);
            return p + Math.round(p * percent / 100.0);
        };
    }
}
  1. Each then... default method returns a new calculator that wraps this: it calls the current pipeline, then applies its rule. That's a decorator written as a lambda, the functional-programming form of the pattern.
package com.handbook.structural.decorator.pricing;

public class PricingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Pricing Rules as Decorators ===");
        long cart = 1_000_00; // INR 1000.00

        PriceCalculator correct = PriceCalculator.base()
                .thenMemberDiscount(10)        // INR 1000 -> 900
                .thenFlatOff(100_00, 500_00)   // festival: INR 100 off above INR 500 -> 800
                .thenGst(5);                   // tax on the discounted price -> 840

        PriceCalculator wrongOrder = PriceCalculator.base()
                .thenGst(5)                    // tax first -> 1050
                .thenMemberDiscount(10)        // -> 945
                .thenFlatOff(100_00, 500_00);  // -> 845

        PriceCalculator plain = PriceCalculator.base().thenGst(5);

        System.out.println("No offers           : INR " + inr(plain.price(cart)));
        System.out.println("Discounts, then GST : INR " + inr(correct.price(cart)));
        System.out.println("GST, then discounts : INR " + inr(wrongOrder.price(cart)) + "  <- same rules, different order");
    }

    private static String inr(long paise) {
        return "%d.%02d".formatted(paise / 100, paise % 100);
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Pricing Rules as Decorators ===
No offers           : INR 1050.00
Discounts, then GST : INR 840.00
GST, then discounts : INR 845.00  <- same rules, different order

Why Decorator here:

  • Rules are independent, stackable, and reorderable, and the order changes the result.
  • Functional decorators (lambdas + default methods) remove the class boilerplate entirely.
  • New rules (a bank-card offer) are one method; existing rules don't change.
Unit Tests: DecoratorTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.structural.decorator;

import com.handbook.structural.decorator.caching.CachingCatalog;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare.CompressingStore;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare.EncryptingStore;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare.InMemoryRecordStore;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.healthcare.RecordStore;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments.FlakyGatewayProcessor;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments.FraudCheckProcessor;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.payments.RetryingProcessor;
import com.handbook.structural.decorator.pricing.PriceCalculator;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class DecoratorTest {

    @Test
    void retrySucceedsWithinLimitAndGivesUpAfter() {
        assertThat(new RetryingProcessor(new FlakyGatewayProcessor(2), 3).pay("O", 1)).isEqualTo("PAID O");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> new RetryingProcessor(new FlakyGatewayProcessor(5), 3).pay("O", 1))
                .hasMessage("gateway timeout");
    }

    @Test
    void fraudCheckShortCircuitsBeforeTheGateway() {
        var neverCalled = new FlakyGatewayProcessor(Integer.MAX_VALUE);
        assertThat(new FraudCheckProcessor(neverCalled, 100).pay("O", 500)).startsWith("BLOCKED");
    }

    @Test
    void storeDecoratorsRoundTripInEitherOrder() {
        String data = "AAAABBBCCD;x";
        RecordStore a = new CompressingStore(new EncryptingStore(new InMemoryRecordStore(), "k"));
        RecordStore b = new EncryptingStore(new CompressingStore(new InMemoryRecordStore()), "k");
        a.write("1", data);
        assertThat(a.read("1")).isEqualTo(data);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> b.write("1", data)) // encrypted Base64 may contain digits
                .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void pricingOrderMatters() {
        long discountFirst = PriceCalculator.base().thenMemberDiscount(10).thenGst(5).price(10_000);
        long taxFirst = PriceCalculator.base().thenGst(5).thenMemberDiscount(10).price(10_000);
        assertThat(discountFirst).isEqualTo(9_450);
        assertThat(taxFirst).isEqualTo(9_450); // percentages commute...
        long flatThenTax = PriceCalculator.base().thenFlatOff(1_000, 0).thenGst(5).price(10_000);
        long taxThenFlat = PriceCalculator.base().thenGst(5).thenFlatOff(1_000, 0).price(10_000);
        assertThat(flatThenTax).isNotEqualTo(taxThenFlat); // ...flat amounts do not
    }

    @Test
    void cachingCallsTheSourceOncePerKey() {
        AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
        CachingCatalog c = new CachingCatalog(sku -> sku + calls.incrementAndGet());
        c.describe("a");
        c.describe("a");
        assertThat(calls).hasValue(1);
        assertThat(c.stats()).isEqualTo("hits=1 misses=1");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Form Example Classic class-based with an abstract base decorator Example 1 Direct implementation (no base class) Example 2: each decorator implements the interface and holds a field Functional (lambdas, Function.andThen, default methods) Example 3; also UnaryOperator<String> pipeline = trim.andThen(lower) Dynamic proxies / AOP Spring @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Retryable: decorators generated at runtime Resilience4j Decorators.ofSupplier(call).withRetry(..).withCircuitBreaker(..).withBulkhead(..).decorate()

Decorators and Spring. Spring AOP proxies are decorators: @Transactional wraps your bean with "begin, call, commit or roll back". You can also write decorators manually with @Primary beans that take the original bean as a constructor argument.

Equality and identity. A decorated object is a different object. decorated.equals(original) is usually false, and instanceof ConcreteComponent fails on the wrapper. Don't rely on concrete types once you decorate.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example java.io BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream, GZIPInputStream, CipherInputStream all wrap an InputStream; same for readers and writers JDK collections Collections.unmodifiableList, synchronizedMap, checkedList wrap collections Servlet API HttpServletRequestWrapper, HttpServletResponseWrapper Spring TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy, LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy; BeanPostProcessors that wrap beans; AOP proxies Spring Session Wraps HttpSession Resilience4j / Micrometer Retry, circuit breaker, timer decorators around calls Caffeine / Spring Cache @Cacheable and cache-loading wrappers

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Add behavior without modifying the class (OCP) Many small objects; stack traces get deep Combine features at runtime in any order Order matters and is easy to get wrong Each concern in one class (SRP), testable on its own Removing a decorator from the middle of a stack is awkward Avoids 2ⁿ subclasses Identity and instanceof checks break on wrapped objects Big interfaces mean every decorator must forward every method (use a base class)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Wrong order

Encrypt-then-compress (no compression), retry-outside-circuit-breaker (retries hammer an open circuit), tax-before-discount (wrong prices). Write down the intended order and test it (see pricingOrderMatters).

Retrying non-idempotent operations

A retry decorator around "charge card" can double-charge. Retry only idempotent calls, or send an idempotency key.

Forgetting to forward some methods

In interfaces with many methods, a decorator that only overrides one and forgets the others breaks behavior silently. Extend a forwarding base class that delegates everything.

Decorators with hidden state

A caching decorator that never evicts is a memory leak; a retry decorator with a shared counter isn't thread-safe. Decorators are real components; give them the same care.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Resilience stacks are decorator stacks, and the order is documented. Resilience4j's recommended order (outermost to innermost) is roughly: Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( call ) ) ) ) ). Reasoning: retries should see the circuit breaker's "open" error and stop; time limits apply per attempt; the bulkhead limits concurrent calls. Be ready to defend whichever order you choose.

Decorators vs. AOP vs. middleware. All three wrap behavior around calls. Use explicit decorators when the composition is part of the domain (pricing rules) or changes per tenant; use AOP for uniform infrastructure (transactions, metrics) across many beans; use middleware/filters (servlet filters, gateway filters) at process or network boundaries.

Observability. With deep stacks, name each layer in logs and metrics (payment.retry.attempts, payment.fraud.blocked) so you can tell which layer acted.

Performance. Each layer is a virtual call; the JIT usually inlines small, monomorphic stacks. Deep or megamorphic stacks (many decorator types at one call site) can hurt hot paths. Measure before collapsing layers.

War story: the retry that DDoS'ed our own database

A team added a retry decorator (5 attempts, no backoff) around a repository call, then a second team added a retry decorator at the service layer (3 attempts), and an HTTP client retried too (3 attempts). When the database slowed down, each user request turned into up to 45 queries. The slowdown became an outage. Fix: one retry layer only (at the edge), exponential backoff with jitter, a retry budget, and a circuit breaker inside the retry so retries stop when the database is clearly down. Lesson: decorators compose multiplicatively. Draw the whole stack before adding a layer.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Decorator Proxy Adapter Composite Chain of Responsibility Interface Same as wrapped Same as subject Different Same as children Same handler interface Purpose Add behavior Control access (lazy, remote, security, cache) Make it fit Part-whole trees Pass the request along until handled Who creates the wrapper? The client composes stacks Usually the framework or factory, hidden from the client Integration code Tree builder Pipeline setup Calls the inner object? Almost always Maybe (may deny or defer) Always (translated) Calls all children Handlers may stop the chain

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Wrap an object with the same interface to add behavior; wrappers can be stacked.
  • Is-a and has-a the component, so decorators wrap decorators.
  • Order matters: compress then encrypt; discounts then tax; think about where retries sit.
  • Java I/O is the classic example; Spring AOP and Resilience4j are the modern ones.
  • vs Proxy: add behavior vs. control access.
PaymentProcessor p = new FraudCheck(new Retrying(new Logging(new Gateway()), 3), 50_000);

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a MetricsProcessor that counts successes and failures, and decide where it belongs in the stack.
  • Replace the toy cipher in EncryptingStore with AES-GCM from javax.crypto.
  • Add a bank-card offer (thenCardCashback) to PriceCalculator with a maximum cashback.
  • Add TTL-based expiry to CachingCatalog using an injectable Clock.

Composite Next: Facade

docs.title: Facade
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner Structural Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Facade gives a simple, high-level interface to a complex set of classes or services. Use it when clients need to do one thing ("place order", "start playback", "open account") that takes many steps across many subsystems.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: placing a grocery order means reserving stock, charging the card, booking a delivery slot and notifying the customer, and if the payment fails, releasing the stock. If the Android app, the iOS app and the web app each do these steps themselves, you get three slightly different checkouts, three places to fix bugs, and clients coupled to four services.

Formal definition (GoF):

Provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A hotel concierge

You tell the concierge "I'd like dinner at 8 and a taxi to the airport tomorrow at 6." They call the restaurant, the taxi company and the front desk. You never deal with any of them directly, though you still could if you wanted to.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Client
    class Facade {
        +doTask()
    }
    class SubsystemA
    class SubsystemB
    class SubsystemC
    class SubsystemD
    Client --> Facade
    Facade --> SubsystemA
    Facade --> SubsystemB
    Facade --> SubsystemC
    Facade --> SubsystemD
Participant Responsibility Facade Knows which subsystems to call, in what order, and how to handle failures; exposes task-level methods Subsystems Do the real work; don't know the facade exists Client Calls the facade (and can still use subsystems directly for advanced needs)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// In the Android app's checkout screen...
if (inventory.reserve(sku, qty)) {
    try {
        String pay = payments.charge(customer, amount);
        String slot = delivery.scheduleSlot(address);
        notifications.send(customer, "Order confirmed " + slot);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        // forgot to release inventory here; the iOS app remembered
    }
}
// ...copied into the iOS app, the web app, and the partner API
  • Duplicated workflows that drift apart (one client forgets compensation).
  • Tight coupling: every client depends on four services.
  • Changing the workflow (add fraud check) means changing every client.

docs.title: Example 1: One-Tap Checkout (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce app wants "one-tap reorder". Behind the button: reserve stock in the dark store, charge the saved card, book a delivery slot, notify the customer. Out-of-stock and declined cards are common, and when the payment fails, the reserved stock must be released or it shows as unavailable to other customers. Mobile, web and the voice assistant all call the same facade.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App
    participant F as CheckoutFacade
    participant I as Inventory
    participant P as Payments
    participant D as Delivery
    participant N as Notifications
    App->>F: placeOrder(...)
    F->>I: reserve(sku, qty)
    alt out of stock
        F-->>App: failure
    else reserved
        F->>P: charge(customer, amount)
        alt declined
            F->>I: release(sku, qty)
            F->>N: "Payment failed"
            F-->>App: failure
        else charged
            F->>D: scheduleSlot(address)
            F->>N: "Order confirmed"
            F-->>App: success
        end
    end

Full Code:

CheckoutFacade.javaSubsystems.javaCheckoutDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout;

import com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout.Subsystems.DeliveryService;
import com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout.Subsystems.InventoryService;
import com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout.Subsystems.NotificationService;
import com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout.Subsystems.PaymentService;

/** Facade: one call for the app; the workflow and its failure handling live here. */
public class CheckoutFacade {

    public record Result(boolean success, String message) {
    }

    private final InventoryService inventory;
    private final PaymentService payments;
    private final DeliveryService delivery;
    private final NotificationService notifications;

    public CheckoutFacade(InventoryService inventory, PaymentService payments,
                          DeliveryService delivery, NotificationService notifications) { // (1)!
        this.inventory = inventory;
        this.payments = payments;
        this.delivery = delivery;
        this.notifications = notifications;
    }

    public Result placeOrder(String customerId, String address, String sku, int qty, int amountInr) { // (2)!
        if (!inventory.reserve(sku, qty)) {
            return new Result(false, sku + " is out of stock");
        }
        String paymentId;
        try {
            paymentId = payments.charge(customerId, amountInr);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            inventory.release(sku, qty); // (3)!
            notifications.send(customerId, "Payment failed, nothing was charged");
            return new Result(false, "payment failed: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        String slot = delivery.scheduleSlot(address);
        notifications.send(customerId, "Order confirmed, arriving " + slot);
        return new Result(true, "confirmed " + paymentId + " " + slot);
    }
}
  1. Subsystems are injected, so the facade is easy to test with fakes and doesn't hide how it's wired.
  2. A task-level method: the client says what it wants, not how.
  3. Compensation lives in one place. Every client gets the correct failure handling for free.
package com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** The subsystems: each is a separate service with its own API. Kept in one file for the demo. */
public final class Subsystems {

    private Subsystems() {
    }

    public static class InventoryService {
        private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MILK-1L", 10, "EGGS-12", 0, "BREAD-WW", 5));

        public boolean reserve(String sku, int qty) {
            int available = stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
            if (available < qty) {
                return false;
            }
            stock.put(sku, available - qty);
            System.out.println("  [inventory] reserved " + qty + " x " + sku);
            return true;
        }

        public void release(String sku, int qty) {
            stock.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum);
            System.out.println("  [inventory] released " + qty + " x " + sku);
        }
    }

    public static class PaymentService {
        public String charge(String customerId, int amountInr) {
            if (amountInr > 5_000) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("card declined");
            }
            System.out.println("  [payment] charged INR " + amountInr + " to " + customerId);
            return "PAY-" + customerId + "-" + amountInr;
        }
    }

    public static class DeliveryService {
        public String scheduleSlot(String address) {
            System.out.println("  [delivery] slot booked 6-8 PM for " + address);
            return "SLOT-18-20";
        }
    }

    public static class NotificationService {
        public void send(String customerId, String message) {
            System.out.println("  [notify] " + customerId + ": " + message);
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout;

import com.handbook.structural.facade.checkout.Subsystems.*;

public class CheckoutDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: One-Tap Checkout ===");
        CheckoutFacade checkout = new CheckoutFacade(new InventoryService(), new PaymentService(),
                new DeliveryService(), new NotificationService());

        System.out.println("Order A:");
        System.out.println("=> " + checkout.placeOrder("CUST-1", "Koramangala", "MILK-1L", 2, 136));
        System.out.println("Order B:");
        System.out.println("=> " + checkout.placeOrder("CUST-2", "Indiranagar", "EGGS-12", 1, 90));
        System.out.println("Order C:");
        System.out.println("=> " + checkout.placeOrder("CUST-3", "HSR Layout", "BREAD-WW", 3, 9_000));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: One-Tap Checkout ===
Order A:
  [inventory] reserved 2 x MILK-1L
  [payment] charged INR 136 to CUST-1
  [delivery] slot booked 6-8 PM for Koramangala
  [notify] CUST-1: Order confirmed, arriving SLOT-18-20
=> Result[success=true, message=confirmed PAY-CUST-1-136 SLOT-18-20]
Order B:
=> Result[success=false, message=EGGS-12 is out of stock]
Order C:
  [inventory] reserved 3 x BREAD-WW
  [inventory] released 3 x BREAD-WW
  [notify] CUST-3: Payment failed, nothing was charged
=> Result[success=false, message=payment failed: card declined]

Order C shows the facade's value: the payment failed, and the stock was released without the app knowing it had been reserved.

Why Facade here:

  • A multi-step workflow that every client needs, with one correct failure path.
  • Clients depend on one interface instead of four services.
  • Adding a fraud check later is a change in the facade only.

docs.title: Example 2: Press Play (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: Before a streaming player shows the first frame, it needs: an entitlement check (is this a premium title?), a DRM license (security level depends on the device), the best CDN edge for the viewer's city, a starting bitrate for their bandwidth and HDR support, and subtitle tracks for their locale. Smart TVs, phones and browsers each used to call all five services, and each platform team got it slightly wrong. A PlaybackFacade gives every player one call.

Design:

flowchart LR
    TV[Smart TV app] --> F[PlaybackFacade.start]
    Phone[Mobile app] --> F
    Web[Browser] --> F
    F --> E[Entitlements]
    F --> D[DRM license server]
    F --> C[CDN selector]
    F --> B[Bitrate ladder]
    F --> S[Subtitles]

Full Code:

PlaybackFacade.javaPlaybackSubsystems.javaPlaybackDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.facade.streaming;

import com.handbook.structural.facade.streaming.PlaybackSubsystems.*;

import java.util.List;

/** Facade used by every player app (TV, mobile, web): one call returns everything to start playback. */
public class PlaybackFacade {

    public record PlaybackSession(String license, String cdnEdge, String rendition, List<String> subtitles) {
    }

    public record Client(String userId, String device, String city, int bandwidthKbps, boolean hdr, String locale) {
    }

    private final EntitlementService entitlements = new EntitlementService();
    private final DrmLicenseServer drm = new DrmLicenseServer();
    private final CdnSelector cdn = new CdnSelector();
    private final BitrateLadder ladder = new BitrateLadder();
    private final SubtitleService subtitles = new SubtitleService();

    public PlaybackSession start(String titleId, Client c) {
        if (!entitlements.canWatch(c.userId(), titleId)) {
            throw new SecurityException(c.userId() + " is not entitled to " + titleId);
        }
        return new PlaybackSession(
                drm.license(titleId, c.device()),
                cdn.bestEdge(c.city()),
                ladder.startingRendition(c.bandwidthKbps(), c.hdr()),
                subtitles.tracks(titleId, c.locale()));
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.facade.streaming;

import java.util.List;

/** Complex subsystems a player needs before the first frame. */
public final class PlaybackSubsystems {

    private PlaybackSubsystems() {
    }

    public static class EntitlementService {
        public boolean canWatch(String userId, String titleId) {
            return !titleId.startsWith("PREMIUM") || userId.endsWith("-premium");
        }
    }

    public static class DrmLicenseServer {
        public String license(String titleId, String device) {
            return (device.equals("browser") ? "Widevine-L3" : "Widevine-L1") + ":" + titleId;
        }
    }

    public static class CdnSelector {
        public String bestEdge(String city) {
            return switch (city) {
                case "Mumbai" -> "edge-bom-2";
                case "Chennai" -> "edge-maa-1";
                default -> "edge-del-1";
            };
        }
    }

    public static class BitrateLadder {
        public String startingRendition(int bandwidthKbps, boolean supportsHdr) {
            if (bandwidthKbps >= 15_000) {
                return supportsHdr ? "2160p HDR" : "2160p";
            }
            return bandwidthKbps >= 5_000 ? "1080p" : bandwidthKbps >= 1_500 ? "720p" : "480p";
        }
    }

    public static class SubtitleService {
        public List<String> tracks(String titleId, String locale) {
            return locale.equals("hi-IN") ? List.of("hi", "en") : List.of("en");
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.facade.streaming;

import com.handbook.structural.facade.streaming.PlaybackFacade.Client;

public class PlaybackDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Press Play ===");
        PlaybackFacade playback = new PlaybackFacade();

        Client tv = new Client("u42-premium", "smart-tv", "Mumbai", 25_000, true, "hi-IN");
        Client phone = new Client("u77", "browser", "Delhi", 3_000, false, "en-IN");

        System.out.println("TV    : " + playback.start("PREMIUM-SERIES-S2E1", tv));
        System.out.println("Phone : " + playback.start("MOVIE-1207", phone));
        try {
            playback.start("PREMIUM-SERIES-S2E1", phone);
        } catch (SecurityException e) {
            System.out.println("Phone : blocked - " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Press Play ===
TV    : PlaybackSession[license=Widevine-L1:PREMIUM-SERIES-S2E1, cdnEdge=edge-bom-2, rendition=2160p HDR, subtitles=[hi, en]]
Phone : PlaybackSession[license=Widevine-L3:MOVIE-1207, cdnEdge=edge-del-1, rendition=720p, subtitles=[en]]
Phone : blocked - u77 is not entitled to PREMIUM-SERIES-S2E1

Why Facade here:

  • Five subsystems, one question: "how do I start playing this title on this device?"
  • Returns a single, immutable PlaybackSession record, which is easy to serialize as one API response (this is also how a Backend for Frontend works).
  • Platform teams stop re-implementing (and mis-implementing) entitlement and DRM rules.

docs.title: Example 3: Open a Bank Account (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: Opening a savings account involves KYC verification (PAN and Aadhaar format checks, in reality calls to government APIs), a credit bureau score, account creation in the core banking system, and debit card issuance (Platinum for scores of 750+). The same flow is used by the mobile app, branch tablets and partner fintech APIs. Compliance wants the KYC rule enforced identically everywhere.

Design:

flowchart TB
    A[Applicant] --> F[AccountOpeningFacade.open]
    F --> K{KYC ok?}
    K -- no --> R[Rejected]
    K -- yes --> C[Credit bureau score]
    C --> CB[Core banking: open account]
    CB --> CA[Issue debit card<br/>Platinum if score >= 750]
    CA --> OK[Account opened]

Full Code:

AccountOpeningFacade.javaOnboardingSubsystems.javaOnboardingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.facade.banking;

import com.handbook.structural.facade.banking.OnboardingSubsystems.*;

/** Facade used by the mobile app, branch tablets and partner APIs alike. */
public class AccountOpeningFacade {

    public record Applicant(String name, String pan, String aadhaarLast4) {
    }

    private final KycService kyc = new KycService();
    private final CreditBureau bureau = new CreditBureau();
    private final CoreBanking core = new CoreBanking();
    private final CardService cards = new CardService();

    public String open(Applicant a) {
        if (!kyc.verify(a.pan(), a.aadhaarLast4())) {
            return a.name() + ": rejected, KYC failed";
        }
        int score = bureau.score(a.pan());
        String account = core.openSavingsAccount(a.name());
        String card = cards.issueDebitCard(account, score >= 750); // business rule lives in the facade
        return "%s: account %s opened, credit score %d, %s".formatted(a.name(), account, score, card);
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.facade.banking;

/** Subsystems involved in opening a bank account. */
public final class OnboardingSubsystems {

    private OnboardingSubsystems() {
    }

    public static class KycService {
        public boolean verify(String pan, String aadhaarLast4) {
            return pan.matches("[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]") && aadhaarLast4.matches("\\d{4}");
        }
    }

    public static class CreditBureau {
        public int score(String pan) {
            return pan.startsWith("ABC") ? 790 : 640;
        }
    }

    public static class CoreBanking {
        private int next = 1001;

        public String openSavingsAccount(String name) {
            return "SB-" + next++;
        }
    }

    public static class CardService {
        public String issueDebitCard(String accountNo, boolean premium) {
            return (premium ? "Platinum" : "Classic") + " debit card for " + accountNo;
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.facade.banking;

import com.handbook.structural.facade.banking.AccountOpeningFacade.Applicant;

public class OnboardingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Open an Account in One Call ===");
        AccountOpeningFacade onboarding = new AccountOpeningFacade();
        System.out.println(onboarding.open(new Applicant("Kavya", "ABCPK1234Q", "5678")));
        System.out.println(onboarding.open(new Applicant("Imran", "XYZPI9876L", "1234")));
        System.out.println(onboarding.open(new Applicant("Test User", "BAD-PAN", "12")));
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Open an Account in One Call ===
Kavya: account SB-1001 opened, credit score 790, Platinum debit card for SB-1001
Imran: account SB-1002 opened, credit score 640, Classic debit card for SB-1002
Test User: rejected, KYC failed

Why Facade here:

  • Regulatory consistency: one implementation of the KYC gate for every channel.
  • Channels (app, branch, partners) stay thin; the onboarding team can change vendors behind the facade.
  • The facade is the natural place for orchestration-level rules (card tier by score).
