docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Facade with injected subsystems (Example 1) vs. facade that owns its subsystems (Examples 2, 3). Prefer injection for testability; owning is fine for small, internal helpers.
  • Multiple facades over the same subsystems for different audiences (an admin facade and a customer facade).
  • Records as results: return one immutable result (PlaybackSession) instead of making the client gather pieces.
  • Service layer = facade: in Spring apps, an @Service that orchestrates repositories and clients for a use case is a facade. Annotate it @Transactional and the whole use case runs in one transaction.
  • Network-level facades: an API Gateway or Backend for Frontend (BFF) is a facade over microservices (covered in the Microservices section).

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Facade over SLF4J Logging back-ends (its name literally means Simple Logging Facade for Java) Spring JdbcTemplate Connection, PreparedStatement, ResultSet, exception translation, resource cleanup Spring RestClient / RestTemplate HTTP client libraries, message converters, error handling Spring JavaMailSender JavaMail sessions, MIME messages, transports java.net.http.HttpClient Connections, HTTP/2, TLS, redirects javax.faces.context.FacesContext JSF request, response, application state java.util.concurrent.Executors Static facade over ThreadPoolExecutor configuration Hibernate Session / JPA EntityManager Persistence context, SQL generation, caching, flushing

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Simple API for common tasks Can become a god object if every feature is added to it Decouples clients from subsystem details (Law of Demeter) May hide useful subsystem features (keep subsystems accessible) One place for workflows, ordering and compensation Another layer to maintain and version Easier to change subsystems behind it If it does too little, it's just pass-through boilerplate

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
The god facade

AppFacade with 140 methods covering orders, users, payments and reports is a monolith in one class. Make facades per use case or bounded context (CheckoutFacade, OnboardingFacade).

Pass-through facades

A facade whose every method just calls one subsystem method adds nothing. A facade earns its place by combining steps or simplifying a complex API.

Hiding failures

A facade that swallows subsystem exceptions and returns "success" makes debugging impossible. Translate failures into clear results or domain exceptions (Example 1's Result).

Distributed transactions in disguise

A facade calling four remote services can't make them atomic. Design compensation explicitly (Example 1), or use the Saga pattern for long-running flows.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Facade vs. orchestrator vs. saga. In-process, a facade orchestrates local calls and can use one database transaction. Across services, the same idea becomes an orchestrator (Saga orchestration) that must handle partial failure, retries, idempotency and timeouts. Be explicit in design reviews about which you're building.

Application services in DDD / Clean Architecture. The "use case" or "application service" layer is a set of facades: each method is one use case (PlaceOrder, OpenAccount), coordinating domain objects and ports. Controllers stay thin; domain objects stay free of orchestration.

API design. Facades define what clients can do. Design them around tasks, not entities (placeOrder, not createOrder + addLine + submit), return complete results, and version them carefully; mobile apps live in the wild for years.

Performance. A facade calling five independent services can call them in parallel (CompletableFuture, structured concurrency with virtual threads), turning the sum of latencies into the maximum. Example 2's DRM, CDN, bitrate and subtitle lookups are independent and could all run concurrently.

War story: three checkouts, three bugs

A retailer's Android, iOS and web apps each orchestrated checkout themselves. Only iOS released reserved stock on payment failure. During a sale, Android and web payment failures left thousands of items "reserved" but never sold; the site showed popular items out of stock while the warehouse was full. Lost sales were estimated in crores of rupees. Fix: a server-side CheckoutFacade (later a saga orchestrator) owning the workflow and compensation; all apps switched to a single POST /checkout; reservations got a TTL as a safety net. Lesson: workflows belong on the server, in one place, not copied into every client.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Facade Adapter Mediator Proxy API Gateway Wraps Many subsystems One class Colleagues that talk to each other One subject Many services (network) Interface New, simpler Converted to an expected one Mediator interface Same as subject HTTP routes Who talks to whom Client → facade → subsystems (subsystems unaware) Client → adapter → adaptee Colleagues → mediator → colleagues (two-way) Client → proxy → subject Client → gateway → services

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One simple, task-level interface over many subsystems.
  • Holds the workflow, ordering and compensation; subsystems don't know it exists.
  • Doesn't block direct access to subsystems.
  • Avoid god facades (split per use case) and pass-through facades.
  • Real life: SLF4J, JdbcTemplate, Spring @Service use cases, API Gateway / BFF.
Result r = checkoutFacade.placeOrder(customer, address, sku, qty, amount);

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a fraud check to CheckoutFacade without changing any client.
  • Make PlaybackFacade call DRM, CDN, bitrate and subtitles in parallel with virtual threads.
  • Return a typed result (sealed interface: Booked, NoDriver) from RideBookingFacade instead of a String.

Decorator Next: Flyweight

docs.title: Flyweight
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Structural Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Flyweight saves memory by sharing the common, immutable part of many similar objects instead of copying it into each one. Use it when you have a huge number of objects whose state splits cleanly into a shared part (intrinsic) and a per-object part (extrinsic).

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a ride-hailing map shows 10,000 cars. If each car object carries its own 16 KB icon bitmap, that's 160 MB for three distinct pictures (Auto, Mini, Sedan). Only position and heading differ per car. Share the three icons, keep a tiny marker per car, and memory drops to well under 1 MB.

Formal definition (GoF):

Use sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently.

The two kinds of state:

Intrinsic Extrinsic Meaning Same for many objects Unique to each object/use Where it lives Inside the flyweight (shared) Outside: in a context object, or passed as method arguments Must be Immutable Anything Map example Icon bitmap, vehicle type Latitude, longitude, heading

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Printing type

Old printing presses didn't carve a new letter "e" for every "e" on the page. They had a tray of reusable metal letters (shared, intrinsic) and arranged them in positions (extrinsic). One "e" design, used thousands of times.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class FlyweightFactory {
        -Map~Key, Flyweight~ pool
        +get(key) Flyweight
    }
    class Flyweight {
        -intrinsicState (immutable)
        +operation(extrinsicState)
    }
    class Context {
        -extrinsicState
        -Flyweight flyweight
        +operation()
    }
    class Client
    Client --> Context
    Context --> Flyweight : shares
    Client ..> FlyweightFactory : get(key)
    FlyweightFactory o--> Flyweight
Participant Responsibility Flyweight Immutable, shared intrinsic state; operations take extrinsic state as parameters Flyweight factory Creates each flyweight once per key and returns the shared instance Context Small per-object data (extrinsic) + a reference to its flyweight Client Gets flyweights from the factory, never with new

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
record CarMarker(String driverId, double lat, double lng, int heading, byte[] iconBitmap) {}

for (Driver d : drivers) {
    markers.add(new CarMarker(d.id(), d.lat(), d.lng(), d.heading(),
            loadIcon(d.type())));       // 16 KB copied 10,000 times, and loaded from disk 10,000 times
}
  • Memory explosion: identical data duplicated thousands of times.
  • Slow: identical data loaded or created over and over, and more GC pressure.

docs.title: Example 1: 10,000 Live Cars on the Map (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: A ride-hailing ops dashboard shows every active car in Bengaluru, updated every few seconds. There are three vehicle types, each with a 64×64 RGBA icon (16 KB). Cars move constantly (position and heading change), but their icons never do. The dashboard runs on modest laptops in the ops centre, so memory matters.

Design:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Markers["10,000 CarMarker records (extrinsic)"]
        M1["D0: lat, lng, heading"]
        M2["D1: lat, lng, heading"]
        M3["D2: ..."]
        M4["D3: ..."]
    end
    subgraph Icons["3 shared VehicleIcon flyweights (intrinsic)"]
        A[Auto 16 KB]
        B[Mini 16 KB]
        C[Sedan 16 KB]
    end
    M1 --> A
    M2 --> B
    M3 --> C
    M4 --> A

Full Code:

VehicleIcon.javaIconFactory.javaCarMarker.javaRideMapDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.ridemap;

/** Flyweight: heavy, immutable, shared. Holds only INTRINSIC state (what every Mini looks like). */
public final class VehicleIcon {

    private final String type;
    private final byte[] bitmap; // a 64x64 RGBA icon = 16 KB

    VehicleIcon(String type) {
        this.type = type;
        this.bitmap = new byte[64 * 64 * 4];
    }

    public String type() {
        return type;
    }

    public int sizeBytes() {
        return bitmap.length;
    }

    public String drawAt(double lat, double lng, int heading) { // (1)!
        return "%s icon at (%.4f, %.4f) facing %d deg".formatted(type, lat, lng, heading);
    }
}
  1. Extrinsic state (position, heading) is passed in, never stored in the flyweight. That's what makes it safe to share.
package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.ridemap;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

/** Flyweight factory: creates each icon once and hands out the shared instance. */
public final class IconFactory {

    private final Map<String, VehicleIcon> icons = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public VehicleIcon icon(String type) {
        return icons.computeIfAbsent(type, VehicleIcon::new); // (1)!
    }

    public int distinctIcons() {
        return icons.size();
    }
}
  1. computeIfAbsent on a ConcurrentHashMap creates each icon at most once, even when many threads ask at the same time.
package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.ridemap;

/** Context object: small, one per car. EXTRINSIC state + a reference to the shared flyweight. */
public record CarMarker(String driverId, double lat, double lng, int heading, VehicleIcon icon) {

    public String render() {
        return driverId + ": " + icon.drawAt(lat, lng, heading);
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.ridemap;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class RideMapDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: 10,000 Live Cars on the City Map ===");
        IconFactory factory = new IconFactory();
        String[] types = {"Auto", "Mini", "Sedan"};
        List<CarMarker> markers = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
            double lat = 12.90 + (i % 100) * 0.001;
            double lng = 77.55 + (i / 100) * 0.001;
            markers.add(new CarMarker("D" + i, lat, lng, (i * 37) % 360, factory.icon(types[i % 3])));
        }

        markers.subList(0, 3).forEach(m -> System.out.println(m.render()));
        long iconBytes = factory.icon("Mini").sizeBytes();
        long withoutFlyweight = markers.size() * iconBytes;
        long withFlyweight = factory.distinctIcons() * iconBytes + markers.size() * 48L; // ~48 B per marker
        System.out.println("Markers on map       : " + markers.size());
        System.out.println("Icon objects created : " + factory.distinctIcons());
        System.out.printf("Memory without sharing: ~%,d KB%n", withoutFlyweight / 1024);
        System.out.printf("Memory with flyweight : ~%,d KB%n", withFlyweight / 1024);
        System.out.println("Same Mini icon shared? " + (markers.get(1).icon() == markers.get(4).icon()));
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: 10,000 Live Cars on the City Map ===
D0: Auto icon at (12.9000, 77.5500) facing 0 deg
D1: Mini icon at (12.9010, 77.5500) facing 37 deg
D2: Sedan icon at (12.9020, 77.5500) facing 74 deg
Markers on map       : 10000
Icon objects created : 3
Memory without sharing: ~160,000 KB
Memory with flyweight : ~516 KB
Same Mini icon shared? true

About 300× less memory for the same picture on screen. (The marker size is an estimate; measure real numbers with JOL or a heap dump.)

Why Flyweight here:

  • Huge count (10,000+) of objects with heavy, identical parts.
  • Clean split: icon = intrinsic, position = extrinsic.
  • The icon is naturally immutable.

docs.title: Example 2: Styled Text in a Collaborative Editor (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: A Google-Docs-style editor stores formatting for every character. A 3-page contract has about 3,000 characters but only 3 distinct styles (bold heading, body text, grey italic footer). Storing a separate style object per character wastes memory on the server (which holds thousands of open documents) and makes "are these two runs the same style?" an expensive deep comparison.

Design:

flowchart LR
    C1["'C' (pos 0)"] --> S1["TextStyle(Inter, 12, bold)"]
    C2["'l' (pos 1)"] --> S1
    C3["'T' (pos 10)"] --> S2["TextStyle(Inter, 12, regular)"]
    C4["'h' (pos 11)"] --> S2
    C5["'C' (pos 1000)"] --> S3["TextStyle(Inter, 10, italic, grey)"]

Full Code:

TextStyle.javaDocument.javaEditorDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.editor;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

/** Flyweight: a record gives value equality for free, which makes interning trivial. */
public record TextStyle(String font, int sizePt, boolean bold, boolean italic, String color) {

    private static final Map<TextStyle, TextStyle> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public static TextStyle of(String font, int sizePt, boolean bold, boolean italic, String color) {
        TextStyle candidate = new TextStyle(font, sizePt, bold, italic, color);
        return POOL.computeIfAbsent(candidate, k -> k); // (1)!
    }

    public static int pooled() {
        return POOL.size();
    }
}
  1. Interning with a record: records get equals/hashCode from their components, so a freshly built style finds its equal twin in the pool, and the pool returns the shared one. The candidate object is garbage straight away. This is exactly how String.intern() works.
package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.editor;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.IdentityHashMap;
import java.util.List;

/** A collaborative document: each character points to a shared style. */
public class Document {

    private record StyledChar(char ch, TextStyle style) { // extrinsic: the char; intrinsic: the style
    }

    private final List<StyledChar> chars = new ArrayList<>();

    public Document type(String text, TextStyle style) {
        for (char c : text.toCharArray()) {
            chars.add(new StyledChar(c, style));
        }
        return this;
    }

    public int length() {
        return chars.size();
    }

    public int distinctStyleObjects() {
        IdentityHashMap<TextStyle, Boolean> seen = new IdentityHashMap<>();
        chars.forEach(c -> seen.put(c.style(), true));
        return seen.size();
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.editor;

public class EditorDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Docs SaaS: Styled Text in a 3-Page Contract ===");
        Document doc = new Document();
        for (int page = 1; page <= 3; page++) {
            doc.type("Clause " + page + ": ", TextStyle.of("Inter", 12, true, false, "#111111"));
            doc.type("The supplier shall deliver goods within 10 days. ".repeat(20),
                    TextStyle.of("Inter", 12, false, false, "#111111"));
            doc.type("Confidential", TextStyle.of("Inter", 10, false, true, "#888888"));
        }
        System.out.println("Characters in document   : " + doc.length());
        System.out.println("Style objects referenced : " + doc.distinctStyleObjects());
        System.out.println("Styles in the pool       : " + TextStyle.pooled());
        System.out.println("Bold style interned?     : "
                + (TextStyle.of("Inter", 12, true, false, "#111111") == TextStyle.of("Inter", 12, true, false, "#111111")));
    }
}

Output:

=== Docs SaaS: Styled Text in a 3-Page Contract ===
Characters in document   : 3006
Style objects referenced : 3
Styles in the pool       : 3
Bold style interned?     : true

Why Flyweight here:

  • Thousands of characters, a handful of styles.
  • Interned styles make "same style?" an identity check (==), which is fast for merging runs.
  • Styles are value objects, immutable by nature.

docs.title: Example 3: Product Data Across Dark Stores (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce company runs 200 dark stores, each stocking the same 50 fast-moving products (in reality thousands). Name, long description, image URL and nutrition JSON are identical in every store; only price and stock differ by store. The pricing service holds every store's listings in memory for fast lookups. Without sharing, each listing carries its own copy of the catalog text.

Design:

classDiagram
    class StoreListing {
        <<record>>
        storeId
        priceInr
        stock
    }
    class ProductInfo {
        <<record, flyweight>>
        sku
        name
        description
        imageUrl
        nutritionJson
    }
    class Catalog {
        -Map~String, ProductInfo~ bySku
        +product(sku) ProductInfo
    }
    StoreListing --> ProductInfo : shares
    Catalog o--> ProductInfo

Full Code:

Catalog.javaProductInfo.javaStoreListing.javaDarkStoreDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.grocery;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Flyweight factory keyed by SKU. In production: a cache in front of the catalog service. */
public class Catalog {

    private final Map<String, ProductInfo> bySku = new HashMap<>();
    private int loads;

    public ProductInfo product(String sku) {
        return bySku.computeIfAbsent(sku, s -> {
            loads++;
            return new ProductInfo(s, "Product " + s, "A long marketing description... ".repeat(10),
                    "https://cdn.example.com/" + s + ".jpg", "{\"kcal\":120,\"protein\":4}");
        });
    }

    public int loads() {
        return loads;
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.grocery;

/** Flyweight: catalog data that is identical in every store. */
public record ProductInfo(String sku, String name, String description, String imageUrl, String nutritionJson) {
}

package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.grocery;

/** Extrinsic, per-store data, plus a reference to the shared product info. */
public record StoreListing(String storeId, ProductInfo product, int priceInr, int stock) {
}

package com.handbook.structural.flyweight.grocery;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.IdentityHashMap;
import java.util.List;

public class DarkStoreDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: 50 Products in 200 Dark Stores ===");
        Catalog catalog = new Catalog();
        List<StoreListing> listings = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int store = 1; store <= 200; store++) {
            for (int p = 1; p <= 50; p++) {
                int price = 40 + p + (store % 5); // prices vary slightly by store
                listings.add(new StoreListing("DS-" + store, catalog.product("SKU-" + p), price, (store * p) % 30));
            }
        }
        IdentityHashMap<ProductInfo, Boolean> distinct = new IdentityHashMap<>();
        listings.forEach(l -> distinct.put(l.product(), true));

        StoreListing a = listings.get(0);
        StoreListing b = listings.get(50); // same SKU-1, next store
        System.out.println(a.storeId() + " " + a.product().sku() + " INR " + a.priceInr() + " stock " + a.stock());
        System.out.println(b.storeId() + " " + b.product().sku() + " INR " + b.priceInr() + " stock " + b.stock());
        System.out.println("Shared ProductInfo instance? " + (a.product() == b.product()));
        System.out.println("Store listings      : " + listings.size());
        System.out.println("ProductInfo objects : " + distinct.size());
        System.out.println("Catalog loads       : " + catalog.loads());
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: 50 Products in 200 Dark Stores ===
DS-1 SKU-1 INR 42 stock 1
DS-2 SKU-1 INR 43 stock 2
Shared ProductInfo instance? true
Store listings      : 10000
ProductInfo objects : 50
Catalog loads       : 50

10,000 listings share 50 product objects, and the catalog was loaded only 50 times instead of 10,000.

Why Flyweight here:

  • A classic data-modelling split: global catalog data vs. per-store data.
  • Cuts memory and load calls to the catalog service.
  • Records make both parts immutable and easy to reason about.
Unit Tests: FlyweightTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.structural.flyweight;

import com.handbook.structural.flyweight.editor.TextStyle;
import com.handbook.structural.flyweight.grocery.Catalog;
import com.handbook.structural.flyweight.ridemap.IconFactory;
import com.handbook.structural.flyweight.social.Hashtag;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class FlyweightTest {

    @Test
    void factoryReturnsSharedInstances() {
        IconFactory f = new IconFactory();
        assertThat(f.icon("Mini")).isSameAs(f.icon("Mini"));
        assertThat(f.icon("Mini")).isNotSameAs(f.icon("Auto"));
        assertThat(f.distinctIcons()).isEqualTo(2);
    }

    @Test
    void equalStylesAreInterned() {
        assertThat(TextStyle.of("A", 1, true, false, "c")).isSameAs(TextStyle.of("A", 1, true, false, "c"));
    }

    @Test
    void catalogLoadsEachProductOnce() {
        Catalog c = new Catalog();
        c.product("X");
        c.product("X");
        assertThat(c.loads()).isEqualTo(1);
    }

    @Test
    void hashtagsInternUnderConcurrency() {
        Set<Hashtag> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                ex.submit(() -> seen.add(Hashtag.of("#Concurrency")));
            }
        }
        assertThat(seen).hasSize(1);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Hashtag.of("no-hash")).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Interning with records (Example 2): value equality makes a Map<T, T> pool trivial.
  • Bounded or weak pools: a pool that grows forever is a memory leak. For unbounded key spaces, use a size-limited cache (Caffeine) or weak references (Guava Interners.newWeakInterner()).
  • Enum as flyweights: enum constants are the simplest flyweights, a fixed set of shared instances.
  • Primitive arrays as a data-oriented alternative: for millions of points, a structure-of-arrays layout (double[] lats, lngs) beats any object model. Know when to leave OOP behind.
  • Project Valhalla (future): value classes will let the JVM flatten small objects, reducing the per-object overhead that often motivates Flyweight.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text:
Where Flyweight JDK Integer.valueOf(-128..127), Long.valueOf, Character.valueOf, Boolean.valueOf caches JDK String.intern() and the string constant pool; compact strings JDK Enum constants; Collections.emptyList(); Optional.empty() JDK java.time.ZoneId.of(...), ZoneOffset caching Text rendering Glyph caches in Java2D, browsers, and editors Games / maps Shared meshes, textures and icons (the GoF example is glyphs in a document editor) Guava Interners, ImmutableList.of() singletons

Classic trap

Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b is true (cached flyweights), but with 128 it's false. Always compare wrappers with equals(). This comes up in service-company interviews all the time.

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Large memory savings with many similar objects More complex model: state is split in two Fewer allocations, less GC pressure Extrinsic state must be passed around, which complicates APIs Fast identity comparison of interned values The factory needs thread-safety and a size or eviction policy No benefit with few objects or little shared state, only complexity

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Mutable flyweights

If anyone can change a shared icon or style, the change appears everywhere. Flyweights must be immutable: final fields, records, defensive copies of arrays.

Unbounded pools

Interning user-provided strings (hashtags, search terms) without a limit is a memory leak and a denial-of-service vector. Bound it, or use weak references.

Premature flyweighting

The JVM is very good at small objects. Measure with a heap histogram (jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram) before adding a factory and splitting state.

Identity comparisons outside the pool

== only works if every instance came from the factory. One new TextStyle(...) bypassing of() breaks it. Keep constructors private when you rely on identity.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Measure first. Use JOL (Java Object Layout) to see real object sizes (headers, padding, compressed oops) and a heap dump analyser (Eclipse MAT) to find duplicate data: MAT's "duplicate strings" and "retained size by class" reports point directly at Flyweight opportunities.

Flyweight at the data layer. The same idea appears as normalization in databases (store product data once, reference it by ID), dictionary encoding in columnar formats (Parquet, Arrow), and string deduplication in G1 (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication), which the JVM does for you.

Caches are flyweight factories with eviction. In services, the "factory" is often a cache keyed by ID (Example 3). Design for invalidation (product name changed) and for the memory budget (max size, weigher).

Concurrency. Immutable flyweights are inherently thread-safe; the only shared mutable structure is the factory's map. ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent gives "create at most once per key", but keep the creation function fast, because it runs while that map bin is locked.

War story: the interner that ate the heap

A social app interned every hashtag in posts and search queries with String.intern()-style pooling to "save memory". A spam campaign generated millions of random hashtags (#a8f7d...). The pool grew without bound, full GCs took seconds, and the search service fell over during a trending event. Fix: intern only tags from an allow-list of trending and known tags; everything else used plain strings; the pool became a bounded Caffeine cache with weak values; input validation rejected tags over 50 characters. Lesson: a flyweight pool is a cache. Bound it, and never key it by untrusted input without limits.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Flyweight Singleton Object Pool Prototype Instances Few shared, one per distinct intrinsic state Exactly one Several, borrowed exclusively Many copies Mutable? No Maybe Yes, while borrowed Yes Used by Many at the same time Everyone One borrower at a time Each copy's owner Goal Save memory One global instance Avoid expensive creation, limit count Avoid expensive setup

Often combined with: Factory (to create and share flyweights), Composite (shared leaf nodes in big trees, like characters in a document), State/Strategy (stateless strategies and states are flyweights).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Share the common, immutable (intrinsic) part; keep the unique (extrinsic) part outside.
  • A factory creates each flyweight once per key (computeIfAbsent).
  • Worth it only with many objects and heavy shared state; measure first.
  • Bound the pool; never intern untrusted input without limits.
  • JDK: Integer.valueOf cache (127 vs 128 trap), the String pool, enums.
VehicleIcon icon = icons.computeIfAbsent(type, VehicleIcon::new);

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Measure CarMarker and VehicleIcon sizes with JOL and update the estimate in the demo.
  • Make the TextStyle pool bounded with Caffeine and weak values.
  • Rewrite the map with structure-of-arrays (double[]) for 1 million cars and compare memory.

Facade Next: Proxy

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Structural Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A proxy is a stand-in with the same interface as the real object that controls access to it: creating it lazily, checking permissions, calling it over the network, caching, or logging. Spring's @Transactional, Hibernate's lazy loading and every gRPC client stub are proxies, so understanding this pattern explains a lot of "framework magic".

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: sometimes you can't, or shouldn't, hand clients the real object directly. It may be expensive to create (an 8 MB image), sensitive (a bank account), or in another process (a remote service). You want clients to use it as if it were the real thing, while something in between decides when, whether, and how the real object is used.

Formal definition (GoF):

Provide a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.

The common kinds of proxy:

Kind Controls Example below Virtual proxy When the real object is created (lazily) Example 1 Protection proxy Whether the caller may use it Example 2 Remote proxy Where it lives (another process or machine) Example 3 Caching proxy Reusing results Decorator page's challenge, Spring @Cacheable Logging / monitoring proxy Recording calls Coding challenge (dynamic proxy) Smart reference Reference counting, locking, lazy init of associations Hibernate lazy collections

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A company's receptionist

You want to meet the CEO. The receptionist (proxy) looks like the way in: you talk to them as if they were the office. They check whether you have an appointment (protection), call the CEO only when it's your turn (virtual), or connect you by video if the CEO is in another city (remote). The CEO's job doesn't change at all.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Subject {
        <<interface>>
        +request()
    }
    class RealSubject {
        +request()
    }
    class Proxy {
        -RealSubject real
        +request()
    }
    class Client
    Client --> Subject
    Subject <|.. RealSubject
    Subject <|.. Proxy
    Proxy --> RealSubject : controls access
Participant Responsibility Subject The interface clients use Real subject Does the actual work; contains no access-control code Proxy Same interface; decides when and whether to forward, and may add work around the call Client Can't tell (and shouldn't care) whether it holds the proxy or the real subject

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public String withdraw(User user, String acc, long amount) {
    if (amount > 50_000 && !user.roles().contains("MANAGER")) throw new SecurityException();
    if (!user.roles().contains("TELLER") && !user.roles().contains("MANAGER")) throw new SecurityException();
    // ...actual business logic, mixed with security checks...
}
// Every method repeats checks. Someone adds a new method and forgets them.
  • Cross-cutting code mixed with business logic (security, laziness, networking).
  • Easy to forget in one method, which becomes a security hole.
  • Business classes become hard to test in isolation.

docs.title: Example 1: Lazy Posters on the Home Screen (Streaming) — Virtual Proxy
docs.text:
Scenario: A streaming app's home screen has rows of 40 titles each. High-resolution posters are 8 MB each to download and decode. Users usually see the first few tiles and scroll a little. Creating all posters up front means 320 MB of downloads per row, a slow start-up and wasted mobile data. Search and analytics only need the title, never the image.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant UI as Home screen
    participant P as LazyPoster (proxy)
    participant R as HighResPoster (real)
    UI->>P: new LazyPoster("Title 1")
    Note over P: nothing downloaded
    UI->>P: title()
    P-->>UI: "Title 1" (no download)
    UI->>P: render()
    P->>R: new HighResPoster(...) [8 MB download]
    P->>R: render()
    R-->>UI: pixels
    UI->>P: render() again
    P->>R: render() (already loaded)

Full Code:

LazyPoster.javaHighResPoster.javaPoster.javaHomeScreenDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

/** Virtual proxy: same interface, creates the real poster only when it is actually shown. */
public class LazyPoster implements Poster {

    private final String title;
    private HighResPoster real; // (1)!

    public LazyPoster(String title) {
        this.title = title;
    }

    @Override
    public String title() {
        return title; // (2)!
    }

    @Override
    public String render() {
        if (real == null) {
            real = new HighResPoster(title); // (3)!
        }
        return real.render();
    }
}
  1. The real subject starts as null: nothing expensive has happened yet.
  2. Cheap requests are answered by the proxy itself, without creating the real object.
  3. The real object is created on first use and then reused. For multi-threaded access, use the holder idiom or a lock (see Singleton).
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

/** Real subject: expensive to create (downloads and decodes an 8 MB image). */
public class HighResPoster implements Poster {

    private final String title;
    private final byte[] pixels;

    public HighResPoster(String title) {
        this.title = title;
        System.out.println("  [download] 8 MB poster for '" + title + "'");
        this.pixels = new byte[8 * 1024]; // scaled down for the demo
    }

    public String title() { return title; }

    public String render() { return "[poster: " + title + ", " + pixels.length / 1024 + "K px]"; }
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

public interface Poster {

    String title();

    String render();
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class HomeScreenDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Home Screen with 40 Titles ===");
        List<Poster> row = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 40; i++) {
            row.add(new LazyPoster("Title " + i));
        }
        System.out.println("Home screen built with " + row.size() + " posters (nothing downloaded yet)");

        System.out.println("User sees the first 3 tiles:");
        row.subList(0, 3).forEach(p -> System.out.println("  " + p.render()));
        System.out.println("User scrolls back to tile 1:");
        System.out.println("  " + row.get(0).render() + "  <- no second download");
        System.out.println("Search index uses titles only: " + row.get(39).title());
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Home Screen with 40 Titles ===
Home screen built with 40 posters (nothing downloaded yet)
User sees the first 3 tiles:
  [download] 8 MB poster for 'Title 1'
  [poster: Title 1, 8K px]
  [download] 8 MB poster for 'Title 2'
  [poster: Title 2, 8K px]
  [download] 8 MB poster for 'Title 3'
  [poster: Title 3, 8K px]
User scrolls back to tile 1:
  [poster: Title 1, 8K px]  <- no second download
Search index uses titles only: Title 40

40 posters on the screen, 3 downloads. Scrolling back doesn't download again.

Why a virtual proxy here:

  • The real object is expensive and often never needed.
  • Clients (the UI) keep using the Poster interface unchanged.
  • This is exactly how Hibernate lazy loading works: your entity's getOrders() returns a proxy collection that queries the database on first access.

docs.title: Example 2: Role-Based Access at the Branch Counter (Banking) — Protection Proxy
docs.text:
Scenario: Bank branch software lets tellers check balances and make withdrawals up to INR 50,000; bigger withdrawals need a manager. Interns can't access accounts at all. The core account service is shared with ATMs and internet banking, which have their own rules, so it must contain no branch-specific security code. Auditors want access rules in one reviewable place.

Design:

flowchart LR
    T[Teller anita] --> P1[SecuredAccountService<br/>user = anita, TELLER]
    M[Manager vikram] --> P2[SecuredAccountService<br/>user = vikram, MANAGER]
    I[Intern sam] --> P3[SecuredAccountService<br/>user = sam, INTERN]
    P1 --> C[CoreAccountService<br/>pure business logic]
    P2 --> C
    P3 -. denied .-x C

Full Code:

SecuredAccountService.javaCoreAccountService.javaAccountService.javaBranchDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

import java.util.Set;

/** Protection proxy: checks the caller's roles before forwarding to the real service. */
public class SecuredAccountService implements AccountService {

    public record User(String name, Set<String> roles) {
    }

    private static final long TELLER_LIMIT_INR = 50_000;

    private final AccountService target;
    private final User user;

    public SecuredAccountService(AccountService target, User user) {
        this.target = target;
        this.user = user;
    }

    @Override
    public long balance(String accountNo) {
        require("TELLER", "MANAGER");
        return target.balance(accountNo);
    }

    @Override
    public String withdraw(String accountNo, long amountInr) {
        if (amountInr > TELLER_LIMIT_INR) {
            require("MANAGER"); // (1)!
        } else {
            require("TELLER", "MANAGER");
        }
        return target.withdraw(accountNo, amountInr);
    }

    private void require(String... anyOf) {
        for (String role : anyOf) {
            if (user.roles().contains(role)) {
                return;
            }
        }
        throw new SecurityException(user.name() + " lacks role " + String.join("/", anyOf)); // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Rules can depend on arguments, not just on the method: large withdrawals need a stronger role.
  2. Denials throw before the real subject is touched, so a denied call has no side effects.
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Real subject: pure business logic, no security code. */
public class CoreAccountService implements AccountService {

    private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>(Map.of("SB-1001", 250_000L));

    public long balance(String accountNo) {
        return balances.get(accountNo);
    }

    public String withdraw(String accountNo, long amount) {
        balances.merge(accountNo, -amount, Long::sum);
        return "withdrew INR " + amount + ", new balance INR " + balances.get(accountNo);
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

public interface AccountService {

    long balance(String accountNo);

    String withdraw(String accountNo, long amountInr);
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

import com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.SecuredAccountService.User;

import java.util.Set;

public class BranchDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Branch Counter ===");
        AccountService core = new CoreAccountService();
        AccountService asTeller = new SecuredAccountService(core, new User("anita", Set.of("TELLER")));
        AccountService asManager = new SecuredAccountService(core, new User("vikram", Set.of("MANAGER")));
        AccountService asIntern = new SecuredAccountService(core, new User("sam", Set.of("INTERN")));

        attempt("Teller checks balance  ", () -> "INR " + asTeller.balance("SB-1001"));
        attempt("Teller withdraws 20,000", () -> asTeller.withdraw("SB-1001", 20_000));
        attempt("Teller withdraws 80,000", () -> asTeller.withdraw("SB-1001", 80_000));
        attempt("Manager withdraws 80,000", () -> asManager.withdraw("SB-1001", 80_000));
        attempt("Intern checks balance  ", () -> "INR " + asIntern.balance("SB-1001"));
    }

    private static void attempt(String label, java.util.function.Supplier<String> action) {
        try {
            System.out.println(label + " -> " + action.get());
        } catch (SecurityException e) {
            System.out.println(label + " -> DENIED (" + e.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Branch Counter ===
Teller checks balance   -> INR 250000
Teller withdraws 20,000 -> withdrew INR 20000, new balance INR 230000
Teller withdraws 80,000 -> DENIED (anita lacks role MANAGER)
Manager withdraws 80,000 -> withdrew INR 80000, new balance INR 150000
Intern checks balance   -> DENIED (sam lacks role TELLER/MANAGER)

Why a protection proxy here:

  • Security is separated from business logic: CoreAccountService is reused by ATM and online channels with different proxies.
  • Access rules live in one auditable class.
  • In Spring, @PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER')") generates this kind of proxy for you.

docs.title: Example 3: Calling the Inventory Service (Logistics) — Remote Proxy
docs.text:
Scenario: An order service checks stock in the inventory service, which runs in another cluster. Order-service developers want to write inventory.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG") as if it were a local call. Behind it, the call must be marshalled into a request, sent over the network, and the response unmarshalled. Network failures must surface as a clear domain error (InventoryUnavailableException), not a raw IOException deep in business code.

Design:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Order service code
    participant P as InventoryClientProxy (stub)
    participant N as Network (Transport)
    participant S as Inventory server
    O->>P: availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG")
    P->>P: marshal: "availableUnits|BLR-1|RICE-5KG"
    P->>N: send(request)
    N->>S: handle(request)
    S-->>N: "OK|120"
    N-->>P: "OK|120"
    P->>P: unmarshal: 120
    P-->>O: 120

Full Code:

InventoryClientProxy.javaInventoryServer.javaInventoryApi + TransportRemoteDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

import java.io.IOException;

/**
 * Remote proxy (a "client stub"): looks like a local InventoryApi, but marshals each
 * call into a network request and turns network failures into a clear domain error.
 */
public class InventoryClientProxy implements InventoryApi {

    public static class InventoryUnavailableException extends RuntimeException {
        public InventoryUnavailableException(String message, Throwable cause) {
            super(message, cause);
        }
    }

    private final Transport transport;

    public InventoryClientProxy(Transport transport) {
        this.transport = transport;
    }

    @Override
    public int availableUnits(String warehouse, String sku) {
        String request = "availableUnits|" + warehouse + "|" + sku; // (1)!
        try {
            String response = transport.send(request);
            String[] parts = response.split("\\|");
            if (!parts[0].equals("OK")) {
                throw new InventoryUnavailableException("Server error: " + response, null);
            }
            return Integer.parseInt(parts[1]); // (2)!
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new InventoryUnavailableException("Inventory service unreachable: " + e.getMessage(), e); // (3)!
        }
    }
}
  1. Marshalling: the method call becomes a message. Real stubs use JSON over HTTP, or Protobuf over gRPC.
  2. Unmarshalling the response back into a Java value.
  3. Transport errors become a domain exception. The caller learns "inventory is unavailable", not "socket closed".
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

import java.util.Map;

/** The real subject, running in another process. Here it parses the wire format directly. */
public class InventoryServer implements InventoryApi {

    private final Map<String, Integer> stock = Map.of("BLR-1:RICE-5KG", 120, "BLR-1:OIL-1L", 0);
    private int calls;

    public int availableUnits(String warehouse, String sku) {
        return stock.getOrDefault(warehouse + ":" + sku, 0);
    }

    /** What the HTTP endpoint would do: decode, call, encode. */
    public String handle(String request) {
        calls++;
        String[] parts = request.split("\\|"); // "availableUnits|BLR-1|RICE-5KG"
        return "OK|" + availableUnits(parts[1], parts[2]);
    }

    public int calls() {
        return calls;
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

/** The interface both the client and the server agree on. */
public interface InventoryApi {

    int availableUnits(String warehouse, String sku);
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

/** Network abstraction: sends a request string, receives a response string (HTTP/gRPC in real life). */
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Transport {

    String send(String request) throws java.io.IOException;
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

import com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote.InventoryClientProxy.InventoryUnavailableException;

import java.io.IOException;

public class RemoteDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Order Service Calling the Inventory Service ===");
        InventoryServer server = new InventoryServer();
        Transport network = request -> {
            System.out.println("  [wire] -> " + request);
            String response = server.handle(request);
            System.out.println("  [wire] <- " + response);
            return response;
        };
        InventoryApi inventory = new InventoryClientProxy(network); // the order service only sees InventoryApi

        System.out.println("Rice in BLR-1: " + inventory.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG"));
        System.out.println("Oil in BLR-1 : " + inventory.availableUnits("BLR-1", "OIL-1L"));

        InventoryApi duringOutage = new InventoryClientProxy(request -> {
            throw new IOException("connect timed out after 2000 ms");
        });
        try {
            duringOutage.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG");
        } catch (InventoryUnavailableException e) {
            System.out.println("During outage: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("Server handled " + server.calls() + " calls");
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Order Service Calling the Inventory Service ===
  [wire] -> availableUnits|BLR-1|RICE-5KG
  [wire] <- OK|120
Rice in BLR-1: 120
  [wire] -> availableUnits|BLR-1|OIL-1L
  [wire] <- OK|0
Oil in BLR-1 : 0
During outage: Inventory service unreachable: connect timed out after 2000 ms
Server handled 2 calls

Why a remote proxy here:

  • Location transparency: business code uses an interface, not HTTP.
  • Marshalling and error translation live in one generated or hand-written class.
  • This is what gRPC stubs, Spring Cloud OpenFeign and Spring 6 HTTP interface clients (@HttpExchange) generate for you.

Remote calls are not local calls

A remote proxy makes a network call look local, but it can fail, time out and be slow (the "fallacies of distributed computing"). Always add timeouts, retries for idempotent calls, and circuit breakers. Never call a remote proxy in a tight loop without thinking.

Unit Tests: ProxyTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy;

import com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.CoreAccountService;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.SecuredAccountService;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.dynamic.LoggingProxy;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote.InventoryClientProxy;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote.InventoryServer;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming.LazyPoster;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ProxyTest {

    @Test
    void lazyPosterDoesNotLoadForTitleOnly() {
        LazyPoster p = new LazyPoster("X");
        assertThat(p.title()).isEqualTo("X");
        assertThat(p.render()).contains("X");
    }

    @Test
    void protectionProxyEnforcesLimits() {
        var teller = new SecuredAccountService(new CoreAccountService(), new SecuredAccountService.User("t", Set.of("TELLER")));
        assertThat(teller.withdraw("SB-1001", 50_000)).contains("withdrew");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> teller.withdraw("SB-1001", 50_001)).isInstanceOf(SecurityException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void remoteProxyMarshalsCalls() {
        InventoryServer server = new InventoryServer();
        var client = new InventoryClientProxy(server::handle);
        assertThat(client.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG")).isEqualTo(120);
        assertThat(server.calls()).isEqualTo(1);
        var broken = new InventoryClientProxy(r -> "ERR|db down");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> broken.availableUnits("a", "b")).hasMessageContaining("db down");
    }

    @Test
    void dynamicProxyLogsAndRethrowsOriginalException() {
        List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
        var secured = new SecuredAccountService(new CoreAccountService(), new SecuredAccountService.User("x", Set.of()));
        var proxied = LoggingProxy.wrap((com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.AccountService) secured,
                com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.AccountService.class, log::add);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> proxied.balance("SB-1001")).isInstanceOf(SecurityException.class);
        assertThat(log).singleElement().asString().contains("threw java.lang.SecurityException");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Three ways to build proxies in Java:

Mechanism How Limits Hand-written (Examples 1–3) Implement the interface, forward calls One class per interface JDK dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) One InvocationHandler for any interface, generated at runtime (coding challenge) Interfaces only Bytecode subclassing (CGLIB, ByteBuddy) Generates a subclass at runtime Can't proxy final classes or methods; needs a non-private constructor

Spring AOP uses JDK proxies when your bean implements an interface and CGLIB subclasses otherwise (Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB: proxyTargetClass = true).

The self-invocation trap (Spring)

@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async work because callers hold a proxy. If a method calls another @Transactional method on this, the call bypasses the proxy, and the annotation is silently ignored. Fix: move the method to another bean, or inject the bean's own proxy. Almost every Spring interview at 5+ years asks about this.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Kind of proxy Spring AOP: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @Retryable, @PreAuthorize Protection / caching / smart proxies around beans Spring @Configuration classes CGLIB proxy so @Bean methods return singletons Spring Data repositories The interface you declare is implemented by a generated proxy Hibernate / JPA Lazy entity proxies (getReference), lazy collections (PersistentBag) gRPC, OpenFeign, Spring @HttpExchange, Java RMI Remote proxies (client stubs) JDK java.lang.reflect.Proxy; Collections.unmodifiableList (protection) Mockito Mocks and spies are runtime-generated proxies HikariCP ProxyConnection: close() returns the connection to the pool

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Controls access without changing the real subject Extra indirection; possible latency (remote) or complexity Separates cross-cutting concerns (security, laziness, remoting) Behavior can be surprising (self-invocation, lazy-init exceptions) Clients unchanged: same interface Dynamic proxies only work with interfaces; CGLIB can't handle final Enables lazy loading, caching, auditing transparently Debugging generated proxies is harder (stack traces, $Proxy12)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Spring self-invocation

Calling a proxied method from inside the same bean bypasses the proxy. Transactions, caching and security silently don't apply.

LazyInitializationException

A Hibernate lazy proxy accessed after the session or transaction closed throws. Fetch what you need inside the transaction (fetch joins, entity graphs, DTO projections), and don't rely on Open Session in View.

Hiding expensive remote calls

for (Order o : orders) inventory.availableUnits(...) looks innocent but makes N network calls. Offer batch methods on remote interfaces.

Identity and equals

proxy == real is false, getClass() returns the proxy class, and Hibernate proxies may not be initialized when equals is called. Use IDs and instanceof carefully.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Proxies at every level of the stack:

Level Proxy Object Spring AOP, Hibernate lazy loading Process Sidecars (Envoy in Istio/Linkerd) intercept all traffic for mTLS, retries, metrics Network Reverse proxies (Nginx), API gateways, forward proxies, CDNs (caching proxies) Database PgBouncer, ProxySQL, RDS Proxy (connection pooling and routing)

The same trade-offs apply at each level: transparency vs. surprise, added latency, and a new failure point.

Designing remote interfaces for proxies. Coarse-grained operations (reserveItems(List<Item>)) instead of chatty ones; idempotency keys on writes; explicit timeouts and deadlines propagated across calls; versioned schemas (Protobuf field numbers).

Lazy loading strategy in JPA. Default @ManyToOne is eager (a common performance trap); set fetch = LAZY and fetch explicitly per use case with entity graphs or join fetches. Watch for N+1 queries caused by proxies initializing one by one. Enable Hibernate statistics in tests to catch them.

War story: the @Transactional that wasn't

A wallet service had transfer() call this.debit() and this.credit(), each annotated @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) to "isolate" them. transfer() itself wasn't transactional. Because of self-invocation, neither inner annotation applied: there was no transaction at all. When credit() failed on a constraint, debit() had already committed. Money vanished from wallets for 3 days before reconciliation caught it. Fix: @Transactional on transfer() (one transaction for both legs), inner methods moved to a separate LedgerService bean, and an integration test asserting rollback when credit fails. Lesson: annotations are proxies. If the call doesn't go through the proxy, the annotation doesn't exist.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Same interface, controls access: virtual (lazy), protection (security), remote (stub), caching, logging.
  • The real subject stays free of cross-cutting code.
  • Java: hand-written, java.lang.reflect.Proxy (interfaces), CGLIB/ByteBuddy (subclasses).
  • Spring: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize are proxies; self-invocation bypasses them.
  • vs Decorator: control access vs. add behavior.
T proxy = (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[]{iface}, (p, m, a) -> m.invoke(target, a));
